When input costs rise, farmers absorb the shock first; retail price rises lag by months, and farm-gate price rises lag further still. Norco's warning — supply shortages within 12 months — is what happens when that lag breaks the farm economy.

timeline.heading: THE $1 MILK LEGACY
timeline.body: From 2011 to 2019, Coles sold home-brand milk at A$1 per litre — a loss-leader price that pushed processors to cut farm-gate rates below production cost. Hundreds of dairy farms exited the industry. The residual capacity has no buffer: any new cost shock now passes through directly or breaks the chain.

blocks.question: For how many years did Coles sell home-brand milk at A$1 per litre before ending the policy?
blocks.explanation: The A$1/litre policy ran from 2011 to 2019 — roughly 8 years of loss-leader pricing that hollowed out Australian dairy farm margins.

2026-04-22-coles-adds-20c-to-the-price-o.label: Oil shocks & the dairy supply chain

timeline.heading: THE BOTTLENECK
timeline.body: Hormuz is 33 km wide at its narrowest, but the shipping lanes are just 3 km each — two inbound, two outbound, separated by a 3 km buffer. Roughly a fifth of global oil consumption passes through daily.

timeline.heading: WHY IRAN HOLDS THE NORTHERN SHORE
timeline.body: Iran's coastline runs along the entire northern edge of the strait. The deepest shipping channel hugs the Iranian side, which is why IRGC fast-attack boats, anti-ship missiles, and island garrisons can threaten traffic from positions extremely hard to suppress.

timeline.heading: THE IRGC IS NOT THE NAVY
timeline.body: Iran has two parallel maritime forces. The regular **Artesh** navy operates frigates and submarines for blue-water deterrence. The **IRGC Navy** — a separate chain of command reporting directly to the Supreme Leader — runs the swarm of small fast-attack craft in the Gulf. Hormuz is the IRGC's turf, which is why escalations here bypass the foreign ministry.

blocks.text: The **IRGC** was designated a foreign terrorist organization by the US in 2019 — the first time that label was applied to part of another state's armed forces.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988, Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. Oil prices spiked briefly but markets adapted — tankers were reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags and escorted by warships. The lesson planners took: disruption is easier to threaten than to sustain.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL REGIME
timeline.body: Under UNCLOS Article 38, ships have a right of transit passage through international straits — coastal states cannot suspend passage or impose conditions. Iran signed UNCLOS in 1982 but never ratified it, and has long argued Hormuz is governed by its own domestic law, not the convention.

blocks.question: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, what right do ships have through international straits like Hormuz?
options: Innocent passage, which coastal states can suspend
Transit passage, which cannot be suspended
Free passage only with coastal state permission
No right — it depends on bilateral treaties
blocks.explanation: UNCLOS Article 38 grants transit passage through straits used for international navigation, and unlike innocent passage it cannot be suspended by the coastal state.

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: Lloyd's of London war-risk premiums — not the shots themselves — are what close a shipping lane. Once premiums spike, commercial vessels reroute regardless of the actual threat level. The financial chokepoint is tighter than the physical one.

timeline.heading: THE ATTACK SURFACE
timeline.body: A DeFi vault is a smart contract that pools user deposits and deploys them to earn yield. Unlike a bank, there is no human in the loop — the contract's code is the vault. Any bug in that code is the vault's entire security perimeter.

blocks.text: In traditional finance, a bug gets patched overnight. In DeFi, a bug is **public, on-chain, and exploitable by anyone** the moment it ships — often before the team knows it exists.

timeline.heading: WHY $10 BILLION AND COUNTING
timeline.body: DeFiLlama's running tally of hacks and exploits crossed $10bn in cumulative losses. The pattern is structural: new chains attract new protocols, new protocols ship fast, auditors are scarce, and composability means one broken contract can drain a dozen others that trusted it.

timeline.heading: THE SUI CONTEXT
timeline.body: Sui is a newer Layer-1 blockchain built around the Move language, originally developed at Meta for the abandoned Diem project. Move was designed specifically to prevent common Solidity bugs like reentrancy — but new languages ship with new, less-understood failure modes.

timeline.heading: THE CONTAGION PATTERN
timeline.body: KelpDAO was breached over the weekend; Volo fell days later. Exploits often cluster because attackers reuse the same exploit class across protocols sharing code, libraries, or oracle dependencies. One vulnerability found on Monday is hunted across the ecosystem by Friday.

timeline.heading: WHY FREEZES ARE RARE
timeline.body: Volo recovered $500k through ecosystem partners — typically centralized exchanges that blacklist the attacker's withdrawal addresses. This works only when the attacker tries to cash out through a KYC'd venue. Funds routed through privacy-preserving mixers or cross-chain bridges are almost never recovered.

blocks.question: Why do most DeFi hack recoveries fail?
options: Attackers exit through mixers and cross-chain bridges before freezes
blocks.explanation: Recovery depends on catching funds at a KYC'd exchange. Mixers and bridges break the forensic trail faster than blacklists can propagate.

timeline.heading: THE POST-MORTEM RITUAL
timeline.body: After every major DeFi exploit, the protocol publishes a post-mortem detailing the exact bug, the attacker's path, and proposed remediations. These documents are how the industry learns — but they also reveal that most exploits fall into a small handful of repeated categories: price-oracle manipulation, reentrancy, access-control errors, and flawed upgradeability.

timeline.heading: THE ADDITIONALITY TEST
timeline.body: A carbon credit is only valid if the emissions cut would not have happened anyway. If a pig farm already profits from capturing methane to burn as fuel, the credit buyer pays for nothing new. This is the single hardest question in offset markets — and the easiest to fudge.

blocks.text: The technical term is **additionality**: the project must be *additional* to business-as-usual. Fail this test and the credit is, in climate terms, fiction.

timeline.heading: WHY METHANE
timeline.body: Methane traps roughly 80x more heat than CO2 over 20 years. A ton of captured methane generates far more credits than a ton of avoided CO2, which is why livestock-waste projects became a magnet for offset developers in the 2010s.

timeline.heading: THE CDM PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The UN's Clean Development Mechanism, launched under Kyoto in 2005, funneled billions into Chinese industrial-gas projects. A 2015 Stockholm Environment Institute study found that 73% of CDM credits issued likely did not represent real reductions — factories were found to have manufactured refrigerant gases solely to destroy them for credits.

timeline.heading: THE CERTIFIER PROBLEM
timeline.body: Gold Standard, Verra, and the other major registries are paid by the project developers whose credits they certify. The conflict is structural: stricter validation means fewer credits issued, which means less revenue for the certifier. Auditors rarely visit the sites they approve.

timeline.heading: WHO BUYS AND WHY
timeline.body: Corporations buy offsets to claim 'net zero' without cutting operational emissions. Shell alone retired over 20 million credits in 2022 — more than any other company. The market grew on the premise that a ton avoided in Guangdong is equivalent to a ton emitted in Rotterdam. Additionality failures break that equivalence.

blocks.question: What makes a carbon credit 'additional'?
options: The emissions cut would not have happened without the credit revenue
The credit is verified by a third party
The project is located in a developing country
blocks.explanation: Additionality means the climate benefit is caused by the credit — not something that would have happened anyway for other economic reasons.

timeline.heading: THE STRUCTURAL FLAW
timeline.body: Additionality is counterfactual — it asks what would have happened in a world that doesn't exist. Developers write baseline scenarios that maximize credit issuance; certifiers rarely have the data to challenge them. The problem isn't fraud in most cases; it's that the entire accounting framework rewards optimistic storytelling.

timeline.heading: THE DUAL SYSTEM
timeline.body: Nigeria runs two parallel land regimes. Statutory title comes from the 1978 Land Use Act, which vests all land in state governors as trustees. Customary tenure predates the state entirely — land belongs to the lineage, the clan, or the community, with living members as stewards rather than owners.

blocks.text: The governor holds land *in trust* for the people — a colonial-era fiction that gives state executives enormous discretion over who gets a **Certificate of Occupancy**.

timeline.heading: WHY CONSENT IS COLLECTIVE
timeline.body: Under customary tenure, land is held by the dead, the living, and the unborn. A chief or family head is a custodian, not a proprietor. Selling or leasing without broad community ratification is treated as a breach of trust, not a legitimate commercial act — which is why Nigerian courts routinely void such transfers even when signed by traditional rulers.

timeline.heading: THE 2008 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Nigerian Supreme Court jurisprudence on joint family ownership — reinforced in cases like Ekpendu v. Erika and successive rulings through the 2000s — holds that no single family head can alienate ancestral land without the concurrence of principal members. A signature at the top is not consent from the bottom.

blocks.question: Under Nigerian customary land law, who must consent to a valid lease of ancestral land?
options: The principal members of the landowning family or community
Any adult member who holds a title
blocks.explanation: Supreme Court rulings hold that customary land is jointly owned; principal members of the family or community must concur for any alienation to bind.

timeline.heading: THE LAND USE ACT TRAP
timeline.body: The 1978 Act was meant to simplify land administration but instead created a layer where governors can override customary claims by issuing statutory certificates to investors. Communities often learn of 'leases' only when bulldozers arrive — because the paperwork was filed in the state capital, not the village.

timeline.heading: THE 99-YEAR SIGNAL
timeline.body: Ninety-nine years is the maximum leasehold term the Land Use Act permits for statutory grants. In practice it functions as freehold — longer than any living signatory will survive. When chiefs sign 99-year deals over 300 hectares, they are alienating the unborn generations customary law is designed to protect.

blocks.label: Enugu State, southeast Nigeria
blocks.caption: Akpawfu sits in Nkanu East, Igbo heartland

timeline.heading: THE IGBO CONTEXT
timeline.body: Southeastern Nigeria's Igbo communities historically organized land through the umunna — the patrilineal kindred — with decisions made in open assembly. Colonial and post-colonial administrations imposed a 'paramount chief' model that concentrated authority in individuals the British found easier to negotiate with. Disputes like Akpawfu's are partly a legacy of that flattening.

timeline.heading: THE DEPENDENCY
timeline.body: The EU imports roughly 60% of its energy. Before 2022 it bought 40% of its natural gas from Russia; after the Ukraine invasion, it replaced pipeline gas with seaborne LNG — much of it passing through Hormuz or the Red Sea. Trading one chokepoint for another is the structural story of European energy since 2022.

blocks.text: The EU did not *reduce* import dependence after 2022 — it **rerouted** it. Gas arrives on tankers now instead of pipelines, which means every maritime chokepoint became a European energy chokepoint.

timeline.heading: THE HORMUZ EXPOSURE
timeline.body: Roughly 20% of global oil and a growing share of LNG transits the Strait of Hormuz — a 33-km-wide channel between Iran and Oman. Qatar, which supplies nearly half of EU LNG imports by some measures, has no alternative export route; its gas either crosses Hormuz or stays in the ground.

timeline.heading: WHY TAX ELECTRICITY BELOW FOSSIL FUELS
timeline.body: In most EU states, electricity carries higher taxes and levies than the natural gas or heating oil it competes with — a legacy of treating power as a luxury and fuel as a necessity. A household swapping a gas boiler for a heat pump often pays more per unit of delivered heat, even when the heat pump is more efficient. Inverting that ratio is the single biggest lever for electrification without new subsidies.

blocks.question: Why does a heat pump often cost more to run than a gas boiler in the EU today?
options: Heat pumps are less efficient than gas boilers
Electricity is taxed more heavily than gas per unit of energy
Gas is subsidized directly by the EU
blocks.explanation: Modern heat pumps deliver 3-4 units of heat per unit of electricity, but EU tax structures were built when electricity was the premium good — so the efficient technology often loses on price.

timeline.heading: THE ACQ COMMUNAUTAIRE PROBLEM
timeline.body: EU energy tax rules are set by the 2003 Energy Taxation Directive, which requires unanimity to amend. A single member state — Hungary, Ireland, or any other — can block a tax shift indefinitely. This is why the Commission prefers regulatory tools (efficiency standards, emissions trading) over fiscal ones, even when tax reform is the cleaner instrument.

blocks.text: The *unanimity rule* on tax matters is the single most important constraint on EU fiscal policy — and the reason Brussels pushes **regulation** where it cannot push **taxation**.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The 1973 oil shock drove France to build 56 nuclear reactors in 15 years, Denmark to invent modern wind power, and Germany to pass its first energy efficiency laws. Every major leap in European energy policy has been crisis-driven. The 2022 REPowerEU plan was the Ukraine-war analog; AccelerateEU is positioned as the Iran-war one.

timeline.heading: THE POSTWAR CEILING
timeline.body: West Germany's 1955 rearmament was conditional. Allied partners — especially France — accepted a German army only inside NATO's integrated command, never as a national force. Every German defense decision since has operated under that implicit ceiling: strong enough to deter, never strong enough to act alone.

blocks.text: The doctrine had a name: *Einbindung* — **binding in**. German military power would exist only as a component of Western collective defense, never as a sovereign instrument.

timeline.heading: THE PEACE DIVIDEND
timeline.body: The Bundeswehr had 500,000 troops at reunification in 1990. By 2015 it was 178,000, with helicopters that couldn't fly and submarines that couldn't dive. Germany spent three decades treating its military as a line item to cut, not a capability to maintain.

timeline.heading: THE ZEITENWENDE
timeline.body: Three days after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Chancellor Scholz announced a €100 billion special fund for the Bundeswehr and called the moment a Zeitenwende — a turning point. It was the largest single defense commitment in postwar German history, and it broke with 70 years of deliberate military restraint.

blocks.question: What triggered Germany's 2022 Zeitenwende defense pivot?
blocks.explanation: Scholz announced the €100bn fund on February 27, 2022 — three days after Russian forces crossed into Ukraine.

timeline.heading: CONSCRIPTION'S GHOST
timeline.body: Germany suspended conscription in 2011, ending a tradition that tied the citizen to the state through uniformed service. Rebuilding to 460,000 troops without conscription means competing with private employers for recruits — which is why senior officers wanted an even higher ceiling written into the plan.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: Germany sits on NATO's central front. In a conflict with Russia, Polish and Baltic defenders need German reinforcements moving east within days, not weeks. The Bundeswehr's job is not primarily to fight on German soil — it is to be the logistical and combat spine that keeps the eastern flank from collapsing.

timeline.heading: THE FISCAL CONSTRAINT
timeline.body: Germany's constitutional debt brake caps federal deficits at 0.35% of GDP. The 2022 special fund was only possible through a one-time constitutional amendment. Sustaining a 460,000-troop force for fifteen years requires either permanent tax increases, structural spending cuts elsewhere, or another constitutional carve-out — each politically costly.

blocks.text: The debt brake — *Schuldenbremse* — was written into the **Grundgesetz** in 2009 after the financial crisis. Amending it requires a **two-thirds majority** in both chambers, which no single governing coalition has held since.

timeline.heading: WHY mRNA FOR FLU
timeline.body: Traditional flu vaccines are grown in chicken eggs over six months — a pipeline that collapses if the pathogen is avian influenza itself, which kills the eggs. mRNA platforms skip the biological substrate entirely: synthesize the genetic instructions, inject them, let human cells make the antigen.

blocks.text: The egg-based bottleneck is why a severe **H5N1** pandemic was always going to outpace the legacy vaccine infrastructure. mRNA was built precisely for this scenario.

timeline.heading: THE SPEED DIFFERENTIAL
timeline.body: Moderna designed its COVID-19 vaccine sequence in 48 hours after China published the SARS-CoV-2 genome in January 2020. First human doses were injected 63 days later. Egg-based flu vaccines take roughly six months from strain selection to first dose — a timeline set by chicken biology, not regulation.

timeline.heading: CEPI's ROLE
timeline.body: The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations was founded in Davos in 2017 after the West African Ebola outbreak exposed how slowly the world responds to new pathogens. It is funded by Norway, Germany, Japan, the UK, the Gates Foundation, and Wellcome — a deliberately non-US-dependent consortium built for exactly the scenario now unfolding.

timeline.heading: THE BARDA MODEL
timeline.body: The US Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority, created in 2006, has been the primary buyer of pandemic countermeasures for two decades — guaranteeing markets for vaccines no private firm would otherwise develop. Canceling contracts signals the end of that guarantee, and private pharma responds to withdrawn guarantees by shelving programs.

timeline.heading: H5N1's CASE FATALITY
timeline.body: Of roughly 900 confirmed human H5N1 cases since 2003, about half have died. The virus has not yet achieved efficient human-to-human transmission — the mutation that would make a pandemic — but dairy cattle outbreaks across US herds in 2024–2025 multiplied the mammalian hosts in which that mutation could emerge.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of confirmed human H5N1 infections since 2003 have been fatal?
blocks.explanation: WHO data tracks ~900 confirmed cases with roughly half fatal — though confirmed cases skew toward severe hospitalizations, so true case fatality is likely lower.

timeline.heading: THE SOVEREIGNTY SHIFT
timeline.body: For two decades, pandemic vaccine capacity meant American capacity. The UK running Moderna's late-stage H5N1 trial is the first time a major mRNA platform has shifted its pivotal studies to a non-US health system — a quiet but structural relocation of biosecurity capability across the Atlantic.

timeline.heading: THE ONE-CHINA SQUEEZE
timeline.body: Beijing's precondition for diplomatic ties with any state is formal non-recognition of Taipei. Since 1971, when the UN seat flipped to the PRC, the number of states recognizing Taiwan has fallen from 68 to 12. The attrition is not accidental — it is the single most sustained diplomatic campaign in modern history.

blocks.text: The PRC's rule is binary: a state recognizes **either** Beijing **or** Taipei, never both. Every switch is permanent.

timeline.heading: WHY ESWATINI HOLDS OUT
timeline.body: Eswatini is Africa's last absolute monarchy and Taiwan's only remaining ally on the continent. King Mswati III has personally vetoed switching recognition despite repeated Chinese overtures. Taipei funds hospitals, scholarships, and agricultural projects — small money globally, structurally significant for a country of 1.2 million.

timeline.heading: THE DEBT-TRAP LEVER
timeline.body: Roughly 60% of African sovereign debt to bilateral creditors is held by China. Beijing does not need to threaten war or sanctions — it can simply refuse to restructure loans that countries cannot repay on original terms. Airspace denial is a small ask in exchange for debt relief.

blocks.label: Eswatini's landlocked neighborhood
blocks.caption: Overflight permission from any of these states requires going through Beijing.

timeline.heading: HOW OVERFLIGHT SOVEREIGNTY WORKS
timeline.body: Under the 1944 Chicago Convention, every state controls the airspace above its territory absolutely. Civilian transit rights exist only through bilateral agreements, which any state can revoke. A head-of-state flight typically requests clearance weeks in advance; denial is a diplomatic signal, not a technical obstacle.

blocks.question: Under international law, which body grants overflight rights for a head-of-state flight?
blocks.explanation: The Chicago Convention codified absolute airspace sovereignty — every state grants or denies overflight on its own terms.

timeline.heading: THE LONG ATTRITION
timeline.body: Taiwan lost Burkina Faso (2018), São Tomé (2016), Gambia (2013), Senegal (2005), and Liberia (2003) to Chinese checkbook diplomacy. The continent-wide shutout is the end state of a 20-year campaign, not a sudden pivot. Eswatini's isolation in the region makes even a state visit logistically impossible without Beijing's acquiescence.

timeline.heading: THE WITHDRAWAL LOOPHOLE THAT ISN'T
timeline.body: Article 127 of the Rome Statute says withdrawal takes effect one year after notification — and explicitly does not discharge obligations arising while the state was a party. A leader cannot commit crimes, withdraw, and walk free. The treaty was drafted with exactly this evasion in mind.

blocks.question: When the Philippines withdrew from the ICC in 2019, what happened to jurisdiction over earlier acts?
options: Jurisdiction ended on the withdrawal date
Jurisdiction survived for acts committed while a member
Jurisdiction required UN Security Council renewal
Jurisdiction transferred to Philippine domestic courts
blocks.explanation: Rome Statute Article 127(2) preserves the court's jurisdiction over crimes committed during membership, regardless of later withdrawal.

timeline.heading: THE DRUG WAR NUMBERS
timeline.body: Philippine police acknowledge roughly 6,200 killings in anti-drug operations from 2016 to 2022. Human rights groups put the real figure between 12,000 and 30,000 once vigilante killings are counted. The gap between official and independent tallies is itself evidence the prosecution will use.

blocks.text: Duterte's own campaign language — promising to *"fatten the fish in Manila Bay"* with bodies — is part of the ICC record. The **command responsibility** doctrine means a head of state can be liable for subordinates' crimes if he knew or should have known and failed to prevent them.

timeline.heading: WHY THE ICC HAS LIMITED REACH
timeline.body: The court has no police force. It relies on member states to arrest suspects on their territory. The United States, China, Russia, and India are not members — a fugitive in any of them is effectively beyond reach. Duterte's arrest happened only because a successor government cooperated.

timeline.heading: COMPLEMENTARITY
timeline.body: The ICC only acts when national courts are unable or unwilling to prosecute. Duterte's case cleared this bar because Philippine domestic investigations were judged insufficient — a finding Manila contested but could not reverse. The principle reserves sovereignty for states that genuinely police their own.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT SHADOW
timeline.body: Only a handful of former heads of state have faced international prosecution: Milošević died mid-trial at the ICTY; Charles Taylor was convicted by the Sierra Leone special court; Hissène Habré was convicted in Senegal under universal jurisdiction. Duterte would be the first former Asian head of state tried at the ICC itself.

blocks.label: heads of state tried by international tribunals

timeline.heading: THE CONFIRMATION STAGE
timeline.body: Pre-trial confirmation is not a verdict — it is a filter. Prosecutors must show substantial grounds to believe the accused committed the crimes charged. Roughly a quarter of ICC cases have collapsed at this stage, most famously Kenya's Uhuru Kenyatta, where witness intimidation gutted the evidence.

timeline.heading: THE MERIT ORDER
timeline.body: Grid operators rank every power plant by marginal cost — hydro and nuclear first, then coal and gas, then expensive oil-fired peakers last. Dispatching in this order minimizes system cost. Bypassing it is not just inefficient; it inverts the logic that makes a unified grid cheaper than isolated generation.

blocks.text: The merit order is why a national grid exists at all: pooling demand lets the *cheapest* generator in the country serve the next marginal kilowatt-hour, not just the cheapest plant near you.

timeline.heading: THE CAPACITY TRAP
timeline.body: Pakistan signed dollar-denominated **capacity payments** with independent power producers in the 1994 and 2002 power policies — the state pays whether or not the plant generates. Installed capacity now exceeds peak demand, yet distributors claim shortages. The fixed payments must be made regardless; every idle megawatt raises the per-unit tariff on electricity actually sold.

blocks.text: Capacity payments mean Pakistan pays roughly **$2 billion a year** for electricity it never consumes — a structural cost baked into every bill, denominated in dollars the country does not easily earn.

timeline.heading: CIRCULAR DEBT
timeline.body: Distribution companies (DISCOs) under-collect from consumers, cannot pay generators, who cannot pay fuel suppliers. The resulting IOU chain — Pakistan's 'circular debt' — exceeded PKR 2.6 trillion by 2024. Every off-grid bilateral deal that bypasses cheaper plants inflates this debt further, because the expensive power still gets paid for, eventually, by the Treasury.

timeline.heading: WHY OFF-GRID LOOKS ATTRACTIVE
timeline.body: For an individual DISCO, bilateral contracts with specific plants can guarantee supply during load-shedding and sidestep grid operator allocations. The cost passes to consumers through fuel price adjustments; the procurement decision sits with the DISCO. The incentive to cheat the merit order is structural, not individual corruption.

blocks.question: In a merit-order dispatch system, which plant runs last?
options: The plant with highest marginal cost
blocks.explanation: Merit order dispatches by marginal cost — cheapest first, most expensive peakers only when demand requires them.

timeline.heading: THE IMF DIMENSION
timeline.body: Pakistan's $7bn IMF programme agreed in 2024 makes power sector reform a structural benchmark. Tariff hikes to close the circular debt gap are politically toxic; distribution-company privatisation has stalled for two decades. Finding DISCOs buying outside the merit order is exactly the kind of governance failure the Fund cites when releasing tranches becomes conditional.

timeline.heading: WHY TPUS EXIST
timeline.body: Google built the first TPU in 2015 because running neural networks on general-purpose GPUs was too slow and power-hungry at search scale. A TPU is an ASIC — an application-specific chip — that does matrix multiplication and almost nothing else, trading flexibility for throughput per watt.

blocks.text: The tradeoff is stark: a GPU runs any workload; a TPU runs *one kind* of math but runs it **~3-5× more efficiently** at that single task.

timeline.heading: THE SYSTOLIC ARRAY
timeline.body: TPUs use a systolic array — a grid of thousands of multiply-accumulate units where data flows rhythmically between neighbors, like blood through a heart. The architecture dates to a 1978 paper by H.T. Kung at Carnegie Mellon; Google was the first to commercialize it at scale.

timeline.heading: WHY SCALE IS THE MOAT
timeline.body: Training a frontier model requires tens of thousands of accelerators wired together with high-bandwidth interconnect. The bottleneck is rarely the chip itself — it is the network between chips. A million-chip pod is a networking feat as much as a silicon feat.

timeline.heading: THE AGENT SHIFT
timeline.body: Classic SaaS sells seats — one login per human. Agents that act across Gmail, Docs, Drive, and Meet collapse that model: the unit of consumption becomes a task, not a seat. Whoever owns the graph of your work owns the surface agents run on.

blocks.question: What is the primary constraint preventing a single AI agent from acting seamlessly across Gmail, Docs, and Drive today?
options: Lack of a unified permission and data graph across apps
blocks.explanation: The hard part is the graph — unified identity, permissions, and context across apps. Model capability is largely sufficient; integration is the moat.

timeline.heading: THE MICROSOFT FRONT
timeline.body: Workspace vs. Microsoft 365 is a two-decade trench war. Microsoft has ~400M paid seats; Google has ~300M. Migration tools are the weapon — the switching cost is not the software but the years of email history, shared drives, and calendar links that must move without breaking.

timeline.heading: THE CAPEX RACE
timeline.body: Hyperscalers are spending over $300bn combined on AI infrastructure in 2026. The bet is that whoever has the most compute when agents become useful captures the enterprise workflow layer — a market worth trillions in seat revenue over a decade.

timeline.heading: THE FEDERATION ACCOUNT
timeline.body: Nigerian states get most of their money not from taxes they collect but from monthly transfers out of the Federation Account — oil revenue pooled in Abuja and distributed via FAAC. Governors receive lump sums with minimal conditionality, which makes discretionary spending on fleets and entourages politically easy and fiscally invisible.

blocks.text: The mechanism is called **FAAC** — the Federation Account Allocation Committee. It meets monthly, divides oil receipts among the three tiers, and leaves governors with *unrestricted* cash.

timeline.heading: THE GOVERNOR'S POWERS
timeline.body: Under Nigeria's 1999 Constitution, state governors control security votes — cash disbursements that require no receipts and no legislative oversight. Combined with appointment power over commissioners, judges' welfare packages, and board seats, the governor is closer to a regional sovereign than an American-style state executive.

timeline.heading: THE MPI NUMBER
timeline.body: The Multidimensional Poverty Index measures more than income — it counts deprivation in health, education, living standards, water, sanitation, and housing. Niger State's 69.1% rate means roughly seven in ten residents are deprived on multiple dimensions simultaneously, not just poor on a single income threshold.

blocks.question: What does Nigeria's Multidimensional Poverty Index measure?
options: Deprivation across health, education, and living standards
blocks.explanation: The MPI counts simultaneous deprivations across multiple dimensions — a household can be income-poor, school-poor, and water-poor at once, and each deprivation is weighted.

timeline.heading: THE NAIRA CONTEXT
timeline.body: Since the 2023 devaluation under Tinubu, the naira has lost more than half its dollar value. A fleet of imported SUVs — nearly all vehicles at this tier are imported — costs roughly three times in naira what it would have pre-float. The optics of billions in naira on cars are sharper precisely because each unit now buys so much less.

timeline.heading: THE PATRONAGE LOGIC
timeline.body: Official vehicles in Nigerian politics are not transport — they are status instruments distributed to keep coalitions intact. Judges, legislators, and traditional rulers receiving cars from a governor become stakeholders in his political survival. This is the same logic that drove the 'Ghana-Must-Go' bag era: governance as redistribution among elites, not service delivery.

timeline.heading: THE NORTHERN BELT
timeline.body: Niger State sits in Nigeria's Middle Belt — agricultural, majority-Muslim, and increasingly contested by bandit groups and ISWAP-linked cells. Poverty and insecurity compound: displaced farmers cannot plant, tax bases erode, and state revenue depends ever more on FAAC transfers rather than internal generation.

blocks.label: Niger State sits in Nigeria's Middle Belt

timeline.heading: THE SPLIT
timeline.body: Islamic State West Africa Province broke from Boko Haram in 2016 after a leadership dispute with Abubakar Shekau. ISWAP rejected Shekau's indiscriminate killing of Muslim civilians as un-Islamic and pledged allegiance to Baghdadi. The split produced two rival jihadist factions competing for the same territory.

blocks.text: The doctrinal wedge was *takfir* — Shekau declared ordinary Muslims apostates and legitimate targets; **ISWAP** rejected this, which is why it now governs villages Boko Haram would have burned.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: The insurgency operates across the Lake Chad Basin, where Nigeria, Niger, Chad, and Cameroon meet. Borders are porous, the lake itself has shrunk 90% since the 1960s, and fighters move between countries faster than any single national army can pursue.

timeline.heading: THE GOVERNANCE MODEL
timeline.body: ISWAP taxes fishermen, farmers, and traders in areas it controls — issuing receipts, settling disputes, and providing a crude form of order. In parts of Borno and the lake islands, it functions as a shadow state that collects revenue more reliably than Abuja does.

timeline.heading: THE STATE ABSENCE
timeline.body: Askira Uba sits in southern Borno, far from the Maiduguri-centered military response. Nigeria's federal structure means emergency response runs through NEMA, state agencies, and local government — each underfunded, each blaming the others. A village attack can go unreported to Abuja for days.

blocks.question: Roughly how many Nigerians have been displaced by the Boko Haram/ISWAP insurgency since 2009?
blocks.explanation: UN estimates put internal displacement above 2 million in the northeast, with millions more affected across the Lake Chad Basin.

timeline.heading: THE SIXTEEN-YEAR WAR
timeline.body: The insurgency began in 2009 with the extrajudicial killing of Boko Haram founder Mohammed Yusuf in police custody. What started as a local grievance against state brutality has outlasted four Nigerian presidents and consumed an estimated $9 billion in military spending. The violence has become structural, not episodic.

timeline.heading: THE STATUTE
timeline.body: The Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 is the constitution of the regulatory state. It forces agencies to explain their reasoning, accept public comment, and act on a factual record — not on political whim.

blocks.text: The APA's core test: agency action must not be *arbitrary and capricious*. Courts read this as a demand for **reasoned decisionmaking** — a record showing the agency considered the relevant facts, not just followed orders.

timeline.heading: STATE FARM
timeline.body: The 1983 Supreme Court ruling in Motor Vehicle Manufacturers v. State Farm set the standard: an agency reversing course must examine the evidence and articulate a rational connection between facts and choice. 'The President told me to' is not a rational connection.

blocks.question: Under State Farm, what must an agency show when it reverses a prior rule?
options: That the President ordered the change
A rational connection between facts in the record and the new policy
That the new rule has majority public support
blocks.explanation: State Farm requires reasoned analysis grounded in the administrative record — political direction alone is insufficient under the APA.

timeline.heading: WHAT AN EXECUTIVE ORDER CAN AND CANNOT DO
timeline.body: Executive orders direct the executive branch but cannot override statutes. An EO can tell Interior to reconsider renewable permits; it cannot itself satisfy the APA's requirement that Interior justify the outcome with facts and analysis.

timeline.heading: THE INJUNCTION SCOPE
timeline.body: After the 2024 decision narrowing universal injunctions, federal courts increasingly limit relief to named plaintiffs. A trade-group-only injunction means non-member developers still face the blocked rules — and the government can relitigate or appeal without a nationwide freeze.

timeline.heading: THE SLOW-WALK LOOPHOLE
timeline.body: Even when rules fall, agencies retain vast discretion over permit timing, environmental review depth, and information requests. Enforcement by delay is hard to challenge in court because no single decision triggers reviewable final action.

timeline.heading: THE CHEVRON SHIFT
timeline.body: Loper Bright (2024) ended Chevron deference, meaning courts no longer defer to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes. This cuts both ways: it constrained Biden-era climate rules and now constrains the current administration's rollback rules with equal force.

timeline.heading: THE MUON
timeline.body: A muon is a heavier cousin of the electron — same charge, but 207 times the mass. It lives for 2.2 microseconds before decaying. Because it is so much heavier, it couples more strongly to hypothetical new particles, which makes it a sensitive probe of physics beyond the Standard Model.

blocks.text: The muon's mass ratio is why it matters: sensitivity to new physics scales roughly as *mass squared*, giving muons a **~43,000×** advantage over electrons as a probe.

timeline.heading: WHAT g-2 MEASURES
timeline.body: Spin a charged particle in a magnetic field and it precesses. The Dirac equation predicts a gyromagnetic ratio of exactly 2. The real value deviates slightly — the 'anomalous magnetic moment,' or g-2 — because the particle is constantly emitting and reabsorbing virtual particles from the quantum vacuum.

timeline.heading: WHY VIRTUAL PARTICLES MATTER
timeline.body: The quantum vacuum is not empty. Pairs of particles flicker in and out of existence, and the muon interacts with all of them as it precesses. Every known particle contributes a calculable bump to g-2. If an unknown particle exists, it would show up as a discrepancy between theory and experiment.

timeline.heading: THE HADRONIC PROBLEM
timeline.body: Electromagnetic and weak contributions to g-2 can be calculated to extraordinary precision. But hadronic contributions — virtual quarks and gluons — cannot be computed perturbatively because the strong force gets stronger at low energies. This single term has dominated the theoretical uncertainty for twenty years.

blocks.question: Why is the hadronic contribution to muon g-2 so hard to calculate?
options: The strong force weakens at low energies, making math diverge
The strong force strengthens at low energies, breaking perturbation theory
Quarks are too light to simulate
Gluons do not interact with muons
blocks.explanation: Asymptotic freedom means QCD is weak at high energies and strong at low energies — the opposite of QED — so standard perturbative expansions fail for low-energy hadronic loops.

timeline.heading: LATTICE QCD
timeline.body: Lattice chromodynamics discretizes spacetime into a grid and solves the strong-force equations numerically on supercomputers. It is the only first-principles method that works in the non-perturbative regime. The Penn State recalculation uses lattice QCD to pin down the hadronic vacuum polarization term that had driven the anomaly.

timeline.heading: WHY 'HALF A SIGMA' MATTERS
timeline.body: In particle physics, a discovery of new physics requires a 5-sigma discrepancy between theory and experiment. The old muon g-2 gap was around 4.2 sigma — tantalizing but not conclusive. Closing it to 0.5 sigma means theory and experiment now agree; the anomaly that inspired a generation of beyond-Standard-Model papers has effectively dissolved.

timeline.heading: WHAT SURVIVES
timeline.body: The Standard Model is now consistent with g-2, but it still cannot explain dark matter, neutrino masses, the matter-antimatter asymmetry, or why gravity is so weak. One door closed; the building still has holes.

timeline.heading: WHO THE NUBA ARE
timeline.body: The Nuba are roughly 50 distinct ethnic groups — speaking dozens of languages — who took refuge in the Nuba Mountains over centuries to escape slave raids from the north. They are predominantly Muslim, with Christian and traditional minorities, and have long been treated by Khartoum as racially African despite sharing the faith of the Arab-identifying center.

blocks.text: The label *Nuba* is a geographic collective, not a single ethnicity — a fact that has repeatedly frustrated attempts by outsiders to negotiate with them as one bloc.

timeline.heading: WHY SOUTH KORDOFAN IS THE FAULT LINE
timeline.body: When South Sudan seceded in 2011, the border was drawn north of the Nuba Mountains — leaving a population that had fought alongside the southern SPLA stranded inside Sudan. The SPLM-North insurgency began within weeks of independence and has never ended.

blocks.label: the Nuba Mountains sit north of the 2011 border

timeline.heading: THE 1990s PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Under Bashir, Khartoum declared jihad against the Nuba in 1992 and imposed a total blockade — no food, no journalists, no aid — for most of the decade. African Rights and later the UN documented forced relocations to 'peace camps' and mass atrocities that many scholars classify as genocide. The current detentions sit inside that institutional memory.

timeline.heading: MILITARY INTELLIGENCE AS A PARALLEL STATE
timeline.body: Sudan's Military Intelligence Directorate runs detention sites outside the regular prison system, answerable only to the army command. Since the April 2023 war with the RSF began, MI facilities have proliferated — and with the ICRC and UN largely expelled from government-held areas, no independent body verifies who is held, where, or on what charge.

timeline.heading: WHY KADUGLI MATTERS
timeline.body: Kadugli is the South Kordofan state capital and the army's main garrison in the Nuba Mountains. UN peacekeepers (UNMIS) were stationed there in 2011 and documented mass graves before being expelled — a template the current blackout echoes.

blocks.question: Why were UN peacekeepers expelled from Kadugli in 2011?
options: They documented mass graves after fighting broke out
Their mandate expired at South Sudan's independence
They were withdrawn over funding disputes
blocks.explanation: UNMIS staff photographed mass graves near Kadugli in mid-2011; Khartoum terminated the mission shortly after, and no replacement force was permitted.

timeline.heading: THE DOCUMENTATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: With foreign journalists barred and humanitarian access blocked, diaspora-run monitors like the Nuba Mountains Observatory have become the primary evidence trail. Their methodology — named victims, dated incidents, cross-checked with families — is the same approach Syrian Archive pioneered, and the same approach ICC prosecutors have come to rely on when states close the door.

timeline.heading: THE FATWA POSTURE
timeline.body: Supreme Leader Khamenei issued a fatwa in the mid-2000s declaring nuclear weapons haram under Islamic law. Iranian diplomats cite it constantly; Western analysts dismiss it as rhetorical cover. The ambiguity is the point — it lets Tehran claim principled restraint while preserving every technical capability short of weaponization.

blocks.text: The doctrine is called *taqiyya*-compatible by critics and *principled* by supporters — either way, it is **unwritten**, which means it can be revised by the same authority that issued it.

timeline.heading: THE 90% THRESHOLD
timeline.body: Weapons-grade uranium is ~90% U-235. Iran has been enriching to 60% — a level with no civilian use. The jump from 60% to 90% is technically trivial compared to the jump from 3.67% (reactor grade) to 60%. Most of the centrifuge work is already done.

blocks.question: What enrichment level is considered weapons-grade uranium?
blocks.explanation: Weapons-grade is ~90% U-235. The hardest centrifuge work is getting from natural uranium to 60% — the final jump to 90% is comparatively fast.

timeline.heading: THE JCPOA GHOST
timeline.body: The 2015 nuclear deal capped Iranian enrichment at 3.67% and stockpiles at 300kg for 15 years. Trump withdrew in 2018; Iran responded by exceeding every limit. Any new deal negotiates against a baseline far worse than 2015 — Iran now has knowledge, stockpile, and advanced centrifuges it did not have a decade ago.

timeline.heading: WHY ISLAMABAD
timeline.body: Pakistan is the only Muslim nuclear power, maintains working relations with both Tehran and Washington, and has brokered back-channels before — most famously Kissinger's 1971 opening to China. Its utility is geographic and diplomatic: close enough to Iran to be trusted, distant enough from Washington to provide cover.

timeline.heading: THE HORMUZ LEVERAGE
timeline.body: Every Iranian negotiator carries the strait in their pocket. Roughly 21% of global oil consumption transits Hormuz; Iran's coastline runs its entire northern edge. The threat need not be executed to move markets — insurance premiums and tanker rates shift on rhetoric alone.

timeline.heading: THE SURRENDER QUESTION
timeline.body: Prediction markets price the odds of Iran surrendering its enriched uranium stockpile at single digits. The market reflects a structural truth: a regime that built the program through four decades of sanctions does not dismantle it under a 72-hour ultimatum.

timeline.heading: WHAT A PIT IS
timeline.body: A plutonium pit is the grapefruit-sized hollow sphere at the core of every modern warhead. When conventional explosives compress it, the plutonium reaches supercritical density and triggers fission — which in a thermonuclear weapon then ignites the fusion secondary.

blocks.text: The pit is the *primary*; the hydrogen-isotope stage it ignites is the *secondary*. Every US warhead since the 1950s has used this **two-stage Teller-Ulam** design.

timeline.heading: WHY PRODUCTION STOPPED
timeline.body: The US made pits at Rocky Flats in Colorado until 1989, when an FBI raid found widespread environmental violations — plutonium in the groundwater, illegal incineration, contaminated soil. The plant never reopened. For over 30 years, the US stockpile has run on pits made before the Berlin Wall fell.

timeline.heading: THE AGING QUESTION
timeline.body: Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,000 years, but the metal itself self-irradiates and develops microscopic voids over decades. JASON, the Pentagon's scientific advisory group, concluded in 2006 that existing pits remain reliable for at least 85 years — which is why the urgency of new production is a policy choice, not a physics deadline.

timeline.heading: THE TWO-SITE STRATEGY
timeline.body: Los Alamos in New Mexico and the Savannah River Site in South Carolina are being rebuilt to produce 30 pits each per year. The split is deliberate — a single-site failure cannot halt the program — but Savannah River is years behind schedule and billions over budget.

blocks.label: pit production sites: Los Alamos NM, Savannah River SC

timeline.heading: THE STOCKPILE PARADOX
timeline.body: The US already holds roughly 3,700 active warheads plus thousands of retired pits warehoused at Pantex in Texas. New production at 60/year adds to an arsenal that New START caps at 1,550 deployed strategic warheads — meaning every new pit made is either a replacement or a hedge against a future treaty collapse.

timeline.heading: WHO PAYS THE CLEANUP
timeline.body: The $400M cleanup cut targets the Office of Environmental Management, which handles Cold War waste at Hanford, Savannah River, and Oak Ridge. Hanford alone holds 56 million gallons of radioactive sludge in aging tanks — the largest environmental liability in US government history, estimated at $500+ billion to remediate.

blocks.question: How many plutonium pits does the US already hold in warehoused storage at Pantex, Texas?
blocks.explanation: The Union of Concerned Scientists estimates ~15,000 pits sit unused at Pantex — decades of surplus from the Cold War drawdown.

timeline.heading: THE ULCC BARGAIN
timeline.body: Ultra-low-cost carriers unbundle everything — seats, bags, water — and pack planes tighter than legacy carriers. The model works only at high load factors and low fuel prices. When either slips, ULCCs have no premium cabin to cushion the fall.

blocks.text: Spirit's seat pitch runs **28 inches**, versus **31–32** on legacy carriers. The math: more seats per plane means lower cost per seat — but zero margin for a demand shock.

timeline.heading: THE CHAPTER 11 RITUAL
timeline.body: US airlines have used bankruptcy as a balance-sheet tool for forty years — Continental (twice), TWA (three times), United, Delta, American, US Airways. Chapter 11 lets them shed pensions, renegotiate leases, and void labor contracts while still flying. Spirit's second filing in under two years is unusual only in speed, not kind.

timeline.heading: WHY WASHINGTON INTERVENES
timeline.body: Airlines are politically protected because route maps map onto congressional districts. A Spirit collapse means lost service to secondary cities — Myrtle Beach, Kalamazoo, Bristol — where no legacy carrier will replace the frequency. The 2020 CARES Act sent $54 billion to airlines on the same logic.

timeline.heading: WARRANTS, NOT LOANS
timeline.body: An option warrant gives the government the right to buy equity at a fixed strike price later. If Spirit recovers, taxpayers capture upside; if it fails, the warrants are worthless. This is the structure Treasury used on AIG in 2008 and on the Detroit automakers in 2009 — the state as reluctant shareholder.

timeline.heading: THE JETBLUE PROBLEM
timeline.body: JPMorgan's warning is the moral hazard point: once the government rescues one distressed carrier, every distressed carrier has a template. JetBlue posted losses through 2024–25 after a blocked Spirit merger; Frontier's margins are structurally thinner than Spirit's. A $500 million precedent prices the next ask.

blocks.question: Which US airline has NEVER filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy?
blocks.explanation: Southwest has never filed Chapter 11 — the only major US carrier with that record, a product of its fuel-hedging discipline and single-fleet cost structure.

timeline.heading: THE DEREGULATION INHERITANCE
timeline.body: The 1978 Airline Deregulation Act ended federal route and fare controls, letting carriers compete on price. It killed Pan Am, Eastern, and TWA; it also created the hub-and-spoke system and the ULCC niche. Every bailout since has been a partial re-regulation — the state picking which survivors the market was about to cull.

timeline.heading: THE CORE PROBLEM
timeline.body: Knot theory studies closed loops in three-dimensional space. Two knots are equivalent if one can be deformed into the other without cutting. Deciding whether two tangled loops are the same knot is deceptively hard — the question has occupied mathematicians since Lord Kelvin proposed in 1867 that atoms were knots in the ether.

blocks.text: A knot *invariant* is a quantity you compute from a knot diagram that stays the same no matter how the loop is deformed. If two knots have different invariants, they are definitively different. If they share the same invariant, they *might* be the same — the invariant may simply be too weak to tell them apart.

timeline.heading: THE LADDER OF INVARIANTS
timeline.body: Each generation of invariant catches knots the previous one missed. The Alexander polynomial (1928) was the first systematic tool. The Jones polynomial (1984) earned Vaughan Jones the Fields Medal by distinguishing knots Alexander could not. Khovanov homology (1999) refined Jones into a richer structure — but pairs of knots share Khovanov signatures and still resist separation.

timeline.heading: WHY IT'S HARD
timeline.body: The space of knot diagrams is infinite — any knot has infinitely many equivalent drawings via Reidemeister moves. A good invariant must be computable from any diagram yet return the same answer for all of them. Proving an invariant is well-defined is often harder than defining it.

timeline.heading: THE DNA CONNECTION
timeline.body: DNA inside a cell is a closed loop millions of base pairs long, and replication requires untangling it. Enzymes called topoisomerases cut, pass, and rejoin strands to change the knot type. Knot invariants let biologists classify the substrates and products of these enzymes — telling which topological moves the cell can actually perform.

blocks.text: A single human cell packs roughly **two meters** of DNA into a nucleus ~6 microns across. Topoisomerase inhibitors like *etoposide* and *doxorubicin* — used in chemotherapy — work by trapping the enzyme mid-cut, leaving the DNA knotted and killing the dividing cell.

timeline.heading: THE QUANTUM CONNECTION
timeline.body: Edward Witten showed in 1989 that the Jones polynomial emerges naturally from Chern-Simons quantum field theory — a link between knot topology and physics that nobody had anticipated. Topological quantum computers, now being built by Microsoft and others, encode qubits in the braiding of quasiparticles; the computation literally *is* knot manipulation.

timeline.heading: THE KHOVANOV BARRIER
timeline.body: Khovanov homology is a categorification of the Jones polynomial — it replaces each polynomial coefficient with a vector space, capturing strictly more information. Yet computational experiments found knot pairs with identical Khovanov homology that topologists suspected were distinct. Closing that gap has been an open problem for over two decades.

blocks.question: Why do mathematicians keep inventing new knot invariants?
options: Older invariants are computationally too slow
Some distinct knots share the same value under existing invariants
New invariants are required by the axioms of topology
blocks.explanation: An invariant that can't distinguish two genuinely different knots is said to be incomplete. Each new invariant aims to separate pairs that previous tools collapsed together.

timeline.heading: THE COLLAPSE
timeline.body: Lebanon's banking system froze in October 2019. Banks imposed informal capital controls overnight — depositors could no longer withdraw their dollars, and the lira lost over 98% of its value against the dollar within four years. Savings accumulated over decades evaporated in months.

timeline.heading: LOLLARS
timeline.body: Dollars trapped inside Lebanese banks became known as *lollars* — digital dollars that could only be withdrawn in lira at a fraction of their value. A depositor with $100,000 on paper might access perhaps $15,000 in real purchasing power. The term is Lebanese gallows humor for a currency that exists only as a database entry.

blocks.text: The gap between a **lollar** and an actual US dollar banknote — a *fresh dollar* in Beirut slang — became the single most important price in the economy.

timeline.heading: THE CASH ECONOMY
timeline.body: With banks untrusted, Lebanon reverted to physical cash. By 2023 the IMF estimated roughly half of GDP circulated outside the banking system. Salaries paid in envelopes, rent in stacks of hundreds, businesses keeping dollars under mattresses or in safes. This is the vacuum apps like Whish Money filled.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of Lebanon's economy was operating in cash outside the banking system by 2023?
blocks.explanation: The IMF estimated cash transactions reached roughly half of GDP — an extraordinary figure for a middle-income country, and the substrate that made mobile wallets essential.

timeline.heading: WHY NO DEPOSIT INSURANCE
timeline.body: Lebanon's National Institute for the Guarantee of Deposits exists on paper, but it covers lira deposits up to 75 million — worth about $830 at current rates. Dollar deposits have no coverage at all. Fintech platforms like Whish operate entirely outside this already-hollow framework.

timeline.heading: THE REGULATORY GAP
timeline.body: Mobile money providers across weak-state contexts — M-Pesa in Kenya, bKash in Bangladesh, Whish in Lebanon — typically operate under central bank licenses that predate social engineering fraud. Rules cover solvency and anti-money-laundering; they rarely require compensation when a user is tricked into authorizing a transfer themselves.

timeline.heading: WHY WHATSAPP
timeline.body: Lebanon has one of the world's highest WhatsApp penetration rates — over 90% of smartphone users. When a financial platform's support channel runs on the same app fraudsters use to impersonate it, the attack surface is the entire customer base. There is no out-of-band verification the average user trusts more than the in-band impersonator.

timeline.heading: THE MANDATE
timeline.body: UNIFIL was created by UN Security Council Resolution 425 in March 1978, after Israel's first invasion of Lebanon. Its original task was to confirm Israeli withdrawal and help Lebanon restore authority in the south — a mandate that has been renewed every year for nearly five decades without ever being fulfilled.

blocks.text: The mission is *interim* in name only. 1978 was supposed to be months; it is now the **longest-running active UN peacekeeping deployment** in the Middle East.

timeline.heading: THE 2006 REWRITE
timeline.body: After the 34-day war between Israel and Hezbollah, Resolution 1701 expanded UNIFIL from a few thousand observers to roughly 10,000 troops with a mandate to help keep the area south of the Litani River free of armed groups other than the Lebanese army. In practice, Hezbollah never left; UNIFIL patrols around it.

blocks.label: UNIFIL's operating theatre and top troop contributors

timeline.heading: THE CAST
timeline.body: France has anchored UNIFIL since its founding — a legacy of the French Mandate over Lebanon (1920–1943). Italy and France together contribute the bulk of European troops; the overall force is commanded on rotation, currently under an Italian general.

timeline.heading: HEZBOLLAH'S POSTURE
timeline.body: Hezbollah was born in 1982 in direct response to Israel's invasion and occupation of southern Lebanon. Its founding doctrine treats the south as a resistance zone, not a neutral one — which structurally puts any foreign force, UN or otherwise, in the way of its freedom of movement.

timeline.heading: WHY FRANCE IS DIFFERENT
timeline.body: Macron's public accusation against Hezbollah is a sharp break from UNIFIL's usual posture of diplomatic ambiguity. French troops have been targeted before — most infamously the 1983 Drakkar barracks bombing in Beirut that killed 58 French paratroopers, attributed to a Hezbollah precursor group. For Paris, this history is living memory, not archive.

blocks.question: What was the 1983 Drakkar bombing?
options: An attack on French UNIFIL troops in southern Lebanon
A truck bombing of French paratroopers in Beirut
An Israeli airstrike on a French embassy convoy
A Syrian artillery strike on a French patrol
blocks.explanation: The Drakkar bombing hit the French contingent of a separate multinational force in Beirut, not UNIFIL — but it shaped French threat perception of Hezbollah for a generation.

timeline.heading: THE RENEWAL CLIFF
timeline.body: UNIFIL's mandate must be renewed annually by the Security Council. The US under Trump and Israel have both signaled they see the mission as ineffective cover for Hezbollah; France and Italy have been its strongest defenders. An August 2026 non-renewal would end the mission entirely.

timeline.heading: THE GEN Z UPRISING
timeline.body: Nepal's 2025 protests began after the government blocked 26 social media platforms. Within days the movement escalated into an anti-corruption revolt that burned the parliament building and forced PM K.P. Sharma Oli to resign. What started as a digital freedom protest became a generational rejection of the political class.

blocks.text: The movement became known as the ***Nepo Kid*** protests — videos contrasting the lavish lifestyles of politicians' children against median incomes of roughly **$1,400/year** went viral and crystallized public rage.

timeline.heading: THE MAYOR WHO BECAME PM
timeline.body: Balendra Shah — known as Balen — is a rapper and structural engineer who won Kathmandu's mayoralty in 2022 as an independent at age 32. When the Gen Z protests toppled the old order, the army and protest leaders settled on him as a consensus caretaker PM. He is the youngest head of government in Nepal's history.

blocks.question: What was Balendra Shah's profession before entering politics?
blocks.explanation: Balen built a following as a battle rapper and trained as a civil engineer — an outsider profile that was central to his appeal against Nepal's entrenched political dynasties.

timeline.heading: WHY THE HOME MINISTRY MATTERS
timeline.body: Nepal's Home Ministry controls the police, the Department of Money Laundering Investigation, and internal intelligence. A home minister under a laundering probe is not a peripheral scandal — it is the ministry that would normally investigate itself. Losing it forces the PM to hold the portfolio directly to preserve the probe's credibility.

timeline.heading: THE DYNASTIC CAPTURE
timeline.body: Since the 2008 abolition of the monarchy, power has rotated among three parties — the Nepali Congress and two communist factions (UML and Maoist Centre) — led by the same handful of men: Oli, Prachanda, Deuba. Each cycle produced new coalitions but the same leaders. Gen Z's grievance was not ideology; it was the closed circle itself.

blocks.label: the old guard Gen Z rejected

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHIC SQUEEZE
timeline.body: Nepal is landlocked between India and China, with all sea access running through Indian ports. Every government must balance Delhi and Beijing simultaneously — aid, infrastructure loans, open borders for migrant workers. Domestic instability is immediately read in both capitals as an opening.

timeline.heading: THE REMITTANCE ECONOMY
timeline.body: Remittances from Nepali workers abroad — mostly in the Gulf, Malaysia, and India — equal roughly a quarter of GDP, one of the highest ratios in the world. This is the structural backdrop to the anti-corruption rage: a generation works abroad in construction and domestic service to send money home, while the political class in Kathmandu is seen living off that flow.

timeline.heading: WHY NORTH KOREA STEALS CRYPTO
timeline.body: UN sanctions cut North Korea off from the global banking system. The regime generates hard currency through counterfeiting, arms sales, and — since 2017 — cryptocurrency theft. The UN Panel of Experts estimated DPRK cyber operations funded roughly 40% of the weapons program as of 2023.

blocks.text: The Lazarus Group umbrella — run out of the **Reconnaissance General Bureau** — has stolen an estimated **$3B+** in crypto since 2017, making Pyongyang the most prolific state-level crypto thief on record.

timeline.heading: THE SHIFT TO PERSONAL DEVICES
timeline.body: Exchanges hardened after the 2022 Ronin Bridge heist ($625M) and 2024 DMM Bitcoin theft ($305M). Cold storage, multi-sig approvals, and transaction monitoring pushed attackers down the stack — from platforms to the phones in users' pockets, where a single compromised device yields keys directly.

timeline.heading: HOW INFOSTEALERS WORK
timeline.body: Infostealer malware scrapes browser-saved passwords, clipboard contents, session cookies, and wallet seed files from an infected device. Crypto wallets are a prime target because possession of the seed phrase equals possession of the funds — no password reset, no bank intermediary, no reversal.

timeline.heading: THE TRANSPARENCY PARADOX
timeline.body: Every blockchain transaction is public and permanent. Pseudonymous addresses provide privacy, but the transaction graph — who sent what to whom — is visible to everyone. This makes cryptocurrency simultaneously the easiest financial system to use anonymously and the easiest to trace forensically.

timeline.heading: THE LAUNDERING PIPELINE
timeline.body: Stolen coins move through mixers (Tornado Cash, sanctioned in 2022), cross-chain bridges, and over-the-counter brokers in jurisdictions with weak KYC. DPRK operators have industrialized this pipeline — the gap between theft and cash-out has compressed from months to weeks.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of DPRK weapons program funding came from cyber operations by 2023, per the UN Panel of Experts?
blocks.explanation: The UN Panel estimated cyber theft — primarily crypto — funded roughly 40% of the weapons program, making hacking a core pillar of the regime's military economy.

timeline.heading: WHY PHONES ARE SOFT TARGETS
timeline.body: Mobile wallets sit on devices that users also use to browse, message, and install apps. A single malicious APK, phishing link, or trojanized Telegram client can compromise the keys. Unlike exchange accounts, there is no institution to notice the drain or freeze the transfer.

timeline.heading: THE WOUND
timeline.body: On 22 April 2025, gunmen killed 26 tourists in the Baisaran meadow above Pahalgam — the deadliest attack on civilians in Kashmir since the 2008 Mumbai siege. India attributed it to The Resistance Front, widely assessed as a Lashkar-e-Taiba front organization.

blocks.text: **Lashkar-e-Taiba** (LeT) was founded in the late 1980s in Pakistani Punjab and is designated a terrorist group by the UN, US, EU, and India. Pakistan formally banned it in 2002; analysts say it operates through rebranded fronts like *The Resistance Front* and *Jamaat-ud-Dawa*.

timeline.heading: OPERATION SINDOOR
timeline.body: India's May 2025 response — named for the vermilion mark Hindu widows traditionally remove — struck targets across Pakistani Punjab and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. It was the first Indian strike on the Pakistani heartland (not just Azad Kashmir) since the 1971 war.

timeline.heading: THE INDUS LEVER
timeline.body: The 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, gave Pakistan the three western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) and India the three eastern ones. Roughly 80% of Pakistan's irrigated agriculture depends on the western rivers. India suspended its participation in the treaty after Pahalgam — the first such move in 65 years.

timeline.heading: THE ESCALATION LADDER
timeline.body: India and Pakistan have fought four wars (1947, 1965, 1971, 1999) and several limited engagements. Since both went nuclear in 1998, the doctrine has been calibrated escalation — strikes calibrated to punish without crossing the threshold that triggers nuclear response. Sindoor pushed that ceiling higher than any prior episode.

timeline.heading: WHY KASHMIR
timeline.body: At Partition in 1947, the princely state of Jammu & Kashmir had a Muslim majority but a Hindu maharaja, who acceded to India under invasion pressure. The UN-mandated plebiscite never happened. The Line of Control froze the dispute in 1949; neither side recognizes it as a border.

timeline.heading: THE 2019 INFLECTION
timeline.body: India revoked Article 370 in August 2019, stripping J&K of its special autonomous status and splitting it into two union territories ruled directly from Delhi. Farooq Abdullah, the former chief minister quoted in this story, was placed under house arrest for months. The constitutional change reframed Kashmir from a disputed territory to an internal administrative matter — a position Pakistan rejects.

blocks.question: What did India's August 2019 revocation of Article 370 do to Jammu & Kashmir?
options: Stripped its special autonomy and split it into two union territories
blocks.explanation: Article 370 had given J&K its own constitution and autonomy since 1949. Its revocation placed the region under direct rule from Delhi.

timeline.heading: THE TRC BARGAIN
timeline.body: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996–2002) offered amnesty in exchange for full disclosure of politically motivated crimes. The deal was explicit: confess the act, prove the political motive, walk free. Refuse to apply, or lie, and prosecution was supposed to follow.

blocks.text: The bargain was *conditional* amnesty — unique in transitional justice. Chile and Argentina granted blanket amnesties; South Africa required perpetrators to name victims, describe methods, and submit to cross-examination in public hearings.

timeline.heading: THE UNFINISHED LIST
timeline.body: Roughly 300 apartheid-era cases were explicitly handed to the National Prosecuting Authority when the TRC closed — perpetrators who refused amnesty, were denied it, or never applied. Two decades later, fewer than a dozen have gone to trial. Most suspects have since died.

blocks.question: Of the ~300 apartheid-era cases referred by the TRC to prosecutors, roughly how many reached trial in the following 20 years?
blocks.explanation: The vast majority stalled. The Khampepe-style inquiries now probing why are the state's first serious attempt to explain the gap.

timeline.heading: THE SCORPIONS
timeline.body: The Directorate of Special Operations — the Scorpions — was an elite prosecutor-led unit that combined investigation and prosecution under one roof, modeled on the US FBI. It pursued senior ANC officials for corruption, which made it politically inconvenient, and was dissolved by parliament in 2009.

timeline.heading: THE TURF PROBLEM
timeline.body: South African law enforcement fractured after 1994 into overlapping units — SAPS detectives, the Scorpions, the NPA's Priority Crimes Litigation Unit. Apartheid-era cases required cross-unit cooperation between bodies whose leaders were competing for budget, headlines, and survival.

timeline.heading: THE MBEKI YEARS
timeline.body: Allegations of political interference cluster around Thabo Mbeki's presidency (1999–2008). Victims' families argue senior ANC figures, some of whom had their own amnesty applications or pre-1994 operational histories, quietly signaled that prosecutions should not proceed. The current judicial inquiry is the first official test of that claim.

timeline.heading: WHY IT STILL MATTERS
timeline.body: The TRC's legitimacy rested on a promise: amnesty for those who confessed, prosecution for those who didn't. If the second half never arrives, the first half becomes indistinguishable from impunity — and every future transitional-justice bargain is weakened by the precedent.

timeline.heading: THE STATUTORY HOOK
timeline.body: Section 237(a)(4)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act lets the Secretary of State personally deem a noncitizen deportable if their presence is believed to produce 'potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.' No crime, no hearing, no evidence standard — the Secretary's determination is itself the trigger.

blocks.text: The clause is known in immigration bar shorthand as the ***foreign policy ground***. It was written in 1990 with Cold War defectors in mind and sat nearly dormant for three decades before recent administrations revived it.

timeline.heading: WHAT A GREEN CARD ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: Lawful Permanent Resident status is a statutory privilege, not a constitutional right. The holder can work, travel, and live indefinitely in the US, but can be stripped of the card and removed through immigration proceedings. Only citizenship — naturalization — is irrevocable absent fraud.

timeline.heading: THE DUE PROCESS FLOOR
timeline.body: The Supreme Court held in Landon v. Plasencia (1982) that returning permanent residents are entitled to due process at the border. But immigration courts sit inside the Executive Branch (the DOJ's EOIR), not the independent judiciary — the judge hearing your case reports up to the same administration seeking your removal.

blocks.question: Which branch of the US government employs immigration judges?
options: The Judicial Branch, like federal district judges
The Executive Branch, inside the Department of Justice
blocks.explanation: Immigration judges are DOJ employees in the Executive Office for Immigration Review — they can be reassigned or fired by the Attorney General.

timeline.heading: THE IRANIAN DIASPORA IN AMERICA
timeline.body: Roughly half a million Iranian-Americans live in the US, with the densest concentration in Los Angeles — 'Tehrangeles' — where a wave arrived after the 1979 revolution. Most are secular, middle-class, and include many who fled the very regime they are now sometimes accused of representing.

timeline.heading: THE SURNAME PROBLEM
timeline.body: Persian family names are drawn from a relatively small pool of roots — geographic, tribal, or religious — and a shared surname implies no familial connection. Mistaking two Hamidehs for relatives of a general is the cultural equivalent of assuming every American named Smith is related.

timeline.heading: THE 1952 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Mass deportation orders driven by ideology rather than conduct are not new. The McCarran-Walter Act of 1952 let the Attorney General deport LPRs for suspected communist sympathies; in Galvan v. Press (1954) the Supreme Court upheld it, holding that immigration is a plenary power of the political branches. That doctrine — that courts defer almost totally to the executive on who may stay — has never been overruled.

timeline.heading: DETENTION MEDICAL CARE
timeline.body: ICE's own 2024 oversight reports documented chronic delays in specialist referrals and medication access at contract detention facilities. Untreated chronic conditions — hypertension, diabetes, blood disorders — are the single largest category of medical grievances filed by detainees, and deaths in ICE custody have repeatedly been traced to missed or delayed care.

timeline.heading: THE SUNSET CLAUSE
timeline.body: USMCA is the first major trade pact with a built-in expiration. Article 34.7 requires a joint review every six years; if all three parties don't agree to extend, the deal terminates after sixteen years. The 2026 review is the first test of this mechanism.

blocks.text: The clause was a US demand in 2018 — designed precisely so Washington could **reopen terms periodically** without abrogating the treaty outright.

timeline.heading: WHY CANADA IS EXPOSED
timeline.body: Roughly 75% of Canadian exports go to the United States. No other G7 economy is so dependent on a single trading partner. The asymmetry is the entire negotiating problem: the US can threaten tariffs as leverage; Canada cannot credibly threaten the reverse.

timeline.heading: NAFTA TO USMCA
timeline.body: NAFTA (1994) created a continental free-trade zone with minimal rules-of-origin requirements. USMCA (2020) tightened those rules — autos must now have 75% North American content (up from 62.5%) and 40-45% must be made by workers earning at least $16/hour. The shift was designed to pull manufacturing back from Mexico to the US.

timeline.heading: THE CHAPTER 19 FIGHT
timeline.body: Canada's red line in every renegotiation since 1988 has been binational dispute panels — the mechanism that lets Canadian exporters challenge US anti-dumping duties outside US courts. Washington has tried to kill it three times; Ottawa has held the line each time, because without it Canadian softwood lumber, steel, and dairy would face uncontested US trade remedies.

timeline.heading: THE LEVERAGE ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: The US runs a goods deficit with Canada driven almost entirely by oil — Canada is the largest single supplier of crude to US refineries, especially Midwest ones engineered for heavy Canadian grades. This is Ottawa's one structural card: those refineries cannot quickly switch feedstock.

blocks.question: What share of US crude oil imports comes from Canada?
blocks.explanation: Canada supplies roughly 60% of US crude imports — more than all OPEC countries combined, and the Midwest refinery complex is purpose-built for heavy Canadian grades.

timeline.heading: CARNEY'S BACKGROUND
timeline.body: Mark Carney is the only person to have run two G7 central banks — the Bank of Canada (2008–2013) and the Bank of England (2013–2020). He took the prime ministership in 2025 with a mandate built explicitly around managing the US relationship through the USMCA review.

timeline.heading: WHAT ENSO ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation is a sloshing of warm water across the equatorial Pacific. Trade winds normally pile warm water in the west near Indonesia; when they weaken, that warm pool migrates east toward South America. The ocean surface warms, and the atmosphere above follows.

blocks.text: Meteorologists track it via the *Oceanic Niño Index* — a running average of sea-surface temperature anomalies in the **Niño 3.4** region of the equatorial Pacific. Above **+0.5°C** is El Niño; below **−0.5°C** is La Niña.

timeline.heading: WHY IT DOMINATES THE ANNUAL RECORD
timeline.body: The ocean stores roughly 1,000 times more heat than the atmosphere. El Niño releases a sliver of that stored heat to the air; La Niña absorbs it. This is why individual years wobble around the warming trend — the underlying greenhouse forcing is monotonic, but ENSO decides which year prints a new record.

timeline.heading: THE LAG
timeline.body: Peak global temperatures arrive several months after peak Pacific warming. An El Niño that peaks in late 2026 exports its heat to the global atmosphere through early-to-mid 2027, which is why forecasters already pencil in 2027, not 2026, as the candidate record year.

blocks.question: How much of Earth's excess climate heat does the ocean absorb?
blocks.explanation: Over 90% of the heat trapped by greenhouse gases ends up in the oceans. The atmosphere gets only a few percent — which is why tiny ocean shifts swing global air temperatures.

timeline.heading: THE TELECONNECTIONS
timeline.body: A warm eastern Pacific reshuffles weather worldwide: drought across Indonesia, Australia, and southern Africa; heavy rain on the Pacific coast of South America; a weaker Indian monsoon; milder winters across northern North America. The 2015–16 El Niño contributed to Ethiopia's worst drought in fifty years.

timeline.heading: THE SUPER EL NIÑO
timeline.body: Three events since 1950 qualify as 'super' — 1982-83, 1997-98, and 2015-16. Each reset the global temperature record and triggered coral bleaching, fisheries collapse off Peru, and cascading food-price shocks. They arrive roughly every 15-20 years, and the warming baseline means each new one starts from a hotter floor.

timeline.heading: THE DOCTRINE
