Bridges are the most-attacked surface in crypto — Ronin lost $625M, Wormhole $325M, Nomad $190M — because compromising the keys mints unbacked tokens that drain the destination chain.

timeline.heading: HOW CONTAGION WORKS
timeline.body: Aave accepts a token as collateral. A bridge minting that token is exploited, flooding markets with unbacked supply. The collateral's price holds briefly on Aave's oracle while attackers borrow against it, then collapses — leaving the protocol with bad debt the borrower will never repay.

timeline.heading: THE GOVERNANCE LAG
timeline.body: Aave's treasury cannot just write a check. Any disbursement requires a token-holder vote, typically a 3-day discussion plus a 3-day on-chain vote. The exploit happens in seconds; the rescue takes a week. This is the structural cost of decentralization.

blocks.question: Why can't Aave instantly tap its treasury to cover a shortfall?
options: The treasury is held by a third-party custodian
Disbursements require a token-holder governance vote
Smart contracts cannot move funds without an oracle update
US regulators have frozen the treasury
blocks.explanation: AAVE token-holders must vote on any treasury action, which typically takes about a week between proposal and execution.

timeline.heading: THE ARBITRUM SECURITY COUNCIL
timeline.body: Most L2s, including Arbitrum, retain a multisig 'Security Council' that can pause contracts or freeze funds during emergencies. The trade-off the ecosystem accepts: a small group of trusted humans can override the code to prevent disaster — but that same group could, in theory, refuse to release funds or seize them. Aave's request to Arbitrum is a public test of that trust.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: After 2016's DAO hack drained $60M, Ethereum hard-forked the chain to reverse the theft — splitting the network and birthing Ethereum Classic. The lesson the industry took: voluntary consortium rescues, even imperfect ones, are preferable to rewriting history.

timeline.heading: WHY AT BIRTH
timeline.body: Hepatitis B transmits vertically — an infected mother passes it to the newborn during delivery. The window to intervene is hours, not days. A vaccine dose plus immunoglobulin within 12 hours of birth blocks roughly 90% of perinatal transmission; wait a week and the virus has already established chronic infection.

blocks.text: The clinical term is *perinatal transmission* — exposure during the birth process itself, distinct from *horizontal* spread later in life through blood or sex.

timeline.heading: WHY CHRONIC IS THE WHOLE GAME
timeline.body: An adult who catches hepatitis B usually clears it; fewer than 5% become chronic carriers. An infected newborn is the inverse: roughly 90% become chronic. Of those, 25% die prematurely from cirrhosis or liver cancer. The birth dose exists because the infant immune system loses this fight almost every time.

timeline.heading: THE 1991 DECISION
timeline.body: Before universal birth-dose policy, the US screened only mothers known to be high-risk. It missed too many — a third of perinatal infections came from mothers with no flagged risk factor or whose status was never tested. The 1991 ACIP recommendation moved to universal coverage precisely because targeted screening had failed.

blocks.question: Why did the US move from risk-based screening to universal birth-dose vaccination in 1991?
options: Targeted screening missed too many infected mothers
A new vaccine technology became available
blocks.explanation: Roughly one-third of perinatal infections came from mothers whose risk status was unknown or untested — universal coverage closed that gap.

timeline.heading: WHO ACIP IS
timeline.body: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices is a 15-member federal panel whose recommendations determine which vaccines insurers must cover without copay under the ACA, what the Vaccines for Children program distributes free, and what schools require. A vote to drop a recommendation cascades through the entire access system, not just clinical guidance.

timeline.heading: THE GLOBAL CONTEXT
timeline.body: The WHO recommends universal birth-dose hepatitis B vaccination; 113 countries follow it. Taiwan was the first to adopt it nationally in 1984 and saw childhood liver cancer rates fall by roughly 70% within a generation — one of the cleanest cause-and-effect results in vaccine history.

timeline.heading: THE SPARK
timeline.body: In March 2011, security forces in Daraa detained roughly 15 schoolboys for spraying anti-regime graffiti. They were tortured for weeks. When their families came to plead for their release, Atef Najib — Bashar al-Assad's maternal cousin and the city's political security chief — reportedly told them to forget their sons and have new ones. The protests that followed became the Syrian uprising.

blocks.text: The 13-year-old whose tortured body was returned to his family — **Hamza al-Khatib** — became the uprising's first icon. His name carried the revolution before any political program did.

timeline.heading: THE MUKHABARAT ARCHITECTURE
timeline.body: Assad-era Syria ran on four overlapping intelligence services — Military Intelligence, Air Force Intelligence, General Security, and Political Security — each reporting directly to the presidency, each with its own detention network, each empowered to arrest without judicial oversight. Overlap was the design: no single branch could become a coup threat, and citizens could never be sure which service was watching.

timeline.heading: THE ALAWITE INNER CIRCLE
timeline.body: The Assad regime concentrated security command in the Alawite minority — roughly 10 percent of Syria's population — and within that, in extended family. Najib was Anisa Makhlouf's nephew; the Makhloufs and Assads filled the senior intelligence and Republican Guard posts for four decades. The trial of a cousin is therefore not symbolic — it is the first prosecution of the regime's bloodline.

timeline.heading: DARAA, THE HAWRAN PLAIN
timeline.body: Daraa sits on Syria's southern border with Jordan, in the agricultural Hawran plain — historically Sunni, tribal, and economically marginalized under decades of drought and Damascus-centric investment. That the uprising began here, not in Aleppo or Homs, surprised the regime; the Hawran's tribal networks extend across the Jordanian border, and grievances spread faster than the security services could contain them.

timeline.heading: TRANSITIONAL JUSTICE, NO PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Post-conflict states have tried three models: South Africa's truth commission with conditional amnesty, Rwanda's gacaca community courts processing hundreds of thousands of cases, and Iraq's de-Baathification by administrative purge. Each has known failures — amnesty alienates victims, gacaca produced uneven verdicts, de-Baathification gutted the state. Syria, with tens of thousands of Mukhabarat officers and over 100,000 documented disappearances, has chosen none of these yet.

blocks.question: What did the families of the detained Daraa schoolboys reportedly hear from Atef Najib in 2011?
options: A promise to investigate within 48 hours
To forget their sons and have new ones
That the boys had already been transferred to Damascus
An offer of compensation in exchange for silence
blocks.explanation: The reported insult — said to fathers begging for tortured children — became the moment Daraa's tribal networks turned irreversibly against the regime.

timeline.heading: THE CAESAR FILES
timeline.body: In 2013, a Syrian military photographer codenamed Caesar defected with roughly 55,000 images of detainees who had died in custody — emaciated bodies numbered like inventory. The archive, authenticated by forensic experts, is the most extensive photographic record of state torture since the Nazi camps and forms the documentary backbone for any Mukhabarat prosecution to come.

timeline.heading: THE COINBASE PREMIUM
timeline.body: Coinbase is the largest US-regulated spot exchange; Binance dominates offshore. When Coinbase prints higher than Binance for the same Bitcoin, US institutions are bidding harder than the rest of the world. When the premium flips negative, the marginal US buyer has stepped back.

blocks.text: The premium is a *flow* indicator, not a *price* indicator — it shows **who** is buying, not how much Bitcoin is worth.

timeline.heading: WHY WHALES MATTER MORE HERE
timeline.body: Bitcoin ownership is extremely concentrated: roughly 2% of addresses hold over 90% of the supply. A single Bitfinex wallet holding 79,000 BTC controls more coin than most countries' strategic reserves hold in gold equivalent. When that wallet sits at peak exposure, its rebalancing decisions move the market on their own.

timeline.heading: THE ABSORPTION RATIO
timeline.body: Miners produce roughly 450 new BTC per day. For prices to rise, net new demand — primarily ETF inflows and corporate treasuries — must exceed that issuance. When the absorption ratio collapses from multiples of issuance toward 1x, prices stop rising even before they fall.

timeline.heading: THE LEVERAGE OVERHANG
timeline.body: Most Bitcoin trading volume is perpetual futures, not spot. When funding rates stay positive for weeks, longs are paying shorts to keep positions open — a crowded trade. Pullbacks in this regime tend to cascade through liquidations rather than orderly selling.

blocks.question: What does a sustained NEGATIVE Coinbase premium typically signal?
options: US institutional demand is weakening relative to offshore
Bitcoin's underlying network is being attacked
Coinbase is losing market share to competitors
The Federal Reserve is cutting interest rates
blocks.explanation: The premium tracks WHERE buying is concentrated. Negative means offshore (Binance, Bitfinex) is bidding harder than US regulated venues — institutional caution.

timeline.heading: THE MACRO BACKDROP
timeline.body: Bitcoin pays no yield. When real Treasury yields are high, the opportunity cost of holding a zero-coupon asset is measurable, and capital rotates back to bonds. The 10-year real yield is the single best macro predictor of crypto risk appetite.

timeline.heading: WHAT A GATEKEEPER IS
timeline.body: The DMA designates a small set of platforms as 'gatekeepers' based on size thresholds: €7.5bn EU turnover, 45 million monthly EU users, and a 'core platform service' like an OS, app store, or search engine. Designation triggers obligations no other firm faces.

timeline.heading: WHY HOTWORDS MATTER
timeline.body: On Android, only Google Assistant (now Gemini) can wake from a locked screen, listen continuously for trigger phrases, and read on-screen context across apps. Rivals run as foreground apps, killed when the screen locks. The privilege is not a feature — it is access to the OS event loop.

blocks.text: The technical term is *privileged system intent* — Android reserves certain broadcasts (screen-on, hotword-detected, accessibility-service) for apps signed with the platform key. Third-party assistants live one ring out from the kernel; the gatekeeper sits inside it.

timeline.heading: THE 10% HAMMER
timeline.body: DMA fines scale to 10% of global annual turnover, 20% for repeat offenses. For Alphabet's ~$350bn revenue, a single violation can cost $35bn — larger than any GDPR fine ever issued. Brussels designed the cap to make compliance cheaper than defiance.

blocks.label: max DMA fine vs notable EU penalties

timeline.heading: THE INTEROPERABILITY DOCTRINE
timeline.body: DMA Article 6(7) requires gatekeepers to grant rivals 'effective interoperability' with hardware and OS features. This goes further than US antitrust, which historically forbids only active exclusion. The EU mandates active sharing — a positive duty, not just a negative restraint.

blocks.question: What does DMA Article 6(7) require gatekeepers to do for rivals?
options: Stop blocking competitors from app stores
Actively share OS and hardware interfaces
Pay a licensing fee to smaller firms
blocks.explanation: Article 6(7) imposes a positive duty of effective interoperability — sharing access, not merely refraining from exclusion.

timeline.heading: THE BRUSSELS EFFECT
timeline.body: When the EU sets a compliance regime that costs more to fragment than to apply globally, firms tend to roll out the EU version everywhere. GDPR did this to privacy notices; DMA is doing it to platform architecture. The 450-million-person market sets the floor for what's technically possible elsewhere.

timeline.heading: THE LAST VOTE
timeline.body: The 2006 legislative elections — the last Palestinian national vote — were won by Hamas with 44% to Fatah's 41%. The US, EU, and Israel had pushed for the election expecting a Fatah win; when Hamas took the legislature, the same powers imposed sanctions and froze tax transfers. The lesson absorbed by every faction since: elections only count if the right side wins.

timeline.heading: THE OSLO ARCHITECTURE
timeline.body: The Palestinian Authority was created by the Oslo Accords (1993-95) as an interim self-government body — explicitly time-limited to five years pending final-status negotiations. Thirty years later, the interim is the structure. The PA has municipal authority but no sovereignty over borders, airspace, water, or the population registry.

blocks.text: The PA collects taxes through Israel under the **Paris Protocol** — Israel withholds VAT and customs on PA-bound goods, then transfers them monthly. These *clearance revenues* are roughly **65%** of PA budget, and Israel has frozen them repeatedly as leverage.

timeline.heading: WHO CONTROLS WHAT
timeline.body: Gaza's electricity comes primarily from Israeli grid feeds and a single Gaza power plant that runs on Israeli-supplied fuel. Water comes from the coastal aquifer (over-pumped, brackish) plus Israeli Mekorot pipelines. The crossings — Erez, Kerem Shalom, Rafah — are controlled by Israel and Egypt. A municipal council elected inside this envelope governs garbage collection and street repair, not statehood.

timeline.heading: THE LEGITIMACY DEFICIT
timeline.body: Mahmoud Abbas's four-year term as PA president expired in 2009. He has remained in office for seventeen years past the constitutional limit, citing the impossibility of holding elections under occupation. Polls consistently show majority Palestinian support for his resignation. The municipal vote in Deir al-Balah is the first ballot most Gazans under 35 have ever cast.

timeline.heading: THE 22.7% NUMBER
timeline.body: Turnout that low in a high-stakes vote signals either fear, fatigue, or boycott. Hamas did not field slates and discouraged participation; many Gazans live displaced from their registered municipalities; nine UN tents cannot replace the polling infrastructure of a functioning state. The number is a measure of conditions, not enthusiasm.

blocks.question: When was the last time Gaza held any kind of election before this week's vote?
blocks.explanation: The 2005 municipal elections were the last Gaza-wide vote. The 2006 legislative election was Palestine-wide, not Gaza-only, and Hamas's takeover in 2007 ended electoral politics entirely until now.

timeline.heading: THE BLESSED LAND
timeline.body: Palestine — al-ard al-mubaraka, the blessed land — is named in Surah al-Isra as the territory around al-Aqsa whose precincts Allah has blessed. Classical scholars including Ibn Kathir read this geography as inseparable from the broader region of al-Sham. For the Muslim reader, a municipal vote in Deir al-Balah is a small civic act on land whose significance in Islamic tradition vastly exceeds the boundaries of any administrative council.

timeline.heading: THE CHOKEPOINT IN NUMBERS
timeline.body: Hormuz normally carries 80-100 tanker transits a day moving roughly 21 million barrels — about a fifth of global oil consumption. A collapse to single digits is not a slowdown; it is a closure that war-risk insurance pricing has already enforced regardless of what mines remain.

timeline.heading: WHY MERZ BREAKS WITH WASHINGTON
timeline.body: Germany's strategic memory of Iraq 2003 is institutional. Schröder refused to join; the refusal defined a generation of German foreign policy as distinct from Atlanticist reflex. Merz, a CDU Atlanticist by instinct, invoking that comparison signals the rift is structural, not personal.

blocks.text: German strategic culture distinguishes *Bündnistreue* — alliance loyalty — from automatic military alignment. Merz is asserting the former while denying the latter.

timeline.heading: THE SEQUENCING DISPUTE
timeline.body: Tehran's offer — peace deal first, nuclear concessions second — inverts the standard non-proliferation template (verify, then normalize). Rubio's rejection follows the JCPOA-era logic: leverage evaporates the moment sanctions lift, so concessions must come before relief.

blocks.question: What was the JCPOA's core sequencing principle that Rubio is restating?
options: Verification of nuclear limits preceded sanctions relief
Both happened simultaneously on signing day
blocks.explanation: The 2015 deal required IAEA verification of nuclear rollback before economic sanctions were lifted — Tehran's current proposal would reverse that order.

timeline.heading: THE CAST AT THE TABLE
timeline.body: The diplomatic geometry is unusual: a German chancellor publicly dissenting, an Iranian foreign minister flying to Moscow, a US secretary of state holding the line, and a US president offering personal diplomacy via phone. Each node has a distinct interest.

timeline.heading: THE STRAIT'S GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: Hormuz sits between Iran and Oman. The deepest channels hug the Iranian coast; the shipping lanes are 3 km wide each. Saudi and Emirati bypass pipelines could reroute roughly a third of Gulf exports — the rest has no alternative route to tidewater.

timeline.heading: THE RUSSIA HEDGE
timeline.body: Iran's pivot to Moscow in moments of Western pressure is now reflexive — Shahed drones flowed to Russia for Ukraine; Russian air defense and economic backstops flow back. The 2025 strategic partnership treaty formalized what was already operational.

timeline.heading: THE TRUST CHAIN
timeline.body: Modern software is assembled from thousands of third-party packages, each pulling in dozens more. A single compromised dependency anywhere in that tree executes with the same privileges as your own code. There is no sandbox by default.

blocks.text: A typical Node.js project pulls in **1,000+ transitive dependencies** from authors the developer has never heard of. Trust is not verified — it is *inherited* through the dependency graph.

timeline.heading: WHY THE LEGITIMATE PACKAGE IS THE ATTACK
timeline.body: Typosquatting — registering 'reqeusts' to catch typos for 'requests' — is the old technique. The new technique is hijacking the real package: steal the maintainer's signing key or compromise their CI pipeline, then publish a poisoned version under their genuine name. Every existing user auto-updates into the trap.

timeline.heading: THE GITHUB ACTIONS PIVOT
timeline.body: GitHub Actions runs CI/CD jobs in ephemeral cloud VMs with access to repository secrets — npm tokens, AWS keys, signing certificates. A flaw that lets one workflow read another's secrets effectively hands attackers the keys to every project that runs on the same infrastructure.

timeline.heading: THE SOLARWINDS PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In 2020, attackers compromised SolarWinds' build server and inserted a backdoor into Orion updates signed with the real corporate certificate. 18,000 organizations — including the US Treasury, State, and Homeland Security — installed the malicious update. The lesson: signing proves origin, not safety.

timeline.heading: WHY ROTATION IS NON-NEGOTIABLE
timeline.body: Once credentials touch a compromised runner, they must be assumed exfiltrated and used. Attackers exfiltrate first, exploit later — sometimes months later, after the incident is forgotten. Rotation invalidates whatever they captured; auditing logs alone does not.

blocks.question: After running a poisoned CI build that may have leaked AWS keys, what's the right response?
options: Audit CloudTrail logs and rotate only if suspicious activity appears
Rotate immediately — assume the keys are already in attacker hands
Restrict the keys to specific IPs and keep monitoring
Re-run the build with the clean version to overwrite the leak
blocks.explanation: Exfiltration leaves no reliable trace at the runner. Once a secret touches a compromised process, it must be treated as already stolen — rotate, don't audit-and-wait.

timeline.heading: THE STRUCTURAL FIX
timeline.body: Reproducible builds, hardware-backed signing keys, and SLSA provenance attestations let downstream users verify that a published artifact actually came from the claimed source code. Adoption is uneven; most package registries still trust whoever holds the upload token.

timeline.heading: THE DURAND LINE
timeline.body: The 2,640-km border was drawn in 1893 by British colonial administrator Mortimer Durand, slicing through Pashtun tribal lands. Afghanistan has never formally recognized it — every Kabul government, from monarchy to Taliban, has rejected it as a colonial imposition.

timeline.heading: WHO THE TTP IS
timeline.body: Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan formed in 2007 as a coalition of Pakistani Pashtun militants modeled on the Afghan Taliban but with a different target: the Pakistani state. They share ideology and ethnic ties with the Afghan Taliban, but operationally they are distinct.

blocks.text: The Afghan Taliban call themselves the **Islamic Emirate**; the Pakistani group calls itself **Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan** — the *Pakistani Taliban Movement*. Same ideology, different state target.

timeline.heading: THE SANCTUARY PROBLEM
timeline.body: For two decades Pakistan accused Afghanistan of harboring TTP fighters in Kunar and Nangarhar — the same charge the US made about al-Qaeda before 2001. After 2021, the Afghan Taliban inherited the territory and the accusation. Kabul denies harboring; Islamabad's strikes say otherwise.

timeline.heading: THE PASHTUN BELT
timeline.body: Roughly 50 million Pashtuns live in the contiguous belt straddling the Durand Line — about 15 million in Afghanistan, 35 million in Pakistan. The line cuts through tribes whose families and grazing lands sit on both sides. Border control as Westphalian states understand it has never functioned here.

timeline.heading: WHY CHINA BROKERED
timeline.body: Beijing has $62 billion committed to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor and growing mining interests in Afghanistan. Repeated TTP attacks have killed Chinese engineers in Pakistan; instability on the Afghan side threatens Mes Aynak copper. China is the only outside power with leverage on both governments simultaneously.

blocks.question: Which power brokered the March 2026 Pakistan-Afghanistan ceasefire?
blocks.explanation: China brokered the ceasefire, leveraging its CPEC investments in Pakistan and mining interests in Afghanistan — the only outside power with concurrent influence on both.

timeline.heading: THE HISTORICAL RHYME
timeline.body: Pakistan supported the Afghan Taliban through the 1990s as strategic depth against India. After 2001 it played both sides — hosting US logistics while sheltering Taliban leadership in Quetta. The current crisis is partly the bill arriving for that two-decade hedge.

events.label: Taliban takes Kabul with ISI support

timeline.heading: THE AMYLOID HYPOTHESIS
timeline.body: For thirty years, Alzheimer's research bet on a single idea: sticky amyloid-beta plaques accumulate between neurons, trigger inflammation, and kill cells. Drugs that targeted the plaques directly — solanezumab, bapineuzumab, gantenerumab — failed clinical trials repeatedly through the 2010s.

timeline.heading: WHAT MICROGLIA ACTUALLY DO
timeline.body: Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells — about 10% of all brain cells. They patrol continuously, extending and retracting processes every few minutes, sampling the extracellular space. When they detect debris or pathogens, they engulf and digest it. They are the brain's professional janitors.

timeline.heading: THE LIPID SIGNAL
timeline.body: Microglia don't randomly find plaques. They are summoned by N-acyl amino acids — lipid messengers released by stressed neurons that bind microglial receptors and direct them to damage sites. Without the signal, microglia drift past plaques without engaging.

blocks.text: PM20D1 is the enzyme that **cleaves** these lipid signals into their active form. It's the molecular siren that tells microglia *where to go*.

timeline.heading: WHY ANTIBODIES FAILED THE TARGET
timeline.body: For a decade, researchers tried to block PM20D1 with antibodies — large protein molecules that bind extracellular targets. But PM20D1 acts inside vesicles and at membrane interfaces where antibodies cannot reach. The drug class was wrong for the biology.

timeline.heading: THE MOUSE-TO-HUMAN GAP
timeline.body: Mouse Alzheimer models accumulate plaques on accelerated timelines under genetic forcing. Roughly 99% of Alzheimer drugs that work in mice fail in humans — the disease in people involves decades of vascular, metabolic, and inflammatory damage that the models do not capture.

blocks.question: Roughly what fraction of Alzheimer drugs that succeed in mouse models go on to fail in human trials?
blocks.explanation: The translational failure rate in Alzheimer's is among the worst in medicine — over 99% of mouse-validated candidates fail human Phase 2 or 3.

timeline.heading: THE BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER
timeline.body: Even if a small molecule activates PM20D1 perfectly in a dish, it must cross the blood-brain barrier — a tight junction of endothelial cells that excludes roughly 98% of small-molecule drugs and nearly all large biologics. This is why CNS drug development costs more and fails more than any other therapeutic area.

timeline.heading: THE DOCTRINE
timeline.body: For nearly fifty years, the Fourth Amendment did not protect information you voluntarily shared with a third party. Bank records (US v. Miller, 1976), phone numbers dialed (Smith v. Maryland, 1979) — once you handed data to someone else, you had no reasonable expectation of privacy in it. This is the third-party doctrine.

blocks.text: The doctrine was built for an era when *third party* meant your bank teller or telephone operator — not an ad-tech SDK silently logging your GPS coordinates 1,400 times a day.

timeline.heading: THE CARPENTER CRACK
timeline.body: In Carpenter v. United States (2018), the Court ruled 5-4 that police need a warrant to obtain 127 days of cell-site location records from a carrier. Roberts wrote that location data is so revealing — tracing 'familial, political, professional, religious, and sexual associations' — that the third-party doctrine cannot mechanically apply.

blocks.text: When the Government tracks the location of a cell phone it achieves near perfect surveillance, as if it had attached an ankle monitor to the phone's user.
blocks.speaker: Chief Justice Roberts, Carpenter v. United States

timeline.heading: THE BROKER LOOPHOLE
timeline.body: Carpenter covered carriers, not apps. Data brokers buy precise GPS pings from weather, prayer, and game apps via the ad-tech bidstream, then sell the resulting bundles to anyone with a purchase order — including ICE, CBP, the FBI, and the Defense Intelligence Agency. The legal theory: a purchase is not a search.

people.name: DIA
people.role: told Congress it buys US-person data

blocks.label: agencies that bought broker location data

timeline.heading: GEOFENCE WARRANTS
timeline.body: A geofence warrant asks Google (or another platform) for every device that crossed a defined polygon during a defined window. The Fifth Circuit ruled them categorically unconstitutional in 2024; the Fourth Circuit upheld them. That circuit split is what brought the question to the Supreme Court.

blocks.question: What makes a geofence warrant constitutionally unusual under traditional Fourth Amendment doctrine?
options: It targets a place and time, not a named suspect
It must be signed by a federal judge
blocks.explanation: Traditional warrants particularize a person or thing to be seized. Geofence warrants reverse the logic — they identify suspects by who was present, which critics argue is a general warrant the Fourth Amendment was written to forbid.

timeline.heading: THE MOSAIC THEORY
timeline.body: Individual data points may be innocuous — one GPS ping, one license plate scan. Aggregated over weeks, they reveal mosques attended, doctors visited, lovers met, protests joined. Justice Sotomayor named this in her US v. Jones (2012) concurrence; it is the doctrinal seed Carpenter grew from.

timeline.heading: WHY IT MATTERS NOW
timeline.body: Closing the broker loophole would force federal agents to obtain warrants for the same location data they currently buy with appropriated funds. Congress tried this with the Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act in 2024 and failed. A Supreme Court ruling would impose what legislation could not.

timeline.heading: THE LEGACY RAIL
timeline.body: International wires move through correspondent banking — a chain of banks that each hold accounts with the next, passing messages over SWIFT and settling balances at the end of the day. Each hop adds fees, compliance checks, and a cutoff window aligned to New York business hours.

blocks.text: SWIFT is **only a messaging network** — it moves instructions, not money. Actual settlement happens through *nostro/vostro* accounts the correspondent banks hold for each other.

timeline.heading: WHY WEEKENDS MATTER
timeline.body: Fedwire and most central-bank settlement systems close evenings and weekends. A wire sent Friday afternoon in New York typically clears Monday in the receiving country. Stablecoins settle on public blockchains that never close, which is the structural advantage Western Union is buying.

timeline.heading: THE REMITTANCE MARKET
timeline.body: Global remittances run roughly $700bn a year, with the World Bank's measured average cost around 6.4%. The corridor most exposed is small-ticket cross-border to lower-income countries — exactly the corridor Western Union built its 170-year-old network on.

timeline.heading: THE RESERVE MECHANIC
timeline.body: A regulated dollar stablecoin holds reserves — typically short-dated US Treasuries and bank deposits — equal to tokens outstanding. The issuer earns the yield on those reserves. At current Treasury rates this is the most profitable part of the business; the payment rail is a customer-acquisition funnel for the float.

timeline.heading: WHY SOLANA
timeline.body: Settlement finality on Solana is roughly 400 milliseconds, with fees typically under a cent. Ethereum mainnet costs more and confirms in tens of seconds. For a remittance flow priced against Western Union's existing per-transaction fee, the chain choice is essentially a unit-economics decision.

timeline.heading: THE GENIUS ACT
timeline.body: The 2025 GENIUS Act gave US-issued payment stablecoins a federal charter framework: 1:1 reserves in cash and short Treasuries, monthly attestations, and bankruptcy priority for token-holders. Before the law, no major correspondent bank could touch the rails on compliance grounds. The law is what made this launch legal at scale.

blocks.question: What backs a fully-reserved US payment stablecoin under the GENIUS Act?
options: Cash and short-dated US Treasuries held 1:1
A pool of crypto collateral over-collateralized 150%
blocks.explanation: GENIUS requires 1:1 reserves in cash and short Treasuries, with monthly attestations — distinct from FDIC-insured deposits or crypto-collateralized models.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE CEASEFIRE ACTUALLY SAYS
timeline.body: The November 2024 deal gave Hezbollah 60 days to withdraw fighters and weapons north of the Litani River, while Israel was to pull back across the Blue Line. The Lebanese Army would deploy into the vacated south alongside UNIFIL. Almost none of the timelines held; Israel retained five 'strategic points' inside Lebanese territory past every deadline.

timeline.heading: THE 1701 INHERITANCE
timeline.body: UN Resolution 1701 ended the 2006 war on similar terms: Hezbollah disarms south of the Litani, Israel withdraws, UNIFIL monitors. It was never enforced. The November 2024 ceasefire is essentially 1701 rewritten with a US-French monitoring mechanism instead of UNIFIL — the same architecture that failed for eighteen years.

blocks.text: The Litani is roughly **30 km** north of the Israeli border. The strip between the river and the Blue Line is what every south Lebanon arrangement since 1978 has tried — and failed — to demilitarize.

timeline.heading: WHY CIVILIAN TOLLS RECUR HERE
timeline.body: South Lebanon's villages sit on a geography that has been buffer zone, occupation zone, and battleground continuously since 1978. Hezbollah's military infrastructure is dispersed through civilian terrain by design — homes, garages, orchards. Strikes on suspected weapons sites and strikes on civilian dwellings become the same coordinates.

timeline.heading: WHY BRAZIL CARES
timeline.body: Lebanon's diaspora in Brazil — roughly 7 million people of Lebanese descent — is larger than Lebanon's domestic population of about 5.5 million. Most descend from Christian and Shia migrants who left during Ottoman conscription drives and the 1975-1990 civil war. Every south Lebanon casualty list includes dual nationals.

timeline.heading: THE SPOILER LOGIC
timeline.body: Ceasefires that lack disarmament timelines incentivize both sides to test the edges. Israel demonstrates that strikes carry no cost; Hezbollah demonstrates it has not been disarmed. The IRA decommissioning took 8 years after Good Friday — armed groups disarm only when politics delivers more than fighting does. Lebanon's politics delivers neither.

blocks.question: How long after the Good Friday Agreement did the IRA fully decommission its weapons?
blocks.explanation: The IRA completed decommissioning in 2005 — 7 years after the 1998 agreement — only after sustained political concessions and independent verification.

timeline.heading: THE TRILLION-DOLLAR MYTH
timeline.body: The $1 trillion figure traces to a 2010 US Geological Survey estimate of in-ground reserves — lithium, copper, iron, rare earths, cobalt. In-ground value is not extractable value. Without roads, rail, power, water, and processing capacity, ore in the Hindu Kush is worth a fraction of ore at a port.

timeline.heading: THE EXTRACTION-TERMS LADDER
timeline.body: Mining contracts sit on a spectrum. At one end: raw ore export at spot price, no processing, low royalties. At the other: domestic smelting requirements, equity stakes for the state, training mandates, technology transfer. Where a country sits on this ladder reflects its leverage — not its geology.

timeline.heading: THE INDONESIA PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In 2014 Jakarta banned raw nickel ore exports outright. Chinese smelters had two choices: build processing plants in Indonesia or lose access. They built. Indonesia now controls roughly half of global refined nickel — a transformation that required state capacity, not just resources.

blocks.text: Indonesia's leverage came from being a *price-setter* in nickel, not a price-taker. Afghanistan's lithium share is too small to coerce buyers — the **Lithium Triangle** of Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia holds over half of global reserves.

timeline.heading: THE SANCTIONS DISCOUNT
timeline.body: Sanctioned states sell at a discount because their buyer pool shrinks. Russian oil trades at $15-25 below Brent. Iranian crude trades wider still. The same logic applies to minerals: only buyers willing to absorb sanctions risk show up, and they price that risk into the contract.

blocks.question: Why do sanctioned exporters typically accept worse contract terms than peers?
options: Their buyer pool shrinks, eliminating competitive bidding
International law caps their royalty rates
They lack physical infrastructure to ship
blocks.explanation: Sanctions don't degrade the ore — they shrink the auction. Fewer bidders means each buyer can dictate terms the seller would otherwise refuse.

timeline.heading: THE RESOURCE CURSE
timeline.body: Countries rich in extractable minerals consistently underperform resource-poor peers on growth, governance, and conflict. The mechanism: resource revenue accrues to whoever controls the mine, not the broader economy, so capturing the state becomes more valuable than building it. Afghanistan's history of warlord-controlled mining predates the Taliban by decades.

events.label: Hajigak iron ore awarded to Indian consortium
Lithium and REE concessions to CN, IR, TR

timeline.heading: WHY CHINA, IRAN, TURKEY
timeline.body: The buyers are precisely the states with the least to lose from US sanctions exposure. China already operates the dormant Aynak copper concession from 2007. Iran shares a 900km border and operates outside the dollar system. Turkey has hedged its sanctions posture for a decade. The cast is the cast that shows up everywhere sanctions push Western capital out.

timeline.heading: THE TEACHER EXCEPTION
timeline.body: US copyright law's work-for-hire doctrine assigns employer ownership of work created within employment scope. But a long-standing 'teacher exception' — rooted in academic custom predating the 1976 Copyright Act — held that lectures, books, and course materials belonged to the professor, not the university. The exception was never codified; it survives by tradition and contract.

blocks.text: The 1976 Act technically *abolished* the teacher exception by omission — courts have split on whether it survives, leaving the question to **faculty handbooks** and union contracts.

timeline.heading: WHY RECORDINGS CHANGED EVERYTHING
timeline.body: A live lecture is ephemeral; a recording is a fixed, reproducible asset. When universities pivoted to recorded instruction during COVID, most updated IP policies to claim ownership of recordings as 'institutional works' — a category broader than work-for-hire. The professor still owns the ideas; the university owns the file.

blocks.question: Under US copyright law, when does a lecture become protected?
options: When 'fixed in a tangible medium' — written, recorded, or transcribed
blocks.explanation: Copyright attaches at fixation, not creation. An unrecorded lecture is unprotected; the moment it's recorded, ownership becomes the contested question.

timeline.heading: THE MOOC PRECEDENT
timeline.body: When Coursera and edX launched in 2012, Stanford, MIT, and Harvard quietly negotiated revenue-sharing agreements with star faculty whose courses drew millions of enrollments. The contracts treated lectures as licensed content, not work-for-hire. ASU's atomic-modules approach skips that negotiation entirely — the precedent it sets is that a university can repackage faculty output without consent.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'ATOMIC' MEANS
timeline.body: AI training pipelines prefer short, self-contained chunks: a 90-second clip explaining one concept, tagged and embeddable. A 75-minute lecture is too long to retrieve; a hundred atomic modules are searchable inventory. The economic value shifts from the lecture to the chunked corpus — and the corpus is what the university now claims to own.

timeline.heading: THE COMPENSATION GAP
timeline.body: Faculty salaries assume teaching, research, and service. They do not assume that recorded lectures will be productized into a separate revenue stream. When Westlaw and LexisNexis built searchable databases from court opinions in the 1980s, judges weren't paid royalties — opinions were public domain. Faculty lectures are not. That distinction is what makes ASU's posture legally fragile and politically combustible.

timeline.heading: THE 2021 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Australia's News Media Bargaining Code was the first law worldwide forcing platforms to pay publishers. Facebook briefly blanked all Australian news pages in February 2021 — including government health and emergency services pages — before backing down and signing deals.

blocks.text: The week-long blackout earned a name: the **Facebook News Ban**. It demonstrated platform leverage but also drew the regulatory backlash that shaped every copycat law since.

timeline.heading: WHY A LEVY, NOT A CODE
timeline.body: The 2021 code let platforms avoid designation by cutting voluntary deals. Meta announced in 2024 it would not renew those deals. A revenue tax flips the default: pay publishers or pay the treasury. Platforms cannot exit by simply refusing to negotiate.

timeline.heading: THE COPYCAT WAVE
timeline.body: Canada's Online News Act (2023) triggered Meta to block news for Canadians entirely — a block still in place. France, Germany, and Spain pursued versions through EU copyright law. Each jurisdiction tests whether platforms will concede or withdraw.

timeline.heading: THE STRUCTURAL ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: Australian newsrooms shed roughly 5,000 jobs in the decade to 2020 as classified and display ad revenue migrated to Google and Meta. The bargaining code's premise: platforms captured value journalism produced. The counter-argument: platforms drive traffic publishers monetize. Both are partly true.

timeline.heading: THE TIKTOK ADDITION
timeline.body: The 2021 code targeted Google and Meta. TikTok was added in 2026 because short-form video now carries a meaningful share of news consumption among under-30s. The levy treats news distribution as the trigger, regardless of platform format.

blocks.question: What did Meta do when Canada passed its 2023 news payment law?
options: Blocked all news links for Canadian users
blocks.explanation: Meta blocked news links on Facebook and Instagram for Canadian users rather than pay — a block still in effect, demonstrating that platforms will exit news rather than concede on principle.

timeline.heading: THREE REVOLUTIONS, ONE PATTERN
timeline.body: Kyrgyzstan is the only Central Asian state to have overthrown its president by street protest — three times. Each Tulip-style uprising replaced one strongman with another who promised reform and consolidated power instead.

events.label: October unrest brings Japarov from prison to presidency

timeline.heading: FROM PRISON TO PRESIDENT
timeline.body: Japarov was serving an 11-year sentence for hostage-taking when October 2020 protesters stormed the prison and freed him. Within weeks he was acting president. The path — prisoner to head of state in under a month — has no parallel in post-Soviet politics.

blocks.text: The bloc that pulled him out was **Mekenchil**, a nationalist party Tashiyev led. The two men's careers fused on the night of the prison break — which is why this dismissal reads less like a cabinet reshuffle and more like a divorce.

timeline.heading: THE GKNB
timeline.body: Tashiyev ran the State Committee for National Security — the GKNB, successor to the Soviet KGB. In Central Asia these agencies don't just collect intelligence; they run anti-corruption prosecutions, control border services, and decide which oligarchs lose assets. Whoever holds the GKNB holds the leash.

timeline.heading: THE TANDEM PROBLEM
timeline.body: Post-Soviet co-rule arrangements are unstable. Putin–Medvedev ended with Putin returning. Nazarbayev's handover to Tokayev collapsed in the 2022 Kazakh unrest. Tandems work until the junior partner builds an independent base — at which point the senior either absorbs or expels him.

timeline.heading: THE NEIGHBORHOOD
timeline.body: Kyrgyzstan sits between Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and China's Xinjiang. It hosts a Russian airbase at Kant, a Chinese-financed rail project, and a US-aligned mining sector — Bishkek's foreign policy is a hedging exercise on every axis.

timeline.heading: WHY 2027 MATTERS
timeline.body: Japarov's referendum-rewritten constitution allows two five-year terms. 2027 is his first re-election test. Removing Tashiyev now — two years out — gives the GKNB time to be staffed with loyalists before the campaign apparatus turns on.

blocks.question: What did Japarov's 2021 constitutional referendum change?
options: Restored a strong presidential system after a decade of parliamentarism
Abolished the presidency in favor of a prime minister
blocks.explanation: The 2010 constitution had made Kyrgyzstan Central Asia's only parliamentary republic. Japarov's referendum reversed that, concentrating power back in the presidency.

timeline.heading: THE RISE OF CJNG
timeline.body: The Jalisco New Generation Cartel emerged around 2009 as a splinter from the Sinaloa-aligned Milenio Cartel. Within a decade it rivaled Sinaloa as Mexico's most powerful trafficking organization, with presence reported in most Mexican states and distribution networks across five continents.

blocks.text: CJNG's signature was *vertical integration* — controlling product from Andean coca and Asian fentanyl precursors through to US street distribution, rather than acting as a transit middleman.

timeline.heading: WHY SUCCESSION FRAGMENTS
timeline.body: Cartels are not corporations with org charts; they are coalitions of regional plaza bosses bound by a charismatic leader's reputation for violence and reliable payment. When the leader dies, the coalition's unity dies with him. The 1989 arrest of Guadalajara Cartel chief Félix Gallardo split his network into the Tijuana, Sinaloa, and Juárez cartels — the structural template for every Mexican succession since.

events.label: Félix Gallardo arrested; Guadalajara Cartel splits
Pablo Acosta killed; Juárez Cartel restructures
Beltrán Leyva killed; faction war erupts
El Mencho dies; CJNG enters succession

timeline.heading: THE PACIFIC ROUTES
timeline.body: Nayarit and Jalisco sit on the Pacific corridor that channels methamphetamine precursors from Asian ports through Manzanillo and Lázaro Cárdenas, then north to the US border. Whoever controls these plazas controls the chemical supply chain that has displaced cocaine as CJNG's main revenue source.

timeline.heading: THE KINGPIN STRATEGY
timeline.body: US and Mexican policy since the 1990s has targeted top leaders for capture or killing — the so-called kingpin strategy. The empirical record is mixed: leaders fall, but homicide rates in their territories typically rise as lieutenants war over succession. The arrest disrupts operations; it rarely shrinks the trade.

timeline.heading: THE BOUNTY ECONOMY
timeline.body: The US State Department's Narcotics Rewards Program has paid over $135M since 1986 for information leading to traffickers. A $5M bounty on a regional successor signals where Washington ranks the threat — El Mencho himself carried a $10M bounty, the same tier as Chapo Guzmán at his peak.

blocks.question: What typically happens to homicide rates in a region after a top cartel leader is captured?
options: They fall as the cartel weakens
They rise as lieutenants war over succession
They stay flat — local violence is unrelated to leadership
blocks.explanation: Studies of Mexico's kingpin strategy consistently find short-term homicide spikes in the captured leader's territory as rivals and internal factions fight to inherit the plaza.

timeline.heading: WHY THIS IS HARDER THAN APOLLO
timeline.body: Apollo used a single Saturn V to send a small lander to the Moon. Artemis uses a giant Starship that's too heavy to reach the Moon on one tank — it must launch, then be refueled in low Earth orbit by a fleet of additional Starships before it can leave for the Moon.

blocks.text: Apollo's lunar module weighed **15 tonnes**. Starship's lunar variant is roughly **100+ tonnes** dry — an order of magnitude heavier, which is why orbital refueling went from optional to mandatory.

timeline.heading: THE REFUELING PROBLEM
timeline.body: Cryogenic propellant — liquid methane and oxygen near -180°C — boils off in sunlight and sloshes unpredictably in microgravity. Transferring it between two docked spacecraft has never been demonstrated at scale. Estimates suggest a single Artemis mission needs 8 to 16 tanker launches in rapid succession before boil-off defeats the effort.

timeline.heading: THE TWO LANDERS
timeline.body: NASA hedged by funding two competing landers — SpaceX's Starship HLS for Artemis III and Blue Origin's Blue Moon for Artemis V. Both require orbital refueling. Both are years behind. The hedge didn't produce redundancy; it produced parallel delays.

timeline.heading: THE CHINA TIMELINE
timeline.body: China's lunar program is methodical: Chang'e robotic landers since 2013, sample return in 2020, far-side sample return in 2024. The crewed Long March 10 and Lanyue lander target 2030 — using a conventional architecture with no refueling required.

timeline.heading: WHY THE GAP MATTERS
timeline.body: No human has left low Earth orbit since 1972. The institutional knowledge of crewed deep-space operations — how to manage radiation, consumables, communication delays — has eroded across two generations of engineers. Both NASA and China are rebuilding capability that was once routine.

blocks.question: How many years has it been since a human last walked on the Moon?
blocks.explanation: Apollo 17's Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt left the lunar surface in December 1972 — over five decades ago.

timeline.heading: THE BUDGET ARITHMETIC
timeline.body: Apollo consumed roughly 4% of the federal budget at peak. NASA today runs at about 0.4% — one-tenth the share — while attempting a more complex architecture with commercial partners on fixed-price contracts. The schedule slips are partly engineering, partly the math of doing more with less.

timeline.heading: WHAT PRO SE MEANS
timeline.body: Pro se — Latin for 'for oneself' — is the right to represent yourself in court without a lawyer. Federal law (28 USC §1654) guarantees it, but judges have long observed that pro se litigants lose at dramatically higher rates than represented parties.

blocks.text: The constitutional floor is *Faretta v. California* (1975) for criminal defendants; civil pro se rights flow from statute, not the Sixth Amendment. The right to self-represent is not a right to competent self-representation.

timeline.heading: WHY HALLUCINATIONS HAPPEN
timeline.body: Large language models are trained to produce plausible-sounding text, not factual citations. When asked for a supporting case, they generate something that looks like a real citation — correct reporter format, plausible court, plausible year — but the case may not exist. The model has no database of real opinions to check against.

blocks.question: Why do AI models invent fake legal citations that look real?
options: They were trained on fake cases by mistake
They predict plausible text, not retrieve verified facts
Court records are not in their training data
blocks.explanation: LLMs generate the most statistically likely next tokens. A citation 'shape' is easy to mimic; the underlying case existing is a separate question the model cannot verify.

timeline.heading: THE MATA PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In Mata v. Avianca (SDNY 2023), two attorneys submitted a ChatGPT-drafted brief citing six fabricated cases. Judge Castel sanctioned them $5,000 and required notification to every judge falsely named as authoring the invented opinions. It became the canonical warning case — and the rate of AI filings still climbed.

timeline.heading: THE VERIFICATION BURDEN
timeline.body: Federal judges and clerks now spend uncompensated time running citations through Westlaw or PACER to verify the cited case exists, says what the brief claims, and was decided as alleged. The burden falls hardest on overworked districts where pro se filings already dominate the civil docket.

blocks.label: share of federal civil cases with a pro se party

timeline.heading: THE ACCESS TRADEOFF
timeline.body: AI lowers the cost of drafting a complaint to nearly zero. For someone who could never afford a lawyer, that is a genuine expansion of access to courts. For the courts themselves, it is a flood of filings whose factual and legal claims must be verified by hand, with the worst-quality work indistinguishable from the merely inexperienced.

timeline.heading: RULE 11 AND ITS LIMITS
timeline.body: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 requires that filings be grounded in fact and warranted by law, with sanctions for violations. But Rule 11 was designed for represented parties, and courts have historically been lenient with pro se filers. Sanctioning a self-represented litigant who cannot pay accomplishes little; the deterrent that works on lawyers does not work on the public.

timeline.heading: THE ASTREINTE MECHANISM
timeline.body: Russian courts use a French-derived legal instrument called an astreinte — a recurring penalty that compounds daily until compliance. Unlike fixed fines, it has no statutory ceiling, which is how a content-moderation dispute scales into nine-figure judgments.

blocks.text: The penalty doubles weekly: 100,000 rubles becomes 200,000, then 400,000. Within months the figure exceeds any plausible fine — *by design*, to coerce compliance from a defendant who has already left the jurisdiction.

timeline.heading: WHY GOOGLE LEFT BUT DIDN'T LEAVE
timeline.body: Google shut its Russian subsidiary in 2022 after bailiffs first seized accounts, filing for bankruptcy locally. But YouTube continued operating for Russian users, and the legal entity's frozen assets — bank accounts, ad revenue receivables, server hardware — remained reachable by Russian courts even as the parent company withdrew operationally.

timeline.heading: THE COMPOUNDING LADDER
timeline.body: The $561M figure represents 62 separate enforcement proceedings, each one a different YouTube channel — mostly Russian state media like RT and Tsargrad — that Google blocked after Western sanctions. Every blocked channel is its own astreinte clock, running in parallel.

timeline.heading: THE ENFORCEMENT THEATER
timeline.body: Russia cannot reach Google's offshore assets — US courts will not enforce a Russian judgment against speech the First Amendment protects. The seizures function domestically: a signal to Russian users that the state acted, and a precedent banks like Sberbank cite when freezing Western firms' rubles.

blocks.question: Why can Russian courts seize $561M from Google despite Google exiting Russia in 2022?
options: Google still operates a Moscow office under a different name
Frozen accounts and receivables of the Russian subsidiary remained in-country
International treaties require Google to comply with Russian judgments
Google chose to pay to avoid criminal charges against staff
blocks.explanation: Google's Russian legal entity filed for bankruptcy but its in-country assets — bank balances, ad receivables — stayed reachable by domestic bailiffs even after operations ceased.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: This is now the largest sustained extraction from a Western tech firm by a sanctioned state. China extracted $2.8B from Alibaba in 2021 — but that was a domestic regulator disciplining a domestic firm. Russia is doing it across a closed border, to a company that no longer operates there.

timeline.heading: THE COPYRIGHT GAP
timeline.body: US copyright protects fixed expression — a specific recording, a specific performance. It does not protect a voice itself. If an AI model trains on a singer's catalog and generates a new song in their style, the original recordings were not copied; a new fixation was created. The statute Congress wrote in 1976 did not contemplate this.

blocks.text: Copyright protects the *recording*, not the *voice*. Trademark protects *source identifiers* — the thing consumers use to recognize who made something. A voice as brand is a trademark argument, not a copyright one.

timeline.heading: THE BETTE MIDLER PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In Midler v. Ford (1988), Ford hired a sound-alike singer to mimic Bette Midler for a commercial after Midler refused. The Ninth Circuit ruled this violated her right of publicity — a state-law tort, not federal IP. Right of publicity remains a patchwork: California protects it robustly, Tennessee passed an ELVIS Act in 2024, Florida barely recognizes it.

blocks.label: Right of publicity by US state

timeline.heading: WHY TRADEMARK IS UNUSUAL HERE
timeline.body: Trademark protects source identifiers — logos, names, packaging — that tell consumers who made a product. Registering a voice as a trademark requires proving the voice itself functions as a brand identifier in commerce. The USPTO has registered sounds (NBC chimes, MGM lion roar) but never the timbre of a living person's speaking or singing voice.

timeline.heading: THE TOM WAITS CASE
timeline.body: Tom Waits won $2.6 million from Frito-Lay in 1992 for a Doritos ad using a sound-alike. The court applied Lanham Act false-endorsement doctrine — implying Waits endorsed the product. Swift's filing tests whether that doctrine, born in the era of human imitators, extends to AI models trained on a catalog without consent.

blocks.question: Which legal theory has historically protected celebrities from voice imitation in ads?
options: Right of publicity + Lanham Act false endorsement
blocks.explanation: Voice itself is not copyrightable. Celebrities have won via state right-of-publicity torts and federal Lanham Act claims for implied endorsement.

timeline.heading: THE NO FAKES ACT
timeline.body: A bipartisan federal bill — the NO FAKES Act — would create the first federal right against AI-generated voice and likeness replicas. It has bounced through committee since 2023 without passage. Until it clears, artists are litigating in a legal vacuum where each circuit court can reach a different answer.

timeline.heading: THE HANDBOOK
timeline.body: South Africa's Ministerial Handbook is the binding rulebook governing what ministers can claim from the state — official residences, vehicles, security, domestic staff at designated seats only. It was tightened in 2019 after a decade of Zuma-era abuses, and explicitly bars state-funded household help at private homes.

blocks.text: The handbook distinguishes a **designated ministerial seat** (Pretoria, Cape Town) from a private residence. State-paid domestic staff are permitted only at the former.

timeline.heading: WHY EAST LONDON MATTERS
timeline.body: Tolashe's home is in East London, Eastern Cape — not a designated seat. Routing a state aide's salary to a private household in a non-seat location is the specific line the handbook draws; the geography is the violation, not just the family transfer.

timeline.heading: THE PAYROLL TRICK
timeline.body: The mechanism — putting a household worker on a department payslip and redirecting the funds — is a recurring South African accountability pattern. The Public Protector's office has flagged similar arrangements across multiple administrations; the structure hides private benefit inside a legitimate payroll line.

blocks.question: Which South African body is constitutionally empowered to investigate misuse of state resources by ministers?
blocks.explanation: The Public Protector is a Chapter 9 institution created by the 1996 Constitution specifically to investigate improper conduct by state organs and officials.

timeline.heading: THE ZONDO SHADOW
timeline.body: The Zondo Commission (2018–2022) documented how state capture under Zuma worked through exactly these small-scale payroll and procurement arrangements scaled across departments. Its findings reset the political cost of being caught — what was once routine is now resignation-grade.

timeline.heading: THE GNU CONSTRAINT
timeline.body: Since the 2024 election, the ANC governs in a Government of National Unity with the DA, which campaigned on clean governance. Each ANC scandal now carries coalition risk the party did not face during its three decades of single-party rule — the DA can extract concessions or trigger reshuffles in ways the opposition never could before.

timeline.heading: THE SEQUENCING PROBLEM
timeline.body: Every nuclear negotiation hinges on what comes first. Iran wants sanctions relief and security guarantees before constraining enrichment; the US wants enrichment caps before relief. Whoever moves first carries the risk that the other walks away after pocketing the concession.

blocks.text: In game theory this is a classic **commitment problem** — both sides prefer a deal to no deal, but neither can credibly promise to follow through once the other has moved.

timeline.heading: THE JCPOA PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The 2015 deal solved sequencing by phasing: Iran shipped out enriched uranium and disabled centrifuges in exchange for staged sanctions relief, verified by IAEA inspectors at each step. Trump withdrew in 2018, demonstrating that even phased deals collapse if a successor administration repudiates them — a memory that now shapes Tehran's reluctance to move first.

timeline.heading: WHY PAKISTAN BROKERS
timeline.body: Pakistan shares a 900km border with Iran, hosts the only Sunni-majority nuclear arsenal, and maintains working relations with Tehran, Riyadh, and Washington simultaneously. Islamabad has brokered Saudi-Iran de-escalation before — a role that depends on its peculiar position as a Sunni state with a 15-20% Shia population that cannot afford sectarian war on its western border.

timeline.heading: THE ENRICHMENT THRESHOLD
timeline.body: Weapons-grade uranium is 90% U-235; reactor fuel is 3-5%; medical isotopes need ~20%. Iran has enriched to 60% — a level with no civilian justification but technically below weapons-grade. The jump from 60% to 90% takes weeks, not years; this is why the US treats enrichment caps as the central constraint and why Iran treats them as its last bargaining chip.

blocks.question: What enrichment level does Iran currently produce that has no civilian justification?
blocks.explanation: 60% has no civilian use — it sits above medical-isotope needs (~20%) but below weapons-grade (90%), making it a deliberate signal of breakout capability.

timeline.heading: THE ENVOY SIGNAL
timeline.body: Cancelling an envoy visit mid-mediation is a calibrated diplomatic punishment — it does not break the channel but registers displeasure. Kushner's role as a personal envoy rather than a State Department official means the cancellation is reversible without bureaucratic friction; the same informality that lets Trump deploy him also lets Trump withdraw him without process.

timeline.heading: THE ARITA HEIST
timeline.body: In early 2024, a finance employee at Arup's Hong Kong office wired $25 million after a video call with what appeared to be the company's CFO and several colleagues. Every face on the call was a deepfake. The fraud is the canonical case study because it required no technical breach — only synthesized faces convincing enough to override a trained professional's skepticism.

blocks.text: The attack vector wasn't the *technology*; it was **plausibility at scale**. Generating one convincing fake video of a CFO used to require a studio. Now it requires a laptop and ten seconds of public footage.

timeline.heading: THE LIAR'S DIVIDEND
timeline.body: Legal scholars Bobby Chesney and Danielle Citron coined this term in 2018: as deepfakes proliferate, genuine recordings of misconduct can be dismissed as fakes. The harm is not just that lies become believable — it is that truths become deniable. Authoritarian leaders caught on tape gain a pre-built escape hatch.

timeline.heading: WHY DETECTION LOSES
timeline.body: Deepfake detection is a generative adversarial problem. Each new detector trains the next generation of fakes to evade it. The defender must catch every attack; the attacker only needs one that works. This is the same asymmetry that makes spam filters a permanent arms race rather than a solved problem.

timeline.heading: THE TRUST SUBSTRATE
timeline.body: Democratic governance assumes citizens share a baseline factual reality — that a video of an official saying X is evidence the official said X. Print, radio, and television each had forgery costs high enough to preserve this assumption. Generative AI collapses those costs to near zero, removing a substrate that institutions never had to defend before.

timeline.heading: THE LATIN AMERICAN STAKES
timeline.body: Public trust in government across Latin America runs at roughly 30% — among the lowest of any region in OECD surveys. Governments deploying AI for welfare eligibility, policing, or healthcare triage in this environment inherit the trust deficit; an algorithmic error reads as confirmation of state malice rather than implementation bug.

blocks.question: What share of citizens in Latin America say they trust their national government?
blocks.explanation: OECD's Trust Survey puts the regional average around 30%, well below the OECD mean of ~40% — a thin substrate on which to layer opaque AI decisions.

timeline.heading: THE PROVENANCE FIX
timeline.body: The C2PA standard (Adobe, Microsoft, BBC, others) cryptographically signs media at the moment of capture, so a downstream viewer can verify it has not been altered. The catch: provenance only certifies authentic content. It cannot prove a fake is fake — it can only prove a real thing is real, which is the opposite problem from the one most people think deepfakes pose.

timeline.heading: THE UNMARRIED WOMAN PROBLEM
timeline.body: Egyptian hotels have long refused rooms to unmarried Egyptian women traveling alone, citing informal 'morality' policies that have no statutory basis. The practice is custom enforced as if it were law — tolerated by tourism authorities for decades.

blocks.text: Foreign women face no such bar. The refusal applies specifically to *Egyptian* women without a male guardian or marriage certificate — a *de facto* mahram requirement imposed by hoteliers, not by Egyptian statute or by classical fiqh on hotel accommodation.

timeline.heading: THE 2011 LAW
timeline.body: Article 161 bis of Egypt's penal code, added after the 2011 revolution, criminalizes discrimination on the basis of sex, origin, language, religion, or creed. For over a decade it sat largely unused — prosecutors brought almost no cases, and no hotel had ever been convicted under it.

timeline.heading: THE CONSTITUTIONAL BACKDROP
timeline.body: Egypt's 2014 constitution, Article 11, commits the state to achieving equality between women and men. But constitutional equality clauses across the Arab world routinely coexist with personal-status laws derived from a conservative reading of fiqh that limit women's autonomy in travel, marriage, and guardianship.

timeline.heading: WHY IN ABSENTIA MATTERS
timeline.body: Egyptian criminal procedure allows conviction in absentia, but the defendant retains an automatic right to a full retrial upon surrender or arrest. The one-year sentence is real but provisional — the appeal is not a formality, it restarts the case from scratch.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT MECHANIC
timeline.body: Egypt is a civil-law system, not common law — there is no formal stare decisis. But a first conviction under a dormant statute reshapes prosecutorial behavior: police take complaints, prosecutors file charges, and hotels adjust policy to avoid being the second test case. The signal travels even without binding precedent.

blocks.question: Why does a first conviction matter so much in a civil-law system without binding precedent?
options: It binds future judges to the same ruling
It shifts prosecutorial and institutional behavior even without binding force
It amends the underlying statute automatically
blocks.explanation: Civil-law systems lack stare decisis, but a first successful prosecution under a dormant law signals to police, prosecutors, and regulated industries that the statute is now live.

timeline.heading: THE JOURNALIST AS PLAINTIFF
timeline.body: Across the Arab world, dormant rights statutes have most often been activated by journalists and lawyers who can absorb the social cost of being the first complainant. Tunisia's 2017 violence-against-women law, Morocco's 2018 Hakkaoui law, and Jordan's 2021 harassment amendments all moved from text to enforcement through individual test cases brought by women in public-facing professions.

timeline.heading: WHY BAIKONUR EXISTS WHERE IT DOES
timeline.body: Rockets launch eastward to borrow Earth's rotation; the closer to the equator, the bigger the free velocity boost. Baikonur sits at 46°N — far from ideal — but Soviet planners picked it in 1955 for secrecy and rail access, not physics. Kazakhstan inherited the world's largest spaceport by accident of Soviet collapse.

timeline.heading: THE LEASE
timeline.body: After 1991 Russia found its premier launch site in a foreign country. The 1994 lease — extended to 2050 — pays Kazakhstan roughly $115m/year plus environmental damages from spent rocket stages falling on Kazakh steppe. Baikonur the city is administered as if it were Russian territory.

blocks.text: The arrangement is unique in international law: a sovereign state leases a *city plus 6,717 km²* to another power, complete with Russian rubles, Russian schools, and Russian police — inside Kazakhstan.

timeline.heading: WHY SOYUZ-5 MATTERS
timeline.body: Soyuz-5 (Irtysh) is Russia's first new medium-lift rocket since the Soviet era, designed to replace the Ukrainian-built Zenit that Russia lost access to in 2014. It launches from a refurbished Zenit pad at Baikonur — one Kazakhstan now has equity in via the joint Baiterek venture, not just rent.

timeline.heading: RUSSIA'S LAUNCH ISOLATION
timeline.body: After February 2022, Roscosmos lost OneWeb, ExoMars, and Soyuz launches from French Guiana. Western commercial payloads vanished. SpaceX captured the freed market. Russia's remaining launch customers are domestic, Iranian, and increasingly dependent on Kazakh goodwill at Baikonur.

timeline.heading: THE LEVERAGE INVERSION
timeline.body: For thirty years the rent flowed one way and the dependency was Kazakh — Baikonur jobs, technology transfer, prestige. Sanctions inverted it. Russia now has nowhere else to launch crewed missions to the ISS or heavy commercial payloads at scale; Vostochny in the Far East remains under-built and over-budget.

blocks.question: Which country's space program is most dependent on a foreign-soil launch facility today?
blocks.explanation: All other major space powers launch from sovereign territory. Russia's flagship cosmodrome sits in a country it once ruled — and now must negotiate with.

timeline.heading: THE ONE-CHINA TRAP
timeline.body: Beijing requires every state that recognizes the PRC to break formal ties with Taipei. The result: countries must choose, and almost all choose the larger market. Taiwan held 22 formal partners in 2016; it has 12 today.

events.label: UN Resolution 2758 transfers China seat to PRC
Tsai elected; Beijing ends diplomatic truce
Panama, Dominican Republic, El Salvador switch

timeline.heading: THE TWELVE
timeline.body: Taiwan's remaining formal partners are mostly small Pacific, Caribbean, and Central American states plus the Holy See. Each switch shrinks the practical meaning of Taiwanese statehood — fewer embassies issuing visas, fewer votes in UN agencies that still admit observers.

blocks.label: Taiwan's 12 remaining formal allies
blocks.caption: Pacific microstates, Caribbean, Central America, Holy See, Eswatini

timeline.heading: AIRSPACE AS LEVERAGE
timeline.body: Under ICAO rules, overflight requires the underlying state's permission. Most Taiwanese presidential trips to Latin America transit US airspace as 'stopovers' — Beijing protests but cannot block. Denying transit through third-country airspace is a newer escalation that exploits Beijing's economic leverage over those states.

blocks.text: The diplomatic term is **transit diplomacy** — Taiwanese presidents use 'refueling stops' in friendly capitals to hold meetings that would otherwise require formal recognition. Each blocked transit narrows that workaround.

timeline.heading: THE STRAIT IS BUSY
timeline.body: Whatever the diplomatic temperature, the Taiwan Strait remains one of the world's most-trafficked waterways. Roughly 40% of global container traffic passes through it; any kinetic move would freeze a chunk of the world economy within days.

timeline.heading: THE SEMICONDUCTOR SHIELD
timeline.body: TSMC alone produces over 90% of the world's most advanced chips. This 'silicon shield' is why Washington's Taiwan policy survives administration changes — a Chinese blockade would halt iPhone, Nvidia, and AMD production within a quarter.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of the world's most advanced (sub-7nm) chips does TSMC produce?
blocks.explanation: TSMC fabs in Hsinchu and Tainan produce more than 90% of leading-edge logic chips — the core of the 'silicon shield' deterrent.

timeline.heading: THE DISTRACTION DIVIDEND
timeline.body: Beijing has long calibrated Taiwan pressure to US bandwidth. The 1995-96 Strait Crisis came as Washington was managing Bosnia; the 2022 Pelosi-visit drills came amid the Ukraine war's first year. Iran consuming Pentagon attention now follows the same pattern.

timeline.heading: THE LOST DECADES
timeline.body: Japan's policy rate has been at or near zero since 1999. An entire generation of traders, borrowers, and savers has never priced money the way the rest of the world does. The BOJ raising to even 1% would be the tightest policy Japan has run since the asset bubble burst in 1991.

blocks.label: BOJ policy rate, the long arc

timeline.heading: THE CARRY TRADE
timeline.body: Borrow yen at near-zero, convert to dollars, buy US Treasuries yielding 4%+. Pocket the spread. This trade has financed everything from emerging-market debt to Silicon Valley venture capital for two decades. When the yen strengthens or the gap narrows, positions unwind violently — August 2024 saw a 12% Nikkei crash in two days as carry trades imploded.

blocks.text: The technical term is **uncovered interest rate parity** — the theory says currencies should adjust so the carry profit disappears. In practice, the *yen* has defied this for decades, which is why the trade keeps working until it suddenly doesn't.

timeline.heading: THE INTERVENTION FLOOR
timeline.body: Japan's Ministry of Finance — not the BOJ — controls currency intervention. The MOF spent roughly $62bn defending the yen in 2024 when it crossed 160 against the dollar. The 159 level is psychologically loaded: traders watch it as the trigger zone where Tokyo sells dollars from its $1.2tn reserve stack.

timeline.heading: WHY A SPLIT VOTE MATTERS
timeline.body: BOJ decisions are usually unanimous — Japanese institutional culture favors consensus. A 6-3 split is the most hawkish dissent since Ueda took over in 2023. Markets read split votes as forward guidance: the dissenters today are usually the majority within two meetings.

blocks.question: What was the BOJ's policy rate from 2016 to 2024?
options: Negative 0.1% — charging banks to park reserves
blocks.explanation: The BOJ charged commercial banks 0.1% on excess reserves to push them to lend, a regime that ended only in March 2024.

timeline.heading: THE INFLATION PUZZLE
timeline.body: Japan finally has the inflation it spent 30 years trying to manufacture — core CPI has run above the 2% target since 2022. But wages haven't kept pace, so real household income is falling. The BOJ is in the unusual position of fighting inflation that arrived too late to be celebrated.

timeline.heading: WHAT A REGULATORY SANDBOX IS
timeline.body: A sandbox is a legal carve-out where a government suspends normal rules so firms can deploy untested products on real users. The UK's FCA pioneered the model in 2016 for fintech; it has since spread to AI, biotech, and crypto. The bargain is faster innovation in exchange for weaker consumer recourse.

blocks.text: The defining feature: liability shifts from the deploying firm to the *user* or *the state*, since normal product-safety law is partially suspended.

timeline.heading: WHY SMALL STATES BID
timeline.body: El Salvador has 6.3 million people and a GDP near $35bn — too small to matter as a market, large enough to serve as a live testbed. Bukele used the same logic with bitcoin in 2021: trade regulatory permissiveness for foreign capital and reputational positioning that larger economies cannot offer.

timeline.heading: THE LIABILITY GAP
timeline.body: In rich-country health systems, an AI diagnostic error routes through medical malpractice law, FDA device approval, and hospital insurance. In a sandbox, those layers are partially suspended. When a triage model misclassifies a stroke as indigestion, who pays the family is a question the contracts rarely answer.

blocks.question: In most AI regulatory sandboxes, who legally bears the cost when a deployed tool causes patient harm?
options: The vendor, under standard product liability
The host government, as the licensing authority
The patient, with limited recourse against either party
Split equally between vendor and government by treaty
blocks.explanation: Sandbox frameworks typically suspend or cap normal liability rules to attract vendors — recourse for end users is the variable that gets traded away.

timeline.heading: THE BITCOIN PRECEDENT
timeline.body: El Salvador made bitcoin legal tender in September 2021. By 2024 the IMF made unwinding the policy a condition of a $1.4bn loan: bitcoin acceptance was rolled back from mandatory to voluntary. The sandbox attracted attention but not the foreign investment promised; the state-built Chivo wallet had documented theft and outage problems that ordinary users absorbed.

timeline.heading: WHY HOSPITALS ARE THE HARDEST CASE
timeline.body: Schools and call centers can absorb AI errors with low downside — a wrong essay grade, a misrouted complaint. Clinical settings cannot. A diagnostic model trained on US or European patient data underperforms on populations it was not trained on; rural Salvadoran patients with different disease prevalence and presentation patterns are exactly the distribution-shift case AI systems handle worst.

timeline.heading: THE SUPPLY-SIDE GAP
timeline.body: Every climate treaty since Rio 1992 has targeted emissions — the demand side. None has capped extraction. A country can sign Paris and simultaneously expand oil drilling without violating any commitment, because the treaty regime regulates burning, not pumping.

blocks.text: The asymmetry is structural: **demand-side** rules let producers externalize the cap onto consumers. **Supply-side** rules force producers to leave reserves in the ground — which is why no major exporter has ever signed one.

timeline.heading: THE NPT ANALOGY
timeline.body: The 1968 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty froze the nuclear club at five states and bound them to disarm in exchange for non-nuclear states forgoing weapons. The fossil fuel framing borrows the bargain: producers wind down, non-producers commit not to develop new reserves, and a just-transition fund compensates the asymmetry.

blocks.text: Each of the Parties to the Treaty undertakes to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament.
blocks.speaker: NPT, Article VI

timeline.heading: WHO IS NOT AT THE TABLE
timeline.body: The three states absent from Bogotá produce roughly 40% of global oil. Without them, any extraction cap is a unilateral disarmament by smaller producers — economically painful, climatically marginal. The treaty's leverage depends entirely on whether their absence becomes diplomatically costly.
