blocks.label: share of US road CO2 by vehicle class

timeline.heading: WHY DIESEL IS HARD TO BEAT
timeline.body: Diesel packs about 45 megajoules per kilogram; lithium-ion cells deliver under 1 MJ/kg. A Class 8 hauling 80,000 lbs over 500 miles needs a battery pack that weighs several tons — every kilogram of battery is a kilogram of payload lost. The physics, not the price, is the constraint.

blocks.text: Tesla's Semi reportedly carries a **~900 kWh** pack — roughly 10× a Model S. That mass alone eats into the **80,000 lb** federal gross-weight limit, though the US has granted EV trucks a **2,000 lb** weight allowance to partially offset it.

timeline.heading: THE TCO CROSSOVER
timeline.body: Trucking is a thin-margin business run on Total Cost of Ownership: fuel, maintenance, driver, financing, depreciation. Diesel is 30-40% of TCO on long-haul; electricity at industrial rates is a fraction of that, and an electric drivetrain has perhaps a tenth the moving parts. The crossover happens when capex amortization beats the fuel savings — sensitive to electricity price, utilization, and charger access.

timeline.heading: THE CHARGING PROBLEM
timeline.body: A Class 8 fast-charge from 20% to 80% draws over a megawatt — enough to power a small town. The bottleneck is not the truck but the grid interconnection: utilities can take 2-4 years to approve and build a substation upgrade. Megawatt Charging System (MCS) standards were only finalized in 2024.

blocks.question: What's the approximate peak power draw of a Class 8 truck megawatt charger?
blocks.explanation: MCS targets up to ~3.75 MW theoretically, but production chargers today deliver around 1 MW — roughly 3× the fastest car DC fast chargers.

timeline.heading: THE COMPETITION
timeline.body: Tesla is not alone or first. Daimler's Freightliner eCascadia, Volvo VNR Electric, and Kenworth/Peterbilt T680E have been in commercial use since 2022. The question is not whether electric trucks work — it's whether Tesla's range claims (500 miles loaded) hold up against incumbents that ship today.

timeline.heading: WHY CALIFORNIA FIRST
timeline.body: WattEV is based in California, which has the Advanced Clean Fleets rule requiring drayage trucks at ports to be zero-emission by 2035, and the largest network of public truck charging in North America. Most early Semi deployments cluster around the LA/Long Beach port complex — the geography of regulation, not market demand.

timeline.heading: THE ORIGINAL BARGAIN
timeline.body: Princeton's 1893 honor code traded faculty surveillance for student self-policing: students sign a pledge and are obligated to report peers. The system survived 133 years because cheating left visible traces — a wandering eye, a passed note, a whispered answer.

blocks.text: The pledge was famously terse: *"I pledge my honor that I have not violated the Honor Code during this examination."* Every blue book carried it; every student signed it.

timeline.heading: WHY PEER REPORTING WORKED
timeline.body: Honor codes function as equilibrium games: they hold when most students believe most others comply. Once perceived cheating crosses a threshold, the cooperative norm collapses — non-cheaters feel like suckers and either start cheating or stop reporting. Game theorists call this a tipping model.

timeline.heading: WHAT AI BROKE
timeline.body: Earlier cheating — crib sheets, copied answers, even contract essay mills — produced artifacts another student could see. A classmate using ChatGPT on a laptop or phone under the desk produces no observable signal. The peer-detection layer the honor code depended on no longer has anything to detect.

blocks.question: Princeton's 2025 senior survey found what share of students had cheated during their time at the university?
blocks.explanation: 30% — high enough that the peer-reporting equilibrium had already collapsed; the proctoring vote ratified a reality, not a hypothetical.

timeline.heading: THE PEER GROUP
timeline.body: Among elite US universities, true unproctored exams were always rare. Caltech and the US service academies maintain honor codes with broad take-home privileges; UVA's single-sanction code (expulsion for any violation) is the strictest; most of the Ivy League proctors normally.

blocks.label: honor code regimes at selective US universities

timeline.heading: THE DETECTION ARMS RACE
timeline.body: AI-detection tools (Turnitin, GPTZero) report false-positive rates that make them legally unusable for discipline — a single wrongful expulsion invites litigation. Watermarking schemes proposed by OpenAI and Google have not shipped at scale. There is currently no reliable forensic method to prove a given essay was AI-generated, which is why universities are retreating to the one thing that works: watching students take the test in person.

timeline.heading: THE DEEPER SHIFT
timeline.body: The proctoring vote is a small instance of a wider pattern: institutions that ran on trust-based verification — open-book exams, take-home finals, unsupervised remote work — are rebuilding surveillance layers they had spent decades dismantling. The cost is not just supervision but the signal that supervision sends about what students are presumed to be.

timeline.heading: WHAT HIPAA ACTUALLY COVERS
timeline.body: HIPAA, passed in 1996, regulates only 'covered entities' — health plans, healthcare providers who bill electronically, and clearinghouses — plus their business associates. A consumer app that collects medical-looking data but never bills insurance or treats patients sits entirely outside the law.

blocks.text: The acronym is *Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act* — its core purpose was making insurance follow workers between jobs. Privacy was a **secondary** add-on, which is why the scope is tied to billing relationships, not to the sensitivity of the data.

timeline.heading: THE CONSUMER-APP GAP
timeline.body: Fitness trackers, period apps, mental-health chatbots, and symptom loggers collect data more intimate than most doctor visits — and none of it is protected health information under federal law. The FTC's Health Breach Notification Rule fills part of the gap by requiring breach disclosure, but it does not restrict what apps can sell.

timeline.heading: WHY THE IMAGES HAVE A PRICE
timeline.body: AI training is the buyer. A labeled medical-image dataset of 150,000 samples would cost a startup hundreds of thousands of dollars to assemble through clinical partnerships and IRB review. Scraped consumer-app uploads bypass the consent, ethics review, and per-image labeling costs entirely.

timeline.heading: THE EUROPEAN CONTRAST
timeline.body: Under the GDPR, health data is a 'special category' requiring explicit consent for each processing purpose — and sale to a third party would require a fresh consent, not a buried terms-of-service clause. California's CMIA and Washington's My Health My Data Act (2024) are the closest US analogues, but they apply only to residents of those states.

blocks.label: who treats health-app data as 'special category'
blocks.caption: EU/UK: explicit consent per purpose. US: patchwork by state.

timeline.heading: THE BANKRUPTCY LOOPHOLE
timeline.body: Even apps with strong privacy policies often carve out an exception for 'transfer of assets' in a sale or bankruptcy. When 23andMe filed for Chapter 11 in 2025, 15 million users' genetic profiles became assets the court could authorize a buyer to acquire — privacy promises do not survive a corporate death.

blocks.question: Which of these health-adjacent apps falls under HIPAA?
options: A period-tracking app on your phone
blocks.explanation: Only the hospital portal involves a 'covered entity' billing insurance. The other three collect equally sensitive data but operate outside HIPAA's scope.

timeline.heading: WHY COUNTS MATTER
timeline.body: Fishery management depends on stock assessments — population counts that determine quotas. Without them, regulators fly blind: by the time a collapse is visible in catch volumes, the breeding population is usually already too depleted to recover quickly.

blocks.text: The classic case is the **Northern cod** off Newfoundland. Catches looked stable into the late 1980s; the 1992 collapse came suddenly, and the moratorium that followed has lasted *over three decades* with the stock still not fully recovered.

timeline.heading: THE SARGASSUM BLOOM
timeline.body: Since 2011, massive sargassum mats — the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt — have stretched from West Africa to the Caribbean. The bloom is fed by Amazon-basin agricultural runoff and warming Atlantic waters. It rots on beaches, releasing hydrogen sulfide, and chokes harbours and reefs.

blocks.label: the Caribbean sargassum corridor
blocks.caption: the belt reaches from West Africa to the Gulf of Mexico

timeline.heading: THE DOLPHINFISH PARADOX
timeline.body: Adult dolphinfish (mahi-mahi) roam the open ocean, but juveniles shelter under floating debris — including sargassum mats. A bloom that suffocates a harbour can simultaneously concentrate the next generation of a commercial fish into a small, easily overfished area.

timeline.heading: THE SIDS PROBLEM
timeline.body: Small Island Developing States contribute under 1% of global emissions but absorb a disproportionate share of climate damage. Their economies are too small to fund redundant monitoring infrastructure, so a single hurricane can knock out the institutions that generate the data needed to argue for climate finance.

blocks.metric: Hurricane damage as share of GDP, single-event peak

timeline.heading: BERYL'S RECORD
timeline.body: Hurricane Beryl (July 2024) became the earliest Category 5 Atlantic hurricane ever recorded, fueled by ocean temperatures more typical of September. The Atlantic hurricane season runs June to November; storms of that intensity historically arrived after August's peak heat.

blocks.question: What made Hurricane Beryl unprecedented when it formed in 2024?
options: It was the earliest Category 5 Atlantic hurricane on record
It was the strongest hurricane ever measured
It was the first hurricane to hit Barbados directly
It was the longest-lasting Atlantic hurricane
blocks.explanation: Beryl reached Category 5 in early July — weeks before the Atlantic basin historically has the heat to sustain that intensity.

timeline.heading: CITIZEN SCIENCE AS STOPGAP
timeline.body: When state monitoring collapses, the alternative is distributed data collection — students, fishers, divers logging counts under researcher protocols. The data is noisier than agency surveys, but a noisy time series beats no time series when you are arguing for international funding.

timeline.heading: WHY DERIVATIVES DOMINATE
timeline.body: In every mature asset class, derivatives volume eventually dwarfs spot. Futures let traders take leveraged positions, hedge inventory, and short without borrowing the underlying — three things spot markets cannot do efficiently. Crypto's 80/20 derivatives-to-spot ratio is not an anomaly; it is the FX and commodity markets' steady state.

blocks.text: The ratio in **FX is roughly 90/10** derivatives-to-spot; in **oil it is closer to 95/5**. Crypto is simply catching up to how grown-up markets actually trade.

timeline.heading: WHAT A BASKET FUTURE IS
timeline.body: A basket future settles against a weighted index of multiple assets, not one. The buyer gets exposure to the whole basket in a single contract — cheaper than buying seven separate futures, and the index methodology smooths idiosyncratic moves in any one token.

timeline.heading: THE CME MOAT
timeline.body: CME is the only US venue where regulated institutions — pension funds, insurers, bank prop desks — can take crypto exposure without touching an unregulated exchange. Mandates and risk committees forbid Binance or Bybit; CME's CFTC registration is the unlock.

blocks.label: crypto derivatives venues by 2024 volume share

timeline.heading: NOTIONAL VS REAL MONEY
timeline.body: Lifetime notional of $7.3 trillion sounds vast but counts the face value of every contract opened, not capital at risk. A trader with $100k margin can open $2m notional at 20× leverage; the notional figure inflates accordingly. Open interest and margin held are the honest measures.

timeline.heading: THE BITCOIN FUTURES PRECEDENT
timeline.body: CME launched Bitcoin futures in December 2017 — within weeks of the price peak. Many academics later argued the launch itself enabled the crash, because shorting became possible for the first time at institutional scale. Price discovery flows where shorts can express conviction.

timeline.heading: WHY JUNE 8
timeline.body: CFTC self-certification for a new contract takes roughly 30 days from filing. Announcing a launch date a month out is the standard signal that filings are already in. The regulatory caveat in CME's statement is procedural ritual, not genuine uncertainty.

blocks.question: Why do regulated US institutions trade crypto through CME instead of Binance?
options: CME is CFTC-registered, satisfying fiduciary mandates
blocks.explanation: Pension funds and insurers have mandates that forbid trading on unregulated venues — CFTC registration is the gating requirement, not price or leverage.

timeline.heading: THE TACTIC
timeline.body: Forced disappearance is detention without acknowledgment — the state holds a person but denies any record of doing so. The legal vacuum is the point: without an admitted arrest, no lawyer can be appointed, no judge can be petitioned, no family can file a habeas claim. The disappeared exist outside the system that would normally protect them.

blocks.text: International law treats *enforced disappearance* as a distinct crime under the **2006 UN Convention** — separate from torture or detention — precisely because the denial itself is what enables every other abuse.

timeline.heading: THE SCALE UNDER SISI
timeline.body: After the 2013 coup that brought Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to power, the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms began documenting hundreds of disappearances per year. The pattern is consistent: pre-dawn raid by National Security, weeks or months of incommunicado holding at undisclosed sites, then either release, transfer to a recognized prison, or — in some cases — appearance in a state-security court already charged.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL ARCHITECTURE
timeline.body: Egypt's 2015 counter-terrorism law allows National Security to hold detainees for up to 14 days without judicial review, renewable. A separate 'pretrial detention' regime — originally capped at two years — has been stretched through rotating case files: when the clock runs out on one charge, a new case is opened on the same person and the count restarts. Detentions of five-plus years without trial are routine.

timeline.heading: WHY FILMMAKERS
timeline.body: Cultural figures are targeted disproportionately because their work travels. A novelist, screenwriter, or director shapes how Egyptians and the diaspora see the state; silencing them is cheaper than censoring every frame they might produce. The 2016 detention of photojournalist Shawkan, the 2019 arrest of activist-blogger Alaa Abd el-Fattah, and the 2020 case against poet Galal el-Behairy follow the same script as Marei's: home raid, no warrant disclosed, disappearance, then charges manufactured later.

timeline.heading: THE SYNDICATE'S LEVERAGE
timeline.body: Egypt's professional syndicates — for doctors, journalists, lawyers, cinema workers — are a holdover from the Nasser-era corporatist state. They are legally empowered to represent their members before the government, which gives them rare standing to demand information the state would otherwise refuse. The Cinema Professions Syndicate pressing prosecutors is not symbolic; it is one of the few channels through which the disappearance can be forced onto the official record.

blocks.question: What makes Egypt's professional syndicates an unusual channel for human-rights advocacy?
options: They are funded by foreign NGOs
They have legal standing to represent members before the state
They control the courts that try their members
blocks.explanation: Syndicates inherit corporatist-era authority to formally represent their professions to the government — giving them access most civil-society groups lack.

timeline.heading: THE MEDICAL DIMENSION
timeline.body: Denying medication to a detainee with thyroid disease is not incidental — untreated hypothyroidism progresses to cardiac and neurological damage within weeks. Human-rights monitors have documented dozens of deaths in Egyptian custody attributable to withheld treatment, including former president Mohamed Morsi, who collapsed in a courtroom cage in 2019 after years of inadequate diabetes care.

timeline.heading: WHAT A BRIDGE ORACLE DOES
timeline.body: A cross-chain bridge locks tokens on chain A and mints wrapped versions on chain B. The oracle is what tells chain B that the lock on chain A actually happened. If the oracle lies — or is tricked — chain B mints tokens backed by nothing.

blocks.text: The wrapped token is only as trustworthy as the **message** that authorized its mint. Bridges are not really moving assets; they are *vouching* that assets exist elsewhere.

timeline.heading: WHY BRIDGES KEEP GETTING DRAINED
timeline.body: Each blockchain is a self-contained ledger that cannot natively read another. The trust layer that bridges this gap — multisigs, validator sets, oracle networks — is where nearly every major DeFi exploit since 2021 has occurred. The protocol is sound; the seam between protocols is not.

timeline.heading: THE DUOPOLY PROBLEM
timeline.body: Cryptography promised disintermediation; the operational reality has converged on a handful of trusted infrastructure providers. When two of the largest US exchanges route their wrapped-asset flows through the same oracle network, a single compromise — software bug, validator collusion, key theft — touches both at once.

blocks.question: Why is concentrating bridge oracles especially dangerous compared to concentrating, say, custody?
options: Oracle networks can mint new tokens out of thin air if compromised; custodians can only steal what they hold
Oracles handle more transactions per second than custodians
Oracles are unregulated while custodians are regulated
blocks.explanation: A compromised custodian loses its deposits. A compromised mint authority can create unbacked tokens until the market notices — which is why bridge hacks routinely exceed exchange hacks in size.

timeline.heading: THE MINT-VS-STEAL GAP
timeline.body: Minting a billion dollars of wrapped tokens is trivial once you control the oracle — it is just a number in a contract. Extracting real value is harder: liquidity pools are shallow, prices crash on sale, exchanges freeze suspicious wallets. The gap between what attackers mint and what they actually withdraw measures how well DeFi's informal defenses work.

timeline.heading: WHY USERS FLED ANYWAY
timeline.body: $3 billion exited LayerZero after a $292 million loss — roughly ten dollars of trust evaporated for every dollar stolen. Bridge users price tail risk asymmetrically: a protocol that has been exploited once is presumed exploitable again, regardless of the patch. Reputation in cross-chain infrastructure is a one-way ratchet.

timeline.heading: THE COUNTING TRICK
timeline.body: National internet penetration statistics typically count any active SIM with data capability as a connected user. A farmer with a 2G phone that loads a text message once a week is counted the same as a Kathmandu professional on fiber. The headline number flatters governments and misleads donors.

blocks.text: The ITU distinguishes between **subscriptions** and **meaningful connectivity** — the latter requires 4G, regular use, an appropriate device, and enough data. By that stricter measure, most of rural South Asia falls off the map.

timeline.heading: THE LAST-MILE ECONOMICS
timeline.body: Backbone fiber is cheap per kilometer across flat terrain; the cost explodes at the last mile, where each household requires its own connection. In mountainous Nepal, a single village may sit 20km from the nearest tower across terrain that needs helicopters to service, making per-user infrastructure cost 10-50x urban rates.

timeline.heading: THE TERRAIN PROBLEM
timeline.body: Nepal compresses elevations from 60m to 8,848m across roughly 200km north-to-south. Radio signals need line-of-sight; mountains break it. Every ridge requires its own tower, every valley its own backhaul link. Geography that took millions of years to form is the binding constraint on what a telecom can deliver this decade.

timeline.heading: WHY SATELLITE ISN'T THE ANSWER YET
timeline.body: Starlink and similar LEO constellations technically cover Nepal, but the terminal costs hundreds of dollars and monthly fees exceed median rural household income. Regulatory licensing has also stalled — Nepal's telecom authority has not granted Starlink an operating license, partly to protect incumbent operators Nepal Telecom and Ncell from competition.

timeline.heading: THE REMITTANCE PARADOX
timeline.body: Remittances from Nepali workers abroad — Gulf states, Malaysia, India — equal roughly a quarter of GDP, the highest dependency ratio of any large economy. Families need internet to receive money transfers, video-call absent parents, and apply for foreign jobs. The households that most need connectivity are the ones whose breadwinners left precisely because the local economy couldn't sustain them.

timeline.heading: THE DIVIDE COMPOUNDS
timeline.body: Once government services move online — tax filing, scholarship applications, land records, agricultural subsidy programs — being offline means being excluded from the state itself. The digital divide stops being about convenience and becomes a citizenship gap.

blocks.question: What fraction of Nepal's GDP comes from remittances sent home by workers abroad?
blocks.explanation: At roughly 25% of GDP, Nepal has one of the world's highest remittance-dependency ratios — second only to a handful of small states like Tajikistan and Tonga.

timeline.heading: WHAT A PANDA BOND IS
timeline.body: A panda bond is a renminbi-denominated bond issued in mainland China by a foreign entity. The category was created in 2005 to internationalize the yuan by letting non-Chinese borrowers tap onshore Chinese savings directly, rather than routing through Hong Kong's offshore market.

blocks.text: Panda bonds sit *onshore* (CNY, regulated by the PBoC and NAFMII); their offshore cousins are **dim sum bonds** issued in Hong Kong (CNH). The two markets price differently because capital controls keep the onshore and offshore yuan partially segmented.

timeline.heading: WHY PAKISTAN ISSUES IN YUAN
timeline.body: Pakistan's dollar borrowing costs are punitive — recent Eurobonds priced in double digits, reflecting near-default risk. A 2.5% yuan coupon is a fraction of that. Beijing's onshore market lets a friendly sovereign borrow at rates Western capital markets would never extend.

timeline.heading: THE DENOMINATION TRADE
timeline.body: Switching debt from dollars to yuan trades one currency mismatch for another. Pakistan earns most foreign revenue in dollars (remittances, textile exports) and only a sliver in yuan. If the rupee falls against the yuan, debt service still gets more expensive — just on a different axis.

timeline.heading: THE OVERSUBSCRIPTION SIGNAL
timeline.body: A 5× oversubscribed book at 2.5% means Chinese institutional investors — banks, insurers, state funds — are willing to hold Pakistani credit at near-policy-rate yields. This is less a market verdict than a political one: Chinese state capital is being directed into a CPEC partner's paper.

timeline.heading: CPEC AS COLLATERAL
timeline.body: The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, launched in 2015, layered roughly $25 billion of Chinese-financed infrastructure across Pakistan — Gwadar port, power plants, the Karakoram highway upgrade. The panda bond extends this relationship into Pakistan's sovereign funding stack itself, not just project finance.

timeline.heading: YUAN INTERNATIONALIZATION
timeline.body: The yuan accounts for about 4% of global payments and roughly 2-3% of central bank reserves, despite China being the world's second-largest economy. Every panda bond, every yuan-settled oil contract, every swap line is a brick in Beijing's slow campaign to build an alternative to dollar hegemony.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of global central-bank reserves is held in renminbi?
blocks.explanation: Despite a decade of internationalization efforts, the yuan remains a marginal reserve currency — the dollar still holds ~58% and the euro ~20%.

timeline.heading: THE PAPAL TRADITION
timeline.body: Modern popes have condemned arms races since Pius XII denounced atomic weapons in 1948. Paul VI told the UN in 1965 'no more war, war never again,' and John XXIII's 1963 encyclical Pacem in Terris argued the nuclear age made just-war doctrine nearly inoperable. Leo's framing extends a 75-year through-line, not a personal stance.

events.label: Paul VI at UN: 'no more war'

timeline.heading: THE 5% TARGET
timeline.body: NATO's old benchmark was 2% of GDP, set in 2014 after Crimea. The new 5% target — 3.5% core defense plus 1.5% related infrastructure — would more than double allied military budgets. Only the United States and Poland currently approach it; for Germany or Italy, hitting 5% means reallocating sums comparable to their entire health budgets.

timeline.heading: WHAT AUTONOMOUS WEAPONS ACTUALLY ARE
timeline.body: A *lethal autonomous weapon system* — LAWS in the UN jargon — selects and engages targets without human intervention at the firing decision. The distinction that matters is between *human-in-the-loop* (operator approves each strike), *human-on-the-loop* (operator can veto), and *human-out-of-the-loop* (machine fires unilaterally). The third category is what Vatican diplomacy has been pressing to ban since 2014.

blocks.text: The Holy See's term of art is **'killer robots'** — adopted deliberately to bypass the technocratic *LAWS* acronym and make the moral question legible to non-specialists.

timeline.heading: THE GENEVA STALEMATE
timeline.body: Negotiations at the UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva have run since 2014 without binding text. Russia, the United States, India, the UK, and Israel — the states with the most advanced autonomous-weapons programs — have blocked a treaty. The Vatican is one of the most consistent voices for a binding ban; it has no army to constrain.

blocks.question: Which body has been negotiating autonomous-weapons rules — without binding result — since 2014?
options: UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (Geneva)
blocks.explanation: The CCW operates by consensus, so any one major military power can — and has — blocked binding text on autonomous weapons.

timeline.heading: THE ENCYCLICAL AS INSTRUMENT
timeline.body: An encyclical is the highest form of papal teaching short of a dogmatic definition — addressed to the whole Church and binding on Catholic moral conscience. Francis used Laudato Si' (2015) to reframe climate as a moral question; the document shifted episcopal politics in dozens of countries. An encyclical on AI and autonomous war would put 1.4 billion Catholics' bishops on record.

timeline.heading: WHY 'BETRAYAL' IS A LOADED WORD
timeline.body: In Vatican diplomatic vocabulary, *tradimento* — betrayal — is reserved for the abandonment of a process, not a disagreement over policy. By using it for European rearmament, Leo is signalling that he views the diplomatic track on Ukraine as having been deliberately closed, not exhausted. The word travels further in Italian and Spanish ecclesial circles than the English translation conveys.

timeline.heading: THE TWO ARMIES
timeline.body: Sudan's war is between two generals who once partnered to overthrow a civilian government. The SAF under Burhan and the RSF under Hemedti jointly crushed the 2019 democracy movement, then turned their shared military infrastructure against each other when a power-sharing deal collapsed in April 2023.

people.name: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan
people.role: SAF commander, de facto head of state

timeline.heading: THE RSF'S ORIGINS
timeline.body: The RSF evolved from the Janjaweed militias that carried out the Darfur genocide beginning in 2003. Bashir armed Arab militias to fight non-Arab rebels, then formalized them as the Rapid Support Forces in 2013. Hemedti, a former camel trader from Darfur, rose from militia commander to the second most powerful man in Sudan — with troops loyal to him personally, not the state.

blocks.text: Nyala is the capital of **South Darfur** — the same region where the original Janjaweed campaigns were waged two decades ago. The RSF has held the city since late 2023, making it one of the largest population centers under paramilitary, not state, control.

timeline.heading: WHY DRONES, WHY NOW
timeline.body: Sudan's army lost its air superiority advantage when the RSF captured most fixed bases in the west. Turkish Bayraktar TB2 and Akinci drones — bought through opaque channels after international pressure on Ankara — let the SAF strike RSF-held cities without basing aircraft in contested airspace. The RSF in turn flies smaller Iranian and Emirati-supplied drones, turning the war into a long-range exchange over civilian neighborhoods.

timeline.heading: THE 80% NUMBER
timeline.body: When drones cause four-fifths of civilian deaths in a conflict, the war has crossed a threshold artillery and ground fire never reach. Drones can be flown from hundreds of kilometers away by operators with no visual on the target; the rules of distinction that international humanitarian law assumes — a soldier seeing what they shoot at — break down entirely.

timeline.heading: THE FORGOTTEN WAR
timeline.body: By every measure of suffering, Sudan is the world's largest current humanitarian catastrophe — over 13 million displaced, famine declared in multiple regions, an economy contracting by double digits. Western coverage remains a fraction of what Gaza or Ukraine receive, in part because no major power has a direct interest in either side winning, and in part because the foreign sponsors — UAE backing the RSF, Egypt and Iran tilting toward the SAF — would be embarrassed by sustained attention.

blocks.question: Which country is the RSF's primary external arms supplier, according to multiple UN panels of experts?
blocks.explanation: The UAE has been repeatedly identified by UN expert panels as funneling weapons to the RSF via Chad, in exchange for gold from Hemedti's family mining operations in Darfur.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Drone bombardment of cities held by an opposing force is no longer exotic — it is now the default of mid-tier wars. Ethiopia used Bayraktars to break the Tigrayan advance in 2021; Russia and Ukraine fire thousands of one-way drones at each other monthly; Yemen's Houthis strike Saudi and Emirati territory. Sudan is the latest battlefield in a global shift: precision air power, once monopolized by superpowers, now belongs to anyone with $5 million and a Turkish export license.

timeline.heading: WHAT A TITANOSAURIFORM IS
timeline.body: Titanosauriforms are the lineage of long-necked sauropods that includes the largest land animals ever to walk the Earth. They emerged in the Late Jurassic and dominated the Cretaceous, eventually producing 70-tonne giants like Argentinosaurus before vanishing with every other non-avian dinosaur 66 million years ago.

blocks.text: The clade name combines *Titanosauria* with the suffix *-formes* — meaning **"shaped like a titanosaur"** rather than necessarily belonging to the titanosaur crown group. It captures an evolutionary grade, not just a single branch.

timeline.heading: WHY THE LOWER CRETACEOUS MATTERS
timeline.body: Sauropod fossils are abundant from the Late Jurassic and the Late Cretaceous, but the ~40 million years between them — the Lower Cretaceous — is comparatively thin. Each new specimen from this gap helps reconstruct how the giants of the Jurassic gave rise to the titanosaurs that ruled the Late Cretaceous.

timeline.heading: THE KHORAT PLATEAU
timeline.body: Northeastern Thailand sits on a sandstone plateau that was a vast river floodplain during the Cretaceous. The Khok Kruat Formation, deposited around 125 million years ago, has yielded fish, crocodyliforms, theropods, and now a second sauropod — a window into a Southeast Asian ecosystem that was geographically isolated from contemporaneous faunas in China and Australia.

timeline.heading: THE NAGA
timeline.body: In Thai and broader Southeast Asian tradition, the naga is a serpent deity associated with rivers, the Mekong, and protective power. Naming a fossil after local mythology — rather than defaulting to Greek or Latin roots — has become standard practice in modern paleontology, anchoring the specimen to the place and people who hold it.

blocks.text: The genus name pairs *Naga* with the Greek *titan* ("giant") — a hybrid that mirrors how the bones themselves bridge **local geology** and a **globally distributed clade**.

timeline.heading: WHY ONLY TWO IN THIRTY YEARS
timeline.body: Sauropod bones are massive but fragile, and complete skeletons are vanishingly rare anywhere on Earth. Tropical weathering, dense vegetation, and limited excavation funding compound the problem in Southeast Asia — most known specimens are partial vertebrae or limb fragments, and a single new genus can take a decade of preparation and comparative study to publish.

blocks.question: What was the first sauropod described from Thailand, 30 years before Nagatitan?
blocks.explanation: Phuwiangosaurus sirindhornae, named in 1994 after the Phu Wiang area and Princess Sirindhorn, was Thailand's first formally described sauropod.

timeline.heading: THE BOTTLENECK
timeline.body: Hormuz is 33 km wide at its narrowest, but the shipping lanes are just 3 km each — two inbound, two outbound, separated by a 3 km buffer. Roughly 21 million barrels of oil pass through daily, about a fifth of global consumption.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY OF LEVERAGE
timeline.body: The strait sits between Iran and Oman, not Iran and any Arab Gulf state. Iran's coastline runs along the entire northern edge, and the deepest shipping channel hugs the Iranian side — which is why Iranian naval positioning matters disproportionately to anyone else's.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL CLAIM
timeline.body: Under UNCLOS Article 38, ships have a right of transit passage through international straits — coastal states cannot suspend passage or impose conditions. Iran signed UNCLOS in 1982 but never ratified it, and has long argued Hormuz is governed by its own domestic law. A 'Strait Authority' that vets transits is the operational expression of that doctrine.

blocks.text: The distinction matters: *innocent passage* (territorial seas) can be suspended; *transit passage* (international straits) cannot. Iran's framing collapses the two — treating the strait as **territorial water** rather than an international corridor.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988, Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. Oil prices spiked briefly but markets adapted — tankers were reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags and escorted by warships. The lesson planners took then still holds: disruption is easier to threaten than to sustain.

events.label: Limpet mines on Gulf of Oman tankers

timeline.heading: WHY IT CAN'T BE BYPASSED
timeline.body: Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline (5 million bbl/day) and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline together could reroute maybe a third of Gulf exports. Fujairah — where this tanker was anchored — is itself the bypass terminal. Seizing a ship there is a deliberate signal that the workaround isn't a workaround.

blocks.label: Hormuz transit vs bypass capacity (mn bbl/day)

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: Lloyd's of London war-risk premiums — not the seizures themselves — are what actually close a shipping lane. Once premiums spike past a threshold, commercial vessels reroute or refuse charter regardless of how many ships are actually being taken. The financial chokepoint is tighter than the physical one.

blocks.question: What historically closes a shipping lane during a Gulf crisis?
options: The number of ships seized or attacked
A spike in Lloyd's war-risk insurance premiums
A formal UN Security Council resolution
The closure of the strait by the coastal state
blocks.explanation: Insurance markets reprice risk in hours. Once war-risk premiums cross a threshold, charterers refuse the route — the lane closes commercially long before it closes physically.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE H200 ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: The H200 is Nvidia's Hopper-generation accelerator with 141GB of HBM3e memory — the part that matters for training large language models is not raw compute but memory bandwidth, which determines how fast parameters can be shuffled during training.

blocks.text: Nvidia's lineup splits along an export-control fence: the flagship **H100/H200/B200** for unrestricted markets, the cut-down **H20** engineered specifically to fall under the US performance ceiling for China. The H200 sits *above* that ceiling — which is why this license is the news.

timeline.heading: THE OCTOBER 2022 REGIME
timeline.body: The Biden administration's October 2022 export controls were the first time Washington restricted commercial semiconductors on national-security grounds since the Cold War. The rules targeted both compute performance and interconnect bandwidth — the latter because clusters matter more than individual chips for frontier AI.

timeline.heading: WHY 25% REVENUE IS UNPRECEDENTED
timeline.body: Demanding a cut of chip sale revenue as a license condition has no clean precedent in export-control history. It blurs the line between security policy and industrial policy — closer to a tariff or a tribute than a non-proliferation measure, and it gives Beijing a clean propaganda line about extortion.

blocks.question: What is the standard tool the US has historically used to restrict dual-use technology exports?
options: The Export Administration Regulations entity list and license denials
blocks.explanation: The EAR and the Commerce Department's entity list have been the workhorse since the 1979 Export Administration Act — license denials, not revenue shares.

timeline.heading: THE TAMPERING CLAIM
timeline.body: Beijing's concern about hardware tampering is not paranoid posturing. Documented US intelligence operations have intercepted shipments to install implants — the 2014 Snowden disclosures revealed the NSA's TAO unit doing exactly this to Cisco routers bound for foreign customers. Once that precedent exists, every adversary assumes it for every shipment.

blocks.text: The technical term is *interdiction* — diverting a shipment mid-transit to modify hardware before it reaches the buyer. After 2014, Chinese state buyers began requiring **domestic inspection and re-flashing** of imported networking gear; extending that posture to AI accelerators is the logical next step.

timeline.heading: THE DOMESTIC SUBSTITUTE
timeline.body: Huawei's Ascend 910C and the in-development 910D are Beijing's answer. They lag Nvidia on raw performance but ship without strings attached, and SMIC's 7nm process — achieved despite ASML EUV restrictions — has proven the supply chain can function under sanctions. Every month of delayed Nvidia imports widens Huawei's domestic market share.

blocks.label: frontier AI accelerators, rough training-relevant specs

timeline.heading: THE HYPERSCALER STACK
timeline.body: The ten licensed buyers are not a random list — they are the firms whose training clusters define Chinese AI capacity. ByteDance trains Doubao on the largest known Chinese cluster; Alibaba's Qwen models are the open-weight benchmark leaders out of China; Tencent, Baidu, and the others backstop the rest of the application layer.

timeline.heading: THE LEVERAGE QUESTION
timeline.body: Export controls work only if the target cannot substitute. If Beijing can credibly threaten to never buy — and accelerate Huawei in the gap — Washington loses the leverage the licenses were meant to monetize. The standoff is a test of whether the 2022 regime has already aged out of usefulness.

timeline.heading: THE PARALLEL ECONOMY
timeline.body: Egypt's armed forces run a sprawling commercial empire: cement plants, pasta factories, gas stations, bottled water, steel, household appliances, even resort hotels. Estimates of its share of GDP range from 2% to over 40% — nobody knows because military firms are exempt from public audit, taxation, and customs duties.

blocks.text: The military's commercial arm operates through holdings like the **National Service Projects Organization (NSPO)** and the **Arab Organization for Industrialization (AOI)** — entities created under Nasser for defense self-sufficiency that quietly expanded into civilian markets.

timeline.heading: WHY THE IMF CARES
timeline.body: Military firms compete with private companies while paying no tax, using conscript labor, and accessing state land for free. The IMF treats this as a structural distortion — private investment cannot price-compete with a tax-exempt rival that wears a uniform. Removing the distortion is a condition of the loan, not a side request.

timeline.heading: THE LOAN AT STAKE
timeline.body: The current $8 billion Extended Fund Facility, signed in March 2024, was Egypt's fourth IMF programme since 2016. Each prior programme attached privatization milestones; each saw them slip. The Fund's reviews release tranches only when targets are met — which is why a stalled sell-off is not a paperwork problem but a payment trigger.

timeline.heading: THE LAND PROBLEM
timeline.body: Many military-owned companies sit on land the army acquired by decree, never registered to a civilian-style title. A buyer cannot list shares on the EGX without clean title; the army cannot produce clean title without subordinating itself to civilian land courts. The stall is legal, but the resistance is institutional.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: When Sisi took power in 2013, the military's economic role expanded sharply — mega-projects (the new capital, Suez Canal extension, road network) routed through army contractors rather than open tender. Reversing that requires the institution that funds the regime's stability to surrender the assets that fund its autonomy.

timeline.heading: THE FISCAL CLIFF
timeline.body: Egypt's external debt exceeds $160 billion. Servicing it consumes roughly half of state revenue. Without the IMF tranche, Cairo faces a choice between dollar shortages (which froze imports in 2022–23) and a fresh devaluation — the pound has already lost two-thirds of its value against the dollar since 2022.

blocks.question: Why are Egyptian military-owned firms a particular problem for private investors?
options: They pay no tax, use conscript labor, and access state land for free
They are required to hire only Egyptian citizens
They must price their goods below cost
blocks.explanation: Military firms operate outside the tax, customs, and labor regimes that bind private competitors — a structural subsidy the IMF treats as a market distortion.

timeline.heading: THE TRUST MODEL
timeline.body: npm has no gatekeeper. Anyone can publish a package; anyone can publish an update. A project pulling in one direct dependency typically inherits hundreds of transitive ones, each maintained by a stranger with publish rights to your build.

blocks.text: A modern React app routinely ships with **1,000+ transitive dependencies**. The user audited *one* — `react` — and inherited the security posture of everyone else.

timeline.heading: THE EVENT-STREAM PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In 2018, a maintainer of the popular event-stream package handed control to a volunteer who'd offered help. Months later, the new owner shipped code that stole Bitcoin wallet keys from a specific downstream app. The package had ~2 million weekly downloads. Nobody noticed for weeks.

timeline.heading: WHY AI VENDORS ARE THE TARGET
timeline.body: AI tooling pulls fresh dependencies aggressively — new SDKs, new model clients, new agent frameworks publish weekly. Developers update without reading diffs. The attack surface is wider and the review cadence is slower than mature ecosystems.

timeline.heading: TYPOSQUATTING VS HIJACK
timeline.body: Two attack shapes dominate. Typosquatting publishes a malicious package with a near-identical name (`reqeusts` for `requests`) and waits for typos. Hijack compromises an existing trusted package via stolen credentials or social engineering — far rarer, far more dangerous.

blocks.question: Which npm attack vector affects the most downstream users when successful?
options: Hijacking the publish credentials of an existing trusted maintainer
Publishing a new malicious package and promoting it
blocks.explanation: Hijacks inherit the victim package's existing install base — millions of automatic updates ship the payload before anyone reviews the diff.

timeline.heading: THE POSTINSTALL HOOK
timeline.body: npm packages can run arbitrary code at install time via the postinstall script. This is how most supply-chain payloads execute — not when you import the package, but the moment you run `npm install`. CI runners, developer laptops, and production build servers all execute it with full user privileges.

timeline.heading: WHY MACOS SPECIFICALLY
timeline.body: Developer machines are high-value targets — they hold SSH keys, cloud credentials, signing certificates, and source code for downstream products. macOS dominates the developer laptop market in San Francisco tech. A payload that profiles `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, and browser keychains on macOS hits the richest credential trove per compromised machine.

timeline.heading: THE ORIGIN
timeline.body: USAID was created by John F. Kennedy in 1961, consolidating Marshall Plan-era aid programs into one civilian agency. Its founding logic was Cold War: development assistance as a counter to Soviet influence in newly decolonized states. Conflict prevention was always a stated co-benefit of the spending, not just a humanitarian one.

blocks.text: The 1961 Foreign Assistance Act explicitly framed aid as serving *both* humanitarian and **national security** ends — a doctrine every administration kept until 2025.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'HIGH-AID REGIONS' MEANS
timeline.body: USAID spending in Africa concentrated in a handful of fragile states — South Sudan, Somalia, DRC, Ethiopia, Sudan. These places host the agency's largest food security, health, and stabilization programs, often running parallel to or substituting for state services in areas the central government cannot reach.

blocks.label: USAID's largest African footprints
blocks.caption: concentrations in fragile and conflict-affected states

timeline.heading: THE CAUSAL CHANNELS
timeline.body: Aid suppresses conflict through several documented mechanisms: food assistance reduces the recruitment pool for armed groups, health programs preserve state legitimacy in remote areas, and cash transfers raise the opportunity cost of joining an insurgency. Removing the inputs reverses each channel within months, not years.

timeline.heading: THE BUDGETARY SCALE
timeline.body: Despite its political prominence, USAID's full budget was roughly $40 billion — under 1% of US federal spending and a rounding error against the Pentagon's $850 billion. The savings from abolition are small; the geopolitical and humanitarian footprint removed is not.

blocks.label: USAID vs other federal lines, FY24 ($bn)

timeline.heading: THE PEPFAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The largest single USAID-administered program is PEPFAR — the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief — launched by George W. Bush in 2003. It is credited with averting roughly 25 million deaths in sub-Saharan Africa. Antiretroviral interruption causes viral rebound within weeks, which is why mortality projections from 2025 cuts compound so quickly.

timeline.heading: THE COUNTERFACTUAL QUESTION
timeline.body: The 6.5% increase is a causal estimate, not a correlation — researchers use the abrupt January 2025 stop-work order as a natural experiment, comparing high-exposure districts to low-exposure ones in the same country. The design isolates the aid shock from broader trends like climate stress or commodity prices.

blocks.question: Why does an abrupt aid cutoff yield a cleaner causal estimate than a gradual one?
options: Abrupt cutoffs are easier to fund as a study
It creates a sharp before/after break uncorrelated with local conditions
blocks.explanation: A sudden, externally imposed stop creates a natural experiment: the timing isn't driven by local violence or politics, so post-cut changes can be attributed to the cut itself.

timeline.heading: THE THREE ALLELES
timeline.body: APOE comes in three flavors — ε2, ε3, ε4 — differing by just two amino acids. ε3 is the common variant (~78% of alleles). ε4 roughly triples Alzheimer's risk per copy; ε2 roughly halves it. One gene, three lifetimes of brain aging.

blocks.label: APOE allele frequency and Alzheimer's risk

timeline.heading: WHAT THE PROTEIN DOES
timeline.body: Apolipoprotein E is the brain's primary lipid shuttle. It packages cholesterol and phospholipids into particles that neurons need to build and repair membranes and synapses. Brain cells cannot import cholesterol from the bloodstream — the blood-brain barrier blocks it — so APOE is the local courier.

timeline.heading: THE AMYLOID HYPOTHESIS
timeline.body: For three decades the dominant theory has been that amyloid-beta plaques drive Alzheimer's. Anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) do clear plaques but produce only modest clinical benefit. The field is increasingly asking what upstream of amyloid actually matters — which is the gap proteomic studies like this one are trying to fill.

blocks.text: The shift from **amyloid-as-cause** to **amyloid-as-symptom** is the most consequential reframing in dementia research since the hypothesis was proposed in 1992.

timeline.heading: WHY PROTEOMICS
timeline.body: Genomics tells you risk; proteomics tells you mechanism. A genome is fixed at conception, but the proteins it expresses shift across tissues, ages, and environments. Reading 7,000+ plasma proteins in thousands of people lets researchers find which molecules actually move between healthy and diseased states — the layer where drugs can intervene.

timeline.heading: THE EARLY-ADULTHOOD CLUE
timeline.body: If ε2's protective proteins appear decades before any dementia onset, the protective mechanism is not a late-life response to damage — it is a lifelong shift in brain maintenance. The therapeutic implication is uncomfortable: meaningful prevention may need to start in the third decade of life, not the seventh.

blocks.question: When do the protective protein signatures of APOE ε2 carriers first appear?
options: Around age 65, near typical Alzheimer's onset
In early adulthood, decades before any symptoms
Only after diagnosis, as a compensatory response
blocks.explanation: The study found upregulation of UNG, VPS29, and BIRC2 in early adulthood — meaning ε2's protection is a lifelong baseline, not a late-life rescue.

timeline.heading: THE MEDIATION FRACTION
timeline.body: 54 of 192 proteins statistically mediate ε2's effect on Alzheimer's risk. Mediation analysis asks: if we held this protein constant, would the genetic effect disappear? A 28% mediation share means most of ε2's benefit flows through measurable, potentially druggable intermediaries rather than through unreachable genetic destiny.

timeline.heading: WHO THE TTP IS
timeline.body: The Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan formed in 2007 as an umbrella for Pashtun militant factions in the tribal belt. It is organizationally distinct from the Afghan Taliban but shares ideology, sanctuary, and personnel across the border.

blocks.text: Islamabad's current state line is *fitna al-Khawarij* — "the sedition of the Kharijites" — a deliberate theological framing that denies the TTP any claim to Islamic legitimacy by invoking the earliest sect classical scholars condemned as extremist.

timeline.heading: THE DURAND LINE
timeline.body: The 2,640 km border between Pakistan and Afghanistan was drawn by British diplomat Mortimer Durand in 1893, cutting through Pashtun tribal lands. No Afghan government — monarchy, communist, mujahideen, or Taliban — has ever recognized it. Militants treat it as a line on a map, not a border.

timeline.heading: THE SANCTUARY PROBLEM
timeline.body: After the 2021 Taliban takeover of Kabul, Pakistan expected its long-standing patronage of the Afghan Taliban to translate into pressure on the TTP. Instead, the Afghan Taliban released TTP prisoners and refused to expel its leadership. The strategic depth Pakistan cultivated for forty years now points back at it.

timeline.heading: THE FATA MERGER
timeline.body: In 2018 Pakistan merged the Federally Administered Tribal Areas — governed since 1901 under the colonial Frontier Crimes Regulation — into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. The merger ended a century of legal exception but left the security vacuum it created unfilled. Bajaur is one of the seven former agencies absorbed in that reform.

timeline.heading: THE ESCALATING ARC
timeline.body: Militant violence in Pakistan collapsed after the 2014 Zarb-e-Azb operation cleared North Waziristan. It bottomed out around 2019 and has climbed steadily since the Afghan Taliban's return. The current cycle is not a flare-up — it is the reversal of a decade of counterinsurgency gains.

timeline.heading: WHY KP BEARS THE WEIGHT
timeline.body: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa hosts the border, the Pashtun population, and the bulk of Afghan refugees. Provincial police are out-armed by militants who carry weapons left behind by NATO. Federal reinforcements are tied up on the eastern border with India — the structural reason no surge has been announced.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE READER SHOULD REMEMBER
timeline.body: The TTP is not Al-Qaeda, not ISIS-K, and not the Afghan Taliban — though it overlaps with all three. It is a domestic Pakistani insurgency whose center of gravity sits on the Afghan side of a border the Afghan state refuses to recognize.

blocks.question: What is the Durand Line?
options: A ceasefire line drawn after the 1971 war
A pipeline route through the tribal belt
blocks.explanation: Drawn by Mortimer Durand in 1893, the line cut through Pashtun tribal territory and has never been recognized by any Afghan government.

timeline.heading: THE DUAL-USE PROBLEM
timeline.body: Routers, switches, and servers are inherently dual-use: the same hardware that runs a hospital network can run a targeting cell. Export controls focus on weapons and chips; general-purpose IT gear flows on commercial terms even when the end user is a military command.

blocks.text: The technical term is **dual-use**: items with civilian utility that also enable military capability. The **Wassenaar Arrangement** covers some categories but exempts most commercial networking hardware.

timeline.heading: THE KILL CHAIN
timeline.body: Modern air operations run on what doctrine calls F2T2EA — find, fix, track, target, engage, assess. Each stage is a data pipeline: sensor feeds, geolocation, identification, weapon assignment, strike, battle damage. Collapsing the cycle from hours to minutes is the entire point of networked warfare.

timeline.heading: WHO BUILDS THE BACKBONE
timeline.body: A handful of Western firms supply the global networking stack used by militaries — Cisco, Juniper, HPE/Aruba, Palo Alto, plus Israeli and increasingly Chinese alternatives. Switching costs are immense: a military that standardizes on one vendor's certificates, training, and management software is locked in for a decade or more.

timeline.heading: THE NUREMBERG PRINCIPLE
timeline.body: International law since 1947 holds that industrialists can be criminally liable when their products knowingly enable atrocities. IG Farben executives were convicted for supplying Zyklon B; bankers were convicted for financing slave labor. The doctrine survives in the Rome Statute's aiding-and-abetting provisions for genocide and war crimes.

timeline.heading: THE ICJ FINDING
timeline.body: In January 2024 the International Court of Justice ruled it plausible that Israel's conduct in Gaza violates the Genocide Convention. The ruling triggered legal obligations for third states under Article 1 of the Convention — including duties on companies operating under their jurisdiction — to prevent acts that could contribute to genocide.

blocks.question: What did the ICJ rule in its January 2024 provisional measures order on South Africa v. Israel?
options: That it was plausible Israel's conduct violated the Genocide Convention
That South Africa lacked standing to bring the case
That Hamas had committed genocide on October 7
blocks.explanation: The provisional measures order did not make a final genocide finding — it found the claims plausible enough to impose binding interim obligations on Israel.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Tech-sector complicity claims are not new. IBM's German subsidiary supplied Hollerith punch-card machines that catalogued Holocaust victims; the company settled a survivor lawsuit in 2001 without admitting liability. Cisco itself faced a US lawsuit alleging its 'Golden Shield' technology helped China persecute Falun Gong practitioners — dismissed on jurisdictional grounds, not on the merits.

timeline.heading: WHY THE DRC KEEPS GETTING EBOLA
timeline.body: Ebola's natural reservoir is fruit bats in Central African rainforests. The DRC sits at the geographic center of that reservoir — every outbreak begins with a spillover event when a hunter, forager, or villager handles infected bushmeat. The country has had 17 outbreaks since 1976 because the virus lives there, not because it travels there.

blocks.label: the Ebola reservoir belt
blocks.caption: every named outbreak has started inside this forest zone

timeline.heading: THE NAME COMES FROM A RIVER
timeline.body: The 1976 index outbreak struck the village of Yambuku in northern Zaire. Researchers named the virus after the nearby *Ebola River* — a tributary of the Congo — to avoid stigmatizing the village itself. The naming convention was deliberate; it set the template for how WHO labels new pathogens to this day.

blocks.text: The 1976 mortality rate was **88%** — 280 dead of 318 infected. Modern outbreaks with rVSV-ZEBOV vaccination and supportive care run closer to **40-50%**.

timeline.heading: THE R0 PARADOX
timeline.body: Ebola's basic reproduction number is roughly 1.5-2.5 — lower than measles (15+), lower than COVID (3-5), even lower than seasonal flu. It spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids, not aerosols. Outbreaks burn out when contact-tracing isolates cases faster than they transmit — which is exactly what conflict zones make impossible.

timeline.heading: WHY ITURI IS HARDER THAN OTHER PROVINCES
timeline.body: Ituri has hosted active armed groups — CODECO, ADF, M23 spillovers — since the late 1990s. Vaccinators and contact tracers cannot enter villages controlled by militias. The 2018-2020 Ebola response in neighboring North Kivu saw health workers murdered on multiple occasions, including a WHO epidemiologist killed in Butembo in 2019. Conflict turns a containable virus into an endemic one.

timeline.heading: THE VACCINE THAT EXISTS
timeline.body: rVSV-ZEBOV (brand name Ervebo) was approved by the FDA in 2019 — the first licensed Ebola vaccine in history. It uses a ring-vaccination strategy: when a case is confirmed, every contact and every contact-of-contact is vaccinated, building an immunological firewall. The strategy worked in West Africa in 2014-16 and again in Equateur Province in 2020. It requires knowing who the contacts are.

blocks.question: What does "ring vaccination" mean in an Ebola response?
options: Vaccinate everyone in the affected country
Vaccinate the case's contacts and their contacts
Vaccinate in concentric geographic rings around the index village
blocks.explanation: Ring vaccination targets the social network around a confirmed case — the people most likely to be exposed — rather than geography or whole populations. It only works if contact tracing functions.

timeline.heading: THE CROSS-BORDER WORRY
timeline.body: South Sudan shares a 600 km porous border with northeastern DRC. Cross-border trade, pastoralist movement, and refugee flows from both directions mean an outbreak in Ituri can become an outbreak in Juba's catchment within weeks. The 2000 Gulu outbreak in Uganda — 425 cases, 224 deaths — began with cross-border movement from southern Sudan.

timeline.heading: WHY A WON STABLECOIN NOW
timeline.body: South Korea's crypto market trades enormous volumes but settles almost entirely in USD-pegged stablecoins like USDT and USDC. Every won-to-crypto trade routes through a dollar intermediary, exporting fees and float to American issuers. A won stablecoin keeps that flow domestic.

blocks.text: The structural pull is the same one driving **euro**, **yen**, and **dirham** stablecoin projects: the dollar's grip on on-chain settlement is a *monetary sovereignty* issue, not just a fintech one.

timeline.heading: THE KIMCHI PREMIUM
timeline.body: Korean crypto prices regularly trade 2-10% above global benchmarks — the so-called kimchi premium. Capital controls on outbound won transfers prevent arbitrageurs from closing the gap. Domestic exchanges like Upbit became closed pools where Korean demand sets its own price.

blocks.label: South Korea crypto exchange market share

timeline.heading: WHY BANKS WERE LOCKED OUT
timeline.body: Since 2017, South Korea required crypto exchanges to partner with a single bank for real-name verified accounts — but banks were forbidden from owning exchanges or issuing crypto products themselves. The wall is now cracking: the Lee Jae-myung government signaled in 2025 that banks could issue won stablecoins under a new framework.

blocks.question: What was required for South Koreans to legally trade crypto on a domestic exchange after 2017?
options: A real-name bank account at the exchange's partner bank
Approval from the Financial Services Commission
blocks.explanation: The real-name account rule tied every trader to one verified bank relationship — designed to block anonymous flows and tax evasion.

timeline.heading: HOW STABLECOINS ACTUALLY WORK
timeline.body: A stablecoin issuer holds reserve assets — typically short-term government bills and bank deposits — and mints one token per unit deposited. The token tracks the peg not by algorithm but by the verifiable promise that the reserve is there. Hana Bank's balance sheet would back the won token directly.

blocks.text: This is why a *bank-issued* stablecoin is structurally different from Tether or USDC: the reserve and the issuer are the same regulated entity, eliminating the **custody risk** that has haunted private stablecoin issuers.

timeline.heading: TOKENIZED SECURITIES
timeline.body: The deal also targets tokenized securities — stocks, bonds, and funds represented as blockchain tokens that settle in seconds rather than the T+2 standard. Korea's Financial Services Commission approved a tokenized securities framework in 2023; major banks have been waiting for infrastructure partners with crypto exchange experience.

blocks.label: East Asian tokenized securities hubs
blocks.caption: Each jurisdiction is racing to set the regional standard before Hong Kong or Singapore lock it in.

timeline.heading: THE IMPORT DEPENDENCE
timeline.body: India imports roughly 85% of its crude oil, the highest dependence of any major economy. There is no domestic cushion — every dollar move in Brent flows through to the pump within weeks.

timeline.heading: THE HORMUZ ROUTE
timeline.body: The majority of India's crude comes from Gulf suppliers — Iraq, Saudi Arabia, UAE — and transits the Strait of Hormuz. Russia became the largest single supplier after 2022, but those barrels arrive via the Suez-Bab el-Mandeb route, which has its own chokepoint risks.

timeline.heading: WHY FUEL IS THE PERFECT TAX
timeline.body: Fuel demand is inelastic — people buy roughly the same amount regardless of price. Governments worldwide exploit this: fuel taxes are cheap to collect (a handful of refineries vs. millions of income earners) and nearly impossible to evade. India's fuel excise generated ₹3.2 trillion in FY2024, roughly 12% of central tax revenue.

timeline.heading: THE HIDDEN STRUCTURE
timeline.body: India deliberately kept petrol and diesel outside the GST (goods and services tax) system. This lets the centre and states stack taxes independently — central excise plus state VAT. At peak in 2020, taxes comprised 65% of petrol's retail price. No other major economy taxes fuel this aggressively relative to base cost.

blocks.text: The split matters politically: when prices rise, the **centre** can blame **states** for VAT, and states can blame the centre for excise. Neither side has to cut.

timeline.heading: THE PASS-THROUGH MECHANISM
timeline.body: State-owned oil marketing companies (Indian Oil, BPCL, HPCL) set retail prices daily based on a 15-day rolling average of import costs plus the rupee-dollar rate. When the rupee weakens against the dollar while crude rises, the squeeze compounds — both sides of the import bill move against the consumer.

timeline.heading: THE 1973 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The first OPEC oil shock quadrupled crude prices and pushed India's import bill from 10% to 40% of export earnings within a year. Indira Gandhi's government responded with petrol rationing, Sunday driving bans, and the nationalization of foreign oil companies — the foundation of today's state-owned OMC system.

blocks.question: What share of India's crude oil consumption is met by imports?
blocks.explanation: India imports ~85% of its crude — among the highest dependence of any major economy, leaving the pump fully exposed to global price moves.

timeline.heading: WHY MINERS PIVOT
timeline.body: Bitcoin miners and AI data centers want the same scarce resource: cheap, abundant electricity at sites with grid connections and cooling. A miner that already owns 500MW of energized capacity can rip out ASICs and rack GPUs faster than a hyperscaler can permit a greenfield campus.

blocks.text: The industry term is *behind-the-meter* power — capacity contracted directly with a generator, bypassing retail tariffs. It's the moat miners actually built, not the **hashrate**.

timeline.heading: THE HALVING SQUEEZE
timeline.body: Bitcoin's block reward halves every four years by protocol design. The April 2024 halving cut miner revenue per block from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC overnight. Unless price doubles to compensate, marginal miners are forced to find another use for their power contracts — or shut down.

timeline.heading: THE CONVERTIBLE NOTE TRICK
timeline.body: A 1% coupon is roughly a third of the Treasury yield — lenders accept it because the note converts to equity if the stock rises past a strike price (here, a 32.5% premium). The issuer gets near-free cash now; existing shareholders eat the dilution if the bet works.

blocks.label: financing cost: convertible vs straight debt

timeline.heading: THE GPU SCARCITY ECONOMY
timeline.body: Nvidia's H100 and successor Blackwell chips are allocated, not sold — the company decides who gets capacity. A multi-billion-dollar Dell purchase plus a direct Nvidia cloud agreement is less a transaction than a place in the queue.

blocks.text: The bottleneck has moved up the stack: from **silicon** (TSMC fab capacity), to **packaging** (CoWoS advanced packaging at TSMC), to **memory** (HBM3e from SK Hynix). Any one of these gates the others.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Core Scientific, Hut 8, TeraWulf, and Applied Digital have all signed AI hosting deals since 2024. Core Scientific signed a $3.5B+ contract with CoreWeave. The pattern is consistent: the value of a miner is now its power contract, not its mining rig.

blocks.question: What asset class do former Bitcoin miners actually compete in once they pivot to AI hosting?
options: Power developers and data center operators
blocks.explanation: The pivot is enabled by energized power capacity and grid interconnects — the same business as traditional colocation operators, not software clouds.

timeline.heading: THE WITHDRAWAL THAT DIDN'T WORK
timeline.body: Duterte withdrew the Philippines from the ICC's Rome Statute in March 2019, effective a year later. The court's jurisdiction nonetheless covers crimes committed while the state was a member — roughly 2011 through March 2019. Withdrawal stops future jurisdiction; it does not erase the past.

blocks.text: The principle is called ***ratione temporis*** — jurisdiction by time. A state cannot retroactively un-consent to crimes already prosecutable while it was a party.

timeline.heading: THE OPERATION
timeline.body: Dela Rosa, as national police chief from 2016, ran Oplan Tokhang — the door-to-door visitation campaign that police records logged as roughly 6,200 killings and human-rights monitors estimated at 20,000–30,000 once vigilante deaths are counted. The gap between the two numbers is the prosecution's case.

timeline.heading: WHY THE COURT MOVED NOW
timeline.body: The ICC operates on complementarity — it only acts when domestic courts are unwilling or unable to prosecute. After years of Philippine inaction, the Pre-Trial Chamber ruled in 2023 that the investigation could proceed because no genuine domestic process existed.

timeline.heading: THE MARCOS PIVOT
timeline.body: Marcos Jr. won the 2022 presidency in alliance with Sara Duterte as VP. That alliance shattered by 2024 over impeachment moves and budget fights. Cooperating with the ICC against Duterte allies is now political subtraction of a rival faction, not just a legal obligation.

timeline.heading: THE WARRANT MECHANIC
timeline.body: ICC warrants have no police force behind them — the court depends on member-state cooperation under Article 89. Once Manila confirms service, the warrant becomes enforceable Philippine process. Flight to a non-cooperating state is the usual escape route; flight inside a cooperating one is just hiding.

blocks.question: How does the ICC actually arrest someone?
options: ICC marshals fly in and detain the suspect
Interpol issues a binding red notice
The host state's own police execute the warrant
UN peacekeepers carry out the arrest
blocks.explanation: The ICC has no police. Every arrest depends on a member state choosing to execute the warrant with its own forces — which is why state cooperation is the whole game.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Duterte was transferred to The Hague in March 2025 — the first former Asian head of state in ICC custody. The dela Rosa warrant signals the court is pursuing the chain of command, not stopping at the principal.

2026-05-15-philippines-icc-warrant-dela-.label: The ICC & the Duterte Drug War

timeline.heading: THE GENEVA FRAMEWORK
timeline.body: The Third Geneva Convention (1949) requires belligerents to repatriate prisoners of war without delay after active hostilities cease. In practice, swaps happen mid-war by mutual agreement — the Convention sets the floor, not the timing.

blocks.text: The legal term is **repatriation**; what Russia and Ukraine do mid-war is technically an *exchange* — soldiers return while the war continues, outside the Convention's post-hostilities trigger.

timeline.heading: WHY THE GULF BROKERS
timeline.body: The UAE has mediated more than 15 Russia-Ukraine prisoner exchanges since 2024, more than any other state. Abu Dhabi maintains working channels with both Moscow and Kyiv, hosts Russian capital that fled Western sanctions, and trades the role for diplomatic prestige unavailable through traditional Western alignment.

timeline.heading: THE NUMBERS GAME
timeline.body: Russia holds an estimated 8,000+ Ukrainian POWs; Ukraine holds roughly 5,000-6,000 Russians. The asymmetry matters: Kyiv has at times exchanged on a 1-for-1 basis using civilian detainees and convicted collaborators to close the gap.

blocks.question: What did Ukraine famously offer in the September 2022 Azovstal commanders exchange?
options: Viktor Medvedchuk, a pro-Russian Ukrainian politician
blocks.explanation: Kyiv handed over Medvedchuk — Putin's goddaughter's father and a former MP — in exchange for 215 Ukrainian fighters, including Azovstal commanders.

timeline.heading: THE TARGETING PATTERN
timeline.body: Russian strikes on Kyiv have followed a recurring rhythm: paired with diplomatic events, prisoner exchanges, or Western aid announcements. Military analysts read this as deliberate signaling — the message that humanitarian gestures do not pause the war.

timeline.heading: THE LONG ARC
timeline.body: Mid-war prisoner exchanges are older than the Geneva system. The American and Confederate armies ran the Dix-Hill Cartel during the Civil War; the Iran-Iraq war's final repatriations dragged on until 2003, fifteen years after the ceasefire.

2026-05-15-russia-ukraine-1000-pow-swap-.label: POW Swaps & the Laws of War

timeline.heading: THE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil moves through the Strait of Hormuz, a 33 km channel between Iran and Oman. The shipping lanes hug the Iranian side, where the water is deepest — which is why Iranian naval positioning matters disproportionately to global energy markets.

timeline.heading: WHY BYPASSES EXIST
timeline.body: After the 1980s Tanker War, Gulf producers learned that a single naval incident could close the strait for weeks. Saudi Arabia built the East-West Pipeline across the peninsula to the Red Sea. The UAE built Habshan-Fujairah to the Gulf of Oman. Both routes share one purpose: deliver oil to a tanker that never enters Hormuz.

timeline.heading: THE CAPACITY MATH
timeline.body: Gulf producers export roughly 17 million barrels per day through Hormuz. Existing bypass routes — the Saudi East-West line and Habshan-Fujairah — can divert about 7 million barrels per day combined. Most of the flow has no alternative, which is why a second UAE pipeline matters out of proportion to its volume.

timeline.heading: THE FUJAIRAH ADVANTAGE
timeline.body: Fujairah sits on the Gulf of Oman, outside Hormuz. It is also the world's second-largest bunkering port after Singapore, with storage capacity exceeding 14 million cubic meters. Oil arrives by pipeline, gets blended and stored, then leaves on tankers bound for Asia without ever entering Iranian-patrolled waters.

blocks.text: Fujairah is one of seven UAE emirates, but the only one with a coastline on the **Gulf of Oman** rather than the Persian Gulf — geography that turned a fishing port into a *strategic redundancy* for the entire federation.

timeline.heading: WHAT INSURANCE DECIDES
timeline.body: Lloyd's of London war-risk premiums — not naval incidents themselves — are what actually close a shipping lane. Once premiums spike past a few percent of cargo value, commercial fleets reroute regardless of how many mines or missiles remain. A pipeline that lands oil at Fujairah lets cargoes load under peacetime premiums even when Hormuz is at war risk.

blocks.question: Which is the largest existing Hormuz bypass route by capacity?
blocks.explanation: The Saudi East-West Pipeline can move about 5 million barrels per day across the peninsula to the Red Sea — the largest single bypass of Hormuz in operation.

timeline.heading: THE MISDIAGNOSIS
timeline.body: Age is a proxy, not a mechanism. The documented harms — sleep loss, comparison spirals, compulsive use — trace to the recommendation engine's optimization for engagement, not to a user's birth year. A 14-year-old and a 40-year-old fed the same algorithmic loop exhibit similar behavioral patterns.

blocks.text: The internal Meta research disclosed by Frances Haugen in 2021 found Instagram made body-image issues worse for *one in three* teen girls — and the cited mechanism was **social comparison amplified by ranking**, not exposure to age-restricted content.

timeline.heading: WHY THE ID MANDATE IS THE POINT
timeline.body: To verify minors, platforms must verify everyone — adults cannot be presumed adult without proof. Every user uploads a passport, driver's license, or biometric scan. The age ban is, in implementation, a universal identity-verification regime sold under a child-safety frame.

timeline.heading: THE COUNTRIES MOVING FIRST
timeline.body: Three jurisdictions have legislated under-16 bans with platform-side enforcement: Australia (passed late 2024, effective 2025), Norway (announced 2024), and Indonesia (drafted 2025). None has paired the ban with rules on how recommendation algorithms rank content for the users who remain.

blocks.label: first movers on platform-enforced age bans

timeline.heading: THE EU PATH NOT TAKEN
timeline.body: The Digital Services Act, in force since 2024, requires very large platforms to assess systemic risks from their recommender systems and offer users a non-profiling feed option. It is the only major regulation that targets the algorithm itself rather than the audience — and the only one industry lobbied hardest against.

timeline.heading: THE COPPA PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The US Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (1998) restricted data collection on under-13s. Platforms responded not by building safer products for children but by setting their minimum age at 13 and looking away. Age gates produce age lies; they do not produce safety.

blocks.question: What did COPPA's under-13 rule actually change about how platforms treat young users?
options: Platforms built dedicated, safer experiences for under-13s
Platforms set a minimum age of 13 and stopped checking
Platforms verified age with government ID
Platforms banned under-13s and enforced it via biometrics
blocks.explanation: COPPA made under-13 data collection legally costly, so platforms set a 13+ minimum and accepted self-declared ages — the harm moved underground rather than away.

timeline.heading: THE LEVER NOBODY PULLS
timeline.body: Three algorithmic changes have shown measurable harm reduction in internal experiments: chronological feeds, friction on infinite scroll, and downranking of engagement-bait. None requires knowing a user's age. None has been mandated by any national law.

timeline.heading: THE LAW
timeline.body: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Economist Charles Goodhart observed this in 1975 watching the Bank of England target money supply aggregates — the moment policymakers picked one, banks restructured around it and the aggregate stopped tracking what it used to track.

blocks.text: The sharper restatement comes from anthropologist Marilyn Strathern: *any measure used for control is unreliable*. The gaming is not a bug in human nature — it is the predictable response to being measured.

timeline.heading: THE SOVIET PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Soviet nail factories famously gamed output quotas: when measured by weight, they produced a few enormous nails; when measured by count, millions of tiny useless ones. The lesson is that workers optimize the proxy, not the underlying goal — and the proxy always diverges.
