blocks.explanation: The Court splits into multiple small benches running in parallel; only constitutional questions are referred to larger 5, 7, or 9-judge benches.

2026-05-17-india-supreme-court-judges-34.label: India's Supreme Court & the Pendency Crisis

timeline.heading: WHY KHIMKI MATTERS
timeline.body: Khimki sits just northwest of Moscow's MKAD ring road, inside the inner suburbs and under the protective umbrella of the capital's air defense system. A drone landing in Khimki is not a stray — it is a drone that flew through the densest concentration of S-400 and Pantsir batteries in Russia.

timeline.heading: THE DISTANCE PROBLEM
timeline.body: Khimki is roughly 450 km from the nearest Ukrainian-controlled territory. A drone that reaches it has crossed the entire Bryansk-Kaluga air defense belt and the Moscow A-135 anti-ballistic ring. Each successful strike is a data point on how far the seams have opened.

blocks.text: Ukraine's long-range strike fleet leans on the **Liutyi** — a domestically built propeller drone with roughly **2,000 km** range, derived from the same aerodynamic family as Iran's *Shahed-136*. Cost per airframe is widely reported in the low **tens of thousands of dollars**; a single S-400 interceptor missile costs **over a million**.

timeline.heading: THE ECONOMICS OF ATTRITION
timeline.body: A cheap drone forces an expensive interceptor. This is the same asymmetry that made naval mines decisive in the Tanker War and that drove the Houthi Red Sea campaign. The defender wins every engagement and still loses the budget war.

timeline.heading: THE TARGETING DOCTRINE
timeline.body: Kyiv's stated policy is to strike military and energy infrastructure inside Russia — refineries, airbases, depots. Civilian apartment buildings in Moscow suburbs are not on that target list; they are typically the result of interception debris, guidance failure, or terminal-phase electronic jamming pushing a drone off course.

timeline.heading: WHY KYIV DOESN'T CLAIM
timeline.body: Ukraine routinely avoids claiming strikes on Russian soil even when authorship is obvious. The ambiguity preserves plausible deniability with Western capitals whose donated weapons carry use restrictions, and denies Moscow a clean propaganda frame for retaliation against named Ukrainian commanders or units.

blocks.question: Why does Kyiv rarely officially claim drone strikes deep inside Russia?
options: The strikes are actually carried out by Russian partisans, not Ukraine
To preserve ambiguity around Western-supplied weapons and use restrictions
Ukrainian law forbids public acknowledgement of cross-border operations
Russia jams claim announcements before they reach foreign media
blocks.explanation: Donor restrictions on Western weapons and the value of strategic ambiguity make non-claiming the default — even when authorship is obvious.

timeline.heading: THE MOSCOW AIR DEFENSE RING
timeline.body: Moscow is the only city in the world ringed by a dedicated nuclear-armed anti-ballistic missile system — the A-135, with 68 silo-based interceptors designed in the Cold War to defeat a US first strike. It was built to stop ICBMs from North Dakota, not propeller drones flying at 200 km/h and 100 meters altitude.

timeline.heading: THE LOAD PROBLEM
timeline.body: A single hyperscale AI datacenter draws 100-300 megawatts — roughly what a city of 200,000 people consumes. A cluster of them on one grid node can exceed the firm capacity the local utility was built to deliver, forcing either new generation or rationing of existing customers.

blocks.text: The constraint is **firm capacity** — power available on the hottest day at peak demand — not nameplate generation. Adding solar doesn't relax it; adding gas peakers or batteries does.

timeline.heading: THE WATER MECHANIC
timeline.body: Evaporative cooling — the cheapest way to shed heat from server rooms — consumes roughly 1.8 liters of water per kilowatt-hour of compute. A 100MW facility running flat out evaporates millions of liters daily, water that exits the watershed as vapor rather than returning to the aquifer.

timeline.heading: THE TAX BARGAIN, REVISITED
timeline.body: Through the 2010s, states competed to attract datacenters with sales-tax exemptions on servers, property-tax abatements, and discounted industrial power rates. The pitch was jobs and ratables; the reality is 30-50 permanent positions per facility and rate-base costs that residential ratepayers absorb when new transmission gets built.

timeline.heading: THE PREEMPTION QUESTION
timeline.body: US zoning power sits with counties and municipalities under state enabling acts — the same authority that governs strip malls and feedlots. There is no federal datacenter siting statute analogous to the Natural Gas Act for pipelines or the Atomic Energy Act for reactors. A county ban is legally durable until a state legislature overrides it.

blocks.text: Compare nuclear plants: the NRC preempts local objections. Compare datacenters: a single county commission can stop a $5bn facility. The asymmetry is why the industry is now lobbying state legislatures, not Washington.

timeline.heading: VIRGINIA AS THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Loudoun County, Virginia hosts roughly 70% of global internet traffic through datacenter alley — the densest concentration on earth. Dominion Energy now warns it cannot meet demand growth without new gas plants; residents have organized against transmission corridors cutting through historic battlefields. The Texas fight is Loudoun's, two years later.

blocks.question: What share of global internet traffic passes through Loudoun County, Virginia?
blocks.explanation: Roughly 70% — a legacy of MAE-East peering in the 1990s and AWS's us-east-1 region anchoring there.

timeline.heading: THE RENEWABLES MISMATCH
timeline.body: Hyperscalers sign power purchase agreements for solar and wind to claim 100% renewable operations, but the grid serves them with whatever's spinning at 3am. The PPAs add green megawatts to the system on average; the actual hourly load is still met by gas, coal, or nuclear. Texas grid operator ERCOT calls this the 24/7 carbon-free gap.

timeline.heading: THE SIX FILOVIRUS SPECIES
timeline.body: What people call 'Ebola' is actually six distinct species in the Ebolavirus genus. Zaire ebolavirus is the deadliest (up to 90% fatality) and the only one with a licensed vaccine — Ervebo. Sudan, Bundibugyo, Taï Forest, Reston, and Bombali strains have no approved vaccine. A new outbreak's first question is always: which species.

blocks.text: The licensed vaccine **Ervebo** protects against *Zaire ebolavirus only*. Cross-protection against Sudan or Bundibugyo strains is minimal — a different outbreak species means starting from zero.

timeline.heading: THE RESERVOIR
timeline.body: Ebola lives in fruit bats — most likely the hammer-headed bat and two epauletted species across Central African forests. Spillover into humans typically begins with a single contact: butchering bushmeat, entering a bat cave, handling a sick primate. Every outbreak traces back to one index case at the forest edge.

blocks.label: the filovirus belt
blocks.caption: forested countries where Ebola has spilled over from bat reservoirs

timeline.heading: WHAT A PHEIC ACTUALLY DOES
timeline.body: A Public Health Emergency of International Concern is a legal designation under the 2005 International Health Regulations. It does not deploy troops or doctors — it triggers reporting obligations, unlocks WHO emergency funding, and authorizes temporary recommendations on travel and trade. Crucially, it signals donors to release contingency budgets that sit dormant otherwise.

timeline.heading: WHY DR CONGO, AGAIN
timeline.body: This is DRC's 15th-recorded Ebola outbreak since the virus was first identified there in 1976 — more than any other country. The Congo Basin's combination of dense forest, bat reservoirs, bushmeat consumption, and weak rural health infrastructure makes recurrence structural, not accidental. The country has institutional memory most others lack; it also has the casualty count to match.

blocks.question: Where was Ebola virus first identified in 1976?
options: Near the Ebola River in what is now DR Congo
In Sierra Leone during a bushmeat survey
In a Sudanese cotton factory outbreak
blocks.explanation: The 1976 outbreak occurred in Yambuku, near the Ebola River in northern Zaire (now DRC) — the virus was named for the river to avoid stigmatizing the village.

timeline.heading: THE CASE FATALITY PROBLEM
timeline.body: Ebola CFR estimates during an active outbreak are always provisional. Deaths are counted faster than recoveries; mild cases go undetected; the denominator is wrong until contact tracing catches up. Historical CFRs have ranged from 25% (Bundibugyo, 2007) to 90% (Zaire, 2003). A 'very high' label this early means the ratio of confirmed deaths to confirmed cases is alarming — not that the true CFR is known.

timeline.heading: THE 21-DAY WINDOW
timeline.body: Ebola's incubation period runs 2 to 21 days. Public health response is built around this: contacts of a confirmed case are monitored for 21 days, and an outbreak is only declared over after 42 days (two incubation cycles) without a new case. The math is unforgiving — one missed contact resets the entire clock.

blocks.text: Survivors remain infectious in *immune-privileged* tissues — eyes, testes, central nervous system — for months. **Sexual transmission** from male survivors has restarted outbreaks more than a year after the original chain was declared closed.

timeline.heading: THE AIRCRAFT
timeline.body: The A-4 Skyhawk was designed by Ed Heinemann at Douglas in the early 1950s as a deliberate rebuke to the trend toward heavier jets — small, simple, and cheap enough that the Navy nicknamed it 'Heinemann's Hot Rod.' It first flew in 1954 and stayed in frontline service somewhere on Earth for over seventy years.

blocks.text: The Skyhawk was so compact its wings did not need to fold for carrier stowage — a structural choice that saved weight and made it **the lightest jet attack aircraft ever fielded at scale**.

timeline.heading: THE FALKLANDS RAID
timeline.body: On 25 May 1982, Argentine A-4s flying at wave-top altitude to evade radar struck HMS Coventry and the supply ship Atlantic Conveyor in San Carlos Water. Many of the bombs they dropped failed to detonate because the low-altitude release left no time for the fuses to arm — a tactical accident of physics that saved several British ships from sinking.

timeline.heading: WHY THE EMBARGO MATTERED
timeline.body: After the war, Britain led a multi-decade arms embargo blocking Argentina from acquiring modern Western fighters with British-made components — ejection seats, radars, avionics. Deals for Israeli Kfirs, Spanish Mirages, and Korean FA-50s collapsed when London vetoed the export licenses on subcomponents. The embargo did not formally end until the F-16 sale cleared in 2024.

timeline.heading: THE F-16 CHOICE
timeline.body: Argentina bought 24 second-hand F-16AM/BM Block 15s from Denmark, which was retiring them as it upgraded to the F-35. Denmark's fleet had been kept to NATO standard through the Mid-Life Update — meaning Buenos Aires is inheriting jets with modernized radar and avionics rather than the airframe Lockheed first delivered in the 1980s.

blocks.label: Skyhawk vs Falcon, by the numbers

timeline.heading: THE REGIONAL CONTEXT
timeline.body: South America has become a continent of light fighters and trainers — Brazil's Gripens, Chile's F-16s, Peru's Mirage 2000s. No regional state maintains a heavy air superiority fleet. The Skyhawk's retirement closes the last chapter of Cold War surplus combat aviation in the southern hemisphere.

timeline.heading: THE LONGEVITY
timeline.body: The A-4 served in eight air forces and saw combat in five wars — Vietnam, Yom Kippur, Falklands, Lebanon, and the Gulf. Israel kept its Skyhawks flying into the 2010s as advanced trainers. Argentina's retirement leaves Brazil's small AF-1 fleet as the last operator anywhere.

blocks.question: In which conflict did A-4 Skyhawks first see major combat?
blocks.explanation: US Navy and Marine A-4s flew thousands of strike sorties over North Vietnam starting in 1964 — nearly two decades before Argentina sent them against the Royal Navy.

timeline.heading: WHAT A LANDING STATION IS
timeline.body: A subsea cable ends at a coastal facility where light pulses are converted to terrestrial fiber. Whoever owns that building controls who can splice in, who gets capacity, and which government can serve a warrant on the traffic. The cable is the pipe; the landing station is the valve.

blocks.text: The distinction matters legally: traffic transiting a cable on the seabed is governed by the **UNCLOS** high-seas regime, but the moment it surfaces it falls under the *landing state's* domestic law — wiretap statutes, data-localization rules, lawful-intercept mandates all attach at the beach manhole.

timeline.heading: WHY 99% OF INTERNATIONAL TRAFFIC RUNS SUBSEA
timeline.body: Satellites carry under 1% of intercontinental data. Around 550 active submarine cables move the rest — every cross-border video call, SWIFT message, and cloud sync. Starlink and successors have not changed this; latency and bulk-capacity economics still favor glass on the seabed by orders of magnitude.

timeline.heading: THE MEDUSA SYSTEM
timeline.body: Medusa is a 7,100km Mediterranean ring backed largely by AFR-IX Telecom and EU recovery funds, designed to land in Portugal, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, France, Italy, Egypt, Greece, and Cyprus. Lebanon bought capacity but is not on the landing list — the cable passes nearby without surfacing.

blocks.label: Medusa landings (and Lebanon, the exception)
blocks.caption: Lebanon subscribes to Medusa capacity but has no shore terminal

timeline.heading: OGERO, THE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: All of Lebanon's existing international cables — IMEWE, CADMOS, BERYTAR — land at facilities operated by Ogero, the state telecom whose budget collapsed with the 2019 currency crisis. The country's bandwidth ceiling is set less by physics than by Ogero's ability to pay for spare parts and diesel for the landing-station generators.

timeline.heading: WHY EGYPT IS THE REAL HUB
timeline.body: Roughly 17% of all global internet traffic crosses Egyptian soil — Telecom Egypt operates the terrestrial fiber crossing between Mediterranean and Red Sea cables, charging transit fees that fund a meaningful share of the state budget. A landing station is not just a building; for the right country it is a recurring revenue stream rivaling the Suez Canal.

timeline.heading: WHAT SUBSCRIBING BUYS
timeline.body: An indefeasible right of use (IRU) gives Lebanon a guaranteed slice of Medusa's capacity, typically for 15–25 years. What it does not give: the ability to deny competitors access, host the splice for lawful intercept, or earn transit fees from neighbors. The country becomes a customer of its own connectivity rather than a node in the regional grid.

blocks.question: Which of these does a landing station give a country that pure cable subscription does not?
options: Faster download speeds for end users
Legal jurisdiction over the traffic at the splice point
A share of the cable's repair costs
Ownership of the seabed the cable rests on
blocks.explanation: Traffic on the seabed is governed by UNCLOS; the moment it surfaces at a landing station, it falls under the landing state's domestic surveillance and data laws.

timeline.heading: WHO HOLDS THE VETO
timeline.body: The UN Security Council has five permanent members — the US, UK, France, Russia, and China — each with an absolute veto. Any one of them can kill a resolution regardless of how the other fourteen members vote. The structure was fixed in 1945 and has never been amended.

timeline.heading: THE DOUBLE VETO PATTERN
timeline.body: Since 2011, Russia and China have coordinated vetoes on roughly two dozen resolutions — Syria chemical weapons, Venezuela elections, Myanmar sanctions, Korea panel renewals. Acting together raises the political cost on Washington of bringing the draft at all; acting alone exposes the vetoing capital to bilateral retaliation.

timeline.heading: THE VENEZUELA PRECEDENT
timeline.body: After 2019 US secondary sanctions tightened on PDVSA, Venezuelan crude was rerouted to China at deep discounts — often $15-20/bbl below Brent — using ship-to-ship transfers and rebranded cargoes labeled as Malaysian or Singaporean origin. The flows survived as long as Maduro did; regime change in 2026 unwound them within months as new licensing favored Western majors.

timeline.heading: WHY IRAN IS THE NEXT VENEZUELA
timeline.body: Chinese teapot refineries in Shandong absorb roughly 90% of Iran's sanctioned crude exports, paid through opaque yuan-denominated channels and Hong Kong intermediaries. A US-backed Hormuz regime that monitored every tanker would do to Iranian-Chinese flows what regime change did to Venezuelan-Chinese flows: collapse them within a quarter.

timeline.heading: WHAT A HORMUZ TOLL WOULD MEAN
timeline.body: A maritime tolling regime — even one framed as freedom-of-navigation enforcement — is functionally a chokepoint where every cargo gets identified, manifested, and either cleared or seized. The legal basis Washington would invoke is UNCLOS transit passage; the practical effect is that sanctioned flows become physically interceptable rather than just legally prohibited.

timeline.heading: THE STRAIT ITSELF
timeline.body: The shipping lanes are 3 km wide each, hugging the Omani side; the deepwater channel passes within 12 nautical miles of Iran's coast. Any inspection regime mounted from Bahrain — where the US Fifth Fleet is headquartered — would operate within range of Iranian shore-based anti-ship missiles and IRGC fast-boat swarms.

timeline.heading: THE RETENTION CHECK
timeline.body: China's veto is not about Hormuz navigation — it is about who controls the inspection list. A regime that decides which tankers pass is a regime that decides which buyers get crude, which is the substance of sanctions enforcement dressed in maritime-safety language.

blocks.question: Why would China veto a US-Bahraini Hormuz inspection resolution?
options: China imports too little Gulf oil to care about the strait
An inspection regime would let Washington identify and block China's sanctioned Iranian crude imports
China and Iran have a formal mutual defense treaty
Russia would block the resolution first, sparing China the vote
blocks.explanation: Roughly 1.5 mn bpd of discounted Iranian crude flows to Chinese teapot refineries through opaque channels — a tolling regime at Hormuz would turn legal sanctions into physical interdiction.

timeline.heading: THE DISEASE
timeline.body: Diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults. High blood sugar damages the tiny vessels feeding the retina; they leak, scar, and eventually detach the light-sensing tissue. Caught early, laser photocoagulation and anti-VEGF injections stop progression. Caught late, the damage is irreversible.

blocks.text: The cruelty is that early-stage retinopathy is **asymptomatic** — by the time vision blurs, the macula is already scarred.

timeline.heading: THE SCREENING GAP
timeline.body: Screening requires a trained ophthalmologist examining a dilated retina, or a fundus camera plus a grader. Bangladesh has roughly one ophthalmologist per 100,000 people; the UK has about six times that. Diabetes prevalence is climbing fastest in exactly the countries with the thinnest specialist coverage.

timeline.heading: WHY CNNS FIT RETINAS
timeline.body: Convolutional neural networks learn spatial hierarchies — edges, then textures, then lesions — by sliding small filters across an image. Retinal pathology is exactly that: microaneurysms are dots, hemorrhages are blots, exudates are bright patches. The pattern vocabulary is finite and visual, which is why fundus reading was the first medical-imaging task to reach specialist-level AI performance, with Google's 2016 JAMA paper as the landmark.

timeline.heading: THE TRANSFER LEARNING TRICK
timeline.body: Training a CNN from scratch needs millions of labeled images. Transfer learning starts from a network pre-trained on ImageNet's 14 million everyday photos, then fine-tunes the final layers on a few thousand retinal images. The early layers — which detect edges and curves — generalize across domains. This is how a Dhaka research team can match a Google-scale lab without Google-scale data.

timeline.heading: WHY ENSEMBLES
timeline.body: Four different CNN architectures vote on each image. Each makes different mistakes; averaging the votes cancels the idiosyncratic errors and keeps the shared signal. The technique is older than deep learning — Netflix's 2009 prize was won by an ensemble — and it routinely buys 1-3 points of accuracy at the cost of compute.

blocks.question: Why does averaging predictions from several different CNNs usually beat the best single model?
options: The models share training data, so errors reinforce
Different architectures make uncorrelated mistakes that cancel on average
Ensembles use more parameters than any single model
Voting eliminates the need for a validation set
blocks.explanation: Diverse models err in different places; averaging keeps the signal they agree on and washes out the noise they don't.

timeline.heading: THE SINGLE-DATASET CAVEAT
timeline.body: A model validated on one dataset has learned that dataset's camera, lighting, and patient demographics as much as the disease itself. The 2018 IDx-DR FDA approval — the first autonomous diagnostic AI cleared in the US — required validation across 10 sites and 900 patients before deployment. Generalization, not peak accuracy, is the gate between a paper and a clinic.

timeline.heading: HOW GRACE WEIGHS WATER
timeline.body: GRACE-FO is a pair of satellites flying 220 km apart in identical orbit. When the lead satellite passes over a mass concentration — a mountain, an aquifer, an ice sheet — it accelerates slightly, changing the distance to its trailing twin. Microwave ranging measures that distance to within a micron. Water is the only mass on Earth's surface that shifts fast enough to show up month-to-month.

blocks.text: The mission name is literal: **Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment**. The first GRACE flew 2002–2017; **GRACE-FO** (Follow-On) launched in 2018 as a NASA–GFZ Potsdam partnership.

timeline.heading: THE RESOLUTION PROBLEM
timeline.body: GRACE's footprint has historically been ~300,000 km² — fine for continents, useless for provinces. Hunan covers ~210,000 km². Resolving groundwater at sub-basin scale required combining gravimetry with hydrological models and surface-water gauges, the methodological advance the Nature study reports.

timeline.heading: DONGTING'S ROLE
timeline.body: Dongting Lake is China's second-largest freshwater lake and the natural overflow basin for the middle Yangtze. It expands from ~2,600 km² in dry season to over 20,000 km² at flood peak — a 7× swing that historically absorbed monsoon surges before they reached Wuhan and Shanghai downstream.

timeline.heading: WHY GROUNDWATER MATTERS FOR FLOODS
timeline.body: A saturated aquifer cannot absorb rainfall — it acts like a full sponge. When groundwater tables sit near the surface before the monsoon, even moderate rain produces runoff because the soil column has no storage left. The 44% figure means groundwater state, not rainfall intensity, was the dominant variable in 2024.

timeline.heading: THE FORECASTING SHIFT
timeline.body: Traditional flood models start with rainfall forecasts and route water through river networks. Satellite gravimetry inverts the question: measure how full the basin already is, then forecast what any given rainfall will do. This is the same conceptual move that turned snowpack measurement into spring-runoff forecasting in the American West a century ago.

blocks.question: What does GRACE-FO actually measure to track groundwater?
options: Radar reflections off the water table
Tiny changes in distance between two satellites
blocks.explanation: Water mass shifts pull the lead satellite forward; microwave ranging detects the micron-scale distance change to its twin.

timeline.heading: THE TINUBU SYSTEM
timeline.body: Lagos has been governed by a single political network since 1999 — Bola Tinubu's Alliance for Democracy, then Action Congress, then ACN, now APC. Every Lagos governor since the return to democracy has been a Tinubu ally; the state's revenue, appointments, and party tickets flow through one structure.

blocks.text: The arrangement has a name in Nigerian political vocabulary: **godfatherism** — where a single patron controls candidate selection, and the elected official owes loyalty upward rather than to voters.

timeline.heading: WHY LAGOS MATTERS
timeline.body: Lagos generates about a third of Nigeria's non-oil GDP and roughly two-thirds of its internally generated state revenue. A party that controls Lagos controls the country's largest tax base and its commercial capital — which is why the Tinubu network's hold on the state has been the foundation of his national rise.

timeline.heading: UNOPPOSED PRIMARIES
timeline.body: An unopposed primary in a one-party state is the visible end of a private negotiation. In APC Lagos, candidate selection happens inside the Governance Advisory Council — the body of Tinubu loyalists that vets every ticket before the formal primary. By the time wards vote, the result has already been set.

timeline.heading: THE SPEAKER'S SEAT
timeline.body: Mudashiru Obasa has held the Lagos State Assembly speakership since 2015 — the longest tenure of any Nigerian state speaker. A speaker controls committee assignments, the legislative calendar, and oversight over the governor's budget. In a machine-state, that position is second in power only to the governor himself.

blocks.question: Since 1999, how many political parties have controlled the Lagos State governorship?
options: Two — APC and PDP have alternated
blocks.explanation: AD → AC → ACN → APC is the same political machine under successive names; PDP has never won Lagos since the Fourth Republic began.

timeline.heading: AGEGE AS A POWER BASE
timeline.body: Agege is a dense mainland Lagos local government — Yoruba-majority, working-class, and one of the highest-turnout zones in the state. Controlling Agege's wards means controlling reliable vote blocks that travel to deliver margins in statewide races. It is the kind of constituency a machine cultivates, not contests.

timeline.heading: THE 2027 ARITHMETIC
timeline.body: If Obasa moves to the federal House of Representatives in 2027, the Lagos Assembly speakership opens for the first time in over a decade. Whoever fills it inherits oversight over Tinubu's home state during his own potential re-election year — making the succession less about Agege and more about which faction sits closest to the presidency.

timeline.heading: THE LAND-AS-CAPITAL PLAY
timeline.body: Sports federations worldwide sit on government-granted urban land allocated decades ago when cities were smaller. As the metro grows around them, the land's market value dwarfs anything the federation could ever earn from its sport. Selling or leasing a fraction to developers funds everything the federation can't extract from gate receipts or sponsorships.

blocks.text: The technical term is *land monetization* — converting a non-cash public asset into operating capital without an explicit budget appropriation. It lets the federation bypass the annual sports ministry allocation entirely.

timeline.heading: WHY LAGOS LAND IS SO VALUABLE
timeline.body: Lagos is projected to be one of the world's three largest cities by 2050, with a metro population already past 20 million. Land prices in serviced areas of the mainland have risen at double-digit rates for two decades. A 40% carve-out in the right location can fund a stadium twice over.

timeline.heading: THE NIGERIAN INFRASTRUCTURE PATTERN
timeline.body: Nigeria's federal sports infrastructure — the National Stadium in Surulere, the Abuja stadium built for the 2003 All-Africa Games — became cautionary tales of state-built, state-neglected facilities. By the 2010s both required hundreds of millions of naira just to make pitches playable. The privatization pivot is a direct response to that maintenance failure.

timeline.heading: THE ACCESS ROAD TELL
timeline.body: In Nigerian construction, the unpaved access road is a leading indicator. Projects that break ground before site logistics are settled — power, water, road, drainage — routinely slip 50-100% past their target. The 24-month timeline assumes the road, the grid connection, and the sand-filling all happen in parallel without dispute.

blocks.question: What share of large Nigerian public-infrastructure projects deliver within their announced timeline?
blocks.explanation: BudgIT and World Bank audits consistently find fewer than one in five major federal projects complete on schedule; the modal slippage is 2-4 years.

timeline.heading: THE OLYMPIC COMMITTEE MODEL
timeline.body: National Olympic Committees are recognized by the IOC as non-governmental, but most receive land and seed funding from the state. The IOC's own Olympic Solidarity program disburses about $590m per quadrennium globally, but the bulk of any committee's revenue comes from sponsorships, broadcast shares, and — increasingly — real estate.

timeline.heading: WHO BENEFITS, WHO PAYS
timeline.body: The athlete-facility upside is real but slow; the housing upside is immediate and captured by the developer and any officials who structured the deal. In Lagos's 2017 Tafawa Balewa Square redevelopment and the Abuja stadium concessions, opacity around valuation and equity splits became the lasting controversy long after the buildings opened.

blocks.text: The phrase to watch in the contract is *consideration in kind* — when the developer's payment is the athlete facility itself rather than cash. It collapses the valuation question into a single negotiation with no market price to check against.

timeline.heading: THE LAST RESERVOIRS
timeline.body: Wild poliovirus type 1 is endemic in only two countries on Earth: Pakistan and Afghanistan. Every other nation has eliminated transmission. The virus survives in a corridor along the Durand Line where vaccination teams cannot operate freely.

timeline.heading: WHY VACCINATORS ARE TARGETS
timeline.body: In 2011 the CIA ran a fake hepatitis B vaccination drive in Abbottabad to collect DNA samples confirming Osama bin Laden's family was hiding there. The operation, exposed months later, weaponized the trust polio teams had spent decades building. The TTP issued formal bans on vaccination in tribal areas; over 100 polio workers and police escorts have been killed in Pakistan since.

blocks.text: The shorthand inside WHO field reports is *the Shakil Afridi effect* — named for the Pakistani doctor the CIA recruited to run the sham drive. He remains imprisoned in Pakistan.

timeline.heading: WHY THE ORAL VACCINE
timeline.body: The oral polio vaccine costs about 15 cents per dose, requires no needle, and a community health worker can administer it in seconds at a doorstep. The injectable version is safer but costs 20 times more and needs trained staff. Eradication campaigns in poor, insecure terrain are only possible because of the oral vaccine's logistics.

timeline.heading: ENVIRONMENTAL SURVEILLANCE
timeline.body: Most polio infections are silent — only about 1 in 200 cases produces paralysis. By the time a child shows symptoms, hundreds in the community are already infected. Sewage sampling for viral RNA is now the early-warning system; a positive environmental sample in Bannu or North Waziristan means transmission is active even before a paralysis case appears.

timeline.heading: THE TRIBAL BELT VACUUM
timeline.body: The districts named in this campaign — North Waziristan, Bannu, and the merged FATA agencies — sit in the security vacuum where the Pakistani state's writ has historically been thinnest. The 2018 merger of FATA into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa brought courts and laws on paper. The TTP's resurgence since 2021 has rolled much of that back, which is why a vaccination drive now needs one soldier for roughly every two vaccinators.

blocks.question: Polio remains endemic in how many countries worldwide?
options: About a dozen across Africa and Asia
blocks.explanation: Nigeria was declared free of wild poliovirus in 2020. Only Pakistan and Afghanistan still report endemic transmission, both concentrated along the Durand Line.

timeline.heading: THE VETO MECHANIC
timeline.body: Any one of the five permanent Security Council members — US, UK, France, Russia, China — can kill any non-procedural resolution with a single negative vote. Abstentions don't count as vetoes; only an explicit 'no' from a P5 member blocks adoption, regardless of how the other 14 council members vote.

blocks.text: The veto was the price the **Soviet Union** demanded at Dumbarton Oaks in 1944 to join the UN at all. Without it, Moscow would have walked — and the institution would have failed before it began.

timeline.heading: THE DOUBLE-VETO PATTERN
timeline.body: Russia and China have voted together on roughly 80% of contested Security Council resolutions since 2011, when they jointly vetoed the first Syria resolution. The alignment is not formal alliance — it is shared interest in blocking Western-led intervention precedents that could one day be turned on Beijing or Moscow.

timeline.heading: WHY HORMUZ IS DIFFERENT
timeline.body: The strait sits between Iran and Oman, not Iran and any Arab state. Iran's coastline runs along the entire northern edge, and the deepest shipping lane hugs the Iranian side. Closing it is geographically trivial for Tehran; reopening it requires either Iranian consent or sustained naval combat in waters Iran has spent forty years mining and fortifying.

timeline.heading: THE TRANSIT-PASSAGE QUESTION
timeline.body: Under UNCLOS Article 38, ships have a right of transit passage through international straits — coastal states cannot suspend it. Iran signed UNCLOS in 1982 but never ratified, and has long argued Hormuz falls under its domestic law, not the convention. The legal ambiguity is the diplomatic opening Russia and China exploit at the Security Council.

blocks.text: In straits used for international navigation... all ships and aircraft enjoy the right of transit passage, which shall not be impeded.
blocks.speaker: UNCLOS, Article 38(1)

timeline.heading: WHAT MOSCOW AND BEIJING GET
timeline.body: Russia ships ~3 mn barrels/day from its own Baltic and Pacific ports — a Hormuz closure tightens global oil and lifts Urals crude prices, partially offsetting sanctions. China imports roughly half its crude from the Gulf and would seem to lose; but Beijing's calculation is strategic, not commercial — blocking a US-led resolution preserves the precedent that Washington cannot use the Council to legitimize Gulf military operations.

blocks.label: Top buyers of Persian Gulf crude (2024, mn bpd)

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR LESSON
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988, Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. Oil prices spiked briefly, then markets adapted — tankers were reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags and escorted by warships. Disruption proved easier to threaten than to sustain, but the reflagging operation took 14 months to organize and cost the US Navy 37 sailors when the USS Stark was hit.

blocks.question: During the 1980s Tanker War, what tactic finally allowed Gulf oil shipments to resume at scale?
options: A UN-brokered ceasefire between Iran and Iraq
Reflagging Kuwaiti tankers under the US flag with naval escort
A Saudi pipeline bypass to the Red Sea
Soviet mediation through the Security Council
blocks.explanation: Operation Earnest Will (1987-88) reflagged 11 Kuwaiti tankers as American, giving the US Navy legal grounds to escort them — a workaround for diplomatic deadlock, not a solution to it.

timeline.heading: THE CHAEBOL ANATOMY
timeline.body: Samsung Electronics is the flagship of the Samsung Group, a family-controlled chaebol that accounts for roughly a fifth of South Korea's GDP and a similar share of its exports. A strike at one company is a macroeconomic event because the company is structurally inseparable from the national economy.

blocks.text: The Korean term *chaebol* literally means *wealthy clan* — a hereditary conglomerate, not a public corporation in the Western sense. The top four (Samsung, SK, Hyundai, LG) account for more than half of the KOSPI's market capitalization.

timeline.heading: WHY MEMORY IS DIFFERENT
timeline.body: Memory chips — DRAM and NAND flash — are commodities sold by the wafer. Unlike logic chips (CPUs, GPUs) where design differentiation rules, memory competes on yield, density, and price per bit. A few weeks of lost output from a top producer moves the spot price within the quarter.

timeline.heading: THE KOREAN DUOPOLY
timeline.body: Samsung and SK Hynix together produce roughly three-quarters of the world's DRAM and over half its NAND. Both fab the bulk of that output inside a 100km corridor south of Seoul — Hwaseong, Pyeongtaek, Icheon. The geographic concentration is the single largest single-point-of-failure in global electronics.

timeline.heading: WHY UNIONS WERE LATE
timeline.body: Samsung Electronics famously operated without a recognized union for nearly fifty years — a deliberate founder-era policy maintained through the 2010s. The National Samsung Electronics Union (NSEU) was only formed in 2019 and held the company's first-ever strike in mid-2024. Korean labor law gives unions the right to strike after mediation fails, but the cultural break is more recent than the legal one.

timeline.heading: HBM AND THE AI BOTTLENECK
timeline.body: High-Bandwidth Memory — DRAM dies stacked vertically and bonded with through-silicon vias — sits beside every AI accelerator Nvidia ships. SK Hynix leads HBM3E; Samsung has spent two years trying to qualify its own stacks into Nvidia's pipeline. A disruption that pulls Samsung further behind on HBM hands SK Hynix structural pricing power over the entire AI training market.

blocks.text: HBM is sold at roughly *5×* the price per bit of standard DDR5 — the margins are why Samsung's qualification delays have been an investor obsession for two years.

timeline.heading: THE PASS-THROUGH
timeline.body: Memory is upstream of nearly every electronic device. A sustained price spike of even 10–15% raises the bill of materials for smartphones, servers, automotive ECUs, and data-center buildouts simultaneously. Hyperscalers buy on long contracts and absorb shocks; consumer electronics OEMs pass them through within a quarter.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of global DRAM output comes from South Korea?
blocks.explanation: Samsung (~43%) and SK Hynix (~34%) together produce close to 77% of global DRAM — the highest single-country concentration of any strategic commodity outside oil.

timeline.heading: WHY TREDEGAR MATTERS
timeline.body: Tredegar is a small ex-mining town in the Welsh valleys with a place in Labour mythology disproportionate to its size. Aneurin Bevan, the postwar health minister who founded the NHS, was born there in 1897 and represented neighbouring Ebbw Vale for 31 years. Losing Tredegar is not losing a marginal — it is losing the birthplace of the British welfare state.

timeline.heading: THE TREDEGAR MODEL
timeline.body: Before the NHS existed nationally, Tredegar had the Tredegar Medical Aid Society — a worker-funded scheme where miners paid a few pence per week for universal medical care for their families. Bevan explicitly said he took this town's model and 'Tredegar-ised' the whole country. The 1948 NHS is, in design, a Welsh mining valley scaled to 50 million people.

blocks.text: Bevan's line to the Commons: *"All I am doing is extending to the entire population of Britain the benefits we had in Tredegar for a generation or more."*

timeline.heading: THE SENEDD'S NEW MATH
timeline.body: The 2026 election was the first under the reformed Senedd: 96 seats (up from 60), elected by closed-list proportional representation in 16 six-member constituencies. The system was designed by a Labour-Plaid cooperation agreement — and produced a result that ended Labour's quarter-century grip on Welsh devolved government.

timeline.heading: WHAT PLAID ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: Plaid Cymru ('Party of Wales') was founded in 1925 as a cultural-linguistic movement to defend the Welsh language, only later adopting independence as a goal. It is social-democratic, pro-EU, and pro-Welsh-speaking — closer ideologically to the SNP than to any English party. Until this election it had never led a Welsh government.

timeline.heading: WESTMINSTER VS CARDIFF
timeline.body: Wales sends 32 MPs to Westminster under first-past-the-post, where Labour still holds most seats. The Senedd uses proportional representation. The two systems can produce wildly divergent results from the same electorate — Welsh voters can return a Labour MP and a Plaid MS on the same day for overlapping territory. This is the structural quirk that lets Labour rule London while losing Cardiff.

blocks.question: Why can the same Welsh voters elect Labour to Westminster but Plaid to the Senedd?
options: Different electorates are registered for each body
Westminster uses first-past-the-post; the Senedd uses proportional representation
Plaid candidates are barred from standing for Westminster seats
Welsh MPs are appointed by the Senedd, not elected
blocks.explanation: FPTP rewards Labour's concentrated valley vote with seats; PR splits the same vote share across multiple parties, letting Plaid, Reform and others convert votes into seats Labour denies them at Westminster.

timeline.heading: THE KINNOCK LINE
timeline.body: Neil Kinnock — Labour leader 1983–1992, born in Tredegar, MP for Bedwellty next door — spent his career arguing that Welsh Labour was the unbreakable spine of the British party. His son Stephen sits in Keir Starmer's cabinet. The family's political home now returns no Labour Members of the Senedd at all.

timeline.heading: THE TWO ARMIES
timeline.body: Sudan's war is between two generals who once partnered to overthrow a civilian government. The SAF (regular army) under Burhan and the RSF (paramilitary) under Hemedti jointly crushed the 2019 democracy movement, then turned their shared military infrastructure against each other in April 2023.

people.name: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan
people.role: SAF commander, de facto head of state

timeline.heading: THE RSF'S ORIGINS
timeline.body: The RSF evolved from the Janjaweed militias that carried out the Darfur genocide beginning in 2003. The Bashir regime armed Arab militias to fight non-Arab rebels, then formalized them as the Rapid Support Forces in 2013. Hemedti, a former camel trader from Darfur, rose from militia commander to the second most powerful man in Sudan — with troops loyal to him personally, not the state.

blocks.text: The RSF is not a wing of the army; it is a **parallel force** that controls its own gold mines in Darfur and answers to Hemedti, not the general staff. That is why the war did not end at the top — there is no single chain of command to cut.

timeline.heading: THE NEIGHBORS' STAKES
timeline.body: Sudan borders seven countries, and almost every one has a reason to intervene. Egypt backs the SAF to keep the Nile flowing and to deny the UAE-aligned RSF a Red Sea foothold. Ethiopia disputes the al-Fashaga borderland and watches the GERD dam from upstream. South Sudan exports its only oil through Sudanese pipelines.

timeline.heading: THE EXTERNAL BACKERS
timeline.body: The proxy war behind the proxy war: the UAE supplies the RSF via Chad and Libya's Haftar; Egypt and Saudi Arabia back the SAF; Iran has resupplied SAF drones after a 2024 rapprochement. The 'civil war' framing understates how thoroughly the conflict is funded from outside.

timeline.heading: THE PARALLEL STATE
timeline.body: The RSF's move to bypass Khartoum's aid channels is part of a wider claim to sovereignty. In February 2025 it signed a charter in Nairobi to form a 'Government of Peace and Unity' in territory it controls — the first serious attempt to partition Sudan along the RSF/SAF line since independence in 1956.

timeline.heading: THE COST
timeline.body: Roughly 12 million people have been displaced — the largest displacement crisis in the world. Famine has been formally declared in parts of Darfur and the Nuba Mountains. The Gezira scheme, Sudan's breadbasket, has been overrun and looted; sorghum (the staple, not wheat) has no domestic substitute at scale.

blocks.question: What is Sudan's staple grain — the one whose collapse has driven the famine?
blocks.explanation: Sorghum, grown largely in the Gezira scheme south of Khartoum, is the caloric floor for most Sudanese. When Gezira fell to the RSF in late 2023, there was no domestic substitute.

timeline.heading: WHY A RUBLE STABLECOIN EXISTS
timeline.body: SWIFT is the messaging network banks use to confirm cross-border payments. After 2022, major Russian banks were cut off, forcing exporters to settle through informal channels — UAE intermediaries, barter, crypto. A ruble-pegged token sidesteps the messaging layer entirely: the settlement happens on a blockchain, with no correspondent bank in the loop.

blocks.text: The token is named **A7A5** — issued out of Kyrgyzstan, denominated in rubles, marketed to Russian exporters dealing with Asian and Gulf counterparties who can't or won't touch dollar rails.

timeline.heading: HOW STABLECOINS ACTUALLY SETTLE
timeline.body: A stablecoin issuer holds reserve assets — usually short-term government paper and bank deposits — and mints one token per unit of currency deposited. The token moves between wallets in seconds, 24/7, with no bank intermediation. Redemption burns the token and returns the underlying. The peg holds only as long as the reserves do.

blocks.label: how a cross-border stablecoin trade settles

timeline.heading: THE DOLLAR DOMINANCE PROBLEM
timeline.body: Nearly all stablecoin volume — over 99% — is denominated in dollars. Tether (USDT) and Circle (USDC) together hold roughly $160bn in US Treasuries, making them collectively a top-20 holder of US government debt. A ruble stablecoin is a structural anomaly: it tries to build sanctions-resistant rails using the same technology that mostly entrenches dollar primacy.

timeline.heading: WHY HONG KONG
timeline.body: Hong Kong passed a stablecoin licensing regime in 2024 and positioned itself as the Asian crypto hub Singapore declined to be. It is also where Russian and Chinese commodity flows now clear in renminbi and rubles rather than dollars — making it a natural booking center for sanctions-adjacent token issuance that mainland China won't host on its own soil.

timeline.heading: THE RETAIL CAP
timeline.body: The Duma's draft bill capping retail accounts at 300,000 rubles — roughly $3,300 — is not consumer protection. It is a firewall: keep the rail open for trade settlement, keep ordinary Russians from using it as a dollar substitute or a capital-flight channel. Every authoritarian state that has tolerated crypto has eventually drawn this same line.

blocks.question: Why do governments that allow stablecoins for trade often cap retail use?
options: To prevent money laundering by criminals
To stop capital flight and preserve domestic currency demand
To protect retail investors from volatility
To comply with international banking standards
blocks.explanation: Stablecoins give citizens a frictionless way to exit the domestic currency. Caps preserve central bank control over the money supply while letting the rail serve trade.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Iran ran a similar experiment after 2018 sanctions, exploring a state-backed crypto rial and tolerating informal USDT corridors through Dubai and Istanbul. The pattern is consistent: sanctioned states don't build alternatives to the dollar — they build workarounds that still ultimately price in dollars or dollar-pegged tokens at the edges.

timeline.heading: THE DISCOVERY
timeline.body: Bacteriophages — viruses that infect bacteria — were independently discovered by Frederick Twort (1915) and Félix d'Hérelle (1917). D'Hérelle coined the name from the Greek phagein, 'to devour,' after watching the agents clear bacterial cultures within hours.

blocks.text: The word *bacteriophage* literally means **bacteria-eater**. Each phage is exquisitely specific — typically infecting one species or even one strain, unlike antibiotics that flatten whole bacterial communities.

timeline.heading: THE SOVIET ARC
timeline.body: The West embraced penicillin after 1928 and largely abandoned phage research. The Soviet Union, cut off from Western antibiotics during the Cold War, kept developing phage therapy. The Eliava Institute in Tbilisi, Georgia, has produced therapeutic phage cocktails continuously since 1923 — a parallel medical tradition Western medicine is only now revisiting as antibiotic resistance accelerates.

blocks.label: the split traditions
blocks.caption: Tbilisi kept the phage line alive while the West went all-in on antibiotics

timeline.heading: THE RUMEN
timeline.body: A cow's rumen is the largest fermentation vat in nature — 100 to 200 liters in an adult, holding 10 to 50 billion microbes per milliliter. Cattle do not digest grass; their microbes do. The rumen breaks cellulose into volatile fatty acids the animal absorbs as energy.

blocks.question: How does a cow extract energy from grass it cannot digest itself?
options: Stomach acid breaks down cellulose directly
Rumen microbes ferment cellulose into fatty acids the cow absorbs
Specialized enzymes in cow saliva digest plant cell walls
Bacteria in the intestine produce glucose from grass
blocks.explanation: Ruminants outsource cellulose digestion to a microbial ecosystem in the rumen, which ferments plant matter into volatile fatty acids — the cow's actual energy source.

timeline.heading: THE CANCER LINK
timeline.body: Streptococcus bovis bacteremia has been associated with colorectal cancer since a 1977 New England Journal of Medicine paper. A bloodstream infection with this organism is a clinical trigger for colonoscopy — the bacteria themselves do not cause the tumor, but their presence in blood signals one is likely already there.

timeline.heading: WHY PHAGE THERAPY IS RETURNING
timeline.body: Antibiotic resistance kills roughly 1.3 million people annually and is projected to surpass cancer by 2050. Phages evolve alongside their bacterial targets — when a strain develops resistance, the phage population mutates in response. This co-evolutionary arms race is the structural advantage antibiotics lack.

timeline.heading: THE BIOFILM PROBLEM
timeline.body: Bacteria in biofilms — slime-encased colonies on surfaces — are up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics than free-floating cells. Most chronic infections (catheter, prosthetic, dental, lung) involve biofilms. Phages can penetrate and dissolve biofilm matrices, which is why anti-biofilm activity is the headline property in any new phage isolate.

timeline.heading: THE ORIGINAL TARGET
timeline.body: CAR-T was built for blood cancers. Engineers extract a patient's T cells, splice in a synthetic receptor that recognizes a tumor marker (usually CD19 on B cells), grow billions of copies, and infuse them back. The FDA approved the first version (Kymriah) in 2017 for pediatric leukemia.

blocks.text: The synthetic receptor is called a **chimeric antigen receptor** because it fuses an antibody's target-recognition domain to a T cell's killing machinery — a chimera in the biological sense.

timeline.heading: WHY B CELLS ARE THE COMMON ENEMY
timeline.body: In lymphoma, B cells are cancerous. In lupus, MS, and myasthenia gravis, B cells produce autoantibodies that attack the patient's own tissue. The same CD19 marker exists on both. A therapy designed to wipe out malignant B cells turns out to wipe out autoimmune ones too.

timeline.heading: RESET, NOT SUPPRESS
timeline.body: Standard autoimmune drugs (steroids, biologics like rituximab) suppress the immune system continuously — patients dose for life and accept infection risk. CAR-T depletes B cells down to zero in weeks; the bone marrow then regenerates a fresh B cell repertoire that, for reasons not fully understood, often comes back without the autoimmune programming.

timeline.heading: THE COST WALL
timeline.body: A single CAR-T dose lists at $400,000–$500,000 in the US, before hospitalization. The cost is structural: each dose is manufactured bespoke from the patient's own cells in a 2–3 week process. Allogeneic ('off-the-shelf') versions use donor cells engineered to evade rejection — same therapy, factory-scale economics.

timeline.heading: CYTOKINE RELEASE SYNDROME
timeline.body: When billions of engineered T cells activate at once, they flood the bloodstream with inflammatory signals. Fever, hypotension, and organ stress follow. CRS is manageable in oncology wards but is the main reason CAR-T has stayed inside hospitals — and the main hurdle for treating autoimmune patients who are otherwise ambulatory.

blocks.question: Why does CAR-T potentially 'cure' autoimmunity while lifelong biologics only suppress it?
options: It permanently edits the patient's DNA
It depletes B cells to zero, and the regenerated repertoire often lacks the autoimmune programming
It replaces the patient's bone marrow
blocks.explanation: CAR-T wipes out the existing B cell population; the marrow then repopulates a fresh repertoire that often returns without the self-attacking clones.

timeline.heading: THE HORMONAL SUBSTRATE
timeline.body: Pregnancy triples estrogen and raises progesterone tenfold, then both crash within 48 hours of delivery. No other physiological event in adult life produces a hormonal swing of that magnitude. The brain's serotonin and GABA systems, which both sex hormones modulate, are destabilized for months on either side of birth.

blocks.text: The clinical term *perinatal* covers pregnancy through the first year postpartum — the period when **suicide is a leading cause of maternal death** in high-income countries, ahead of hemorrhage and hypertension.

timeline.heading: WHY META-ANALYSES MATTER
timeline.body: Individual prevalence studies of perinatal depression have ranged from 5% to 50% depending on the screening tool, cutoff score, and country. A meta-analysis pools the underlying patient data across dozens of studies, weights by sample size, and produces a single estimate with confidence intervals — the closest thing epidemiology has to a verdict.

timeline.heading: THE EDINBURGH SCALE
timeline.body: Most perinatal screening worldwide uses the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, a 10-question instrument designed in 1987. It takes three minutes, requires no clinician, and outperforms standard depression scales in pregnancy because it deliberately excludes somatic symptoms — fatigue, appetite change, sleep disruption — that overlap with normal pregnancy.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHIC INVERSION
timeline.body: Prevalence is highest in South America and sub-Saharan Africa; screening infrastructure is concentrated in Europe, North America, and East Asia. The countries with the most cases have the fewest psychiatrists per capita — Ethiopia has roughly one psychiatrist per million people; the UK has about 150 per million.

timeline.heading: THE IPV LINK
timeline.body: Intimate partner violence in pregnancy is not a separate risk factor stacked on top of mental illness — it is a causal driver. Stress hormones (cortisol, CRH) cross the placenta; chronic activation of the maternal stress axis is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight independent of the mother's diagnosis. The harm compounds across two bodies.

blocks.question: Roughly how much does experiencing intimate partner violence in pregnancy increase the risk of perinatal mental illness?
blocks.explanation: Meta-analyses consistently find IPV during pregnancy roughly triples the odds of depression, anxiety, and PTSD — among the largest modifiable risk factors identified.

timeline.heading: THE TREATMENT DILEMMA
timeline.body: SSRIs cross the placenta. Untreated maternal depression also affects fetal development through cortisol exposure and reduced self-care. Both options carry risk; doing nothing is not the safe choice. Most guidelines now recommend continuing antidepressants through pregnancy when the depression is moderate or severe, a reversal of 1990s practice.

timeline.heading: THE COURT'S JURISDICTION
timeline.body: The ICC prosecutes individuals — not states — for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression. It claims jurisdiction either when the accused's state is a member or when the crime occurred on a member's territory. Palestine acceded in 2015; that is the jurisdictional hook for cases involving Israeli conduct in Gaza and the West Bank, even though Israel itself is not a member.

blocks.text: The doctrine is called ***territorial jurisdiction*** — the same logic that lets a German court try an American tourist who commits a crime in Berlin.

timeline.heading: WHY WARRANTS STAY SEALED
timeline.body: A sealed warrant is invisible until the target crosses a border into a member state's territory, at which point that state has a treaty obligation to arrest. The secrecy is operational: announce a warrant and the target simply never leaves home. Slobodan Milošević was indicted under seal in 1999; the indictment was unsealed only when NATO's bombing campaign made his arrest plausible.

timeline.heading: THE ROME STATUTE MAP
timeline.body: 125 states are parties to the Rome Statute. The US, Israel, China, India, Russia, and most of the Gulf are not. A named official can travel freely among non-members but risks arrest the moment they land in Paris, Berlin, Tokyo, or Pretoria.

blocks.label: non-members of the Rome Statute (selected)
blocks.caption: these states have no obligation to arrest

timeline.heading: THE NETANYAHU PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In November 2024 the ICC issued warrants for Netanyahu and former defense minister Gallant over alleged starvation and civilian-targeting in Gaza, alongside a warrant for Hamas commander Mohammed Deif. It was the first time the court had named a sitting leader of a Western-aligned democracy. France, Germany, and the UK have since equivocated on whether they would honor an arrest on their soil — a stress test the treaty had not faced before.

timeline.heading: WHO ACTUALLY GETS ARRESTED
timeline.body: The court has no police. Every arrest in its history was carried out by a national government — usually after the regime that protected the suspect had already fallen. Charles Taylor was handed over by Liberia's successor government; Bosco Ntaganda walked into the US embassy in Kigali himself. Sitting officials of powerful states have a near-perfect record of avoiding arrest.

blocks.question: How many sitting heads of state have actually been arrested and transferred to The Hague under an ICC warrant?
blocks.explanation: Bashir was indicted in 2009 but traveled freely through member states for years; no sitting head of state has been physically transferred to the court.

timeline.heading: THE US POSITION
timeline.body: The American Service-Members' Protection Act of 2002 — nicknamed the 'Hague Invasion Act' — authorizes the US president to use 'all means necessary' to free any American or allied national held by the ICC. The US has never been a party and signed bilateral immunity agreements with over 100 countries pledging not to surrender Americans to the court.

blocks.text: The statute was passed three months after the Rome Statute entered into force — Washington's signal that the court's authority would not extend to *its* soldiers or *its* allies.

timeline.heading: THE RHETORICAL MOVE
timeline.body: "Freedom of navigation" and "energy market stability" are the standard legal-political wrappers great powers use to justify force in someone else's waters. The framing converts a national interest into a global public good, which lowers the diplomatic cost of intervention.

blocks.text: The State Department term of art is **freedom of navigation operations** (FONOPs) — sailing warships through contested waters to assert that a passage is international. The legal theory is real; the selective application is the political part.

timeline.heading: WHY HORMUZ IS THE LEVER
timeline.body: Roughly a fifth of global oil and a third of seaborne LNG transit the Strait of Hormuz — 33 km wide, shipping lanes only 3 km each. Iran's coastline runs along the entire northern edge and the deepest channel hugs the Iranian side, which is why Tehran's posture moves the global oil price before a single shot is fired.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988 Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. Oil prices spiked but markets adapted — tankers were reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags and escorted by warships. The lesson planners took on both sides: disruption is easier to threaten than to sustain.

events.label: Houthi attacks shut Red Sea, Hormuz traffic rises

timeline.heading: WHY BYPASSES DON'T BYPASS
timeline.body: Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline (5 mn bbl/day) and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah line together could reroute maybe a third of Gulf crude exports. The remaining two-thirds — and nearly all the LNG from Qatar — have no alternative route. There is no engineering solution to the geography.

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: Mines and missiles do not close a shipping lane — Lloyd's of London war-risk premiums do. Once underwriters reclassify a body of water, commercial vessels reroute regardless of how many munitions remain. The financial chokepoint clamps tighter and faster than the physical one.

blocks.question: What actually closes a contested shipping lane to commercial traffic?
options: The number of mines or missiles deployed
A spike in Lloyd's of London war-risk insurance premiums
The closure of the coastal state's ports
blocks.explanation: Once underwriters reclassify a route as war-risk, premiums make voyages uneconomic — commercial vessels reroute long before the physical risk is decisive.

timeline.heading: THE DEADLOCK
timeline.body: Iran's negotiating position pairs sanctions relief with compensation for past damage — a framing the US has never accepted in any nuclear talks since the JCPOA collapsed in 2018. "Energy stability" rhetoric from Washington and Tel Aviv lets Tehran cast itself as the aggrieved party defending its own waters, which strengthens the compensation demand domestically even as it stalls the talks.

timeline.heading: THE ZONING COMPACT
timeline.body: Nigerian party politics runs on an unwritten rule called zoning — the presidency rotates between the Muslim north and the Christian south every two terms, and major offices are distributed across six geopolitical zones. The APC's grip on Jigawa is part of the north-west bloc that delivered Buhari twice and Tinubu once.

blocks.text: Zoning is not in the constitution. It is a *gentleman's agreement* among party elites that has held since the 1999 return to democracy — and breaks loudly when it doesn't.

timeline.heading: THE STAKEHOLDER MEETING
timeline.body: Nigerian primaries are rarely won at the ballot. Candidates are filtered first at closed 'stakeholder' or 'consensus' meetings of traditional rulers, party chieftains, and the state governor. By the time formal voting happens, the outcome is usually pre-arranged — which is why being 'blocked at stakeholders' is a death sentence even before ballots are printed.

timeline.heading: WHY JIGAWA MATTERS
timeline.body: Jigawa sits in the Hausa-Fulani heartland of north-west Nigeria, the demographic engine of every winning presidential coalition since 1999. The state delivered over 90% for Buhari in 2015 and 2019. Tinubu — a southern Yoruba Muslim — needs that bloc intact in 2027, which is why intra-APC churn here registers nationally.

timeline.heading: THE BUHARI INHERITANCE
timeline.body: Muhammadu Buhari, a Fulani Muslim from Katsina, built a personal northern brand — talakawa (common-man) austerity, anti-corruption posture — that outlived his presidency. APC primaries across the north are still partly a fight over who inherits his network of former aides, ministers, and loyalists.

timeline.heading: THE INCUMBENCY RATE
timeline.body: Nigeria's National Assembly turns over faster than most legislatures in the world. Roughly two-thirds of House members lose their seats every cycle — primaries, not general elections, are where most exits happen. Compare that to the US House, where >90% of incumbents who seek re-election win.

timeline.heading: WHAT 2027 TESTS
timeline.body: Tinubu's fuel-subsidy removal and naira float in 2023 cratered northern living standards — the region where staple food inflation hit hardest. The question every APC primary now answers in miniature: does the party's structural lock on the north survive the economic pain it delivered?

blocks.question: What single Tinubu policy is widely credited with the steepest hit to northern Nigerian household purchasing power?
options: Removing the fuel subsidy in May 2023
Imposing a wealth tax on northern elites
blocks.explanation: Petrol prices roughly tripled overnight when the subsidy was scrapped, cascading into transport and food costs that hit the rural north hardest.

timeline.heading: THE BOTTLENECK
timeline.body: Hormuz is 33 km wide at its narrowest, but the shipping lanes are just 3 km each — two inbound, two outbound, separated by a 3 km buffer. Roughly 21 million barrels of oil-equivalent pass through daily, about a fifth of global energy trade.

timeline.heading: WHY LPG NOT OIL
timeline.body: Liquefied petroleum gas — propane and butane — is what fuels Indian kitchens. Roughly 300 million Indian households cook on subsidised LPG cylinders under the Ujjwala scheme. India imports over 60% of its LPG, and Qatar and the UAE are its top suppliers — every cargo that clears Hormuz is a cooking-fuel cargo as much as an energy one.

blocks.text: India's **Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana** put LPG connections into 100m+ poor rural households since 2016, replacing biomass cookstoves. A Hormuz disruption is, in practice, a kitchen-fuel disruption.

timeline.heading: THE QATAR ROUTE
timeline.body: Qatar's Ras Laffan complex is the world's largest LPG export terminal, and almost every molecule leaving it must transit Hormuz — Qatar has no Indian Ocean coastline. Unlike Saudi Arabia (East-West pipeline to the Red Sea) or the UAE (Habshan-Fujairah to the Gulf of Oman), Qatar has no bypass. The strait is not a chokepoint for Doha; it is the only door.

timeline.heading: WHY IT CAN'T BE BYPASSED
timeline.body: Saudi Arabia built the East-West Pipeline (5 million bbl/day capacity) partly as a Hormuz hedge, and the UAE built the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline. Together they could reroute maybe a third of Gulf crude. LPG has even less optionality — gas pipelines are scarce, and the existing bypasses are oil-only.

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: Lloyd's of London war-risk premiums — not the attacks themselves — are what closes a shipping lane. After the May 13 attack off Oman, premiums on Gulf-transit hulls reprice within hours. Once they spike past a threshold, commercial vessels reroute or refuse the voyage regardless of how many tankers actually got hit. The financial chokepoint is tighter than the physical one.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988, Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. Oil prices spiked briefly but markets adapted — tankers were reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags and escorted by warships. The lesson planners took: disruption is easier to threaten than to sustain. India's choice to flag vessels under its own registry and send them through anyway is the modern echo of that reflagging playbook.

blocks.question: During the 1980s Tanker War, how did commercial shipping continue through the Gulf?
options: Tankers reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags with naval escorts
All Gulf oil was rerouted overland via Saudi pipelines
Iran and Iraq agreed to spare commercial vessels
Shipping halted entirely until the war ended in 1988
blocks.explanation: Operation Earnest Will (1987-88) reflagged Kuwaiti tankers under the US flag, allowing the US Navy to escort them legally — the template India is now adapting.

timeline.heading: THE UNENFORCED CLAUSE
timeline.body: Article II Section 26 of the 1987 Constitution prohibits political dynasties — but adds 'as may be defined by law.' Congress, populated by dynasts, has never passed the enabling law in nearly four decades.

blocks.text: The State shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service, and prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law.
blocks.speaker: Philippine Constitution, Article II §26

timeline.heading: THE SCALE
timeline.body: Studies by the Asian Institute of Management estimate roughly 80% of provincial governors and a majority of House members come from dynastic families. The Philippines has one of the highest dynastic shares of any electoral democracy.

blocks.text: Researchers distinguish *thin* dynasties (one relative succeeds another) from **fat** dynasties (multiple relatives hold office simultaneously). The Philippines is unusual globally for how common fat dynasties have become.

timeline.heading: THE MACHINERY
timeline.body: Dynasties run on patronage — local officials control disbursement of pork-barrel funds, public-works contracts, and police postings. An outsider candidate faces not just name recognition gaps but a clientelist network that delivers votes block-by-block.

timeline.heading: THE HOUSES
timeline.body: Marcos and Duterte are the visible apex, but dozens of regional families function the same way. The 2022 ticket — Bongbong Marcos as president, Sara Duterte as vice-president — fused the two largest networks; their 2025 fallout reopened the competition.

timeline.heading: THE 1986 RESET THAT WASN'T
timeline.body: The People Power Revolution ousted Ferdinand Marcos Sr. in 1986 after 21 years and martial law. The 1987 constitution was written to prevent a recurrence — yet by 2022 his son held the presidency. The institutional reforms reset the rules without dismantling the families.

events.label: People Power; family flees to Hawaii

timeline.heading: WHY REFORM STALLS
timeline.body: Every anti-dynasty bill since 1987 has died in committee. The legislators who would vote on it are themselves the targets — a structural conflict of interest with no constitutional court workaround, since the clause is non-self-executing.

blocks.question: Why has the constitutional ban on political dynasties never taken effect?
options: The Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional
It requires an enabling law that Congress has never passed
It was repealed by a 1995 amendment
It only applies to national, not local, offices
blocks.explanation: The clause is non-self-executing — it explicitly defers to a law 'as may be defined by law,' and dynastic legislators have killed every such bill in committee.

timeline.heading: THE ECONOMICS
timeline.body: A Shahed-class long-range drone costs roughly $20,000-$50,000 to build. The Patriot interceptor that shoots it down costs about $4 million. This cost asymmetry — two orders of magnitude — is why drone swarms work even when most are intercepted.

blocks.label: cost per shot, attacker vs defender

timeline.heading: WHY REFINERIES
timeline.body: Refineries are soft targets with hard consequences. The crude distillation unit — a single vertical column hundreds of feet tall — cannot be hardened against overhead attack and takes months to rebuild. Russia has roughly 30 major refineries; Ukrainian strikes have hit more than half since 2024, periodically knocking 10-15% of refining capacity offline.

blocks.text: The bottleneck is the **CDU** — the crude distillation unit. Every barrel a refinery processes passes through one. Damage it and the whole site idles, regardless of how much downstream capacity survives.

timeline.heading: THE RANGE PROBLEM SOLVED
timeline.body: Moscow sits roughly 450 km from the nearest Ukrainian-controlled territory. Early-war drones could not reach it. Ukraine's domestic UAV industry — now producing the Liutyi, Bober, and modified An-196 — extended range past 1,000 km, putting every refinery in European Russia within reach.

timeline.heading: THE DOCTRINE FLIP
timeline.body: For most of military history, strategic bombing required heavy bombers, air superiority, and accepted aircrew losses. Ukraine has demonstrated that a country with no air force and no long-range missiles can still conduct sustained strategic bombing against an adversary's energy infrastructure — using cheap drones built in workshops. The implications for every future war are still being worked out.

timeline.heading: THE SHAHED PIPELINE
timeline.body: Russia's own long-range drone force is built on Iran's Shahed-136, license-produced at the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan as the Geran-2. The Alabuga deal — reportedly worth $1.7 billion — was one of the first major fruits of post-2022 Iran-Russia military cooperation, and it is what enables Russia to launch hundreds of drones per night at Ukrainian cities.

blocks.question: Where is Russia's Shahed-derivative drone factory located?
blocks.explanation: The Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan produces the Geran-2, a license-built version of Iran's Shahed-136.

timeline.heading: THE RETALIATION LADDER
timeline.body: Both sides now follow an unwritten escalation grammar: civilian deaths in one capital invite an energy strike on the other; an energy strike invites a drone swarm on a city. The 556-drone raid following 24 deaths in Kyiv fits this pattern. The danger is that the ladder has no top rung — there is no agreed off-ramp, only diminishing inventories.

timeline.heading: WHAT 400 KG MEANS
timeline.body: A weapon needs roughly 25 kg of uranium enriched to ~90% (weapons-grade). 400 kg of low-enriched material is the feedstock, not the bomb — but at 60% enrichment, the same mass yields enough fissile core for multiple devices once spun a final time.

blocks.text: The distinction the negotiators fight over is **stockpile mass** times **enrichment level**. Both matter; either alone is misleading.

timeline.heading: THE JCPOA BENCHMARK
timeline.body: The 2015 deal capped Iran at 300 kg of uranium enriched to 3.67% — civilian reactor grade. After the US withdrew in 2018, Iran progressively breached every limit; by 2024 the IAEA reported stockpiles above 6,000 kg and enrichment up to 60%, a short technical step from weapons-grade.

timeline.heading: WHY ONE FACILITY
timeline.body: Iran's program is distributed across at least four sites: Natanz (main enrichment), Fordow (buried under a mountain near Qom), Isfahan (conversion), and Arak (heavy water). Consolidating to one site collapses the redundancy that made the program strike-resistant — and makes any future inspection regime far cheaper to verify.

timeline.heading: THE FROZEN ASSETS
timeline.body: Roughly $100bn in Iranian assets sit blocked across South Korean, Japanese, Iraqi, and European accounts — mostly oil-export proceeds Iran could not repatriate under US sanctions. A 25% release cap means Tehran sees ~$25bn against demands for the full balance plus war reparations.

timeline.heading: THE BREAKOUT CONCEPT
timeline.body: "Breakout time" is how long Iran would need — from a given stockpile and centrifuge baseline — to produce enough weapons-grade uranium for one device. JCPOA was designed to keep breakout above 12 months. Post-withdrawal estimates collapsed it to weeks. Every kilogram and every centrifuge in the talks maps to days on this clock.

timeline.heading: WHY COMPENSATION IS A DEAL-BREAKER
timeline.body: Accepting compensation for the February strikes would mean the US conceding the strikes were illegal — a precedent Washington has refused since the 1988 Vincennes downing of Iran Air 655. Iran sued at the ICJ then and won a partial settlement, but the US has never paid wartime reparations to a state it considers adversarial.

blocks.question: What did the US ultimately pay after the 1988 Vincennes incident, when a Navy cruiser shot down Iran Air 655?
options: $61.8m in compensation only to victims' families
A formal apology but no money
blocks.explanation: In 1996 the US settled at the ICJ by paying victims' families directly — never the Iranian state — and offered no apology, the template Washington still follows.

timeline.heading: WHAT CALIBRATION MEANS
timeline.body: A model is calibrated when its stated probabilities match observed frequencies — when it says 70% confident, it should be right 70% of the time. Calibration is a separate property from accuracy: a model can be highly accurate but badly calibrated, or vice versa.

blocks.text: The technical term is **expected calibration error** — the average gap between a model's stated confidence and its actual hit rate, measured across binned predictions.

timeline.heading: WHY MODELS HEDGE BADLY
timeline.body: Pretrained language models are typically well-calibrated on raw next-token probabilities. Reinforcement learning from human feedback — the step that makes them helpful and polite — systematically destroys this. Raters reward confident, fluent answers, so the model learns to sound sure even when its underlying probability is mixed.

timeline.heading: THE AUTOMATION BIAS PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Long before chatbots, aviation and medical researchers documented automation bias: humans defer to algorithmic outputs even when their own judgment is correct and the system is visibly wrong. The 1995 grounding of the Royal Majesty cruise ship — crew trusted a GPS feed for 24 hours after the antenna cable disconnected — is the canonical case.

blocks.text: The crew's reliance on the automated position-fixing equipment caused them to disregard or discount visual and other cues that should have alerted them.
blocks.speaker: NTSB Report MAR-97-01, Royal Majesty grounding

timeline.heading: THE FLUENCY HEURISTIC
timeline.body: Decades of psychology show that humans use fluency — how easily information is processed — as a proxy for truth. A grammatical, well-structured sentence reads as more credible than a hesitant one, regardless of content. LLMs are fluency machines; their outputs trigger this heuristic on every token.

timeline.heading: WHERE IT BITES HARDEST
timeline.body: The stakes scale with the consequence of acting on a wrong answer. A wrong recipe wastes dinner; a wrong drug interaction or wrong case citation can kill a patient or sanction a lawyer. Studies of clinicians using diagnostic AI find they over-accept confident-but-wrong suggestions, and under-accept correct ones flagged as uncertain — the exact opposite of the intended workflow.

blocks.question: A model says it is 70% confident in an answer. For the model to be well-calibrated, what should be true?
options: The answer should be correct 70% of the time across many such claims
The answer is correct, with 30% margin of error
The model is hedging — the true probability is higher
70% of users will accept the answer
