options: New plants use carbon capture by default
Renewables fill demand first, so the new plant runs at a low capacity factor
Modern coal plants emit roughly half as much CO2 per kWh
China taxes coal generation but not coal capacity
blocks.explanation: On a renewables-heavy grid, coal sits at the back of the merit order — capacity grows but each plant runs fewer hours, so emissions track output, not nameplate.

timeline.heading: WHAT FLOCK ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: Flock Safety sells automated license plate readers (ALPRs) — solar-powered cameras that photograph every passing vehicle, run optical character recognition on the plate, and upload the read to a searchable cloud database. By 2024 Flock had deployed in 5,000+ US communities, building one of the largest private surveillance networks in the country.

blocks.text: The product is not the camera — it's the **searchable national database** of plate reads, queryable by any subscribing department across jurisdictions.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL HOLE
timeline.body: The Fourth Amendment restricts government searches, not private companies. Flock is a private vendor that collects the data and sells access to police, which has historically let ALPR networks operate without the warrant requirements that would govern a police-owned camera. Courts are only now beginning to test whether aggregated plate data crosses into a constitutionally protected search.

blocks.question: Why have ALPR networks largely avoided Fourth Amendment challenges?
options: License plates are public, so reading them isn't a search
A private company collects the data and sells access to police
Congress passed a 2018 statute authorizing ALPR sharing
The Supreme Court ruled vehicles have no privacy interest
blocks.explanation: The Fourth Amendment binds government actors. Routing collection through a private vendor has been the structural workaround — though Carpenter v. United States (2018) signals courts may treat aggregated location data differently.

timeline.heading: THE CARPENTER PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In Carpenter v. United States (2018), the Supreme Court held that police need a warrant to obtain seven days of cell-site location data, because the aggregate reveals a person's movements in a way any single data point does not. The same logic — that the whole is more invasive than the parts — is what ALPR challenges now invoke against Flock's persistent, cross-jurisdictional plate history.

timeline.heading: THE THIRD-PARTY DOCTRINE
timeline.body: For decades, US law held that information voluntarily shared with a third party (a bank, a phone company) loses its expectation of privacy. This 1979 doctrine is what made warrantless data collection routine. Carpenter punched the first major hole in it; ALPR cases are testing how wide that hole becomes.

timeline.heading: BANDERA IN CONTEXT
timeline.body: A town of 900 banning Flock is unusual but not unique — communities from Seattle suburbs to Norfolk, Virginia have rolled back ALPR deployments after public backlash. The councilmember's counter-proposal — ban the internet, phones, GPS — is a reductio: every modern convenience is also a surveillance vector, so why single out cameras?

blocks.text: The argument has a name in privacy scholarship: *surveillance realism* — the claim that opting out is already impossible, so resistance to any single system is performative.

timeline.heading: THE BLACK BOX PROBLEM
timeline.body: A convolutional network can classify a tumor with high accuracy but cannot say why. In radiology, an unexplained correct answer is nearly useless — the doctor still bears liability and needs to understand the reasoning before acting on it.

blocks.text: This is why medical AI lives or dies on *interpretability*, not just **accuracy**. A 99% accurate black box that flags one wrong patient in a hundred — without explanation — is harder to deploy than a 95% model that shows its work.

timeline.heading: WHAT A SALIENCY MAP IS
timeline.body: A heatmap overlays the scan with the regions the network 'looked at' most. Techniques like Grad-CAM trace the gradient of the prediction back to the input pixels — bright spots mean those pixels moved the output most.

timeline.heading: THE CLEVER HANS PROBLEM
timeline.body: Models often achieve high accuracy by latching onto spurious features — a scanner watermark, a ruler in the corner, patient-positioning artifacts. Saliency maps exposed this in dermatology AI that 'learned' to detect surgical skin markings rather than melanoma. Auditing where the model looks is how you catch it.

blocks.question: Why did an early skin-cancer CNN appear to outperform dermatologists in 2017?
options: It learned to detect surgical ink markings on biopsied lesions
It memorized rare cases from training data
It used multispectral imaging unavailable to humans
It was trained on more images than any human sees in a career
blocks.explanation: The model 'learned' that lesions photographed with rulers and ink marks were more often malignant — clinicians had pre-selected them for biopsy. Classic shortcut learning.

timeline.heading: SHAPE VS FAITHFULNESS
timeline.body: Two failure modes need separate scores. Shape asks: does the highlighted region match the tumor's actual boundary? Faithfulness asks: if we mask that region, does the prediction actually change? A map can score well on one and badly on the other — pretty pictures that don't reflect the model's real reasoning.

timeline.heading: WHY TRANSFORMERS CHANGED RADIOLOGY
timeline.body: Vision Transformers (2020) replaced the convolutional sliding window with global attention — every patch of the image can attend to every other patch. For tumors whose context matters (edema around the mass, midline shift, ventricle compression) this beats CNN's local receptive field. Most state-of-the-art medical imaging models are now hybrids.

timeline.heading: THE 87% CEILING
timeline.body: Expert agreement with AI explanations rarely crosses ~90% in published studies. The residual gap is rarely the model being 'wrong' outright — it is the model attending to features radiologists don't weight, or weighting features radiologists consider incidental. Closing it requires either retraining on radiologist-annotated saliency or accepting that the model and the human reason differently.

timeline.heading: THE 2011 FARE SCHEME
timeline.body: Delhi's auto-rickshaw and taxi fares are set by a state-government committee, not the market. The current meter rates — ₹25 flagfall, ₹9.50/km for autos — were fixed in 2011 and have been revised only once since. Every fuel shock since then has been absorbed by the driver, not the passenger.

blocks.text: The mechanism is a classic **price ceiling**: the state caps what drivers can charge but cannot cap what they pay for fuel, EMIs, or app commissions. The wedge shows up as driver income, then as strikes.

timeline.heading: WHY CNG, NOT PETROL
timeline.body: A 1998 Supreme Court order — responding to Delhi's catastrophic air pollution — forced the entire commercial transport fleet onto compressed natural gas by 2002. Delhi was the first megacity in the world to mandate CNG for public transport. The fleet has run on it ever since.

timeline.heading: THE IMPORT CHAIN
timeline.body: India imports roughly 50% of its natural gas as LNG, priced off oil-linked contracts and the Dutch TTF benchmark. When Brent moves, Indian city-gas distributors like IGL reset CNG pump prices within weeks. A Persian Gulf scare in crude markets becomes a Delhi auto-driver's pay cut by the next month.

timeline.heading: THE APP COMMISSION LAYER
timeline.body: Ola and Uber take 20–30% of each fare as commission, layered on top of the regulated meter. The driver bears the fuel cost, the EMI on the vehicle, and the platform cut — but cannot raise the fare. The aggregator model imported Silicon Valley's take rate into a price-controlled market.

blocks.label: where a ₹100 Delhi auto fare goes

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Delhi's auto-rickshaw unions struck in 2012, 2018, and 2022 — each time after a fuel spike outpaced the fare. Each strike ended with a partial revision or a CNG subsidy, never a structural fix. The committee meets, defers, and the wedge reopens at the next oil shock.

blocks.question: What forced Delhi's entire commercial transport fleet onto CNG by 2002?
options: A 1998 Supreme Court order on air pollution
blocks.explanation: The Supreme Court, ruling on a public-interest petition about Delhi's air quality, ordered the conversion — making Delhi the first megacity to mandate CNG for public transport.

2026-05-21-delhi-cab-auto-strike-iran-wa.label: Delhi's Fare Cartel & the CNG Trap

timeline.heading: THE PATHOGEN
timeline.body: Ebola is a filovirus with case-fatality rates historically between 25% and 90% depending on strain and care quality. It spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids — not airborne — which is why outbreaks burn hottest in hospitals and at funerals where bodies are washed by hand.

blocks.text: The reservoir host is almost certainly the **African fruit bat**; humans catch it from bats, primates, or duikers and then transmit it to each other. The *index case* — patient zero in any outbreak — is usually a hunter, a forager, or a child who handled bushmeat.

timeline.heading: THE RESERVOIR & THE BORDER
timeline.body: Congo's eastern provinces share a porous border with Uganda through dense forest and active trade routes. The 2018-2020 Kivu outbreak killed 2,287 people and crossed into Uganda twice. Geography, not policy, makes spillover near-inevitable once an outbreak takes hold in eastern DRC.

timeline.heading: WHY CASE FATALITY VARIES
timeline.body: Untreated Ebola Zaire kills roughly 80-90% of those infected. With aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and two monoclonal antibody therapies (Inmazeb and Ebanga, approved 2020), mortality drops to around 35% — and below 10% for patients treated within days of symptom onset. The treatment gap, not the virus, drives most deaths.

timeline.heading: THE VACCINE
timeline.body: Merck's rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine, approved in 2019, uses ring vaccination: when a case is confirmed, every contact and every contact-of-a-contact is vaccinated within days. This strategy contained the 2018-2020 Kivu outbreak's worst flares and is the single biggest reason modern Ebola response looks nothing like the 2014 West Africa catastrophe that killed 11,000.

blocks.question: What changed most between the 2014 West Africa outbreak (11,000 deaths) and outbreaks since 2019?
options: A licensed vaccine and ring-vaccination protocol
Genetic mutation made the virus less deadly
Antibiotics became more effective against Ebola
blocks.explanation: rVSV-ZEBOV was approved in 2019; ring vaccination of contacts and their contacts now contains outbreaks that previously spread unchecked. Antibiotics do not work on viruses.

timeline.heading: WHO PAYS
timeline.body: Outbreak response in low-income states runs on donor pledges, not domestic budgets. The UK's $26.87M is large but covers weeks, not months — and the US, historically the largest funder of WHO and global health security, has cut multilateral health contributions sharply since 2025. Surveillance gaps in eastern DRC are not a technical problem; they are a financing one.

timeline.heading: THE FUNERAL PROBLEM
timeline.body: Traditional burial practices across Central and East Africa involve washing and touching the body — exactly when viral load is highest. Roughly 60% of transmission chains in the 2014 outbreak traced back to funerals. Safe-burial teams in protective equipment, negotiated village by village, are the single most effective non-pharmaceutical intervention — and the most culturally fraught.

timeline.heading: THE DURAND LINE
timeline.body: The 2,640-km border between Pakistan and Afghanistan was drawn in 1893 by British colonial administrator Mortimer Durand. No Afghan government — monarchy, republic, communist, mujahideen, or Taliban — has ever formally recognized it. Islamabad treats it as a settled international frontier; Kabul treats it as a colonial imposition that cuts the Pashtun homeland in half.

timeline.heading: THE PASHTUN BELT
timeline.body: Roughly 50 million Pashtuns live astride the line — more inside Pakistan than inside Afghanistan. Tribes like the Wazir, Mehsud, and Afridi straddle the border by family. The TTP (Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan) draws sanctuary from this, and so does Islamabad's claim that any Afghan-side militant base is a legitimate strike target.

blocks.text: The **TTP** is distinct from the Afghan Taliban: it wages war against the *Pakistani* state, but the Afghan Taliban — bound by Pashtunwali codes of *melmastia* (hospitality) and *nanawatai* (asylum) — will not hand over fellow Pashtuns. That refusal is the proximate cause of the airstrikes.

timeline.heading: THE STRIKE DOCTRINE
timeline.body: Pakistan's posture since 2024 has been that TTP safe havens inside Afghanistan are an act of war by omission, justifying cross-border strikes under the customary law doctrine of 'unwilling or unable' — the same logic the US used for drone strikes in FATA from 2004 to 2018. The doctrine is contested in international law; it is invoked anyway because there is no enforcement mechanism that says otherwise.

timeline.heading: THE UNSC PARADOX
timeline.body: The Security Council can debate a UNAMA report but cannot act against a member state without nine affirmative votes and no P5 veto. Pakistan is currently a non-permanent member (2025–26 term); China, its closest strategic partner, holds a permanent veto. The structural arithmetic of the Council is why findings of 750 casualties produce statements rather than sanctions.

blocks.question: Why has the UN Security Council not acted on UNAMA's findings about Pakistani airstrikes?
options: UNAMA reports are classified and cannot be cited at the Council
Pakistan is a P5 member with veto power
China holds a P5 veto and is Pakistan's closest strategic partner
Afghanistan's Taliban government is not UN-recognized, so it cannot file a complaint
blocks.explanation: Pakistan is a non-permanent member without a veto; China's P5 veto, paired with the Beijing-Islamabad alignment, is what blocks Council action.

timeline.heading: UNAMA'S MANDATE
timeline.body: The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan was established in 2002 and is one of the few UN bodies that kept operating after the Taliban's 2021 return. It does not recognize the Taliban government but reports on civilian harm regardless of which side inflicts it — a posture that has drawn criticism from both Kabul and Islamabad at different moments.

events.label: Pakistan inherits the line; Afghanistan rejects it
First major Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan

timeline.heading: THE HOSPITAL PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Strikes on medical facilities are governed by the Fourth Geneva Convention and its 1977 Additional Protocols — hospitals lose protected status only if used for 'acts harmful to the enemy,' and even then a warning must precede attack. The Kunduz hospital bombing by US forces in 2015, which killed 42 MSF staff and patients, became the modern benchmark case; no individual was prosecuted, and MSF's call for an independent fact-finding commission under the Geneva framework was never honored.

timeline.heading: THE BUFFER STATE LOGIC
timeline.body: China's support for North Korea has never been about ideology. A collapsed DPRK means a unified US-allied Korea with American bases on China's border — the Yalu River is 800 km from Beijing. The Kim regime's survival is a geographic buffer, not a political preference.

timeline.heading: THE 1961 TREATY
timeline.body: China and North Korea signed a Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance in 1961 — the only formal mutual-defense treaty Beijing maintains with any country. It has been quietly renewed every 20 years; the next renewal is 2041. Russia signed its own comprehensive partnership with Pyongyang in 2024, the first such pact since the Soviet collapse.

timeline.heading: WHY THE 2019 GAP MATTERS
timeline.body: Xi has not set foot in Pyongyang in nearly seven years — an unusually long gap for treaty allies. During that window, Kim met Putin twice and sent troops and shells to the Russian front in Ukraine. A 2026 Xi visit signals Beijing wants to pull Pyongyang back into China's orbit before Moscow becomes the senior patron.

timeline.heading: THE SANCTIONS WORKAROUND
timeline.body: UN Security Council sanctions on North Korea require Chinese and Russian votes to enforce. Since 2022, Moscow has openly broken the arms-embargo provisions; Beijing has not formally followed but has stopped policing border trade with the same vigor. The sanctions regime exists on paper while the underlying compliance has quietly collapsed.

timeline.heading: WHO TRADES WITH PYONGYANG
timeline.body: Roughly 95% of North Korea's recorded external trade flows through China — fuel, food, machinery in; coal, textiles, seafood out. Russia is a distant second, and rising fast on munitions exchanges. Everyone else combined is a rounding error.

blocks.label: DPRK external trade by partner (2024 est.)

timeline.heading: THE MEDIATION GAMBIT
timeline.body: Seoul's intelligence floating that Beijing may mediate between Pyongyang and Washington is itself a signal — South Korea would rather China brokered talks than Russia did. A Chinese-mediated track keeps the DPRK file inside the older Six-Party framework that ran 2003–2009, where Seoul had a seat. A Russian-mediated track would not.

blocks.question: How many parties sat at the Six-Party Talks on North Korean denuclearization?
options: Four: US, China, North Korea, South Korea
Six: US, China, Russia, Japan, North Korea, South Korea
Five: UN Security Council permanent members plus North Korea
blocks.explanation: The Six-Party Talks (2003–2009) included the two Koreas, China, the US, Russia, and Japan — the format Seoul prefers because it has a seat at the table.

timeline.heading: WHAT A PERP ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: A perpetual future never expires. Instead of converging to spot at settlement like a traditional future, it uses a funding rate paid every eight hours between longs and shorts to tether the contract price to a reference. The reference is the price the contract is supposed to track.

blocks.text: Perps were proposed by economist **Robert Shiller** in 1993 for real estate. Nobody used them. **BitMEX** revived the design for Bitcoin in 2016 — it is now the most-traded instrument in crypto history.

timeline.heading: THE SYNTHETIC TWIST
timeline.body: A normal perp tracks a liquid spot market — BTC, ETH, oil. A pre-IPO perp has no spot to track. The reference is an over-the-counter valuation estimate stitched together from secondary tender offers, 409A filings, and private trades. The contract is a bet on a number the issuer constructs.

blocks.question: What tethers a pre-IPO perpetual future to SpaceX's actual value?
options: An OTC valuation estimate set by the issuer
A peg to the last primary round
blocks.explanation: Private companies have no continuous price. The issuer picks a reference — typically blending secondary tender data and dealer marks — and the funding rate enforces it.

timeline.heading: WHY IT EXISTS
timeline.body: Private companies stay private longer. SpaceX, Stripe, and OpenAI together hold more value than most national stock exchanges, yet retail cannot touch them. Synthetic perps are the gray-market answer — exposure without equity, settled in stablecoins, available to anyone with a wallet.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL GRAY ZONE
timeline.body: In the US, selling derivatives on a specific company's equity to retail without registration runs into securities law. Binance, OKX, and Hyperliquid offer these contracts offshore and geofence US IPs. The contracts are not SpaceX shares; SpaceX has not authorized them; holders have no claim on the company at IPO.

timeline.heading: THE IPO RECKONING
timeline.body: Once SpaceX lists, the perp's reference becomes a real, continuously-quoted public price. The funding rate will have to absorb the gap between the synthetic mark and the opening tape. Pre-IPO perps that mispriced their references at listing have historically seen violent funding spikes as arbitrageurs close the gap.

timeline.heading: WHY $2 TRILLION IS THE NUMBER
timeline.body: A $2 trillion debut would put SpaceX above Saudi Aramco at its 2019 IPO and second only to the largest US megacaps on day one. Most of that value is Starlink, not launch — recurring subscription revenue commands tech multiples, while rocket cadence commands aerospace multiples.

timeline.heading: WHY FENTANYL DISPLACED HEROIN
timeline.body: Fentanyl is roughly 50 times more potent than heroin and 100 times more potent than morphine. A kilogram can be synthesized in a garage from precursor chemicals — no poppy fields, no harvest season, no acres of land. The economics killed heroin as a wholesale product within a decade.

blocks.text: A lethal dose is about **2 milligrams** — a few grains of salt. A kilogram of pure fentanyl contains roughly **500,000** lethal doses, which is why interdiction seizures are measured in kilos, not tons.

timeline.heading: THE PRECURSOR PIPELINE
timeline.body: The synthesis route runs from Chinese chemical suppliers shipping precursors (NPP, 4-ANPP, and substitutes that mutate each time one is scheduled) to Mexican Pacific ports — Manzanillo, Lázaro Cárdenas, Mazatlán — where cartels operate clandestine labs in Sinaloa and Jalisco, then move finished product north through border plazas to US street markets.

timeline.heading: THE CARTEL DUOPOLY
timeline.body: Two organizations dominate the trade: the Sinaloa Cartel — fragmented after the 2023 arrest of Ovidio Guzmán and the 2024 capture of Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada — and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), which has used the rival's weakness to expand into ports and border crossings it never previously controlled.

timeline.heading: THE KINGPIN STRATEGY'S TRACK RECORD
timeline.body: US drug policy since the 1990s has prioritized removing top traffickers — the 'kingpin strategy.' Every major takedown (Pablo Escobar 1993, the Arellano-Félix brothers in the 2000s, El Chapo 2016) has been followed by more violence, not less, as deputies fight over the inheritance. Fragmentation, not consolidation, has been the consistent result.

blocks.question: What has historically followed the capture of a major cartel leader?
options: A sustained drop in drug supply to the US
A spike in violence as factions fight for control
Voluntary surrender of the rest of the organization
blocks.explanation: Every major kingpin removal since Escobar has triggered succession wars. Supply has rarely dipped for long because the market — not the leader — drives the trade.

timeline.heading: WHY THE BORDER ITSELF NOW RETAILS
timeline.body: Historically Mexican cartels wholesaled to US distributors and avoided street-level sales, which attract local law enforcement. The emergence of retail markets in border cities like Tijuana and Mexicali reflects two changes: a domestic Mexican user base that barely existed a decade ago, and US deportees with US distribution experience returning south. The border is becoming a consumption zone, not just a transit corridor.

timeline.heading: THE LAST COLONY
timeline.body: New Caledonia has been French since 1853, annexed under Napoleon III as a penal colony. It remains on the UN list of 17 non-self-governing territories — the formal register of places still to be decolonized — alongside Western Sahara, Gibraltar, and the Falklands.

blocks.label: a French territory in Melanesia
blocks.caption: 3,200 km from Sydney, 16,800 km from Paris

timeline.heading: THE KANAK
timeline.body: The Kanak are the indigenous Melanesian people of the archipelago, present for roughly 3,000 years before French annexation. By 1921, settler arrivals and disease had reduced them to a minority in their own land — a demographic fact that has shaped every subsequent political settlement.

blocks.text: The 1980s independence struggle was led by the **FLNKS** — Front de Libération Nationale Kanak et Socialiste — and ended in the 1988 hostage crisis at *Ouvéa*, where French gendarmes were taken by Kanak militants and the assault to free them killed 19 Kanaks and 2 soldiers.

timeline.heading: THE NOUMÉA ACCORD
timeline.body: The 1998 Nouméa Accord ended decades of violence with a remarkable compromise: it froze the electoral roll for provincial elections to residents present in 1998 and their descendants. The logic was that only those with a stake in the colonial-era settlement should vote on its dissolution — a deliberate restriction of universal suffrage to protect the indigenous voice.

timeline.heading: THE THREE REFERENDA
timeline.body: The Accord mandated up to three independence referenda. All three (2018, 2020, 2021) returned No — but the third, held during COVID with the Kanak in mourning, was boycotted by the independence movement and is considered illegitimate by most Kanaks. Paris counts it; Nouméa's pro-independence camp does not.

timeline.heading: WHY THE ROLL MATTERS
timeline.body: Unfreezing the roll adds roughly 25,000 mostly non-Kanak voters — enough to flip several provincial assemblies. To loyalists, it restores 'one person, one vote.' To Kanaks, it dilutes the indigenous electorate at the exact moment self-determination is being decided. The 2024 attempt triggered riots that killed 14 and caused €2bn in damage.

blocks.question: What did the 1998 Nouméa Accord freeze?
options: The provincial electoral roll to 1998 residents
Land titles held by settler families
blocks.explanation: The frozen roll was the Accord's central concession — restricting provincial-election voting to long-term residents to protect the Kanak share of the electorate.

timeline.heading: THE NICKEL DIMENSION
timeline.body: New Caledonia holds roughly a quarter of the world's known nickel reserves — critical for stainless steel and EV batteries. Paris's reluctance to let go is not only about prestige; it is about resource sovereignty in a metal China currently dominates downstream.

timeline.heading: THE LONG BASELINE
timeline.body: Japan's suicide rate climbed sharply after the 1997 Asian financial crisis and stayed elevated for over a decade, peaking near 34,000 deaths in 2003. A sustained decline followed from 2010 through 2019 — until the pandemic reversed the trend, especially among women.

blocks.label: Japan suicide deaths, key inflection points

timeline.heading: WHY WOMEN, WHY NOW
timeline.body: Men have historically died by suicide at 2-3x the rate of women in Japan, driven by mid-life economic shocks. The pandemic flipped the pattern: female suicides rose sharply while male rates moved less. Researchers point to non-regular employment — disproportionately female — collapsing first, plus caregiving burdens that closed schools shifted onto mothers.

blocks.text: The Japanese term *karōshi* (death from overwork) captures one mode of male occupational stress; the pandemic surfaced a different pattern — **isolation deaths** among women in service-sector and contract roles that lacked the lifetime-employment protections of *seishain* (regular employees).

timeline.heading: THE HIKIKOMORI SUBSTRATE
timeline.body: Before COVID, Japan's health ministry estimated over 1.5 million hikikomori — people, mostly young, who withdraw from society for six months or more. Lockdowns accelerated withdrawal patterns that were already structural, removing the school and workplace anchors that pulled some back into circulation.

timeline.heading: EXCESS MORTALITY, EXPLAINED
timeline.body: Excess mortality measures deaths above a pre-pandemic baseline — it captures total societal stress, not just the virus. Japan's COVID death toll was among the lowest in the OECD, yet its excess suicide count was substantial. The two numbers measure different things: one counts a pathogen, the other counts a society under strain.

blocks.question: Why does excess mortality often exceed confirmed COVID deaths?
options: Undercounted COVID cases plus deaths from delayed care, isolation, and economic stress
Vaccine side effects accumulating over time
blocks.explanation: Excess mortality captures the full societal cost — missed cancer screenings, deferred surgeries, isolation-driven suicides, and economic despair, alongside undercounted infections.

timeline.heading: THE UNEMPLOYMENT DECOUPLING
timeline.body: The Durkheim-era assumption that suicide tracks joblessness held through Japan's 1998 spike — that crisis was unambiguously economic. The pandemic broke the link: unemployment explains less than 10% of the 2020-22 excess. Whatever drove the surge — isolation, caregiving collapse, online amplification of distress — operated through channels the unemployment rate cannot see.

timeline.heading: THE WERTHER EFFECT
timeline.body: Media coverage of high-profile suicides reliably triggers copycat clusters — documented since Goethe's 1774 novel prompted a wave of imitative deaths across Europe. Japan saw measurable spikes after celebrity suicides in 2020. The WHO publishes media guidelines specifically to dampen this contagion; Japanese broadcasters have adopted them unevenly.

timeline.heading: THE EIGHTH WONDER
timeline.body: The Karakoram Highway took 20 years to build (1959–1979) and killed over 800 Pakistani and 200 Chinese workers — roughly one life per kilometer. It crosses the Khunjerab Pass at 4,693m, the highest paved international border crossing on Earth.

blocks.text: Locals call it the **KKH**. The Chinese side calls it the *China–Pakistan Friendship Highway* — the road is infrastructure and diplomatic monument in one.

timeline.heading: THE ONLY LAND BRIDGE
timeline.body: The KKH is the sole overland route between China and Pakistan. Every other border is sealed by the Karakoram, Hindu Kush, or Himalaya ranges. When the road closes, the China–Pakistan relationship has no Plan B except air freight or the long sea route through the Malacca Strait.

blocks.label: the only road from China to Pakistan

timeline.heading: WHY THE SLOPES FAIL
timeline.body: The Karakoram is the youngest, fastest-rising mountain range on Earth — the Indian plate still pushes north at ~4 cm per year. The rock is fractured, the slopes are steep, and seasonal melt saturates loose scree. Landslides are not anomalies on the KKH; they are the operating environment.

blocks.question: Roughly how fast is the Karakoram range still rising as the Indian plate collides with Asia?
options: It stopped rising in the Pleistocene
blocks.explanation: The collision that built the Himalaya and Karakoram is ongoing — the ranges rise several centimeters per year, which is why their slopes are unstable and prone to landslide.

timeline.heading: THE ATTABAD PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In January 2010, a massive landslide near Attabad in Hunza buried 20 people and dammed the Hunza River, creating a lake that submerged 19 km of the KKH for nearly five years. Traffic crossed by boat until China financed five tunnels to reroute the road above the new lake.

timeline.heading: WHY CPEC RUNS THROUGH HERE
timeline.body: The China–Pakistan Economic Corridor — Beijing's $62bn flagship of the Belt and Road — uses the KKH alignment for its northern leg, terminating at Gwadar port on the Arabian Sea. Every weather closure on a Kohistan switchback is a closure on the most strategically advertised overland trade route in Asia.

timeline.heading: GILGIT-BALTISTAN'S STATUS
timeline.body: Gilgit-Baltistan is administered by Pakistan but is not a constitutional province — it sits in a legal limbo tied to the unresolved Kashmir dispute. The KKH is its only road link to the rest of the country, which makes every closure not just an economic event but a political one for a region already arguing for full provincial rights.

timeline.heading: THE COPENHAGEN CRITERIA
timeline.body: Since 1993, any EU candidate must meet three benchmarks: stable democratic institutions, a functioning market economy, and the ability to adopt the acquis communautaire — the ~80,000 pages of accumulated EU law. Ukraine opened formal accession talks in June 2024; full compliance typically takes a decade or more.

blocks.text: The full body of EU law a candidate must absorb is called the ***acquis communautaire*** — divided into 35 negotiating chapters, each closed only when Brussels certifies compliance.

timeline.heading: THE UNANIMITY TRAP
timeline.body: Accession requires unanimous ratification by all 27 member states plus the European Parliament. Hungary has used this veto repeatedly against Ukraine; Cyprus blocked Turkey's chapters for two decades. Any one capital can freeze the process indefinitely — which is why Merz reaches for a route that bypasses ratification.

blocks.label: the veto players Kyiv must clear

timeline.heading: ARTICLE 42(7)
timeline.body: The EU's own mutual-defence clause, hidden in the Lisbon Treaty, obliges members to aid any member under armed aggression 'by all the means in their power.' It is stronger on paper than NATO's Article 5, but has only been invoked once — by France after the 2015 Paris attacks. Extending it to a non-member without voting rights would be unprecedented.

blocks.text: If a Member State is the victim of armed aggression on its territory, the other Member States shall have towards it an obligation of aid and assistance by all the means in their power.
blocks.speaker: Treaty on European Union, Article 42(7)

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENTS FOR TIERS
timeline.body: Europe has built half-memberships before: the European Economic Area (Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) gives single-market access without voting rights; Switzerland runs on 120+ bilateral treaties; the UK post-Brexit invented yet another tier. Each was sold as transitional; each became permanent.

timeline.heading: THE TURKISH GHOST
timeline.body: Turkey opened accession talks in 2005. Twenty-one years later, only one of 35 chapters has been provisionally closed. Ankara was offered 'privileged partnership' — a tier short of membership — and rejected it as a permanent demotion. Kyiv watches this precedent closely.

timeline.heading: WHY MERZ MOVES NOW
timeline.body: Germany's CDU returned to the chancellery in May 2025 after three years of SPD-led coalition. Merz built his campaign on a harder Ukraine line than his predecessor, and the EU's December 2025 enlargement summit is the next forcing function. Acting before then lets Berlin shape the framework rather than inherit one.

blocks.question: Which EU treaty article contains the mutual-defence clause Merz wants to extend to Ukraine?
options: Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty
Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union
Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union
Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union
blocks.explanation: Article 42(7), added by the Lisbon Treaty in 2009, is the EU's own mutual-defence clause — separate from NATO's Article 5. Article 50 is the exit clause; Article 2 lists EU values.

timeline.heading: THE REGULATOR
timeline.body: Ofcom began as a broadcast regulator — television, radio, spectrum licensing. The Online Safety Act of 2023 handed it jurisdiction over global internet platforms overnight, transforming a domestic media watchdog into one of the world's most powerful content regulators.

blocks.text: Ofcom's full name is the *Office of Communications*; before 2023 its biggest fines targeted **British broadcasters**, not Silicon Valley.

timeline.heading: THE 10% RULE
timeline.body: The Act's maximum fine — 10% of global annual revenue or £18 million, whichever is higher — deliberately mirrors the GDPR and EU Digital Services Act penalty structure. The logic is that fines must scale with company size, or trillion-dollar platforms treat them as a cost of doing business.

blocks.label: what 10% of global turnover looks like (2024 revenue)

timeline.heading: WHY RECOMMENDATION FEEDS
timeline.body: The Act targets algorithmic amplification, not user posts. A teenager who searches for harmful content is one problem; a feed that infers their vulnerability from watch-time and serves more is a different problem. Ofcom's draft codes treat the recommender as the regulated product.

timeline.heading: THE BRUSSELS EFFECT, REVERSED
timeline.body: For two decades the EU set global tech rules and the UK followed. The Online Safety Act is the first major post-Brexit divergence: stricter than the EU's Digital Services Act on children, broader in scope, and enforced by a regulator with no equivalent on the continent.

timeline.heading: THE AUSTRALIAN PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Australia passed a world-first under-16 social media ban in November 2024, enforced on platforms rather than parents. The UK consultation closing next week is the first serious test of whether the model travels. If London follows Canberra, Brussels and Washington face pressure to match.

blocks.label: countries moving on under-16 social media access
blocks.caption: Australia banned in 2024; France, Norway, Ireland are in legislative stages.

timeline.heading: TEST YOURSELF
timeline.body: The Online Safety Act applies to any platform with UK users, regardless of where the company is headquartered.

blocks.question: Under the Online Safety Act, what is Ofcom's maximum fine for a platform that ignores its child-safety duties?
options: 10% of global revenue or £18 million, whichever is higher
Criminal prosecution of the CEO only
blocks.explanation: The global-turnover cap is the teeth — a UK-only cap would let trillion-dollar platforms absorb fines as a cost of doing business.

timeline.heading: WHAT A CONJECTURE IS
timeline.body: In mathematics a conjecture is a statement believed true but unproven. It graduates to a theorem when proved, or dies when a single counterexample is found. Disproof by counterexample is logically cheaper than proof — one ugly fact kills an infinity of expected behavior.

blocks.text: The asymmetry is fundamental: a proof must cover *every* case; a counterexample needs only *one*. This is why brute-force search is a natural fit for disproof and a hopeless one for proof.

timeline.heading: THE FOUR COLOR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The 1976 four color theorem was the first major result whose proof depended on a computer — Appel and Haken reduced the problem to 1,936 configurations and let a machine check each one. Mathematicians initially refused to accept it; some still consider it less satisfying than a proof a human can read end-to-end.

timeline.heading: WHY DISCRETE GEOMETRY
timeline.body: Discrete geometry studies finite or countable arrangements — points, lines, polytopes, packings — rather than smooth curves. Its conjectures often reduce to combinatorial search over configurations, which makes them unusually exposed to machine attack: the search space is large but enumerable.

timeline.heading: VERIFIED VS PROVED
timeline.body: Human-verified means a mathematician checked the counterexample's arithmetic and confirmed it violates the conjecture's claim. Formally proved would mean machine-checked in a proof assistant like Lean or Coq, where every inference step is mechanically validated. The distinction matters: verification trusts the human reader; formal proof trusts only the kernel.

timeline.heading: THE NEW ROLE FOR MODELS
timeline.body: Earlier compute-aided maths used hand-written programs to exhaust a finite case list. An LLM-guided search instead proposes parameterizations a human would not think to try, then evaluates them. The model is not proving anything; it is a creative search heuristic over the configuration space.

timeline.heading: WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN
timeline.body: A counterexample to one conjecture is not a general claim that machines now do mathematics. The Riemann Hypothesis, P vs NP, and the abc conjecture remain untouched by this class of method — they resist enumeration because their counterexample, if one exists, lives somewhere unbounded.

blocks.question: Why is disproving a conjecture often easier than proving one?
options: A single counterexample suffices, but a proof must cover every case
Disproofs do not require peer review
blocks.explanation: Logically, refutation needs one instance; proof needs universal coverage. That asymmetry is why brute-force search fits disproof and not proof.

timeline.heading: THE BRETTON WOODS BREAK
timeline.body: From 1944 to 1971, dollars were redeemable for gold at $35/oz. Nixon closed the window when foreign claims exceeded US reserves. The dollar should have collapsed — instead, Washington engineered a replacement anchor.

events.label: Bretton Woods: dollar pegged to gold

timeline.heading: THE 1974 BARGAIN
timeline.body: Treasury Secretary William Simon flew to Riyadh and struck a deal with King Faisal: Saudi Arabia would price oil exclusively in dollars and recycle surpluses into US Treasuries, in exchange for American security guarantees. Every oil importer on Earth then needed dollars to fill their tank.

blocks.text: The arrangement created what economists call **exorbitant privilege** — the US could run permanent trade deficits because global demand for dollars was structurally locked in by the oil trade.

timeline.heading: WHY 2022 BROKE THE SPELL
timeline.body: When the G7 froze $300bn of Russian central bank reserves after the Ukraine invasion, every non-aligned central banker learned the same lesson: dollar reserves are not property, they are a permission. Gold cannot be frozen by a sanctions order in Washington.

blocks.question: What share of global central bank reserves was held in dollars at the petrodollar peak (1999) vs. today?
blocks.explanation: IMF COFER data shows dollar reserves fell from ~72% in 1999 to under 60% by 2024 — a slow, steady drift, not a collapse.

timeline.heading: THE GOLD BID
timeline.body: Central bank gold buying doubled from the long-run average of ~500 tons/year to over 1,000 tons/year after 2022. China, Turkey, India, and Poland led the buying. This is the cleanest signal of reserve-manager intent — gold pays no yield, so accumulating it means you are paying to escape counterparty risk.

blocks.label: Top central bank gold buyers, 2022–2024 (tons added)

timeline.heading: MBRIDGE & THE RAILS PROBLEM
timeline.body: Replacing the dollar requires replacing the plumbing: SWIFT for messaging, CHIPS for settlement, correspondent banks for clearing. Project mBridge — a BIS-incubated CBDC platform built by the central banks of China, Hong Kong, Thailand, and the UAE — moved its first real cross-border transactions in 2023. It is the first credible alternative rail.

timeline.heading: WHY THE CROWN HOLDS
timeline.body: Network effects are sticky. The dollar's role in invoicing, FX markets, and trade finance is roughly 80–90% — far above its reserve share. Until someone offers deep, liquid, freely convertible bond markets at the scale of Treasuries, the dollar declines slowly, not suddenly. The yuan is not convertible; the euro has no unified bond market.

blocks.text: Economists call this *incumbency by inertia* — sterling kept its reserve-currency role for **forty years** after Britain ceased to be the dominant economy. Currency regimes outlive the empires that built them.

timeline.heading: THE GUARDIAN OF THE GENOME
timeline.body: TP53 encodes p53, a transcription factor that halts cell division when DNA damage is detected and triggers apoptosis if repair fails. It is mutated in roughly half of all human cancers — the single most commonly disrupted gene in oncology.

blocks.text: Lab shorthand calls p53 *the guardian of the genome* — a phrase coined by David Lane in **1992** that stuck because it captures the gatekeeping role precisely.

timeline.heading: WHAT LI-FRAUMENI IS
timeline.body: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is a rare autosomal-dominant disorder where one TP53 allele is mutated in every cell from birth. Carriers face a near-100% lifetime cancer risk, with sarcomas, brain tumors, adrenocortical carcinoma, and early-onset breast cancer dominating the spectrum.

blocks.question: At what age does breast cancer risk in Li-Fraumeni carriers typically begin to rise sharply?
blocks.explanation: LFS breast cancers commonly appear in a woman's 20s and 30s — decades earlier than sporadic disease, which is why annual breast MRI screening starts at age 20 for known carriers.

timeline.heading: THE TWO-HIT MECHANISM
timeline.body: Knudson's 1971 two-hit hypothesis explains why one inherited mutation is enough: every cell already carries the first hit, so a single somatic event knocks out the remaining functional copy. Tumors arise stochastically wherever that second hit lands.

timeline.heading: WHY HER2 KEEPS APPEARING
timeline.body: HER2 is a growth-factor receptor on chromosome 17 — the same chromosome that carries TP53. In LFS breast tumors, HER2 amplification dominates the oncogene landscape, possibly because loss of p53 surveillance lets HER2-driven proliferation run unchecked from an early age.

timeline.heading: THE COLD-TUMOR PROBLEM
timeline.body: Low CD8+ T-cell infiltration marks a tumor as immunologically cold — the immune system is not engaging it. Checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab work best in hot tumors with abundant T cells. An LFS-specific immune profile implies these patients may need different therapies than the sporadic-disease playbook assumes.

blocks.text: Oncologists divide tumors into **hot** (T-cell infiltrated, immunotherapy-responsive) and **cold** (immune-excluded, requiring chemotherapy or targeted agents). The distinction now drives trial-arm assignment as much as histology does.

timeline.heading: WHY SEPARATE TRIALS MATTER
timeline.body: Clinical trials enroll for the average patient. When a subpopulation has distinct biology — different drivers, different immune context, different age at onset — pooling them with sporadic cases dilutes the signal in both directions. The history of HER2-positive disease itself is the precedent: separating it from HER2-negative trials in the 1990s is what made trastuzumab's benefit visible.

timeline.heading: THE PETROSTATE TRAP
timeline.body: Venezuela sits on the world's largest proven oil reserves — larger than Saudi Arabia's. Yet output collapsed from 3.2 million barrels/day in 2008 to under 800,000 by the early 2020s. The collapse was not geological; it was the predictable result of expropriating service contractors, purging PDVSA's engineers in 2003, and using the company as a patronage machine.

timeline.heading: THE CARTEL OF THE SUNS
timeline.body: US prosecutors use the name **Cartel de los Soles** for a network of Venezuelan military officers — the 'suns' refer to the rank insignia on a general's epaulette — accused of moving Colombian cocaine through Venezuelan territory since the 1990s. Unlike Mexican cartels, it is not a hierarchical organization but a protection franchise run from inside the armed forces.

blocks.text: In July 2025 the US Treasury formally designated *Cartel de los Soles* as a **Specially Designated Global Terrorist** entity — the first time a foreign government's own military leadership was sanctioned as a terrorist organization rather than a criminal one.

timeline.heading: THE COLECTIVOS
timeline.body: Beneath the military sit the **colectivos** — armed neighborhood groups in Caracas barrios originally formed under Chávez as civilian defense committees. Over two decades they evolved into a parallel security force: they police pro-government zones, suppress protests the National Guard cannot be seen suppressing, and run local extortion economies. Dismantling them would remove the regime's street-level enforcement arm.

timeline.heading: THE NEGOTIATION TEMPLATE
timeline.body: Every Latin American democratic transition since the 1980s — Argentina 1983, Chile 1990, Brazil 1985 — included some form of amnesty or guarantee for the outgoing security apparatus. Pinochet wrote his own immunity into the 1980 constitution before stepping down. The Venezuelan calculus is the same: the people who would need to leave power are the same people who would face prosecution if they did.

timeline.heading: WHO RODRÍGUEZ IS
timeline.body: Delcy Rodríguez and her brother Jorge are the regime's diplomatic and parliamentary faces — fluent, polished, and personally sanctioned by the US, EU, Canada, and UK since 2017–2018 for human rights abuses and corruption. She ran the 2017 Constituent Assembly that sidelined the elected opposition-led legislature; he negotiates with the opposition in Oslo and Mexico City.

timeline.heading: THE DIASPORA SIGNAL
timeline.body: Roughly 7.7 million Venezuelans have left the country since 2015 — the largest displacement crisis in the Western Hemisphere's history, larger than Syria's at its peak. Colombia hosts about 2.9 million, Peru 1.5 million, the US around 770,000. The exit rate is the clearest referendum on the regime's economic management; no statistic Caracas publishes about GDP recovery matters more than this one.

timeline.heading: QUIZ
timeline.body: A quick check on the scale of the exodus.

blocks.question: How many Venezuelans have left the country since 2015?
blocks.explanation: Roughly 7.7 million — larger than Syria's displacement at its peak, and the biggest in the Western Hemisphere's history.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'SOVEREIGNTY' ACTUALLY MEANS HERE
timeline.body: Compute sovereignty is the ability to decide which models run, on whose hardware, under whose law. When workloads sit in AWS Cape Town or Azure Johannesburg, the data is physically in Africa but the control plane — billing, identity, model allowlists, takedown authority — sits in Seattle and Redmond under US jurisdiction.

blocks.text: The distinction matters: **data residency** (where bytes live) is not **operational sovereignty** (who can pull the plug).

timeline.heading: THE CLOUD ACT REACH
timeline.body: The 2018 US CLOUD Act lets US authorities compel American providers to hand over customer data regardless of where the servers physically sit. An African government hosting citizen data on AWS Cape Town has no legal mechanism to block a US subpoena — the contract is with a Delaware corporation.

timeline.heading: THE TWO REGIONS
timeline.body: Sub-Saharan Africa has exactly two hyperscaler cloud regions: AWS in Cape Town (opened 2020) and Microsoft Azure in Johannesburg (2019). Google Cloud's Johannesburg region opened 2024. Every other African country routes through Europe — typically Frankfurt or Dublin — adding 100-200ms of latency that breaks real-time AI inference.

blocks.label: Sub-Saharan hyperscaler footprint
blocks.caption: two cities host the continent's regulated AI compute

timeline.heading: THE LICENSE GATE
timeline.body: Frontier models like Claude, GPT-4, and Gemini are not sold — they are licensed via API or marketplace listings (Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Vertex). The hyperscaler's acceptable-use policy and the model provider's export restrictions both apply. An African fintech cannot deploy a model the US Commerce Department has flagged for a country on its watch list, even on a server in Lagos.

blocks.question: Which entity ultimately decides whether a frontier AI model can be used in a given African country?
options: The US-based model provider and its cloud distributor
blocks.explanation: Model access flows through US export controls and provider terms — the cloud region is the delivery mechanism, not the gatekeeper.

timeline.heading: THE THIRD-OPTION TRAP
timeline.body: Russia's GLONASS and China's BeiDou-linked satellite internet pitches offer an alternative stack — but routing African AI workloads through Moscow or Beijing replaces US extraterritorial reach with Russian or Chinese extraterritorial reach. China's 2017 Cybersecurity Law and 2021 Data Security Law require Chinese cloud providers to hand data to state authorities on request, with no judicial intermediary.

blocks.label: who can compel disclosure under each stack

timeline.heading: THE NON-ALIGNMENT PRECEDENT
timeline.body: This is the 1960s Non-Aligned Movement problem in a new register. Then it was military bases and arms supply; now it is GPUs and inference endpoints. The structural pattern repeats: small states with no domestic capability must rent the capability from a great power, and the rent is paid in policy alignment.

timeline.heading: THE VERBAL MEMORY ADVANTAGE
timeline.body: Women outperform men on verbal memory tests across the lifespan — recalling word lists, stories, and names. The gap appears in childhood and persists into old age, and it is one of the most robust sex differences in cognitive psychology.

blocks.text: The advantage is specifically *verbal* — spatial and mathematical reasoning show the opposite or no gap. It's a domain effect, not a general intelligence effect.

timeline.heading: THE MASKING MECHANISM
timeline.body: Standard Alzheimer's screening leans heavily on verbal memory tasks like word-list recall. A woman with significant hippocampal atrophy can still score in the normal range because she started from a higher baseline — the disease eats into her reserve before it crosses the diagnostic cutoff.

timeline.heading: COGNITIVE RESERVE
timeline.body: The brain compensates for damage until it can't. Education, bilingualism, and social engagement build reserve that delays symptoms even as pathology accumulates. The 1986 Nun Study autopsied sisters who tested cognitively normal in life yet had brains full of Alzheimer's plaques — reserve had hidden the disease entirely.

timeline.heading: WHO GETS ALZHEIMER'S
timeline.body: Nearly two-thirds of Alzheimer's patients are women. Part of this is longevity — women live longer, and age is the dominant risk factor — but lifetime risk remains higher even after adjusting for survival. The APOE4 risk allele also confers a steeper risk increase in women than in men.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of Alzheimer's patients in the US are women?
blocks.explanation: Women make up about two-thirds of US Alzheimer's cases — driven by longevity and a steeper APOE4 effect, not just by living longer.

timeline.heading: WHY EARLY MATTERS NOW
timeline.body: The new amyloid-clearing drugs — lecanemab and donanemab — only slow decline in early-stage disease. Once neurons are gone, clearing the plaque does nothing. A 2.7-year diagnostic delay is the difference between a treatable window and a closed door.

timeline.heading: THE CUTOFF PROBLEM
timeline.body: Medicine has a long history of male-default reference ranges — cardiac troponin, creatinine, even heart-attack symptom checklists were calibrated on male cohorts. Sex-specific thresholds in cardiology took decades to adopt; cognitive screening is on the same path, a generation behind.

timeline.heading: THE IMF CONDITION
timeline.body: Egypt's $8bn IMF program, expanded in March 2024 after the pound's devaluation, requires phasing out energy subsidies that historically consumed roughly a fifth of state spending. Tariff hikes for industry and households are not policy choices — they are program benchmarks tied to disbursement tranches.

blocks.text: The technical name is **cost-recovery pricing**: the tariff must cover the *delivered* cost of generation plus transmission, not the politically-set floor that's prevailed for decades.

timeline.heading: WHY GAS DRIVES THE TARIFF
timeline.body: Roughly 80% of Egypt's electricity comes from natural gas. Domestic production from the offshore Zohr field has been declining since 2022, forcing Egypt to import LNG at world prices. The tariff hike is downstream of the gas bill — when imports are priced in dollars and the pound has halved, the subsidy gap explodes.

timeline.heading: WHY FERTILIZER IS THE PRESSURE POINT
timeline.body: Ammonia and urea production is the most gas-intensive industry on earth — natural gas is both fuel and feedstock. Egypt is one of the world's larger urea exporters; when domestic energy costs rise, producers chase dollar revenue abroad. The squeeze on summer planting is the predictable second-order effect.

timeline.heading: THE 1977 SHADOW
timeline.body: Every Egyptian government since Sadat has had to weigh subsidy cuts against the memory of the 1977 Bread Intifada — riots that erupted within hours of subsidy cuts on bread, sugar, and cooking oil, killing at least 79 and forcing reversal within 48 hours. The current playbook — hike industrial rates first, household rates incrementally — exists to avoid that detonation.

blocks.text: The price of bread is the price of stability.
blocks.speaker: Egyptian fiscal proverb, post-1977

timeline.heading: THE POUND PASS-THROUGH
timeline.body: Industrial electricity is denominated in Egyptian pounds, but the LNG cargoes that fuel the grid are paid in dollars. The pound's collapse from ~30 to over 50 per dollar in March 2024 means the same import bill is now ~70% more pounds — the tariff is doing arithmetic the currency already did.

timeline.heading: WHO ABSORBS THE COST
timeline.body: Heavy industry — iron, cement, fertilizer, aluminum — runs on thin margins where energy is 30-60% of production cost. They have three options: pass the hike to domestic buyers (inflation), export more to earn dollars (shortage), or curtail output (unemployment). Each route hands the government a different political problem.

blocks.question: Why does an industrial electricity tariff hike tend to TIGHTEN domestic fertilizer supply?
options: Producers shut down to protest the hike
Producers export more to earn dollars that offset the higher pound costs
The grid can no longer supply fertilizer plants reliably
The IMF requires reduced domestic fertilizer use
blocks.explanation: When local costs rise but global urea prices are set in dollars, exporting becomes the rational hedge — leaving less for the domestic market.

timeline.heading: THE 50 LINE
timeline.body: The Purchasing Managers Index surveys procurement officers — the people who place factory orders before output shows up in GDP. A reading above 50 means expansion, below 50 contraction. At 47.5, the eurozone's composite is signalling that activity is shrinking now, months before the official quarterly numbers can confirm it.

blocks.text: PMI is a **diffusion index**: it counts the share of firms reporting *better* conditions minus those reporting *worse*. It measures breadth of change, not magnitude — which is why it leads GDP by 3–6 months but can't tell you how deep a slump goes.

timeline.heading: STAGFLATION'S TEMPLATE
timeline.body: Stagflation — rising prices alongside falling output — broke the post-war consensus that you could trade a little inflation for a little growth. The 1973 OPEC embargo quadrupled crude in six months; by 1975 every major European economy was simultaneously in recession and double-digit inflation. The textbooks had no model for it; the policy response took a decade.

timeline.heading: THE ECB'S SINGLE MANDATE
timeline.body: The European Central Bank, modelled on the Bundesbank, has one statutory target: price stability, defined as 2% inflation. The Federal Reserve has two — price stability and maximum employment. In a stagflation, that legal difference becomes decisive: the Fed can rationalise tolerating inflation to protect jobs; the ECB legally cannot.

timeline.heading: WHY EUROPE FEELS IT FIRST
timeline.body: Europe imports roughly 90% of its crude and most of its natural gas. After cutting Russian pipeline gas in 2022, the bloc rebuilt around LNG cargoes — many routed through the Strait of Hormuz and the Suez–Bab el-Mandeb corridor. A Middle East war hits Europe's input costs before it shows up in American or Chinese inflation prints.

timeline.heading: THE EURO AS SHOCK ABSORBER
timeline.body: A weaker euro magnifies imported inflation — every barrel of oil and tonne of LNG is invoiced in dollars. When the ECB is forced to choose growth over inflation, the currency typically weakens, which feeds back into the very price pressures it was trying to ignore. The June rate decision is, in effect, also a currency decision.

timeline.heading: THE TRAP
timeline.body: There is no clean answer to stagflation. Raise rates to fight imported inflation and you deepen the recession; cut rates to support growth and you entrench the inflation. Volcker's 1981 solution worked but cost the deepest US recession since the 1930s. No European policymaker has been willing to repeat it.

blocks.question: In a stagflation, what does the textbook Phillips Curve predict?
blocks.explanation: The Phillips Curve predicts a tradeoff — more jobs, more inflation. Stagflation broke it: both rose at once, which is why the 1970s forced economists to rebuild the model around inflation expectations.

timeline.heading: THE WET-BULB CEILING
timeline.body: Healthy humans cannot survive sustained wet-bulb temperatures above 35°C — the body cannot shed metabolic heat once the air is as wet and hot as your skin. Dry 50°C with low humidity is survivable in shade with water; 40°C at high humidity is not.

blocks.text: The threshold is set by physics, not fitness: at **35°C wet-bulb**, sweat stops evaporating. Core temperature climbs roughly **0.1°C per minute** with no recovery path short of active cooling.

timeline.heading: WHY NIGHTS MATTER MORE THAN DAYS
timeline.body: The human body tolerates daytime extremes if it can dump accumulated heat overnight. When minimums stay above 30°C, that recovery window closes. Mortality data from the 2003 European heatwave, the 2010 Russian heatwave, and the 2015 Karachi heatwave all track nighttime temperature more tightly than daytime peaks.

timeline.heading: THE 2015 KARACHI PRECEDENT
timeline.body: A June 2015 heatwave killed more than 1,200 people in Karachi over five days. It coincided with Ramadan — fasting workers lost their hydration window — and with grid failures that knocked out fans and pumps. The morgue at Edhi overflowed; bodies were stacked in cold storage trucks. Every variable that drove that toll is present again.

blocks.question: What made the June 2015 Karachi heatwave so deadly compared to similar temperatures elsewhere?
options: Higher absolute peak temperatures than ever recorded in South Asia
Overlap with Ramadan fasting plus rolling power cuts to fans and water pumps
A novel virus that amplified heat-stress mortality
Unusually low humidity that dehydrated victims faster
blocks.explanation: Ramadan removed the daytime hydration window; load-shedding removed fans and pumped water — the two compounding stressors drove deaths far above what the raw temperature predicted.

timeline.heading: WHO IS EXPOSED
timeline.body: Heat mortality clusters among outdoor laborers, the elderly, and those without air conditioning. In Pakistan roughly 60% of the workforce is in agriculture or construction — outdoors, during peak heat, with no practical option to stop working.

timeline.heading: THE GRID FEEDBACK LOOP
timeline.body: Extreme heat drives AC demand, which overloads Pakistan's chronically under-supplied grid, which triggers load-shedding, which removes fans and water pumps from the homes that needed them most. The grid fails hardest exactly when survival depends on it.

timeline.heading: JACOBABAD, EARTH'S FRONTIER
timeline.body: Jacobabad in upper Sindh has crossed the 35°C wet-bulb threshold multiple times in the last decade — one of only a handful of inhabited places on Earth to do so. Climate models projected such crossings for mid-century; they began arriving in the 2010s.

timeline.heading: THE STRUCTURAL DEFICIT
timeline.body: Pakistan grows enough wheat and rice in normal years but imports nearly all its edible oil, pulses, and increasingly sugar. A bad domestic harvest does not just dent supply — it forces dollar outflows the central bank can barely spare.

blocks.text: Pakistan is the world's **fourth-largest palm oil importer**, sourcing nearly all of it from *Indonesia* and *Malaysia*. Edible oil alone runs $3–4bn a year — more than the country's entire textile machinery import bill.

timeline.heading: THE SUGAR REVERSAL
timeline.body: Pakistan was a sugar exporter as recently as the 2010s, with government-backed cane support prices producing structural surpluses. A 100-fold jump in sugar imports in one year signals not a market move but a policy and harvest failure stacking on top of each other.

timeline.heading: THE DENOMINATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: Pakistan borrows in both rupees and dollars. Rupee debt can theoretically be inflated away, but that destroys domestic purchasing power. Dollar debt cannot — a falling rupee makes every imported tonne of palm oil or sugar more expensive in local currency, feeding food inflation that hits the poorest hardest.

timeline.heading: WHY THE IMF CARES
timeline.body: Pakistan's IMF program is built around a primary surplus target and reserve floors. Food imports of $7.85bn are roughly half the State Bank's gross reserves at a typical IMF-review snapshot — meaning the food trade gap is not a side issue, it is the binding constraint on the program.

blocks.label: where Pakistan's food dollars go
blocks.caption: Palm oil from Indonesia/Malaysia; pulses and sugar via India and Gulf re-exporters.

timeline.heading: THE 1977 RHYME
timeline.body: Bhutto's last months in office saw flour shortages that Zia's coup later cited as evidence of administrative collapse. Bread and sugar prices in Karachi and Lahore predate the IMF era as a recurring stress test of state legitimacy — every Pakistani government since has treated atta and cheeni prices as politically untouchable.

blocks.question: Pakistan's sugar imports jumped from 3,000 tonnes to 309,000 tonnes in one year. What does this most directly signal?
options: A collapse in the domestic support-price/harvest system
blocks.explanation: A 100x swing reflects domestic supply failure plus policy mismanagement — Pakistan had been structurally self-sufficient in sugar via cane support prices.

timeline.heading: THE WITHDRAWAL LOOPHOLE THAT WASN'T
timeline.body: Article 127 of the Rome Statute lets a state quit the ICC with one year's notice, but explicitly preserves jurisdiction over crimes committed while membership was active. Duterte announced withdrawal in March 2018; it took effect March 2019. Every killing before that date remains prosecutable forever.

blocks.text: The drafters anticipated exactly this scenario — a leader committing atrocities, then trying to *withdraw retroactively*. Article **127(2)** closes the door.

timeline.heading: THE DRUG WAR AS POLICY
timeline.body: From 2016 to 2022, Philippine police acknowledged killing roughly 6,000 people in anti-drug operations; human rights groups put the true total above 30,000 once vigilante killings are counted. The ICC investigation focuses on whether the killings constituted a state policy of murder — the threshold for crimes against humanity.

blocks.label: official vs estimated drug war deaths, 2016–2022

timeline.heading: THE COMPLEMENTARITY PRINCIPLE
timeline.body: The ICC is a court of last resort. It can only act when national courts are 'unwilling or unable' to prosecute. The Marcos government's argument that domestic remedies suffice has now been rejected by the Philippine Supreme Court itself — making the jurisdictional question politically harder to contest.

timeline.heading: WHY SENATORS ARE HARD TO ARREST
timeline.body: Philippine senators enjoy parliamentary immunity for offenses punishable by under six years — not a shield here, since crimes against humanity carry no such ceiling. The harder barrier is political: the Senate has historically resisted surrendering its own, and ICC arrests depend entirely on cooperative national police.

blocks.question: The ICC has no police force of its own. How does it actually arrest suspects?
options: Interpol Red Notice combined with state police cooperation
ICC marshals deployed from The Hague
Bounty hunters licensed by the Assembly of States Parties
blocks.explanation: The ICC depends entirely on member-state police forces — which is why suspects can remain at large for years in cooperative or uncooperative jurisdictions.

timeline.heading: THE REGIONAL CONTEXT
timeline.body: Southeast Asia is the world's least-ICC-aligned region. The Philippines was the only ASEAN founding member of the court; its 2019 exit left zero current members in the bloc. Domestic accountability for state violence is correspondingly thin across the region.

blocks.label: ASEAN: ICC membership status
blocks.caption: None currently members; only the Philippines (2011–2019) ever joined

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT THAT MATTERS
timeline.body: Only one sitting head of state has ever been transferred to The Hague during their term — Côte d'Ivoire's Laurent Gbagbo in 2011, after losing an election and a civil war. Every other indicted leader (Bashir, Putin, Netanyahu) has remained at large. A senator-rank target is unusual precisely because mid-tier officials are politically cheaper to surrender than presidents.

timeline.heading: WHY REFINERIES, NOT WELLS
timeline.body: Crude oil is useless to an army. Tanks, jets, and trucks need diesel, kerosene, and gasoline — products only refineries make. Striking a wellhead halts future export revenue; striking a refinery starves the front line within weeks.

blocks.text: Ukraine's doctrine inverts the Allied WWII playbook: the **Oil Campaign of 1944** bombed Ploiești's refineries, not Romania's wells, and Wehrmacht fuel stocks collapsed within months.

timeline.heading: THE BOTTLENECK
timeline.body: Russia has roughly 30 major refineries concentrated in European Russia and the Volga basin. Each is a sprawling, fixed installation of cracking towers, hydrotreaters, and distillation columns — bespoke equipment with multi-year lead times, much of it Western-built and now sanctioned.

timeline.heading: THE RANGE PROBLEM
timeline.body: Syzran sits roughly 850 km from the Ukrainian border. Hitting it requires long-range strike drones — Ukrainian designs like the Liutyi and modified An-196 with ranges of 1,000+ km, built indigenously after Western partners declined to supply equivalent missiles.

blocks.question: Why has Ukraine built its own long-range strike drones rather than buying Western cruise missiles?
options: Cost — drones are 50× cheaper per shot
Western partners refused to supply weapons that strike deep inside Russia
Drones evade Russian air defenses better
blocks.explanation: Each factor matters: Storm Shadow and ATACMS came with range restrictions on Russian territory, a Shahed-class drone costs ~$50k vs. millions for a cruise missile, and slow low-flying drones often slip under radar coverage tuned for jets.

timeline.heading: THE REVENUE LINK
timeline.body: Russia's federal budget draws roughly a third of revenue from oil and gas. Refined product exports — diesel especially — were a major workaround after the EU's crude embargo, sold to refining-short buyers in Turkey, Brazil, and India. Disabling refineries hits both domestic supply and export earnings at once.

timeline.heading: THE REPAIR CYCLE
timeline.body: After each strike Russia patches damaged units, but sanctioned catalyst and Western spare parts force cannibalization across sites. Strikes in 2024 took roughly 14% of Russian refining capacity offline at the peak; gasoline shortages forced an export ban that summer.

timeline.heading: THE HISTORICAL ECHO
timeline.body: In 1941 Stalin evacuated entire factories east of the Volga to put them beyond German bomber range. The Volga refineries — Syzran, Samara, Novokuibyshevsk — were built or expanded in that strategic depth. Drone warfare has now collapsed the geography that protected them for eighty years.

timeline.heading: WHERE KASSALA SITS
timeline.body: Kassala lies in Sudan's far east, against the Eritrean border and far from the Khartoum-Omdurman war front. Its relative distance from the main RSF-SAF battles has made it a refuge city — and a sensitive one, because the army controls it and tolerates little dissent about how it's run.

timeline.heading: THE TWO ARMIES
timeline.body: Sudan's war is between two generals who once partnered to overthrow a civilian government. The SAF under Burhan and the RSF under Hemedti jointly crushed the 2019 democracy movement, then turned on each other in April 2023 when a transition deal collapsed.

people.name: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan
people.role: SAF commander, de facto head of state

timeline.heading: THE RSF'S ORIGINS
timeline.body: The RSF evolved from the Janjaweed militias that carried out the Darfur genocide beginning in 2003. Bashir armed Arab militias to fight non-Arab rebels, then formalized them as the Rapid Support Forces in 2013. Hemedti, a former camel trader, rose from militia commander to the second most powerful man in Sudan — with troops loyal to him personally, not the state.

timeline.heading: THE INFORMATION WAR
timeline.body: In civil wars where both sides claim legitimacy, the first casualty is forensic truth. A *landmine* implies RSF infiltration eastward; a *drone strike* implies a specific actor with specific capabilities. Detaining a witness within 24 hours is less about the witness than about which narrative is allowed to set.

blocks.text: The distinction matters: **landmines** suggest territory contested or recently passed through; **drones** point to a deliberate, attributable strike from a known operator — Sudan's war now sees both Turkish-supplied SAF drones and UAE-linked RSF drones.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL VEHICLE
timeline.body: Sudan's 1996 Press and Publications Act and the 2020 Cybercrimes Law both criminalize 'spreading false news' — vague enough to cover almost any post a security service dislikes. Detentions are typically incommunicado and rarely produce a trial; the punishment is the process.

timeline.heading: WHY IT WORKS
timeline.body: Authoritarian regimes don't suppress dissent by convincing the population — they suppress it by raising the personal cost of a single Facebook post until silence becomes rational. One arrest broadcast through a community deters thousands of unwritten posts.

blocks.question: What does the Sudanese army gain most from arresting a witness who disputed the official blast account?
options: A criminal conviction that establishes the official version as legal truth
Deterrence — making other potential witnesses self-censor before posting
Intelligence about a specific opposition cell
Compliance with the 2020 Cybercrimes Law's reporting requirements
blocks.explanation: The arrest's value is the chilling effect on everyone else who saw the blast, not the case against the individual — which is why trials rarely follow.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: Matsu is a Taiwanese archipelago lying just 10 km off China's Fujian coast — closer to Fuzhou than to Taipei. Its 14,000 residents depend on two submarine cables snaking across one of the world's busiest fishing grounds for everything from banking to hospital records.

timeline.heading: WHY CABLES, NOT SATELLITES
timeline.body: Roughly 99% of intercontinental data moves through ~500 submarine cables, not satellites. A single fiber pair carries terabits per second; even Starlink's entire constellation cannot match one modern cable's capacity. Cables are also a hundred times cheaper per bit — which is why every island, every continent, every financial center is wired, not beamed.

blocks.text: The technical term is **landing station** — the coastal facility where a cable terminates. Cut the cable offshore and the landing station goes dark; there is no wireless fallback at carrier scale.

timeline.heading: GREY-ZONE COERCION
timeline.body: Grey-zone tactics sit deliberately below the threshold of armed conflict: actions damaging enough to coerce but ambiguous enough to deny. A fishing trawler dragging an anchor across a cable is plausibly an accident; the same vessel doing it twice, in the same place, to the same cable, is not. Attribution is the entire battlefield.

blocks.question: What makes 'grey-zone' actions strategically valuable to the actor using them?
options: They cause more damage than conventional strikes
They stay below the threshold that triggers a treaty response
They are cheaper than diplomatic pressure
They cannot be detected by the targeted state
blocks.explanation: Grey-zone tactics work precisely because they're ambiguous — clear enough to coerce, deniable enough to avoid triggering Article 5-style obligations or formal sanctions.

timeline.heading: THE 2023 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In February 2023, both Matsu cables were severed within six days — one by a Chinese fishing vessel, one by a Chinese cargo ship, per Taiwan's Coast Guard. Repairs took over 50 days because the world's small fleet of cable-repair ships was booked elsewhere; the Pacific has fewer than 60 such vessels and most are leased years in advance.

timeline.heading: THE ATTRIBUTION GAME
timeline.body: International law on subsea cables traces to the 1884 Convention for the Protection of Submarine Cables — written for telegraph lines and never meaningfully updated. It criminalizes 'wilful or culpably negligent' cable damage but provides no enforcement mechanism in another state's EEZ. Taiwan logging vessel AIS data, hull photos, and anchor scars is building the only kind of case that can be made: evidentiary, public, slow.

timeline.heading: THE TAIWAN STRESS TEST
timeline.body: Matsu is widely read as a live-fire rehearsal. If China can sever an outer island's connectivity without consequence, the same playbook scales to the 14 international cables landing on Taiwan proper. A pre-invasion blackout — banks frozen, command-and-control degraded, social media silenced — is a doctrine, not a hypothetical; it appears in PLA writings on 'informationized warfare.'

timeline.heading: WHY A PARALLEL STACK
timeline.body: US export controls under the Foreign Direct Product Rule reach any chip, software, or satellite component touched by American technology — even when built abroad. A parallel stack is the only way for sanctioned states to escape that extraterritorial reach.

blocks.text: The doctrine is called *extraterritoriality*: a US-origin transistor in a Dutch lithography machine makes the **entire downstream product** subject to Washington's licensing regime.

timeline.heading: THE SATELLITE INTERNET RACE
timeline.body: Low Earth Orbit constellations need thousands of satellites to provide continuous coverage. SpaceX's Starlink has launched the bulk of all active satellites; China's Guowang and Qianfan projects together target similar scale by the 2030s. Russia's Sfera has slipped repeatedly and orbits a fraction of what was promised.

timeline.heading: THE STARLINK PROBLEM FOR MOSCOW
timeline.body: Ukraine's battlefield dependence on Starlink — and Elon Musk's unilateral authority to switch it off — made every adversary of the US realize that orbital comms are a strategic vulnerability. Russia and China both want sovereign alternatives; neither can build one alone at competitive cost.

timeline.heading: WHY OPEN-SOURCE MATTERS
timeline.body: GitHub, owned by Microsoft, complies with US sanctions and has restricted access for users in Iran, Crimea, and parts of Russia. China's Gitee and Russia's GitFlic are the domestic mirrors — but the world's developers, libraries, and CI tooling still orbit GitHub. A genuine alternative requires not just a server but an entire ecosystem.

blocks.question: Which country had the largest GitHub user base affected by US sanctions restrictions?
