blocks.explanation: GitHub restricted Iranian accounts in 2019 under OFAC sanctions; the policy was partially reversed in 2021 after developer protests, but the precedent stuck.

timeline.heading: THE BLOC GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: The target market is the Global South — countries that want connectivity and code repositories without accepting US licensing terms. Iran, Cuba, Myanmar, and most recently the Sahel juntas have all sought alternatives to Western digital infrastructure.

timeline.heading: THE HISTORICAL RHYME
timeline.body: The Soviet bloc built parallel standards for everything — Comecon computers ran clones of IBM mainframes, the OGAS network was a proposed Soviet internet that Brezhnev killed in 1970. Every tech bifurcation in history has produced two viable stacks only when the smaller bloc had genuine industrial depth. Russia today does not; China does.

timeline.heading: WHAT A PITOT TUBE DOES
timeline.body: A pitot tube is a forward-facing probe that measures airspeed by comparing ram air pressure against static pressure. Every fixed-wing aircraft since the 1930s relies on it. When it ices over, the airspeed reading goes wrong — sometimes to zero, sometimes frozen at the last valid value.

blocks.text: The instrument is named for *Henri Pitot*, the 18th-century French engineer who built the first version to measure river current speed in the Seine.

timeline.heading: THE THALES AA MODEL
timeline.body: AF447's Airbus A330 used Thales AA-model pitot probes. By 2008, Airbus and Air France had logged multiple in-flight icing incidents at high altitude with that specific model. A replacement program to the Thales BA model was underway but not yet mandatory when the aircraft went down on June 1, 2009.

timeline.heading: THE HANDOFF PROBLEM
timeline.body: When the airspeed reading failed mid-Atlantic, the A330's autopilot disengaged and handed control to pilots cruising at 35,000 feet at night over the ocean. The crew had never trained for unreliable-airspeed recovery at cruise altitude — simulator scenarios at the time covered the maneuver near the ground, where the aerodynamics are different.

timeline.heading: THE STALL THAT FOLLOWED
timeline.body: The pilot flying pulled back on the sidestick and held nose-up inputs for nearly the entire descent. The A330 stalled and fell 38,000 feet in 3 minutes 30 seconds, wings level, into the Atlantic. Cockpit voice recorders, recovered two years later from 3,900 metres of seawater, captured a crew that never identified the stall.

timeline.heading: WHY THE VERDICT IS UNUSUAL
timeline.body: French courts had acquitted both firms in 2023; this appeals reversal is the first time a Western manufacturer and a flag carrier have been jointly convicted of corporate manslaughter over a commercial crash. Aviation safety jurisprudence has historically treated crashes as systemic learning events, not criminal ones — the fear being that criminal exposure suppresses the candid reporting that makes aviation safe.

blocks.question: What is the standard global framework for investigating commercial aviation crashes?
blocks.explanation: ICAO Annex 13 mandates that crash investigations focus on prevention, not liability — evidence gathered cannot normally be used in criminal proceedings. The French case ran in parallel under domestic criminal law.

timeline.heading: THE BLACK BOX RECOVERY
timeline.body: The flight data and cockpit voice recorders sat on the mid-Atlantic ridge for 23 months before a fourth search, using autonomous underwater vehicles, located them in May 2011. Without that recovery, the icing-induced airspeed failure would likely have remained a leading hypothesis but never a proven chain — and this verdict would not have been possible.

timeline.heading: WHAT PULWAMA WAS
timeline.body: On 14 February 2019, a convoy of 78 buses carrying Indian paramilitary police was struck by a vehicle-borne suicide bomber on the Jammu-Srinagar highway. Forty CRPF personnel died — the deadliest attack on Indian security forces in Kashmir's three-decade insurgency. Jaish-e-Mohammed claimed responsibility within hours.

timeline.heading: THE BALAKOT REPLY
timeline.body: Twelve days after Pulwama, Indian Mirage 2000s crossed the Line of Control and struck what India said was a JeM training camp at Balakot — the first Indian airstrike inside undisputed Pakistani territory since 1971. Pakistan responded the next day; an Indian MiG-21 was downed and its pilot captured, then released within 60 hours. The episode rewrote the unwritten rules between two nuclear states.

timeline.heading: WHO JAISH-E-MOHAMMED IS
timeline.body: JeM was founded in 2000 by Masood Azhar, released by India a year earlier in the IC-814 hijacking exchange. The group is headquartered in Bahawalpur, Punjab, and was designated a terrorist organization by the UN in 2001 — though Azhar himself was only listed in 2019 after years of Chinese vetoes at the Security Council were withdrawn.

blocks.text: JeM is doctrinally distinct from **Lashkar-e-Taiba**: Lashkar grew out of the Ahl-e-Hadith tradition, JeM out of the *Deobandi* madrassa network, which gives it deeper recruitment reach into Pakistani Punjab.

timeline.heading: WHY MUZAFFARABAD
timeline.body: Muzaffarabad is the capital of Azad Jammu and Kashmir, the slice of Kashmir Pakistan administers. It has long hosted militant infrastructure — training camps, safehouses, organizational headquarters — at distances from the Line of Control measured in tens of kilometers. Targeted killings of militant figures inside AJK, attributed to unknown gunmen, have become a recognizable pattern since roughly 2023.

timeline.heading: THE PATTERN OF UNCLAIMED KILLINGS
timeline.body: Since 2023, at least a dozen India-designated militants — figures from JeM, Lashkar, and Hizbul Mujahideen — have been shot dead inside Pakistan by unidentified gunmen, often outside mosques or homes. India denies involvement; Pakistan has publicly accused Indian intelligence of running a covert assassination program on its soil, echoing accusations leveled by Canada and the United States in the same period.

blocks.question: What was India's most consequential domestic response to the Pulwama attack?
options: Withdrawal from the Indus Waters Treaty
Revocation of Article 370, ending Kashmir's special autonomous status
Closure of the Wagah border crossing
Suspension of cricket ties with Pakistan
blocks.explanation: On 5 August 2019, six months after Pulwama, India abrogated Article 370 of its constitution, stripping Jammu & Kashmir of statehood and the special autonomy it had held since 1949.

timeline.heading: THE NUCLEAR FLOOR
timeline.body: India and Pakistan have fought four wars and maintained one of the world's most active militarized borders, yet neither has crossed the threshold to general war since both went overtly nuclear in 1998. The Pulwama-Balakot exchange tested how much conventional escalation that floor permits — and the answer, so far, has been: more than analysts assumed, but less than either side's rhetoric suggests.

timeline.heading: THE BROKER PROBLEM
timeline.body: For most of the 20th century, Central Asian states reached Africa through Moscow's diplomatic networks, and Francophone Africa reached Asia through Paris. Both regions inherited foreign ministries shaped around metropoles, not peer-to-peer ties.

blocks.text: The technical term is **hub-and-spoke diplomacy** — capitals talk to the former imperial center, not to each other. Decolonizing the network means building *direct* embassies, which is exactly what Bishkek is doing now.

timeline.heading: WHY KYRGYZSTAN, NOT KAZAKHSTAN
timeline.body: Kazakhstan has the oil, Uzbekistan has the population, but Kyrgyzstan has the smallest stake in Russian or Chinese alignment and the most freedom to experiment. Small states in multipolar moments often move first precisely because they have the least to lose.

timeline.heading: THE TURKIC BRIDGE
timeline.body: Kyrgyzstan is a member of the Organization of Turkic States, which since 2009 has linked Ankara, Astana, Tashkent, Baku, and Bishkek. Turkey's own pivot into Africa — embassies grew from 12 in 2002 to over 44 today — gives the Turkic bloc a ready-made template and existing logistical rails to plug into.

blocks.label: the Turkic states
blocks.caption: Bishkek's nearest diplomatic neighborhood

timeline.heading: THE NON-ALIGNED ECHO
timeline.body: The 1955 Bandung Conference brought 29 Asian and African states together to articulate a third path between Washington and Moscow. The Soviet republics were absent — they were on one side of the Cold War, not seeking exits from it. Today's Central Asia–Africa overture is, in a real sense, the conversation that 1955 excluded.

blocks.question: Which conference, in 1955, first formally linked Asian and African states outside the two Cold War blocs?
blocks.explanation: Bandung (Indonesia, 1955) gathered 29 newly independent Asian and African states and became the founding moment of the Non-Aligned Movement.

timeline.heading: WHAT AFRICA OFFERS
timeline.body: 54 UN votes — more than any other continental bloc — plus critical minerals (cobalt, lithium, manganese) that Central Asia's nascent processing industries want to source outside Chinese supply chains. The relationship is not yet about trade volume; it is about voting blocs and raw-material optionality.

blocks.text: Africa's *54 UN General Assembly votes* are the single largest regional bloc — larger than Asia's 47 or Europe's 43. For small states seeking visibility on resolutions about sovereignty, sanctions, or great-power competition, that bloc is the most valuable asset on the diplomatic map.

timeline.heading: WHY EUROPE IS UNUSUALLY EXPOSED
timeline.body: The Eurozone imports roughly 90% of its crude and over 80% of its natural gas. Unlike the US, which became a net energy exporter in 2019, Europe has no domestic cushion — every dollar of oil above trend is a direct transfer out of the bloc.

timeline.heading: THE STAGFLATION TRAP
timeline.body: An oil shock raises prices and cuts growth simultaneously — the textbook stagflation pattern. Central banks face an impossible choice: hike to defend the currency and crush demand further, or hold to support growth and let inflation expectations unmoor.

blocks.text: The term *stagflation* was coined in 1965 by UK politician Iain Macleod and entered the economic canon after the **1973 OPEC embargo** broke the post-war Phillips-curve consensus that inflation and unemployment moved in opposite directions.

timeline.heading: THE 1973 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: When OPEC quadrupled oil prices after the Yom Kippur war, West German growth collapsed from 5% to under 1% within a year, and the Bundesbank tightened into the recession. The episode shaped the ECB's founding charter: a single mandate of price stability, even at the cost of growth.

timeline.heading: WHY HORMUZ MATTERS TO BRUSSELS
timeline.body: Roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil and a third of global LNG transits the Strait of Hormuz. Europe's marginal barrel — the one that sets the price — comes from the Gulf even when the average barrel does not.

timeline.heading: THE ECB'S CONSTRAINT
timeline.body: Unlike the Fed, the ECB has only an inflation mandate — no employment mandate. When energy lifts headline CPI above target, the legal framework pushes toward hiking even into a slowdown. The euro's weakness against the dollar compounds the imported-inflation problem.

timeline.heading: THE FISCAL ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: Energy shocks hit Eurozone members unevenly — Germany's industrial base bleeds more than France's nuclear-powered grid, and Italy's debt-to-GDP leaves little room to subsidize bills. Brussels-level forecasts mask divergences that strain the common currency.

blocks.question: What was novel about the ECB's mandate when it was founded in 1998?
options: It had a dual mandate for inflation and employment, like the Fed
It had a single mandate for price stability, modeled on the Bundesbank
It targeted exchange-rate stability against the dollar
It explicitly included financial stability as a co-equal goal
blocks.explanation: The ECB inherited the Bundesbank's single-mandate model — a legacy of Weimar hyperinflation and the 1970s oil shocks that prioritized inflation control above all else.

timeline.heading: THE DSA ARCHITECTURE
timeline.body: The Digital Services Act, in force since 2024, designates platforms with over 45 million EU users as Very Large Online Platforms — VLOPs — subject to systemic risk audits, researcher data access, and fines up to 6% of global turnover. Google, Meta, and TikTok all qualify.

blocks.text: For Meta, 6% of 2024 global turnover is roughly **$10 billion** per violation — an order of magnitude above any GDPR fine ever levied.

timeline.heading: THE NOTICE-AND-ACTION REGIME
timeline.body: DSA Article 16 requires platforms to remove illegal content 'expeditiously' once notified. The 27% removal rate the consumer groups reported is the operative number — it converts a complaint into evidence that the notice-and-action system is failing at scale, which is itself a DSA violation independent of the ads.

blocks.question: Under the DSA, what triggers platform liability for illegal content?
options: Failing to act expeditiously after notification
blocks.explanation: The DSA preserves the hosting safe harbor from the e-Commerce Directive — liability attaches only when a platform fails to act on a valid notice.

timeline.heading: THE COUNTRY-OF-ORIGIN PROBLEM
timeline.body: Most US platforms route their EU operations through Ireland for tax reasons, which historically made Ireland's Data Protection Commission the lead regulator for GDPR complaints — and a notorious bottleneck. The DSA breaks this: enforcement against VLOPs sits with the European Commission directly, not the host-country regulator.

blocks.label: where EU tech enforcement actually happens

timeline.heading: WHY SCAM ADS PERSIST
timeline.body: Programmatic advertising auctions buyers in milliseconds across thousands of demand-side platforms. The platform serving the ad often does not know the advertiser's true identity until after the impression — by design. KYC for advertisers exists on paper; in practice, shell entities and stolen payment cards route around it routinely.

timeline.heading: THE FINE THAT MATTERS
timeline.body: GDPR's 4% cap produced headline fines but rarely changed behavior — most were appealed for years and settled lower. The DSA's 6% applies to global, not European, turnover and is paired with the threat of temporary service suspension in the EU. The deterrent is the suspension, not the cash.

blocks.label: Maximum fine exposure (6% of 2024 global revenue)

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT OF BEUC
timeline.body: The European Consumer Organisation — BEUC — is a federation of 45 national consumer groups across 32 countries. Its complaints have historically seeded major EU actions: the 2018 Google Android antitrust case, the 2022 dark-patterns guidelines, and several DSA risk-assessment audits all traced back to BEUC filings.

timeline.heading: WHY PRESERVATIVES EXIST
timeline.body: Before refrigeration, salt, sugar, and smoke were the only ways to stop microbial growth. Industrial preservatives — nitrites, sorbates, benzoates — emerged in the early 20th century to extend shelf life across global supply chains. The same compounds that prevent botulism in cured meats are now suspected of cardiovascular harm at chronic doses.

blocks.text: **Sodium nitrite** does two jobs in cured meat: it blocks *Clostridium botulinum* and fixes the pink color consumers associate with freshness. Removing it is harder than it sounds — the alternative is botulism risk.

timeline.heading: THE COHORT METHOD
timeline.body: NutriNet-Santé is a French prospective cohort — volunteers log dietary intake repeatedly over years while researchers track health outcomes. Unlike a randomized trial, cohorts cannot prove causation, but they can detect associations across populations large enough to control for confounders like smoking, exercise, and income.

timeline.heading: WHY 29% MATTERS
timeline.body: In epidemiology, a 29% relative risk increase across a population of 112,400 is a substantial signal — large enough to survive adjustment for diet quality, BMI, and lifestyle. For comparison, the relative risk of hypertension from high sodium intake sits around 20-30%. Preservatives may be operating in the same magnitude class as salt itself.

blocks.question: In nutritional epidemiology, what does a 'prospective cohort study' do that a retrospective study cannot?
options: Prove direct causation between exposure and outcome
Track exposures before outcomes occur, reducing recall bias
Eliminate the need for control groups
Test interventions in a controlled setting
blocks.explanation: Prospective cohorts log exposures in real time, so participants who later develop disease cannot misremember their diet — a major flaw in retrospective designs.

timeline.heading: THE NITRITE PARADOX
timeline.body: Sodium nitrite is the most studied compound on the list. It prevents botulism, a paralytic disease that killed thousands before industrial curing. The WHO classified processed meats as Group 1 carcinogens in 2015 largely because of nitrite-derived nitrosamines. Regulators have known about the tradeoff for decades; the political question is whether cardiovascular risk shifts the calculus.

timeline.heading: THE ASCORBIC ACID SURPRISE
timeline.body: Ascorbic acid is vitamin C — the same compound in oranges. As an additive, it functions as an antioxidant that prevents fats from going rancid. Its appearance on a hypertension-risk list is the study's most counterintuitive finding and the one most likely to be a confounder: foods that need ascorbic acid added are often the same ultra-processed foods that drive blood pressure through other mechanisms.

blocks.text: This is the *correlation-vs-causation* trap in nutritional science: the additive may be a **marker** of ultra-processing rather than the **cause** of the harm.

timeline.heading: THE REGULATORY ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: The EU operates on the precautionary principle — additives must be proven safe before approval, and re-evaluations can restrict them on emerging evidence. The US FDA largely grandfathers compounds under the GRAS (Generally Recognized As Safe) designation, where manufacturers self-certify safety. The same compound can carry different legal status on either side of the Atlantic.

blocks.label: how each system handles a suspect additive

timeline.heading: TWO STATIONS BOLTED TOGETHER
timeline.body: The ISS is functionally two stations sharing a truss: the US Orbital Segment (with European, Japanese, and Canadian modules) and the Russian Orbital Segment. They use different software, different docking standards, and different atmospheric pressures historically — a Cold War compromise frozen into orbiting hardware.

blocks.text: The Russian segment provides *propulsion and reboost*; the US segment provides *power and attitude control*. Neither half can fly alone — separation has been studied and rejected as infeasible without years of refit.

timeline.heading: WHERE THE LEAK IS
timeline.body: The cracks are in the PrK transfer tunnel connecting the Zvezda service module to a docking port. Zvezda launched in 2000 and was already a decade old at launch — built in the 1980s as a backup for the Soviet Mir-2 program that never flew.

events.label: Repurposed for ISS after USSR collapse

timeline.heading: THE RISK MATRIX
timeline.body: NASA's 5x5 risk matrix scores likelihood and consequence each 1-5. A '5' in both axes is the agency's highest category — reserved for events that are both probable and catastrophic. The Columbia foam strike, in hindsight, would have scored similarly.

timeline.heading: WHY NOTHING REPLACES IT
timeline.body: Commercial successors — Axiom, Orbital Reef, Starlab, Vast's Haven — exist on paper and in early hardware. None has flown a crewed module. The ISS retirement date has slipped repeatedly because the gap between 'ISS works' and 'commercial station ready' keeps widening.

timeline.heading: THE DEORBIT PROBLEM
timeline.body: The ISS masses 420 tonnes. Letting it fall uncontrolled would scatter debris across hundreds of kilometers. NASA awarded SpaceX an $843M contract in 2024 to build a deorbit vehicle — a one-shot tug that will push the station into a Pacific reentry corridor known as Point Nemo, the spacecraft graveyard farthest from any inhabited land.

timeline.heading: WHO STAYS, WHO GOES
timeline.body: Russia has announced it will leave the ISS partnership after 2028 to build its own station, ROSS. The US-Russian crew-swap agreement — each side flies the other's astronauts as insurance against a single-vehicle failure — survived the Ukraine war as one of the last functioning bilateral programs.

blocks.question: Which country operates the only other crewed space station currently in orbit?
blocks.explanation: China's Tiangong has been continuously crewed since 2022 — making it the second operational crewed station after the ISS.

timeline.heading: TWO DISEASES, TWO MECHANISMS
timeline.body: Dementia (mostly Alzheimer's) is driven by amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the cortex — memory and reasoning erode first. Parkinson's begins in the substantia nigra, where dopamine-producing neurons die — movement fails before cognition. They share an aging substrate but progress through different brain regions on different timelines.

blocks.text: The two are sometimes confused because late-stage Parkinson's can develop dementia (*Lewy body dementia*) and late Alzheimer's can produce motor symptoms — but the **first decade** of each disease looks nothing like the other.

timeline.heading: WHY INCIDENCE CAN FALL WHILE PREVALENCE RISES
timeline.body: Incidence is new cases per year. Prevalence is people currently living with the disease. Better treatment of heart disease and stroke means more people survive to ages where dementia would once have killed them indirectly — so prevalence rises even as age-adjusted incidence drops. The same arithmetic has played out across the UK, US, and Nordic registries since the 2000s.

timeline.heading: THE DIAGNOSIS WAVE
timeline.body: A sudden tripling of dementia rarely reflects a biological surge. It usually means the health system started looking — new screening protocols, insurance reimbursement for cognitive testing, public awareness campaigns. Korea launched its National Dementia Plan in 2008 and expanded free screening through public health centers in the 2010s. The 2018 peak likely marks the moment detection caught up with reality.

blocks.question: When a country's dementia incidence triples then falls, what most often explains the curve?
options: An environmental toxin that was identified and removed
A new screening program that first detected, then saturated, the existing pool of cases
A genetic shift in the population
A change in the definition of dementia by the WHO
blocks.explanation: Once a screening program reaches everyone it can reach, the apparent incidence drops back toward the true underlying rate — the curve reflects measurement, not biology.

timeline.heading: THE FASTEST-AGING COUNTRY ON EARTH
timeline.body: Korea's fertility rate is roughly 0.75 — the lowest ever recorded for a major economy. The share of Koreans over 65 has doubled in 17 years. Any age-related disease will rise in raw counts for decades regardless of what age-adjusted rates do, because the denominator is shifting.

timeline.heading: THE RURAL SURVIVAL GAP
timeline.body: Once diagnosed, where you live shapes how long you live. Rural Korean counties have fewer neurologists per capita, longer drives to memory clinics, and thinner home-care networks. The survival gap between Seoul and a depopulating southern county can run several years for the same diagnosis at the same age — a pattern mirrored in rural Japan, Appalachian US, and the German Länder.

timeline.heading: WHY PARKINSON'S FELL
timeline.body: Parkinson's incidence has dropped quietly across several high-income countries, and no one is sure why. Leading hypotheses: declining smoking rates correlate paradoxically with rising Parkinson's (nicotine appears mildly protective of dopamine neurons), reduced pesticide exposure in agriculture, and better treatment of vascular risk factors that mimic or trigger parkinsonian symptoms.

timeline.heading: THE STRANDED CAPACITY PARADOX
timeline.body: Nigeria has roughly 13,000MW of installed generation capacity but typically dispatches only 4,000-5,000MW. The gap is not a shortage of plants — it is a shortage of working gas pipelines, functioning transmission lines, and creditworthy buyers downstream.

blocks.text: Nigeria's per-capita electricity consumption is **~150 kWh/year** — roughly *one-twentieth* of South Africa's and less than a single American refrigerator uses in a year.

timeline.heading: THE CIRCULAR DEBT LOOP
timeline.body: Generators sell power to the national grid operator, which sells to DISCOs, which bill consumers. Each link underpays the next. When generators cannot pay gas suppliers, supply gets cut — which is exactly what stranded Alaoji for three years.

timeline.heading: THE PRIVATIZATION THAT WASN'T
timeline.body: Nigeria broke up the state monopoly NEPA in 2013, selling generation and distribution to private investors while keeping transmission state-owned. The reform assumed tariffs would rise to cost-recovery levels. Politically, they never could — so the unbundled system inherited the old deficits in new packaging.

timeline.heading: WHY GAS-FIRED, NOT HYDRO
timeline.body: Nigeria sits on Africa's largest proven natural gas reserves — about 209 trillion cubic feet. Most plants in the south, including Alaoji, are gas-fired and clustered near Niger Delta wellheads. The constraint has never been fuel availability; it is the pipeline network and the willingness of producers to deliver without prepayment.

timeline.heading: THE NAIRA SQUEEZE
timeline.body: Tinubu's 2023 float roughly tripled the naira-dollar rate. Gas contracts and plant maintenance are dollar-denominated; tariffs are naira-denominated. Every devaluation widens the gap the federal budget must absorb to keep generators solvent.

timeline.heading: QUICK CHECK
timeline.body: Most of Nigeria's power crisis is not about building more plants.

blocks.question: What is the main reason Nigeria dispatches less than half its installed power capacity?
blocks.explanation: Nigeria has ~13,000MW installed but dispatches 4-5,000MW. The binding constraint is the payment chain — gas suppliers and transmission, not generation hardware.

timeline.heading: THE FEDERAL GAP
timeline.body: US federal CSAM law (18 USC §2252) requires an actual minor depicted. The 2002 Supreme Court ruling Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition struck down a 1996 law that had banned synthetic child imagery, holding that without a real victim, the speech is protected.

blocks.text: The controlling precedent is *Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition* — synthetic imagery without an identifiable minor falls outside the **Miller** obscenity test and outside §2252.

timeline.heading: THE MORPH EXCEPTION
timeline.body: Courts have carved one narrow path: if a real child's face is grafted onto a synthetic body, prosecutors can charge under §2256(8)(C) — the 'morphed image' clause upheld in US v. Anderson (2014). Most school deepfake cases fit here, but charging requires the victim be identifiable, which not every case provides.

timeline.heading: THE STATE PATCHWORK
timeline.body: By 2026, roughly 30 states have criminalized non-consensual deepfake imagery, but statutes vary wildly — some are misdemeanors, some felonies, some require intent to harass, some cover only adults. A student crossing a state line, or using a server hosted elsewhere, can land outside any single statute's reach.

timeline.heading: WHY THE APPS EXIST
timeline.body: 'Nudify' apps run on open-weight diffusion models — Stable Diffusion derivatives fine-tuned on explicit imagery and wrapped in a consumer UI. Once weights are released publicly, takedown is effectively impossible; the model propagates through torrents, Hugging Face mirrors, and Telegram channels faster than any platform can moderate.

blocks.text: The pivotal release was **Stable Diffusion 1.5** in late 2022 — the first high-quality image model with *fully open weights*. Every consumer nudify app since traces back to that lineage.

timeline.heading: SECTION 230 AND THE APP STORES
timeline.body: App stores host these tools under Section 230 immunity for third-party content. Apple and Google have removed individual apps after press attention, but the same developers re-list under new names within days. The bottleneck isn't legal — it's that no platform faces liability for hosting the distribution layer.

blocks.question: Why doesn't federal CSAM law cover AI-generated images of fictional minors?
options: The Supreme Court ruled in 2002 that synthetic imagery without a real victim is protected speech
The FBI lacks jurisdiction over digital files
blocks.explanation: Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition (2002) struck down the 1996 Child Pornography Prevention Act's ban on virtual CSAM, holding it swept in protected speech.

timeline.heading: THE SCHOOL DISCIPLINE GAP
timeline.body: Schools can suspend or expel under student conduct codes, but Title IX coverage of deepfake harassment remains untested. The 2024 final rule under Biden expanded sex-based harassment definitions; the 2025 rollback narrowed them again. Districts are writing policy in real time without clear federal guidance.

timeline.heading: THE MOLECULE PROBLEM
timeline.body: Hydrofluorocarbons cool efficiently but trap heat thousands of times more effectively than CO2 per molecule. A leaking supermarket rack can emit the climate equivalent of hundreds of cars in a single year.

blocks.text: A common supermarket refrigerant, **R-404A**, has a global warming potential of roughly *3,900* — meaning one kilogram leaked equals nearly four tonnes of CO2.

timeline.heading: THE GENERATIONAL CASCADE
timeline.body: Refrigerants have been swapped out roughly every generation as each chemistry revealed a new harm. CFCs were banned for destroying the ozone layer; HCFCs were interim; HFCs solved ozone but proved to be extreme greenhouse gases; HFOs and natural refrigerants are the next step.

events.label: AIM Act passed by US Congress

timeline.heading: THE KIGALI AMENDMENT
timeline.body: The 2016 Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol committed nations to cut HFC production 85% by 2047. The US ratified it under bipartisan Senate vote in 2022 — one of the rare climate treaties to clear that bar — because the chemical industry itself backed it, having already patented the replacements.

timeline.heading: WHY INDUSTRY WANTED THE BAN
timeline.body: Honeywell and Chemours hold the patents on HFO replacements. A phase-out of off-patent HFCs forces every supermarket and AC manufacturer onto the new, patented chemistry. The ban was less environmental imposition than market reset — which is why the rollback splits the industry, not unites it.

blocks.text: This is the **Montreal Protocol** template: regulation accelerates when incumbents already own the substitute. It is why ozone diplomacy succeeded where carbon diplomacy stalled.

timeline.heading: WHY GROCERIES
timeline.body: Supermarket refrigeration is the single largest stationary HFC source in the US economy — long racks of open cases, hundreds of fittings per store, leak rates averaging 25% of charge per year. A typical store leaks more refrigerant in a year than a fleet of delivery trucks emits in fuel.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of its refrigerant charge does a typical US supermarket leak each year?
blocks.explanation: EPA's GreenChill program documents average leak rates near 25% annually — the reason supermarkets dominate stationary HFC emissions.

timeline.heading: THE COST CLAIM
timeline.body: Compliance costs for HFC transitions are real but concentrated in capital equipment, not in the per-item margin that sets shelf prices. Grocery markups are set by labor, real estate, and supply chain — refrigerant chemistry sits below the threshold where consumers would notice.

timeline.heading: THE ORIGINAL SIN
timeline.body: The Computer Misuse Act was drafted in 1990 after the Gold and Schifreen case, where two hackers accessed Prince Philip's Prestel mailbox and were acquitted because no law fit. Parliament wrote the statute around 'unauthorised access' as a binary — you either had permission or you didn't. The category of researcher testing without prior permission did not exist in the drafters' minds.

blocks.text: The 1990 law predates the **public web** by a year and **Google** by eight. Every ambiguity in modern security research traces back to a statute written when the internet had ~313,000 hosts.

timeline.heading: THE VERIFICATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: Finding a vulnerability and proving it is exploitable are different acts. A scanner might flag a misconfigured server; confirming an attacker could actually read data requires sending a crafted request and observing the response. Under a 'stop at first suspicion' rule, the second step — the one that distinguishes a real flaw from a false positive — becomes a crime.

timeline.heading: THE JURISDICTION ARBITRAGE
timeline.body: Belgium legalised good-faith research in 2023. The Netherlands has a coordinated disclosure framework backed by prosecutorial guidelines. France's 2016 Digital Republic Act protects researchers who report to ANSSI. A UK flaw found by a Brussels researcher is legal to verify; the same flaw found by a Londoner is not.

blocks.label: the European patchwork
blocks.caption: researcher protections vary by border

timeline.heading: THE DISCLOSURE ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: Vulnerabilities get found either way. The question is whether the finder is a domestic researcher who reports to the vendor, a foreign researcher who publishes on a conference stage, or a criminal who sells to a broker. Criminalising domestic verification doesn't reduce discovery — it shifts the discoverer.

timeline.heading: THE BUG BOUNTY ECONOMY
timeline.body: Legitimate vulnerability markets pay $5,000 to $250,000 per finding through programs like HackerOne and Bugcrowd. Grey-market brokers like Zerodium pay up to $2.5 million for a zero-click iPhone exploit. The price gap between disclosure and exploitation is the real policy lever — and it widens whenever legal risk pushes researchers toward anonymous channels.

timeline.heading: THE CHILLING EFFECT
timeline.body: The CMA has been used against researchers before. In 2018, Robert Riley was prosecuted for testing a council's website after reporting flaws. The TalkTalk breach prosecutions saw teenagers charged for actions adjacent to the kind of probing a professional pentester does daily. The law's vagueness is itself the deterrent — researchers self-censor long before a charge is filed.

blocks.question: What does the UK's Computer Misuse Act 1990 require to establish 'unauthorised access'?
options: Proof the access caused financial damage
Lack of permission from the system owner, regardless of intent
A formal complaint from the affected party
blocks.explanation: The Act is strict-liability on authorisation: intent, harm, and disclosure don't enter the offence definition — only whether the owner consented.

timeline.heading: THE GUJARATI TRADE NETWORK
timeline.body: For centuries before British rule, Gujarati merchants ran the dhow-trade circuit connecting western India to the Arabian and African coasts via the monsoon winds. Aden was a key node — Hindu, Jain, and Parsi traders settled in pockets from Muscat to Zanzibar, building temples, agiaries, and credit houses wherever the trade routes anchored.

timeline.heading: WHY ADEN, SPECIFICALLY
timeline.body: The British seized Aden in 1839 and ran it as part of the Bombay Presidency until 1937 — administratively, Aden was governed from India, not London. Indian rupees were legal tender, Indian civil servants staffed the bureaucracy, and Indian merchants followed the flag. The Hindu temple built in the 1860s was a colonial-era artifact of that administrative link, not an indigenous Yemeni institution.

blocks.text: From 1839 to 1937 Aden was literally a district of **British India** — the only Arab territory ever administered from Bombay. The Hindu presence was a function of that arrangement; when Aden was transferred to direct Colonial Office rule in 1937, the Indian community began its long decline.

timeline.heading: THE DHIMMA TRADITION
timeline.body: Classical Islamic law extended *dhimmi* status — protected non-Muslim subject — primarily to People of the Book (Jews, Christians, Sabians). Hindus presented a doctrinal puzzle that medieval jurists handled pragmatically: the Hanafi school, dominant in Mughal India, eventually treated Hindus as *dhimmis* for taxation and protection purposes. In Yemen, the Zaydi imams and later republican governments inherited a pluralist commercial precedent rather than a theological doctrine — Hindus were tolerated because they were useful traders, not because of a settled juridical category.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE CIVIL WAR ERASED
timeline.body: Yemen's 2015 war between the Houthi movement and the Saudi-led coalition displaced over four million people and collapsed the southern economy. Aden, once the third-busiest bunkering port in the world (after New York and Liverpool in the 1950s), became a contested city under shifting militia control. Heritage sites without active congregations — Jewish synagogues, the Hindu temple, Parsi towers of silence — lost their physical custodians first.

timeline.heading: THE LAST-CARETAKER PATTERN
timeline.body: Across the Muslim world, abandoned minority shrines often survive on the back of a single Muslim caretaker who stayed when the community left — the Jewish quarter of Fez, the Armenian churches of eastern Anatolia, the Yazidi shrines of Nineveh. The pattern is consistent: once the resident community departs, physical survival depends entirely on a local who treats the site as shared heritage rather than foreign property.

blocks.question: What gave Aden its unusual concentration of Hindu, Parsi, and Jewish merchant communities?
options: Ottoman millet protections extended south to Yemen
Administration as part of British India, 1839–1937
A Zaydi imam's edict welcoming Indian traders
Portuguese trading concessions inherited by Britain
blocks.explanation: Aden was governed from Bombay, not London, for nearly a century — Indian rupees were legal tender and Indian merchants followed the colonial administration.

timeline.heading: THE OBLIGATION
timeline.body: Carrier-of-last-resort rules require a designated telephone company to provide service to anyone who requests it within its territory, at regulated rates, regardless of profitability. The doctrine dates to the 1913 Kingsbury Commitment, when AT&T accepted universal service obligations in exchange for being allowed to keep its near-monopoly.

blocks.text: The bargain was explicit: AT&T got to be a **regulated monopoly** instead of being broken up under the Sherman Act, and in exchange it had to serve every farmhouse, not just the profitable urban routes.

timeline.heading: WHY COPPER IS EXPENSIVE
timeline.body: A copper landline network requires physical wire to every premise, powered switches at central offices, and field crews to repair storm damage. Maintenance cost per line rises as subscribers cancel — the same poles and trunks support fewer paying customers each year. Carriers have been trying to retire copper since the early 2010s.

timeline.heading: WHO STILL USES IT
timeline.body: Landline holdouts cluster in three groups: rural households where cellular coverage is weak, elderly users on fixed incomes who never switched, and medical-alert and alarm systems that were engineered around copper's reliable line power. When the grid fails, a copper line keeps working; a VoIP line tied to a powered modem does not.

timeline.heading: THE 911 PROBLEM
timeline.body: Copper landlines provide a fixed physical address to emergency dispatchers automatically. Cellular and VoIP 911 calls rely on handset GPS or registered addresses that may be stale. The FCC has spent fifteen years closing this gap with rules like NG911 and Kari's Law, but parity is not complete.

blocks.question: Why do copper landlines keep working during a power outage?
options: The phone has an internal battery
The central office sends low-voltage DC power down the line itself
Cell towers automatically reroute the call
blocks.explanation: Telephone central offices push about 48 volts DC down the copper pair, with backup batteries and generators — so the phone is powered by the network, not the home.

timeline.heading: THE PREEMPTION FIGHT
timeline.body: Telecom regulation is split: the FCC governs interstate service, state public utility commissions govern intrastate service. AT&T's strategy is to get the FCC to declare that federal deregulation of legacy phone service preempts California's mandate. The same preemption playbook killed state net-neutrality rules in much of the country after 2017.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: When AT&T was broken up in 1984, the regional Bell operating companies inherited universal service obligations as a condition of their monopoly franchises. Forty years of mergers reassembled most of those Bells back into today's AT&T and Verizon — but the obligations attached to the territory, not the corporate structure. Shedding them requires regulators to formally release the carrier, one state at a time.

timeline.heading: THE TREATY'S LOGIC
timeline.body: The 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank after nine years of negotiation, split six rivers between the two states: India got the eastern three (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej), Pakistan got the western three (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab). India retained limited 'non-consumptive' use of the western rivers — hydropower and run-of-river projects, but no storage that would let it withhold flow.

timeline.heading: WHY PAKISTAN IS DOWNSTREAM AND STUCK
timeline.body: Roughly 80% of Pakistan's irrigated agriculture depends on the Indus system, and the western rivers carry the bulk of that flow. Pakistan sits geographically downstream of India on every one of its major water arteries — a structural vulnerability that the treaty was designed to neutralize through legal guarantee rather than physical control.

blocks.text: Pakistan's *Punjab* — literally 'five rivers' — is named for the very tributaries the treaty allocates. Agriculture is roughly **23% of GDP** and **37% of employment**; the Indus is not one input among many, it is the substrate of the state.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'SUSPENSION' ACTUALLY BREAKS
timeline.body: The treaty's value was never the water allocation alone — that's geography. Its value was the data-sharing regime: telemetry on flows, advance notice of releases, design review of new projects, and the Permanent Indus Commission that met annually since 1960 through three wars. Suspension ends the notification protocol, which is why a routine silt flush now arrives as a 3-metre surge with no warning.

events.label: Uri attack: Modi says 'blood and water cannot flow together'

timeline.heading: SILT FLUSHING, EXPLAINED
timeline.body: Himalayan rivers carry extraordinary sediment loads — the Chenab can deposit metres of silt against a dam wall in a single monsoon. Operators must periodically open low-level sluice gates to flush accumulated sediment downstream, or reservoir capacity collapses and turbines abrade. Under the treaty, the timing and volume of these flushes were coordinated with Pakistan; unilaterally, they read as weaponized hydrology even when the engineering is routine.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT THAT WASN'T
timeline.body: No major transboundary water treaty has ever been formally suspended by an upstream state with active downstream dependents. The Nile, Mekong, Tigris-Euphrates, and Jordan basins all have disputes, but the Indus Treaty was the world's textbook case of cooperation surviving hostility. Its unraveling matters beyond South Asia — it tells every upstream state that the legal architecture is optional.

blocks.question: Which institution brokered the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty and remains a guarantor under its terms?
blocks.explanation: The World Bank spent nine years mediating the treaty and committed funding for Pakistan's replacement canal system; it retains a formal role in dispute resolution.

timeline.heading: THE DOCTRINE
timeline.body: The C standard defines certain operations — signed integer overflow, null pointer dereference, reading uninitialized memory — as undefined behavior. The compiler is permitted to assume they never happen, which means it can delete any code path predicated on them occurring.

blocks.text: The key word is ***undefined***, not *unspecified* or *implementation-defined*. The standard explicitly grants compilers the right to do **anything at all** when UB is encountered — including time-traveling optimizations that affect code before the UB.

timeline.heading: THE CLASSIC DELETION
timeline.body: A developer writes `if (x + 1 < x) abort();` to catch signed overflow. The compiler reasons: signed overflow is undefined, so `x + 1` cannot be less than `x`, so the branch is dead code, so the abort is removed. The safety check the developer wrote is silently deleted at compile time.

timeline.heading: THE KERNEL PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In 2009, a Linux kernel bug (CVE-2009-1897) emerged when GCC deleted a null pointer check in tun_chr_poll. The code dereferenced a pointer, then checked if it was null. GCC reasoned that since dereferencing null is UB, the pointer couldn't be null, so the check was removed — turning a defensive guard into an exploitable vulnerability.

timeline.heading: WHY THE STANDARD IS THIS WAY
timeline.body: C was standardized in 1989 across wildly different hardware: ones-complement mainframes, segmented x86, word-addressed DSPs. Making overflow undefined (rather than wrapping) let compilers generate efficient code on every target. The performance gains compounded over decades; reversing the decision now would break optimizations the entire ecosystem depends on.

blocks.question: What does the C standard say a compiler may do when it encounters undefined behavior?
options: Emit a warning and continue with defined semantics
Anything at all, including deleting surrounding code
blocks.explanation: The standard places no constraints on UB — compilers may assume it never occurs and optimize accordingly, which is why safety checks can vanish.

timeline.heading: WHY RUST AND SWIFT EXIST
timeline.body: Both languages were designed with the explicit goal that safe code cannot invoke undefined behavior. Rust's borrow checker and Swift's ownership model enforce at compile time what C leaves to programmer discipline. The cost of C's UB rules — measured in CVEs across decades of kernel, browser, and embedded code — is what justified building entire new toolchains.

blocks.label: how each language treats signed overflow

timeline.heading: THE MITIGATION LANDSCAPE
timeline.body: Compilers added flags — `-fwrapv` forces signed overflow to wrap, `-fno-strict-aliasing` disables type-based optimization, UBSan instruments binaries to catch UB at runtime. None are default. The Linux kernel compiles with `-fno-strict-aliasing` and `-fno-delete-null-pointer-checks` precisely because upstream GCC's defaults are too aggressive for systems code.

timeline.heading: THE MICHIGAN SIGNAL
timeline.body: In the February 2024 Michigan Democratic primary, over 100,000 voters chose 'uncommitted' as a protest against Biden's Gaza policy — more than 13% of the primary electorate. Biden had carried Michigan by roughly 154,000 votes in 2020. The math was visible nine months before November; the campaign treated it as a containable faction rather than a structural warning.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY OF THE LOSS
timeline.body: Arab and Muslim American voters cluster in a handful of decisive precincts — Dearborn and Hamtramck in Michigan, the Philadelphia suburbs in Pennsylvania, the Phoenix metro in Arizona. Dearborn, the only Arab-majority city in the US, swung from Biden +44 in 2020 to Trump +6 in 2024 — a 50-point shift in a single municipality.

blocks.label: Arab American population centers in swing states

timeline.heading: WHAT AN AUTOPSY IS
timeline.body: The party 'autopsy' is a postmortem genre invented after the RNC's 2012 'Growth and Opportunity Project,' which famously urged Republicans to embrace immigration reform — advice Trump promptly ignored on his way to the nomination. The genre's track record is that parties commission them, publish them, and then do what their primary electorate wants anyway.

blocks.text: The 2013 GOP autopsy was so candid about demographic decline it became known internally as the *Growth and Opportunity Project* — and so thoroughly disregarded that operatives joked it should be filed under **fiction**.

timeline.heading: THE COALITION ARITHMETIC
timeline.body: Arab Americans number roughly 3.7 million nationwide and Muslim Americans about 4.5 million. Both are small as national shares but concentrated in Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Ohio — states whose 2020 and 2024 margins were thinner than the local Arab/Muslim electorate. A 10-point swing among 200,000 voters in Wayne County, Michigan is the same arithmetic as a 1-point swing among 2 million Hispanic voters in Florida.

blocks.question: By roughly how many votes did Trump carry Michigan in 2024?
blocks.explanation: Trump won Michigan by about 80,000 votes — smaller than the Dearborn-Hamtramck-Detroit-suburb Arab/Muslim electorate, which broke heavily away from the Democratic ticket.

timeline.heading: THE OMISSION AS POSITION
timeline.body: What an autopsy leaves out is itself a finding. The 2016 DNC review acknowledged the white working class; the 2024 review's silence on Gaza signals which donor and lobbying constituencies still set the boundaries of party self-criticism. AIPAC and allied groups spent over $100 million in the 2024 cycle, primarily in Democratic primaries — a figure that explains the silence more cleanly than any analytical oversight.

blocks.label: Pro-Israel lobby spending in 2024 US elections (selected)

timeline.heading: THE HISTORICAL RHYME
timeline.body: In 1968, Democrats lost a generation of antiwar voters by refusing to break with Lyndon Johnson on Vietnam at the Chicago convention. Humphrey moved toward a bombing halt too late; Nixon won by 0.7 points. The party's postmortem then also under-weighted the war as the cause. Coalitions ruptured by foreign policy tend to be diagnosed as messaging problems for a full cycle before they are diagnosed as policy problems.

events.label: Humphrey loses to Nixon by 0.7 points
McGovern wins nomination on antiwar plank, loses 49 states
Iraq war vote splits Democratic field
Obama beats Clinton partly on Iraq opposition

timeline.heading: THE ENRICHMENT LADDER
timeline.body: Natural uranium is 0.7% U-235. Reactor fuel needs 3-5%. Research reactors use 20%. Weapons-grade is 90%+. The work to go from natural to 20% is roughly 90% of the total separative effort needed to reach weapons-grade — which is why 20% is the diplomatic red line, not 90%.

blocks.text: Iran's stockpile sits at **60% enrichment** — a level with no civilian justification. No power reactor uses it; only a handful of research reactors worldwide ever have. The remaining work to weapons-grade is **a matter of weeks**, not months.

timeline.heading: THE CENTRIFUGE CASCADE
timeline.body: Enrichment works by spinning uranium hexafluoride gas at supersonic speeds in cascades of centrifuges. Each stage marginally separates the lighter U-235 from heavier U-238. The same cascade that produces 5% fuel can produce 90% material — it just needs to be reconfigured and run longer. The equipment does not distinguish civilian from military intent.

timeline.heading: THE JCPOA BASELINE
timeline.body: The 2015 nuclear deal capped Iran's enrichment at 3.67% and its stockpile at 300 kg. After Trump withdrew the US in 2018, Iran progressively breached every limit. By 2024 the stockpile exceeded 6,000 kg across multiple enrichment levels — roughly 20× the JCPOA cap.

timeline.heading: WHY EXPORT MATTERS
timeline.body: Shipping the stockpile to Russia or a third country is the only verifiable way to set Iran's program back by years. Diluting it in-country is reversible in months. The 2015 deal moved 11 tonnes of Iranian uranium to Russia — the single most consequential nonproliferation act of the past decade. Tehran knows it; that's why this is the sticking point.

timeline.heading: THE FACILITIES
timeline.body: Natanz hosts Iran's main centrifuge halls, hardened underground. Fordow sits buried inside a mountain near Qom — built explicitly to survive bunker-buster strikes. Isfahan handles uranium conversion. Together they form a redundant geography: no single strike disables the program.

timeline.heading: THE BREAKOUT QUESTION
timeline.body: 'Breakout time' is how long Iran would need to produce enough weapons-grade material for one bomb. In 2015 it was estimated at 12 months. By 2023 the IAEA assessed it at under two weeks. The stockpile is not theoretical leverage — it is a clock.

blocks.question: What level of uranium enrichment is generally considered 'weapons-grade'?
blocks.explanation: Weapons-grade uranium is conventionally defined as 90%+ U-235. But the hardest separative work is done by 20%; reaching 90% from there is comparatively fast.

timeline.heading: THE HALF-LIFE OF A LINK
timeline.body: Studies of academic citations find that roughly half of URLs cited in court opinions and journal articles are dead within a decade. The web is not a permanent record; it is a constantly decaying one, and decay accelerates when platforms shut down rather than when individual pages rot.

blocks.text: Harvard's Perma.cc project found **49%** of hyperlinks in US Supreme Court opinions written since 1996 no longer point to their original content — a phenomenon researchers call ***link rot***.

timeline.heading: THE ARCHIVE OF LAST RESORT
timeline.body: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, founded by Brewster Kahle in 1996, holds over 900 billion web captures. It is a single nonprofit in San Francisco — not a government program, not a consortium — that has become the de facto backup of the public web, despite running on roughly $30 million a year.

timeline.heading: WHY USENET MATTERS
timeline.body: Before the web, hobbyist discourse lived on Usenet — a distributed message system from 1980 that predates HTTP by nine years. Google bought the DejaNews archive in 2001, ran it as Google Groups, then quietly degraded search and access. Much of pre-2000 internet culture survives only because individuals mirrored it off Usenet before access closed.

timeline.heading: THE PLATFORM RISK
timeline.body: When GeoCities shut down in 2009, Yahoo gave users weeks of notice and deleted 38 million pages. The Archive Team — a volunteer collective separate from the Internet Archive — scrambled to mirror what it could. The pattern has repeated with Google+, Vine, MySpace music, Tumblr's adult archive, and Storify. Platform centralization concentrated culture; platform shutdowns now extinguish it.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL FRAGILITY
timeline.body: The Internet Archive lost a 2023 copyright case (Hachette v. Internet Archive) over its lending library and faces a separate suit from major record labels over its 78rpm record collection. A single adverse judgment could force deletion of holdings that exist nowhere else, because rights holders generally do not preserve what they no longer monetize.

timeline.heading: WHO PRESERVES HOBBY WRITING
timeline.body: National libraries collect books and major newspapers. Universities collect scholarly journals. Almost no institution collects fan forums, hobby blogs, or amateur strategy guides — yet that is where most of the actual writing on the internet happens. Preservation of vernacular culture falls almost entirely on private archivists working without funding or legal protection.

blocks.question: Roughly what fraction of links cited in US Supreme Court opinions since 1996 no longer point to their original content?
blocks.explanation: Harvard's Perma.cc study found ~49% of cited URLs were dead or altered — even in documents meant to stand as permanent legal record.

timeline.heading: THE PERMIT AS REVENUE
timeline.body: Nepal charges $15,000 per Everest permit on the south side. With 494 permits this season, that single fee generates roughly $7.4M — before guide fees, oxygen, helicopters, and lodge revenue that multiply the figure several times over.

blocks.text: Tourism contributes roughly **6–7%** of Nepal's GDP, and Everest expeditions are the single most visible — and most lucrative — slice of it.

timeline.heading: WHY THE SHERPA DO THE WORK
timeline.body: The Sherpa are an ethnic group from the Solukhumbu region who migrated from eastern Tibet roughly 500 years ago. Generations of life above 3,000m bred genetic adaptations — higher nitric oxide levels, more efficient hemoglobin — that let them work at altitudes where outsiders barely survive.

timeline.heading: THE TWO ROUTES
timeline.body: Everest has two standard routes: Nepal's southeast ridge from Base Camp at 5,364m, and Tibet's northeast ridge from the Chinese side. Beijing closes the north route at will for political or logistical reasons, funneling all commercial traffic — and all permit revenue — to Kathmandu.

timeline.heading: THE DEATH ZONE
timeline.body: Above 8,000m, atmospheric pressure is roughly one-third of sea level. The body cannot acclimatize — it deteriorates. Climbers carry bottled oxygen, but supply is finite and the window above the South Col is measured in hours, not days.

timeline.heading: THE TRAFFIC JAM PROBLEM
timeline.body: When Nepal issues hundreds of permits but the weather window is only 5–7 viable summit days per season, climbers queue at the Hillary Step in the death zone. The 2019 season's viral image of a line stretched along the summit ridge killed 11 — most from exhaustion and oxygen depletion while waiting, not from falls.

blocks.question: Most Everest deaths in recent commercial seasons happen because of —
options: Exhaustion and oxygen depletion while waiting in queues
Sudden storms above the South Col
blocks.explanation: With hundreds of permits issued against a 5–7 day weather window, the bottleneck at the Hillary Step now kills more climbers than the mountain's technical hazards.

timeline.heading: THE 1953 FIRSTS
timeline.body: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay summited on 29 May 1953. Hillary received a knighthood; Tenzing, a Nepali-born Sherpa, received the George Medal — a lesser British honor reserved for non-citizens. The two men refused for the rest of their lives to publicly say who stepped onto the summit first.

timeline.heading: THE NAPSTER PLAYBOOK
timeline.body: Sue first, license second is the labels' standard move. RIAA sued Napster into bankruptcy in 2001, then signed the same technology — peer-distributed audio — into iTunes and Spotify within five years. Litigation establishes the price; the deal follows.

timeline.heading: TWO COPYRIGHTS, NOT ONE
timeline.body: Every recorded song has two separately owned copyrights: the underlying composition (lyrics and melody, owned by the publisher) and the master recording (the specific performance, owned by the label). An AI cover needs a license from both, which is why the labels and publishers fight these cases separately.

blocks.text: The compulsory mechanical license under **§115** of the US Copyright Act lets anyone cover a song at a statutory rate — but it covers only the *composition*, not the master, and the Copyright Office has explicitly declined to extend it to AI-generated audio.

timeline.heading: THE TRAINING-DATA QUESTION
timeline.body: UMG's June 2024 suit against Suno alleged the model was trained on copyrighted recordings without permission — the same fair-use question driving the New York Times v. OpenAI case. No US court has yet ruled that training on copyrighted audio is or isn't fair use; the labels are licensing into the uncertainty rather than waiting for a verdict.

timeline.heading: THE VOICE PROBLEM
timeline.body: An AI cover that mimics a specific singer's voice implicates a third right that copyright doesn't cover: the right of publicity. Tennessee's ELVIS Act (2024) was the first state law to explicitly protect a performer's voice from AI cloning. Federal protection still doesn't exist.

blocks.question: Which 2023 viral AI track triggered the major labels' first coordinated takedown of AI music?
options: "Heart on My Sleeve" — fake Drake and The Weeknd
blocks.explanation: "Heart on My Sleeve" hit 600k Spotify streams in April 2023 before UMG forced takedowns across every platform — the incident that made AI voice cloning a board-level issue at the majors.

timeline.heading: WHO ACTUALLY GETS PAID
timeline.body: Spotify pays roughly 70% of revenue to rights holders. Of that, the label takes the largest share; the songwriter and the performer split what remains, often unevenly. An AI cover that requires composition + master + voice licenses means the same stream is taxed three times — and the original artist may not be one of the three payees.

blocks.label: where a $1 Spotify stream flows (typical 2024 split)

timeline.heading: THE SONY-WARNER HOLDOUT
timeline.body: The Big Three labels — UMG, Sony, Warner — together control roughly two-thirds of recorded music. When one cuts a deal first, the other two gain leverage: they can watch the terms, refuse, and demand better. Spotify launched in the US in 2011 only after all three signed; an AI cover product without Sony and Warner catalogs has a similar incompleteness problem.

timeline.heading: WHERE WHEAT BEGAN
timeline.body: The Fertile Crescent — arcing from the Levant through northern Syria into the Zagros foothills — is where humans first domesticated wheat, barley, lentils, chickpeas, and flax roughly 10,000 years ago. The wild ancestors of these crops still grow there, which is why the region's landraces carry genetic diversity found nowhere else on Earth.

timeline.heading: WHAT A LANDRACE IS
timeline.body: A landrace is a crop variety shaped by centuries of selection in one specific place — adapted to that valley's rainfall, that soil's salinity, that pest pressure. Unlike modern hybrid seed, landraces are genetically heterogeneous: a single field carries hundreds of subtly different plants, so a disease or drought never wipes out the whole crop.

blocks.text: Industrial agriculture replaced landraces with **monocultures** — uniform high-yield varieties that maximize output but collapse together. Roughly **75%** of the world's crop genetic diversity was lost in the 20th century, per FAO estimates.

timeline.heading: ICARDA AND THE ALEPPO EVACUATION
timeline.body: The International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas held the world's most important Fertile Crescent seed collection at Tel Hadya, outside Aleppo. As the front lines closed in during 2012, staff shipped roughly 80% of the 150,000 accessions to backup facilities in Morocco and Lebanon — the only major seed-bank evacuation under active wartime conditions in history.

timeline.heading: THE SVALBARD BACKSTOP
timeline.body: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, dug into permafrost on a Norwegian Arctic island in 2008, is the world's seed-of-last-resort. ICARDA became the first depositor to ever WITHDRAW seeds from Svalbard — pulling its own duplicates in 2015 to rebuild the Aleppo collection in exile. The vault was designed to be opened once in a generation; Syria triggered it within seven years.

blocks.question: ICARDA became the first institution to do what at the Svalbard Global Seed Vault?
options: Withdraw seeds to rebuild a lost collection
Build a secondary vault on the same island
blocks.explanation: Svalbard was designed as a deposit-only backup. ICARDA's 2015 withdrawal — to restart its Aleppo work in Morocco and Lebanon — was the first time the vault had been opened for its intended purpose.

timeline.heading: THE SANCTIONS BIND
timeline.body: US and EU sanctions on Syria restrict financial transfers, dual-use equipment, and most institutional partnerships. Humanitarian carve-outs exist on paper but banks routinely refuse Syria-linked transactions to avoid compliance risk — a phenomenon called de-risking. A volunteer agricultural project operates in this gap precisely because it needs no wire transfers and no imported equipment.

timeline.heading: WHY FOOD SOVEREIGNTY MATTERS HERE
timeline.body: Syria's wheat output collapsed from roughly 4 million tonnes pre-war to under 1.5 million by the mid-2020s. A country that fed itself and exported to neighbors became dependent on Russian and Ukrainian imports — leaving its bread supply hostage to a war on the other side of the Black Sea. Reviving local landraces is less nostalgia than strategic autonomy.

blocks.text: The term *food sovereignty* — coined by the peasant movement **La Vía Campesina** in 1996 — goes beyond food security. Security asks whether calories are available; sovereignty asks who controls the seed, the land, and the price.

timeline.heading: WHAT NET MIGRATION ACTUALLY MEASURES
timeline.body: Net migration is arrivals minus departures over twelve months — not visas issued, not asylum claims, not citizenships granted. The ONS estimates it from the International Passenger Survey plus Home Office admin data, so revisions of 50,000+ between provisional and final figures are routine.

blocks.text: The headline figure conflates students, care workers, dependants, and returning Britons into a single number — which is why the political debate fixates on *gross* arrivals while the *net* figure is what gets quoted.

timeline.heading: THE 2022 SPIKE
timeline.body: Net migration ran around 250,000 per year through the 2010s, then jumped to a record 906,000 in the year to June 2023. Three one-off pipelines drove it: the Ukraine and Hong Kong BN(O) schemes, an uncapped post-Brexit student route with dependants, and a Health and Care Worker visa that quietly became the largest single channel.

blocks.label: UK net migration, peak vs reset

timeline.heading: THE CARE-WORKER PIPELINE
timeline.body: Adding care workers to the Shortage Occupation List in 2022 — with dependants permitted and a salary floor near £20,000 — created the fastest-growing visa category in UK history. By 2023 health and care visas alone exceeded 350,000 main applicants and dependants. The 2024 ban on overseas care recruitment closed it at the source.

timeline.heading: THE SETTLED-STATUS LEVER
timeline.body: Indefinite Leave to Remain, the UK's permanent-residency status, currently unlocks after five years of qualifying work or family visas. Doubling it to ten years pushes the point at which migrants gain access to non-contributory benefits and full labour-market mobility further out — without changing how many people enter.

blocks.question: What does extending the ILR qualifying period to ten years primarily do?
options: Reduces the number of new arrivals each year
Delays when current migrants gain permanent rights
Cancels existing visas issued before the change
blocks.explanation: ILR rules govern transition from temporary to permanent status — they affect the stock of long-term residents, not the flow of new arrivals.

timeline.heading: THE POLITICAL LOGIC
timeline.body: Both major UK parties now compete on the same axis. The Conservatives closed the student-dependant route and the care pipeline in 2024; Labour inherited the falling numbers and added the ILR extension. Reform UK's polling surge in 2024–25 made low net migration the price of staying in office, regardless of which party paid it.

events.label: Care worker added to shortage list

timeline.heading: THE STRUCTURAL TENSION
timeline.body: The UK's adult social care sector relies on roughly 150,000 foreign-born workers; vacancy rates jumped after the recruitment ban. NHS England, universities funded by overseas tuition, and food processing all run on visa pipelines the same governments are closing. The migration debate is downstream of a fiscal model that depends on the labour it restricts.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: Belarus shares a 1,084 km border with Ukraine, running from the Polish corner to the Russian one. Chernihiv sits 75 km from that border; Kyiv itself is 140 km. An armored column moving on paved roads from Gomel can reach the outskirts of Kyiv in a day if unopposed — which is exactly what the February 2022 northern thrust attempted.

timeline.heading: THE UNION STATE
timeline.body: Belarus and Russia are formally bound by the 1999 Union State treaty — a supranational arrangement with a shared parliament, joint military doctrine, and integrated air defense. After the 2020 protests, Lukashenko's domestic legitimacy collapsed and Moscow's leverage became near-total. Belarus is sovereign on paper; operationally, the Russian military uses it as forward territory.

blocks.text: The 2022 invasion's northern axis launched from Belarusian soil with no Belarusian troops involved — Minsk provided the **territory**, Moscow provided the **army**. The distinction is what lets Lukashenko deny belligerent status while hosting it.

timeline.heading: THE ORESHNIK
timeline.body: The Oreshnik is an intermediate-range ballistic missile Russia first used in combat against Dnipro in November 2024. It flies at Mach 10+ with multiple independently-targetable warheads and a range covering all of Europe from Belarusian launch sites. Deploying it to Belarus extends Russia's strike reach without moving Russian launchers — a deniability layer wrapped around a hard military fact.

timeline.heading: THE NUCLEAR DRILLS
timeline.body: Russia stationed tactical nuclear warheads in Belarus in 2023 — the first foreign deployment of Russian nuclear weapons since the Soviet collapse. Joint nuclear exercises rehearse the command chain: Russian warheads, Belarusian delivery platforms, dual-key authorization. The doctrine being signaled is escalation control, not first use.

blocks.question: When did Russia first station nuclear weapons in Belarus since the Soviet collapse?
options: Never — the warheads remain on Russian soil
blocks.explanation: The 2023 deployment was the first time Russia stationed nuclear warheads outside its borders since 1991, ending a three-decade nonproliferation posture.

timeline.heading: THE 2022 LESSON
timeline.body: The original northern thrust failed not because Ukraine outfought it but because Russian logistics collapsed on a single highway. The 64-km armored column northwest of Kyiv ran out of fuel and food within a week. Any second attempt would have to solve the rail-gauge bottleneck at the border and the swamp terrain of the Pripyat marshes — constraints that have not changed.

events.label: Belarus protests; Lukashenko leans on Moscow

timeline.heading: WHY BELARUS HESITATES
timeline.body: Lukashenko has kept Belarusian ground troops out of Ukraine for three years despite Russian pressure. The Belarusian army is roughly 48,000 active personnel — small, poorly equipped, and politically unreliable after the 2020 purges. Sending it into Ukraine risks both military embarrassment and the kind of domestic backlash that nearly toppled the regime four years ago.

timeline.heading: THE MLS BARGAIN
timeline.body: A Multiple Listing Service is a private cooperative where competing brokerages agree to share their listings with each other. The bargain is mutual exposure: every member's seller gets every member's buyers. Break the share, break the cooperative.

blocks.text: The technical term for an off-MLS home is a **pocket listing** — a property the agent keeps in their pocket, shown only to a curated set of buyers before (or instead of) hitting the public market.

timeline.heading: DOUBLE-ENDING
timeline.body: US residential commissions run roughly 5-6% of sale price, split between the seller's agent and the buyer's agent. If one agent represents both sides — a *dual agency* or *double-end* — they keep the entire commission. Private listing networks engineer this outcome by design.

blocks.label: who gets paid on a $500k home

timeline.heading: THE BURNETT PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In October 2023, a Missouri jury found the National Association of Realtors and major brokerages liable for $1.8 billion in the Sitzer-Burnett case — ruling that the cooperative commission rule inflated buyer-agent fees. NAR settled nationally for $418 million and agreed to decouple buyer commissions from MLS listings in 2024.

timeline.heading: WHY ZILLOW MATTERS
timeline.body: Zillow aggregates MLS feeds into a single national consumer interface — roughly 200 million monthly visitors. A listing absent from Zillow is, for most buyers, a listing that does not exist. Cutting Zillow off is a structural lever, not a marketing dispute.

blocks.question: Why does removing a home from Zillow effectively hide it from most buyers?
options: Zillow has exclusive MLS licensing rights
Most US buyers begin home searches on aggregators like Zillow, not brokerage sites
Federal law requires listings to appear on Zillow
Zillow owns the underlying MLS databases
blocks.explanation: Surveys consistently show ~75% of US buyers start on portals like Zillow or Redfin; brokerage and MLS sites trail far behind.

timeline.heading: THE ANTITRUST QUESTION
timeline.body: The Sherman Act forbids agreements among competitors that restrain trade. When a regional MLS — itself a cooperative of competing brokerages — collectively withholds inventory from a downstream distributor, the conduct sits squarely in the zone courts have policed since the 1899 Addyston Pipe decision against horizontal collusion.

timeline.heading: THE BRICKING PATTERN
timeline.body: When a connected-hardware vendor shuts down its cloud, the physical device often becomes inert — even if its sensors and radios still work perfectly. The hardware you own depends on a server you don't.

blocks.label: hardware bricked by vendor cloud shutdowns

timeline.heading: WHY THE CLOUD AT ALL
timeline.body: A weather station could in principle stream straight to a local screen. Vendors route it through their servers because the cloud is where the *recurring revenue*, the firmware-update channel, and the data telemetry live — even when the user paid once for a sealed device.

blocks.text: The industry term is **forced obsolescence by cloud dependency** — the device works, the *service contract* doesn't, and there is no legal distinction between the two.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL GAP
timeline.body: US consumer law treats software as licensed, not sold. The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act covers physical defects but says nothing about a manufacturer turning off the server that makes the hardware function. The EU's 2024 Right-to-Repair directive is the first major framework to address this; the US has no federal equivalent.

timeline.heading: THE LOCAL-FIRST ALTERNATIVE
timeline.body: A small open-source ecosystem — Home Assistant, rtl_433, Weewx — captures the radio signals AcuRite stations broadcast and stores readings on the user's own machine. The sensors transmit on 433 MHz in the clear; no cloud is technically required to read them.

blocks.question: What frequency do most consumer weather-station sensors broadcast on, allowing third-party software to receive them directly?
blocks.explanation: 433 MHz is an unlicensed ISM band used by most low-power telemetry — which is why open-source receivers like rtl_433 can decode AcuRite, Oregon Scientific, and LaCrosse sensors without vendor cooperation.

timeline.heading: THE DATA QUESTION
timeline.body: A decade of personal weather readings — frost dates, rainfall totals, microclimate records — lives on AcuRite's servers under their terms. When the app dies, the export path dies with it. The pattern repeats across fitness trackers, smart scales, and home-energy monitors: the user generated the data, the vendor controls the egress.

timeline.heading: THE SCALE PROBLEM
timeline.body: China generates more electricity than the US, EU, and India combined. Even a 1% shift in its power mix moves global emissions more than most countries' entire economies. This is why two provinces can determine whether global CO2 rises or falls.

timeline.heading: WHY INNER MONGOLIA AND SHANDONG
timeline.body: These are China's two largest coal-power provinces. Inner Mongolia hosts the country's biggest open-pit mines and exports power east via ultra-high-voltage lines; Shandong is a heavy-industry corridor running steel, aluminum, and chemicals. Cutting fossil output there moves the national needle in a way that decarbonizing a southern services province cannot.

blocks.label: the two provinces that bent the curve

timeline.heading: THE CURTAILMENT TAX
timeline.body: Curtailment is renewable energy generated but not used — wind farms told to stop spinning, solar panels disconnected — because the transmission grid cannot move the power to where demand is. A 13% curtailment rate means roughly one in eight clean electrons is wasted at the source.

blocks.text: China's curtailment problem is geographic: the best wind sits in the northwest *(Xinjiang, Gansu, Inner Mongolia)*, the best solar in the Tibetan plateau, but **70%+ of demand** is on the eastern seaboard 2,000–3,000 km away.

timeline.heading: THE UHV ANSWER
timeline.body: China has built the world's only at-scale ultra-high-voltage DC grid — power lines running at 800kV-1100kV that move electricity across continental distances with under 5% loss. Over 30 UHV lines now connect western generation to eastern load centers. The remaining curtailment reflects what hasn't been wired yet, not what can't be.

timeline.heading: THE PEAK QUESTION
timeline.body: Beijing pledged in 2020 to peak emissions before 2030 and reach net-zero by 2060. The unresolved question is whether 2024-25 was the peak or a plateau. A two-province decline suggests the curve is bending; thirteen provinces still rising suggests the plateau still has years to run.

blocks.question: When did China commit to peaking CO2 emissions and reaching carbon neutrality?
options: Paris Agreement, 2015 — peak by 2025, neutral by 2050
Xi's UN speech, 2020 — peak before 2030, neutral by 2060
Glasgow COP26, 2021 — peak by 2028, neutral by 2055
Beijing Declaration, 2023 — peak by 2030, neutral by 2070
blocks.explanation: Xi announced the '30/60' targets in a video address to the UN General Assembly in September 2020 — a unilateral commitment that surprised both Western capitals and China's own energy ministries.

timeline.heading: THE COAL FLOOR
timeline.body: Even as renewables surge, China approved more new coal capacity in 2022-23 than the rest of the world combined. The doctrine is energy security first: coal stays as a 'support role' baseload, dispatched less but kept available. Decarbonization in China is additive — clean power layered on top — not substitutive in the way Europe forced its grid to shift.

timeline.heading: THE TWO-TRACK SYSTEM
timeline.body: China sorts students at age 15 via the zhongkao exam.
