timeline.body: PFAS have been detected in rainwater on the Tibetan Plateau, in polar bear livers, in the blood of newborns on every continent. The 3M plant in Minnesota and DuPont's Parkersburg works in West Virginia were the original point sources; six decades later the molecules are everywhere water has flowed.

timeline.heading: THE REGULATORY MOMENT
timeline.body: The US EPA set the first enforceable drinking-water limits for PFOA and PFOS in 2024 — 4 parts per trillion, near the limit of detection. The EU is moving toward a class-wide restriction under REACH. Both regimes assume utilities can remove PFAS; neither has a cheap way to destroy what's removed.

blocks.question: What is the EPA's 2024 enforceable drinking-water limit for PFOA?
blocks.explanation: 4 ppt — roughly one drop in 20 Olympic swimming pools — sits near the floor of what commercial labs can reliably measure.

timeline.heading: INCINERATION DOESN'T WORK
timeline.body: The default disposal route — high-temperature incineration — was assumed to break C-F bonds above 1,000°C. Recent EPA stack testing found incinerators emit shorter-chain PFAS as byproducts, effectively redistributing the problem into the air. This is why a destruction technology that works at ambient temperature matters.

timeline.heading: WHAT HYDROXYL RADICALS DO
timeline.body: The hydroxyl radical (·OH) is one of the most aggressive oxidants in aqueous chemistry — second only to fluorine itself. Photocatalysts like TiO₂ have generated ·OH from UV light since the 1970s, but driving the reaction with visible sunlight, without sacrificial oxidants, and sustaining it for hundreds of hours is the engineering threshold this work claims to cross.

timeline.heading: WHY 'REAL WASTEWATER' IS THE TEST
timeline.body: Lab-grade water contains the target molecule and little else. Municipal wastewater contains organics, salts, metals, and competing radical scavengers that poison most catalysts within hours. The 500-hour figure was achieved in a clean reactor; scaling to a treatment plant is where ninety percent of promising photocatalysts have died for fifty years.

timeline.heading: OMAN, THE QUIET CHANNEL
timeline.body: Every serious US–Iran negotiation in the past two decades has passed through Muscat. Oman maintains diplomatic relations with Tehran, Washington, and Tel Aviv simultaneously — a posture no other Gulf state has held since the 1979 revolution. Sultan Qaboos hosted the secret 2013 talks that produced the JCPOA framework before Geneva was ever announced.

timeline.heading: WHAT AN MOU ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: A Memorandum of Understanding is a non-binding statement of intent. Unlike a treaty, it does not require Senate ratification — which is why every modern US–Iran arrangement has been structured this way. It is also why the JCPOA collapsed in a single executive order in 2018: an MoU binds an administration, not a country.

blocks.text: The American constitutional distinction matters here: a **treaty** needs two-thirds of the Senate; an **executive agreement** or *memorandum* needs only the president's signature — and survives only as long as the next president lets it.

timeline.heading: THE FROZEN ASSETS
timeline.body: Iranian assets have been frozen and partially released in cycles since the 1979 embassy seizure. The pattern repeats because the freeze is the leverage — release it fully and Washington loses its non-military pressure tool. Every deal has unfrozen a portion, never the whole.

timeline.heading: JOINT HORMUZ OVERSIGHT
timeline.body: Iran and Oman already share the Strait of Hormuz — the shipping lanes pass through Omani territorial waters on the southern side, Iranian waters on the northern. A joint maritime oversight body would be the first formal cooperation on the strait since the 1975 Algiers Agreement (which dealt with Iraq, not the Gulf). Most past 'oversight' has been one-sided: Iran's IRGC navy on top, the US Fifth Fleet from Bahrain underneath.

timeline.heading: WHY THE OIC SHOWS UP HERE
timeline.body: The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation has 57 members and rarely produces operational diplomacy — its consensus rule means most resolutions are denominator statements. But it offers a forum where Sunni Gulf monarchies and Shi'a Iran sit at the same table without it being a Western-brokered event, which gives a deal legitimacy that a US-only announcement could not.

blocks.question: What event triggered the founding of the OIC in 1969?
options: An arson attack on al-Aqsa Mosque
blocks.explanation: An Australian visitor set fire to al-Aqsa's pulpit in August 1969; the resulting summit in Rabat established the OIC as a permanent Muslim-state body.

timeline.heading: THE MARKET'S READ
timeline.body: Prediction markets price the gap between announcement and signature. A 'largely negotiated' deal is not a signed one, and the historical base rate for late-stage US–Iran agreements collapsing in the final clauses is high — the 2015 JCPOA itself nearly broke in its last 72 hours over inspection language at Parchin.

blocks.label: US x Iran permanent peace deal by May…

timeline.heading: THE THREE BUCKETS
timeline.body: UN climate finance splits into three categories: mitigation (cutting emissions), adaptation (preparing for impacts you can't avoid), and loss and damage (compensating for harms beyond adaptation). The boundaries between them are political, not physical — and they determine who pays whom.

blocks.text: The distinction matters because *adaptation* is funded as development assistance, while *loss and damage* implies **liability** — an admission that wealthy emitters owe compensation to vulnerable nations.

timeline.heading: THE COP27 BREAKTHROUGH
timeline.body: Developing countries fought for 30 years to get loss and damage recognized as a separate finance stream. Wealthy nations resisted because the framing implies historical responsibility for emissions. The Loss and Damage Fund was finally agreed at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh in 2022 and operationalized at COP28 in Dubai.

events.label: Vanuatu proposes insurance pool for sea-level rise
Bali Action Plan first names loss and damage
Paris Agreement Article 8 — but no liability
COP27 agrees to create the fund

timeline.heading: WHY THE FRAMING FIGHT MATTERS
timeline.body: If a family leaves a flood-prone delta and rebuilds inland, that's adaptation — a success story funded by development aid. If the same family is classified as displaced by climate harm, that's loss and damage — and someone owes them compensation. Same act, opposite political accounting.

timeline.heading: WHO IS MOST EXPOSED
timeline.body: The World Bank's Groundswell report projects up to 216 million internal climate migrants by 2050 across six regions. The bulk are in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America — regions whose cumulative historical emissions are a small fraction of those of OECD countries.

timeline.heading: THE PLEDGE GAP
timeline.body: Total pledges to the Loss and Damage Fund sit around $700 million. UNEP's Adaptation Gap Report estimates developing-country adaptation needs alone at $215–387 billion per year by 2030. The fund is roughly three orders of magnitude short of the problem it was created to address.

blocks.question: Roughly how large is the Loss and Damage Fund relative to estimated annual adaptation needs in developing countries?
options: About a tenth of the annual need
Less than 1% of the annual need
Roughly equal to the annual need
blocks.explanation: ~$700M pledged vs. $215–387bn/yr in adaptation needs — the fund is under 0.5% of one year's requirement, and loss-and-damage needs are larger still.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT PROBLEM
timeline.body: Wealthy emitters fear that accepting climate liability opens the door to unlimited claims — a parallel to tobacco settlements or asbestos litigation. The Paris Agreement's Article 8 explicitly states loss and damage 'does not involve or provide a basis for any liability or compensation.' That carve-out is what made the fund politically possible — and what limits its scale.

timeline.heading: WHAT CMIP IS
timeline.body: The Coupled Model Intercomparison Project is a standardized protocol — every participating modelling centre runs the same scenarios with the same forcings, so outputs can be compared like-for-like rather than as a babel of incompatible runs.

blocks.text: CMIP is run by the **World Climate Research Programme**; its ensembles are the empirical backbone of every IPCC *Assessment Report* since the Second (1995).

timeline.heading: WHY ENSEMBLES, NOT ONE MODEL
timeline.body: No single climate model is right. Each makes different choices about clouds, ocean mixing, ice sheets. Averaging across dozens of independent models cancels out structural biases — the multi-model mean consistently beats any individual member against observations.

blocks.question: Why do climate scientists average across many models instead of picking the best one?
options: The best model changes year to year
Individual models have structural biases that partially cancel in the mean
Computing one model is cheaper than running many
blocks.explanation: Different models err in different directions on clouds, ocean heat uptake, and feedbacks. The multi-model mean is more skillful than any single member.

timeline.heading: THE SCENARIO LADDER
timeline.body: CMIP6 introduced Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) — five storylines about how population, economy, and policy evolve, each paired with a radiative forcing target. SSP1-1.9 is the Paris-compatible low end; SSP5-8.5 is the fossil-fueled high end.

timeline.heading: THE COMPUTE BILL
timeline.body: Five million gigabytes of output is not a storage problem — it is a coordination problem. Centres run on national supercomputers from Exeter to Beijing to Princeton; outputs are federated through the Earth System Grid, which is how a researcher in Nairobi can query a run produced in Tokyo.

timeline.heading: THE POLICY CLOCK
timeline.body: IPCC assessment reports are written on a fixed cadence — AR6 landed in 2021-23, AR7 is due in 2028-29. The fast-track tier exists because national climate plans (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement come due in 2025 and 2030; waiting for the full ensemble would leave policymakers citing a decade-old science base.

timeline.heading: THE HOT-MODEL PROBLEM
timeline.body: A subset of CMIP6 models ran 'hotter' than the geological record can support — climate sensitivity above 5°C per CO2 doubling, which paleoclimate evidence rules out. IPCC AR6 quietly down-weighted these runs rather than reporting a raw mean. CMIP7 protocols tighten the screening upfront.

blocks.text: The technical term is **equilibrium climate sensitivity** (ECS) — the long-run warming from doubled CO2. The IPCC's *likely* range is 2.5–4°C; models above that ceiling are flagged as outliers, not deleted.

timeline.heading: THE FREEZE
timeline.body: Diplomatic ties collapsed in 2023 after Trudeau publicly accused Indian agents of orchestrating the killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar on Canadian soil. Both countries expelled diplomats, visa services froze, and FTA talks were suspended mid-negotiation. The current restart is the first ministerial-level commerce visit since.

timeline.heading: THE MAPLE 8
timeline.body: Canada's eight largest pension funds — CPPIB, CDPQ, OTPP, PSP, BCI, AIMCo, HOOPP, OMERS — collectively manage around C$2.4 trillion. Unlike US pension funds that mostly buy public stocks, the Maple 8 directly own airports, toll roads, ports, and unlisted companies worldwide. They have been among the largest foreign infrastructure investors in India for over a decade.

timeline.heading: WHY URANIUM
timeline.body: Canada is the world's second-largest uranium producer after Kazakhstan, and the Athabasca Basin in Saskatchewan holds the highest-grade ore on Earth — some deposits assay above 15% U3O8, roughly a hundred times the global average. India runs a fleet of pressurized heavy-water reactors that need a steady fuel supply, and was locked out of the global uranium market for 34 years after the 1974 'Smiling Buddha' test until the 2008 NSG waiver.

blocks.text: India is one of only four nuclear-armed states outside the **Non-Proliferation Treaty** (with Pakistan, Israel, and North Korea), yet uniquely received a *country-specific waiver* from the Nuclear Suppliers Group in 2008 — a diplomatic carve-out no other state has obtained.

timeline.heading: THE CRITICAL MINERALS PIVOT
timeline.body: Canada hosts deposits of lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, and rare earths that India needs for EV batteries and electronics manufacturing. Both governments are trying to build supply chains that route around China, which currently refines roughly 60–90% of most critical minerals regardless of where they are mined.

blocks.label: the critical-minerals triangle
blocks.caption: Canada mines, China refines, India and US want to break the chokehold

timeline.heading: WHAT AN FTA WOULD ACTUALLY DO
timeline.body: India–Canada bilateral trade is only about C$13bn — tiny relative to either country's total. The real prize is not tariff reduction but an investment-protection chapter that lets the Maple 8 deploy capital at scale without arbitration risk, and a mobility chapter for the 1.8 million Indian-origin Canadians and the student pipeline that funds Canadian universities.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of Canada's international students come from India?
blocks.explanation: Indian nationals made up roughly 40% of Canada's study-permit holders before the 2023 freeze — the single largest source country, and a major revenue stream for Canadian universities.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: The strait sits between Iran and Oman, not Iran and any Arab Gulf state. Iran's coastline runs along the entire northern edge, and the deepest shipping channel hugs the Iranian side — which is why Iranian naval positioning matters disproportionately.

timeline.heading: THE BOTTLENECK
timeline.body: Hormuz is 33 km wide at its narrowest, but the shipping lanes are just 3 km each — two inbound, two outbound, separated by a 3 km buffer. Roughly 21 million barrels of oil pass through daily, about 21% of global consumption.

blocks.label: Donald Trump announce that the United…

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL FAULTLINE
timeline.body: Under UNCLOS Article 38, ships have a right of transit passage through international straits — coastal states cannot suspend passage or impose conditions. Iran signed UNCLOS in 1982 but never ratified it, and has long argued Hormuz is governed by its domestic law. A toll-free MOU would dodge the unresolved legal question rather than answer it.

blocks.text: The US position rests on *transit passage* — a stronger right than *innocent passage*, which coastal states **can** suspend. Iran's framing of 'managing vessel numbers' is a quiet assertion of the weaker regime.

timeline.heading: WHY MINES, WHY NOW
timeline.body: A single mine costs a few thousand dollars. Clearing it costs millions and weeks. This asymmetry is why mining has been the weapon of choice for weaker naval powers since the American Civil War — and why 'mines cleared' is the concrete deliverable Washington wants in writing.

blocks.question: What actually closes a shipping lane during a Hormuz crisis?
options: Lloyd's of London war-risk insurance premiums
blocks.explanation: Once war-risk premiums spike, commercial vessels reroute regardless of how many mines remain. The financial chokepoint is tighter than the physical one.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988, Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. Oil prices spiked briefly but markets adapted — tankers were reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags and escorted by warships. The lesson planners took: disruption is easier to threaten than to sustain.

timeline.heading: THE PAKISTAN CHANNEL
timeline.body: Islamabad mediating Tehran-Washington is not new — Pakistan brokered the back-channel that produced the 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement under Chinese auspices. Its leverage comes from being one of the few Sunni-majority nuclear states with working diplomatic ties to both Tehran and Washington, and a 959 km border with Iran through Balochistan.

timeline.heading: FRANÇAFRIQUE
timeline.body: For sixty years after independence, France maintained a parallel state across its former African colonies — currency (the CFA franc), garrisons, intelligence networks, and presidential hotlines. The arrangement was called Françafrique. It survived decolonization on paper because the political and economic plumbing never left.

blocks.text: The **CFA franc** was pegged to the French franc, then the euro, with reserves held at the French Treasury — meaning Paris effectively controlled monetary policy for fourteen African states until reforms began in 2019.

timeline.heading: THE COUP BELT
timeline.body: Since 2020, a contiguous strip of the Sahel — Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea, Niger, and Chad's transition — has fallen to military takeovers. The juntas share a script: dissolve parliament, expel French troops, invite Russian security, withdraw from ECOWAS, denounce the CFA.

blocks.label: the Sahel coup belt vs the coast
blocks.caption: juntas in the interior, civilian governments on the Atlantic

timeline.heading: THE AES
timeline.body: In September 2023, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger formed the Alliance of Sahel States (Alliance des États du Sahel). In January 2024 they announced withdrawal from ECOWAS — the West African bloc that had threatened military intervention against Niger's junta. The AES is a mutual-defense pact aimed explicitly at the bloc that tried to reverse the coups.

timeline.heading: WHY NIGER MATTERS TO PARIS
timeline.body: Niger supplied roughly 15–20% of the uranium feeding France's nuclear reactors, mined at Arlit by Orano (formerly Areva). France generates about 70% of its electricity from nuclear power — the highest share of any major economy. Losing Niger meant scrambling for Kazakh and Canadian supply at higher prices.

blocks.question: What share of France's electricity comes from nuclear power?
blocks.explanation: France is the most nuclear-dependent major economy at ~70%, which is why African uranium access has been a strategic priority since the 1960s.

timeline.heading: WAGNER, THEN AFRICA CORPS
timeline.body: Russian influence arrived through Wagner Group contractors — first in Mali (2021), then Burkina Faso and Niger. After Prigozhin's death in 2023, the Kremlin folded Wagner's Africa operations into the Africa Corps under direct GRU control. The model is the same: regime protection, mineral concessions, information operations, no human-rights conditionality.

blocks.text: The Russian pitch is brutal but coherent: *no lectures*, no conditionality, cash for access. Where France attached governance demands to its garrisons, Moscow attaches **nothing** — and that absence is the entire product.

timeline.heading: THE BAZOUM PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Mohamed Bazoum was Niger's first peacefully elected successor to an elected president — a milestone in a country that had seen five coups since independence. He was detained in the July 2023 coup and remains held without trial. ECOWAS threatened military intervention to restore him; the threat collapsed when Nigeria's senate refused to authorize troops and the AES treaty deterred unilateral action.

events.label: Operation Serval: France intervenes in Mali

timeline.heading: THE INSURGENCY
timeline.body: Balochistan has been in active insurgency since 2004 — the fifth uprising since Pakistan's 1948 annexation of the Khanate of Kalat. The Baloch Liberation Army and allied groups target security forces, Chinese workers, and infrastructure that moves resources out of the province.

events.label: Bhutto dismisses Balochistan govt; fourth war

timeline.heading: WHY RAIL
timeline.body: Pakistan Railways runs a single colonial-era trunk line through Balochistan — Quetta to Rohri east, Quetta to Taftan (Iran) west, Quetta to Chaman (Afghan border) north. There is no parallel route. A single charge on any of these branches severs the province from the national grid.

timeline.heading: THE CHAMAN LINE
timeline.body: The Quetta–Chaman branch was built by the British in 1892 to move troops toward Kandahar during the Great Game. It climbs through the Khojak Pass via a 3.9 km tunnel — when completed it was the longest railway tunnel in British India. Its military logic has never changed; its passengers are still largely soldiers and cantonment workers.

blocks.text: The **Khojak Tunnel** appeared on the back of Pakistan's 5-rupee note from 1976 to 2005 — a colonial engineering feat reframed as national heritage, on a line the state can no longer reliably defend.

timeline.heading: THE GRIEVANCE
timeline.body: Balochistan produces most of Pakistan's natural gas and hosts the Reko Diq copper-gold deposit and the Chinese-operated Gwadar port. It is also the poorest province by every human-development metric. The insurgency's core claim — that the province's resources fund a state that returns nothing — is empirically difficult to dispute.

timeline.heading: THE 2025 ESCALATION
timeline.body: In March 2025 the BLA hijacked the Jaffar Express in a tunnel near Sibi, holding hundreds of passengers hostage for over 24 hours before army commandos retook the train. It was the first mass hostage-taking on Pakistan's rail network and signaled a shift from bombings to set-piece operations.

blocks.question: Why does Balochistan's rail network make such an attractive insurgent target?
options: High passenger volume relative to roads
No parallel routes — a single charge severs the province
Trains carry most of Pakistan's natural gas exports
Chinese-funded high-speed lines run through tribal areas
blocks.explanation: Pakistan Railways runs single colonial-era branches through Balochistan with no redundancy; one charge cuts a border crossing for days.

timeline.heading: THE PIVOT
timeline.body: Before the 2022 invasion, Russia supplied under 2% of India's crude. By 2024 it was roughly 35-40%, displacing Iraq and Saudi Arabia as the top source. The shift happened in months, not years — refiners chase the discount, not the flag.

blocks.label: India's crude suppliers, share of imports

timeline.heading: THE PRICE CAP MECHANICS
timeline.body: The G7 set a $60/barrel cap on Russian crude in December 2022. The mechanism: Western shippers and insurers — who dominate the global tanker trade — may only service Russian cargoes priced below the cap. India buys legally under the cap, but most cargoes now move on Russia's *shadow fleet* of older tankers with non-Western insurance, sidestepping the rule entirely.

blocks.text: The **shadow fleet** — roughly 600 aging tankers under flags of convenience — is the structural workaround. Sanctions targeting individual vessels barely dent it; new shells reflag overnight.

timeline.heading: THE REFINER ARBITRAGE
timeline.body: Reliance and Nayara (part-owned by Rosneft) buy discounted Urals crude, refine it, and export diesel and jet fuel to Europe — which still buys Indian refined products even while sanctioning Russian crude. The molecules end up in the same European tank; the legal fiction is the refining step.

blocks.label: Russian crude → European fuel, via India

timeline.heading: WHY INDIA WON'T BUDGE EASILY
timeline.body: India imports over 80% of its crude. Every $10/barrel discount on Russian volumes saves roughly $8-10bn annually at current import levels. For a country running a chronic current account deficit, that's not a marginal saving — it's macroeconomic oxygen.

timeline.heading: THE NON-ALIGNED REFLEX
timeline.body: India's foreign policy doctrine since Nehru has been *strategic autonomy* — formerly called non-alignment. Buying Russian oil while deepening defense ties with the US is not a contradiction in Delhi's framework; it is the framework. The same logic underwrote Soviet arms purchases during the Cold War while India accepted US food aid.

blocks.question: What share of India's military hardware still originates from Russian/Soviet platforms?
blocks.explanation: Roughly 60% of India's military inventory is Russian-origin — tanks, fighters, submarines. Diversification toward US, French, and Israeli platforms is recent and partial.

timeline.heading: THE TARIFF LEVER
timeline.body: The July tariff deadline is the actual pressure point. The US can't sanction India directly without breaking the Quad and pushing Delhi closer to Beijing. Tariffs on Indian goods — textiles, pharmaceuticals, refined fuels — are the calibrated tool: painful enough to negotiate over, reversible enough not to rupture the relationship.

timeline.heading: THE CHAEBOL STRUCTURE
timeline.body: Samsung is the largest of South Korea's chaebol — family-controlled conglomerates that emerged under Park Chung-hee's 1960s industrial policy. The top five chaebol generate revenue equivalent to roughly half of Korean GDP, making labor disputes at Samsung effectively macroeconomic events.

blocks.text: The word *chaebol* literally means **wealth clique** — written with the same characters as Japan's prewar *zaibatsu*, the family conglomerates US occupiers broke up in 1945. Korea kept its version.

timeline.heading: THE NO-UNION DOCTRINE
timeline.body: Samsung operated under a 'no-union management' policy for nearly 50 years after founder Lee Byung-chul declared in 1969 that unions would form at Samsung 'over my dead body.' The first legally recognized union appeared in 2020, after a 2018 conviction of senior executives for sabotaging union drives. The 2024 walkout was the first strike in company history.

timeline.heading: WHO CAPTURES PRODUCTIVITY GAINS
timeline.body: Economists distinguish the labor share of income (wages) from the capital share (profits, dividends). For most of the postwar period these moved together. Since roughly 2000, productivity has continued rising while the labor share has fallen across nearly every advanced economy — the gains accruing to capital owners and a thin layer of high-skill workers.

blocks.question: Since 2000, what has happened to labor's share of national income across most advanced economies?
blocks.explanation: The decoupling of wages from productivity since ~2000 is the central labor-economics fact of the era — it's the gap the Samsung union is trying to claim a piece of.

timeline.heading: THE LUDDITE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Early 19th-century English textile workers smashed power looms not because they misunderstood technology, but because they understood it precisely — the productivity gains went to factory owners while skilled weavers lost wage premiums earned over generations. Every wave of automation since has reopened the same distributional question: who owns the surplus the machine creates?

timeline.heading: WHY AI IS DIFFERENT
timeline.body: Past automation displaced specific tasks — looms replaced weaving, ATMs replaced tellers — and workers bargained over redeployment. Generative AI threatens cognitive tasks broadly across white-collar work, making it harder to define what was 'replaced' and therefore what compensation is owed. The Samsung demand is one of the first formal attempts to write that share into a labor contract.

timeline.heading: THE GERMAN MODEL
timeline.body: Germany's Mitbestimmung (codetermination) law puts worker representatives on the supervisory boards of large firms — half the seats at companies above 2,000 employees. When automation arrives, the negotiation happens inside the boardroom rather than on the picket line. Korea's labor law has no such mechanism; the union must extract concessions externally, strike by strike.

timeline.heading: THE ORIGINAL DESIGN
timeline.body: Gordon Gallup's 1970 test marks an animal with odorless dye in a spot it can only see in a mirror. If the animal touches the mark on its own body — not the mirror — it is inferred to recognize the reflection as itself.

blocks.text: Gallup called it the **mark test**; the inference is that mirror-directed self-touch implies a *concept of self* distinct from the reflected image.

timeline.heading: THE SHORT LIST
timeline.body: For decades, only great apes passed reliably. The list later expanded to a handful of species across very different lineages — convergent evolution, not a shared ancestral trait.

blocks.label: species that have passed the mark test

timeline.heading: THE WRASSE PROBLEM
timeline.body: In 2019 a cleaner wrasse — a fish with a brain the size of a grain of rice — passed the test. Either fish have a self-concept, or the test measures something simpler than selfhood. Most cognitive scientists now suspect the latter.

blocks.question: Which of these passed the mark test most recently before belugas?
blocks.explanation: A 2019 study reported cleaner wrasse touching marks visible only in a mirror — a result that forced a rethink of what the test actually measures.

timeline.heading: THE SENSORY MISMATCH
timeline.body: Dogs fail the mirror test but identify themselves by smell. Belugas navigate by echolocation; their primary self-model may be acoustic, not visual. A vision-only test asks species to introspect in a sense they do not lead with.

timeline.heading: WHAT SETH IS ARGUING
timeline.body: Anil Seth's broader thesis is that consciousness is many overlapping processes — bodily self-modeling, perspective-taking, agency — not a single switch. A mirror response could reflect any one of them, or none, depending on the species' perceptual world.

blocks.text: Seth's framing borrows from Jakob von Uexküll's *Umwelt* — the idea that each species inhabits its own perceptual world, and a test designed in ours is a poor instrument for theirs.

timeline.heading: WHY IT STILL MATTERS
timeline.body: Mirror-test results feed directly into animal-welfare law: jurisdictions that recognize cetacean sentience have used the test as evidence to ban captivity. The methodological critique is not academic — it shapes what zoos and aquaria are permitted to do.

timeline.heading: THE PATHOGEN
timeline.body: Brucella is a small intracellular bacterium that hides inside macrophages — the very immune cells meant to kill it. That intracellular niche is why brucellosis is famously hard to cure: antibiotics that can't penetrate cells fail, and relapse is common even after months of combination therapy.

blocks.text: The standard regimen is **doxycycline plus rifampicin or streptomycin for six weeks minimum** — and even then, relapse rates run 5–10%.

timeline.heading: THE TRANSMISSION ROUTES
timeline.body: Three main channels: drinking raw milk from infected animals, handling birth tissues (placenta, aborted fetuses) where bacterial load is highest, and inhaling aerosols in barns. Pastoralist life touches all three daily — milking by hand, assisting deliveries, sharing shelter with herds at night.

timeline.heading: WHY PLACENTA IS THE HOTSPOT
timeline.body: Brucella concentrates in the placenta of infected ruminants because the bacterium feeds on erythritol, a sugar abundant there. A single infected placenta can shed billions of organisms — which is why women, who handle birthing in most pastoralist cultures, often have higher seroprevalence than men.

blocks.question: Why does Brucella concentrate in ruminant placentas rather than other tissues?
options: The placenta is rich in erythritol, which Brucella metabolizes
The placenta has weaker immune defenses than other organs
Brucella is sexually transmitted between animals
blocks.explanation: Brucella preferentially metabolizes erythritol, a sugar abundant in placental and fetal tissues of ruminants — explaining why abortion is the hallmark of livestock infection.

timeline.heading: THE ONE HEALTH ARGUMENT
timeline.body: Roughly 60% of human infectious diseases are zoonotic — they jump from animals. Vertical health systems that fund human clinics and veterinary services as separate budgets miss the interface where transmission actually happens. The One Health framework, formalized by WHO/FAO/OIE in the 2000s, treats human, animal, and environmental health as a single surveillance problem.

timeline.heading: THE PASTORALIST GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: Northern Kenya's arid lands host roughly 4 million pastoralists — Borana, Somali, Samburu, Turkana — moving cattle, camels, and small stock across the Horn of Africa's rangelands. The same mobility that buffers herds against drought also spreads pathogens across district and national borders faster than any surveillance system tracks them.

timeline.heading: THE VACCINE ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: Livestock vaccines for Brucella (S19 for cattle, Rev-1 for sheep and goats) have existed since the 1940s and are cheap. No licensed human vaccine exists — the live attenuated strains used in animals are too virulent for people. This means the only realistic path to cutting human cases is mass vaccination of the herds, which requires veterinary budgets pastoralist regions rarely receive.

timeline.heading: THE WUI PROBLEM
timeline.body: The wildland-urban interface — where homes meet flammable vegetation — is the most dangerous fire geography on earth. Chile's coastal range has packed informal settlements into steep, eucalyptus-covered slopes, the exact terrain that produces fast-moving crown fires.

blocks.text: Chile's hillsides are dominated by **eucalyptus** and **Monterey pine** — introduced for the timber industry, both more flammable than native sclerophyll forest. The trees shed oil-rich litter and resprout after burns, locking the landscape into a fire cycle.

timeline.heading: WHY VALPARAÍSO BURNS
timeline.body: Valparaíso sits at the foot of forty-two hills, where unplanned settlements (tomas) climbed slopes too steep for fire trucks. Narrow alleys mean a single ignition reaches dozens of homes before any engine arrives. The 2014 fire killed 15; 2024 killed 138 on the same hillsides.

timeline.heading: MANAGED RETREAT
timeline.body: Planners call the policy of relocating households out of hazard zones managed retreat. It is politically toxic everywhere it has been tried — from Louisiana's Isle de Jean Charles to Fukushima's exclusion zone — because it forces the state to decide which communities cease to exist.

blocks.text: The term of art is *managed retreat* — distinguished from *displacement* (involuntary, after disaster) and *adaptation in place* (fortifying what exists). Most governments quietly default to displacement because retreat requires buying out homes before they burn.

timeline.heading: WHO CAN AFFORD TO LEAVE
timeline.body: Climate adaptation is regressive: those with capital relocate to safer ground and bid up its price; those without remain in the hazard zone and rebuild with thinner margins each cycle. The same pattern shows up in Bangladeshi delta villages, California fire country, and Lagos floodplains.

blocks.question: Across studies of post-disaster mobility, who is most likely to relocate permanently after a fire or flood?
options: The poorest residents, who have least to lose
Elderly residents with deep community ties
blocks.explanation: Insurance payouts plus existing savings finance a one-time move; the poorest lack the lump sum, and renters often relocate locally rather than out of the hazard zone entirely.

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE WITHDRAWAL
timeline.body: When insurers stop writing policies in a fire zone — as has happened in parts of California and Australia — property values collapse and the state becomes insurer of last resort. Chile's private insurance market has begun excluding the Valparaíso hills, shifting the cost of every future fire onto the public budget.

timeline.heading: THE BEGIN DOCTRINE
timeline.body: Since Menachem Begin authorized the 1981 strike on Iraq's Osirak reactor, Israeli policy has held that no hostile state in the region may acquire nuclear weapons capability — and that Israel will act unilaterally, preventively, and without warning to enforce that line.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE JCPOA ACTUALLY COVERED
timeline.body: The 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action capped Iran's uranium enrichment at 3.67%, limited its centrifuge count, and put the Fordow facility under IAEA monitoring — in exchange for sanctions relief. Ballistic missiles were addressed only in a separate UN Security Council resolution, and Iran's regional proxies were left out entirely.

blocks.text: The missile clause sat in **UNSCR 2231**, which *called upon* Iran to refrain from missile development — language Tehran's lawyers argued was a request, not a prohibition. The JCPOA itself was silent.

timeline.heading: ENRICHMENT IS NOT A WEAPON
timeline.body: Weapons-grade uranium is 90% U-235. Iran has stockpiled material at 60% — short of the threshold but only weeks of further enrichment away. A bomb also requires weaponization (the explosive package) and a delivery vehicle. The JCPOA's red lines targeted the enrichment step because it is the slowest and most monitorable.

blocks.question: Roughly how enriched must uranium be to be 'weapons-grade'?
blocks.explanation: Weapons-grade is conventionally ~90% U-235. Iran's current 60% stockpile is below the line but technically much closer to 90% than to natural uranium (0.7%).

timeline.heading: THE REGIONAL MISSILE GAP
timeline.body: Iran's ballistic arsenal is the largest in the Middle East — a deliberate compensation for an air force still flying 1970s American jets. Israel's stated war aim was to constrain it; the framework leaves it untouched.

timeline.heading: THE 2015 PRECEDENT FOR UNILATERAL DEALS
timeline.body: Obama signed the JCPOA over Netanyahu's explicit objection — including a March 2015 address to a joint session of Congress arranged without White House coordination. The diplomatic rupture was the deepest in modern US-Israel relations. Trump's current opening repeats the pattern of a US president cutting a deal Jerusalem opposes.

timeline.heading: WHY THE SILENCE
timeline.body: Israeli prime ministers historically respond to US-Iran diplomacy with immediate public pushback. Netanyahu's silence signals either that the deal contains private assurances on uranium removal, or that the political cost of breaking with Trump exceeds the cost of an unsatisfactory deal — a calculation Israeli leaders have rarely been forced to make.

2026-05-24-israel-silence-trump-iran-dea.label: Iran's Nuclear File & the Israeli Calculus

timeline.heading: THE DISTRIBUTION MOAT
timeline.body: GitHub hosts the code, VS Code edits it, Azure runs it. Microsoft controls the three surfaces where a developer spends their day. Owning distribution lets the platform decide which AI assistant a developer encounters first — and which one requires switching workflows to reach.

timeline.heading: THE BUNDLING PLAYBOOK
timeline.body: Microsoft has run this move before. Internet Explorer bundled with Windows killed Netscape in the late 1990s and triggered United States v. Microsoft (2001), the antitrust case that nearly broke the company up. Teams bundled with Office 365 squeezed Slack into filing an EU complaint in 2020. The pattern is consistent: own the surface, default the product, watch the rival shrink.

timeline.heading: THE FRENEMY STRUCTURE
timeline.body: Microsoft is Anthropic's competitor *and* customer *and* infrastructure landlord. It has invested over $13bn in OpenAI, embedded GPT models across its product surface, and simultaneously sold Claude through GitHub Marketplace. Cutting Claude Code is the predictable resolution of a structurally unstable arrangement — the partner with distribution always controls the timing.

timeline.heading: WHY DEVELOPERS RESIST SWITCHING
timeline.body: Coding assistants compete on a narrow axis: how often the suggestion is the one you would have typed. A developer who has tuned muscle memory and prompt habits around one model loses real productivity switching to another, even when the benchmark scores are close. *Switching cost* in this market is measured in days of degraded output, not subscription fees.

blocks.text: The technical term is **lock-in by habituation** — the user, not the data, becomes the moat. It's why Vim users don't switch editors and why a forced AI-tool migration triggers more friction than the per-seat price would predict.

timeline.heading: THE EU ANGLE
timeline.body: The Digital Markets Act (in force 2024) designates Microsoft a 'gatekeeper' for Windows and LinkedIn — but not yet for GitHub or VS Code. The DMA forbids gatekeepers from self-preferencing their own services on designated platforms. If the Commission adds developer-tool surfaces to the list, moves like this one become legally contestable rather than just commercially unpopular.

blocks.question: Under the EU's Digital Markets Act, what is the threshold to designate a platform a 'gatekeeper'?
options: €7.5bn EU revenue and 45m monthly EU users
Any company headquartered outside the EU
Market share above 50% in any EU country
blocks.explanation: The DMA uses revenue and user-base thresholds (€7.5bn EU turnover, 45m monthly EU end-users, 10k business users) — not market share — to designate gatekeepers.

timeline.heading: WHAT MXENES ARE
timeline.body: MXenes are 2D sheets of transition-metal carbides or nitrides, just a few atoms thick. Ti₃C₂ — titanium carbide — is the prototype, discovered at Drexel in 2011 by etching aluminum out of a layered ceramic. Their surfaces are crowded with hydroxyl and oxygen groups, which is why they conduct electricity like a metal yet behave chemically like a sponge.

blocks.text: The name borrows from *graphene* — the *-ene* suffix signals a single-layer 2D material, while **MX** encodes the metal (M) and carbon/nitrogen (X) lattice.

timeline.heading: WHY THE LIVER, WHY MACROPHAGES
timeline.body: The liver filters the entire blood volume every few minutes, and Kupffer cells — its resident macrophages — make up the largest macrophage population in the body. Any nanoparticle injected intravenously is overwhelmingly captured there. What is usually a delivery problem becomes, for a liver-targeted drug, a free ride.

timeline.heading: THE ROS PROBLEM IN MASH
timeline.body: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH) begins as fat accumulation but turns dangerous when stressed hepatocytes leak reactive oxygen species. Macrophages sense the damage and release inflammatory cytokines, which kill more hepatocytes, which release more ROS. The fibrosis that ends in cirrhosis is the scar tissue from this loop.

blocks.question: What distinguishes MASH from simple fatty liver (steatosis)?
options: Inflammation and hepatocyte injury on top of fat
blocks.explanation: Steatosis is fat alone; MASH adds inflammation and ballooning hepatocyte injury — the step that drives fibrosis and cirrhosis.

timeline.heading: WHY MXENES SCAVENGE ROS
timeline.body: Those surface hydroxyl groups donate electrons readily. When a reactive oxygen species — a hydroxyl radical, a superoxide — meets a Ti₃C₂ sheet, it grabs an electron and is neutralized. The sheet itself oxidizes slowly. In effect, the nanosheet acts as a sacrificial antioxidant with a surface area thousands of times larger than a small-molecule drug.

timeline.heading: THE REGULATORY DISTANCE
timeline.body: MASH has only one FDA-approved drug (resmetirom, 2024) after two decades of failed trials. The gap between a mouse study and an approved human therapy in this disease is roughly a decade, because the endpoint regulators accept — fibrosis regression confirmed by biopsy — takes years to measure.

timeline.heading: THE NANOPARTICLE GRAVEYARD
timeline.body: Hundreds of nanoparticle therapies have shown spectacular results in mice and failed in humans. Mouse livers clear particles faster, mouse immune systems tolerate metals differently, and the doses that work in a 25-gram animal rarely scale linearly to a 70-kilogram one. The first question for any new nanomedicine is not whether it works — it is whether it works for reasons that will survive the species jump.

timeline.heading: THE SPLIT
timeline.body: Islamic State West Africa Province broke from Boko Haram in 2016 over a doctrinal dispute: Abubakar Shekau insisted any Muslim who cooperated with the Nigerian state was a legitimate target; ISWAP's leadership, endorsed by IS central, ruled that ordinary Muslims could not be killed indiscriminately. The split made ISWAP more disciplined, not less dangerous.

blocks.text: The cleavage was over *takfir* — the practice of declaring other Muslims apostates. Shekau's maximalism alienated civilians; ISWAP's restraint let it govern them.

timeline.heading: THE LAKE CHAD BASIN
timeline.body: ISWAP operates across the shorelines and islands of Lake Chad — terrain that touches Nigeria, Niger, Chad, and Cameroon. The lake has shrunk by roughly 90% since the 1960s, exposing islands and reed channels that armies cannot patrol but small boats can.

timeline.heading: THE GOVERNANCE MODEL
timeline.body: In territory it controls, ISWAP collects taxes (zakat on cattle and fish), adjudicates disputes through its own qadis, and provides a crude form of order. This is why mass abductions on roads coexist with relative calm in some villages — the group distinguishes between subjects to be governed and travelers to be ransomed or conscripted.

timeline.heading: WHY ROADS
timeline.body: Abductions cluster on highways because highways are where the state's writ thins out fastest. A village can host a permanent garrison; a 200km stretch of road cannot. The Maiduguri–Biu corridor has been a kidnap zone for over a decade — vehicles travel in convoys at scheduled hours or not at all.

blocks.question: What is the original meaning of the name 'Boko Haram' in Hausa?
blocks.explanation: 'Boko' originally referred to Roman-script books used in colonial Western schools; 'haram' means forbidden. The group's founding doctrine rejected secular Western education as religiously impermissible.

timeline.heading: THE CHIBOK ECHO
timeline.body: The 2014 abduction of 276 schoolgirls from Chibok — also in Borno — drew global attention via #BringBackOurGirls. More than a decade later, around 90 remain unaccounted for. Mass abductions on this scale have continued almost yearly since, with diminishing international notice each time.

timeline.heading: THE MULTINATIONAL FORCE
timeline.body: The Multinational Joint Task Force — Nigeria, Niger, Chad, Cameroon, Benin — was reconstituted in 2015 to coordinate operations around Lake Chad. Its effectiveness rises and falls with whichever capital is most willing to deploy. Niger's 2023 coup and Chad's domestic turmoil have repeatedly thinned the force from the non-Nigerian side.

timeline.heading: THE FUNDING MODEL
timeline.body: Most civil aviation authorities run on fees levied directly on the industry they regulate — passenger service charges, overflight fees, ticket sales taxes, and licensing levies. The treasury doesn't fund them; the airlines do. This makes the regulator structurally dependent on the financial health of the carriers it polices.

blocks.text: The Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority statute earmarks **5% of every ticket** sold and a per-passenger service charge as its primary revenue. When carriers withhold remittances, the regulator's own payroll is at risk.

timeline.heading: THE CONFLICT OF INTEREST
timeline.body: A regulator that depends on industry fees becomes a creditor of the firms it oversees. Suspending services to collect a debt is a tool no central bank or treasury would use — but for self-funded regulators, it is sometimes the only leverage available short of revoking an Air Operator Certificate.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'SERVICES' MEANS
timeline.body: Air navigation clearance, airworthiness certification, crew licensing, and route approvals all flow through the authority. Without them an airline cannot legally dispatch a flight. A services suspension is a soft grounding — the planes physically can move, but no insurer will cover a flight without current paperwork.

blocks.question: What typically grounds an airline first when its regulator pulls services?
options: The aircraft are physically locked at the gate
Insurance lapses without current airworthiness paperwork
Pilots refuse to fly in protest
Fuel suppliers cut off the carrier
blocks.explanation: Hull and liability insurance is contingent on a valid Certificate of Airworthiness; the moment certification lapses, the policy voids and the airline cannot legally dispatch.

timeline.heading: THE NAIRA SQUEEZE
timeline.body: Nigerian carriers earn most revenue in naira but pay for leases, spare parts, fuel, and overflight fees in dollars. Years of currency depreciation have compressed cash flow even as ticket prices climbed — leaving regulatory charges as one of the last bills paid.

timeline.heading: THE EID TIMING
timeline.body: Eid al-Adha falls in early June 2026 — one of two annual peaks for domestic Nigerian aviation, alongside Christmas. Lagos-Abuja and Lagos-Kano routes run at near-full loads for the week around the holiday. A suspension that holds through Eid means lost revenue the carriers cannot recover, which paradoxically deepens the arrears the regulator is trying to collect.

timeline.heading: THE TRAPPED-FUNDS BACKDROP
timeline.body: Nigeria has spent the last three years on IATA's trapped-funds list — foreign airlines unable to repatriate ticket revenue from naira accounts. Emirates suspended Nigeria service in 2022 over $85m stuck in the country. The domestic carriers now under suspension operate inside the same dollar-scarce system that drove the foreign airlines out.

blocks.label: Largest blocked-funds markets for foreign airlines, 2024 (IATA)

timeline.heading: THE PROJECT
timeline.body: One Constitution Avenue is a luxury mixed-use tower complex on Islamabad's ceremonial axis — the road that runs between the Supreme Court, Parliament, and the Presidency. The land was leased by the Capital Development Authority in 2007 to a private developer for a 99-year term; the dispute is over which flats the state was owed back as its share of the project.

blocks.label: Islamabad's ceremonial axis
blocks.caption: the contested tower sits among the institutions now adjudicating it

timeline.heading: THE ALLOTMENT
timeline.body: Roughly 240 flats in the completed tower were allotted at below-market rates to sitting judges, federal ministers, senior bureaucrats, and at least one former prime minister. The allotments became public years after the fact, and the original list has never been fully released.

blocks.text: The allotments at issue went to judges of the **same superior courts** now adjudicating the title dispute — a textbook conflict of interest that Pakistani recusal practice has historically been slow to enforce.

timeline.heading: THE NEMO JUDEX RULE
timeline.body: Across common-law systems the principle is nemo judex in causa sua — no one shall be a judge in their own cause. In Pakistan it is codified through Article 4 and Article 10A of the Constitution (due process and fair trial) and the Code of Conduct for Judges, which requires recusal where a judge has any personal or financial interest in the outcome.

blocks.question: What does the legal principle 'nemo judex in causa sua' require?
options: A judge must not hear a case in which they have a personal interest
A judge must give written reasons for every ruling
A judge cannot be removed except by parliament
A judge must follow the precedent of higher courts
blocks.explanation: Nemo judex in causa sua — 'no one shall be a judge in their own cause' — is the foundational recusal rule across common-law systems.

timeline.heading: WHY ARBITRATION
timeline.body: Pakistan's 1940 Arbitration Act (now largely superseded by the 2011 act for international disputes) lets parties to a commercial contract bypass the courts and settle through a private tribunal whose award is enforceable like a decree. Governments use it to escape clogged dockets and to insulate sensitive deals from public hearings — at the cost of transparency.

blocks.text: An arbitration *award* is final and binding once signed: courts may set it aside only on narrow grounds — fraud, misconduct of the arbitrator, or an award that exceeds the submitted dispute. Reopening one a decade later, as the IHC is being asked to do, runs against the entire design of the system.

timeline.heading: THE MINISTER'S DUAL ROLE
timeline.body: Khawaja Asif signed the 2012 award in his then-capacity as Minister for Water and Power, binding the state to the developer's terms. He now sits in cabinet as Defence Minister of the government whose court is being asked to undo that same award — a conflict the bench cannot ignore even if Asif himself is not a party.

timeline.heading: THE BROADER PATTERN
timeline.body: Judicial perks in Pakistan — official residences, plots in Defence Housing Authority schemes, post-retirement consultancies — have long been criticised as a quiet patronage system that ties the bench to the executive that allocates them. The One Constitution Avenue case is unusual only because the perk and the dispute land in the same courtroom.

timeline.heading: WHY LIVESTOCK MATTERS
timeline.body: Livestock is Sudan's second-largest export after gold and the single largest rural employer. Roughly two-thirds of Sudanese households own animals; for Darfuri pastoralists, sheep are not a sideline but the household balance sheet — savings, dowry, and insurance in one form.

blocks.text: Sudan holds one of the largest sheep herds in Africa — historically the country was the **top live-sheep exporter to Saudi Arabia**, with Eid al-Adha demand alone moving millions of head across the Red Sea each year.

timeline.heading: THE EID PREMIUM
timeline.body: Eid al-Adha requires a healthy ram per household that can afford one. Demand concentrates into a two-week window, prices spike predictably, and the Gulf import market — Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait — absorbs the surplus at premium rates. The entire pastoral economy is calibrated around this annual peak.

blocks.label: the Eid livestock corridor
blocks.caption: Sudan historically supplied Gulf Eid demand via Port Sudan

timeline.heading: THE FRAGMENTATION
timeline.body: A 4.4x price gap between Nyala and Khartoum on the same animal is not a market — it is two markets separated by checkpoints, looted trucks, and front lines. In functioning economies, arbitrage closes such gaps in days; in Sudan, the gap is the war.

timeline.heading: THE TWO ARMIES
timeline.body: Sudan's war is between two generals who jointly overthrew a civilian government. The SAF under Burhan holds the center and Port Sudan; the RSF under Hemedti — evolved from the Janjaweed militias of the Darfur genocide — controls most of Darfur, including Nyala. The trade routes between them are the front line.

people.name: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan
people.role: SAF commander, de-facto head of state

timeline.heading: WHY ROUTES MATTER
timeline.body: Sudanese livestock historically moved north along two corridors: Darfur to Omdurman to Port Sudan for Gulf export, and Kordofan to the Nile for domestic markets. Both corridors now cross RSF–SAF lines. A sheep born in Nyala cannot legally, safely, or affordably reach the ships at Port Sudan.

timeline.heading: THE CURRENCY LAYER
timeline.body: SDG 2 million sounds enormous; the Sudanese pound has collapsed against the dollar since the war began. Real prices in hard currency have risen sharply but nowhere near 4x — the headline gap reflects both genuine scarcity and the parallel collapse of the unit of account.

blocks.question: Why does the same sheep cost more than 4x as much in central Sudan as in Darfur?
options: Darfur sheep are a lower-quality breed
War-blocked routes prevent supply from reaching demand
Central Sudan has stronger Eid traditions
blocks.explanation: Arbitrage normally closes such gaps within days. In Sudan, RSF-SAF front lines physically block the trade corridors that once connected Darfur herds to Khartoum and Port Sudan.

timeline.heading: WHAT A CENTRAL BANK ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: A central bank is not a building — it is the monopoly on issuing legal tender, settling interbank payments, and holding reserves. When a rival force replicates those three functions inside the same country, sovereignty has already been partitioned in fact, regardless of what maps still show.

blocks.text: The technical term is **monetary sovereignty** — and unlike territorial sovereignty, it cannot be shared. Two issuers of the 'same' pound produce two currencies, even if both are printed in the same denominations.

timeline.heading: THE TWO ARMIES
timeline.body: Sudan's war is between two generals who jointly overthrew Bashir in 2019, then jointly crushed the civilian democracy movement, then turned on each other in April 2023. The SAF (regular army) under Burhan controls Port Sudan and the east; the RSF under Hemedti — evolved from the Janjaweed militias of the Darfur genocide — controls most of Darfur and much of Khartoum.

people.name: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan
people.role: SAF commander, de-facto head of state

timeline.heading: THE TERRITORIAL SPLIT
timeline.body: The official Central Bank of Sudan relocated to Port Sudan on the Red Sea coast after Khartoum fell. The RSF runs its parallel monetary system out of Nyala in South Darfur. The two issuing centers sit nearly 2,000km apart with active front lines between them.

timeline.heading: THE BANKNOTE RECALL WEAPON
timeline.body: In 2024 the SAF-controlled central bank announced a redesign of the 1,000-pound note, giving holders a short window to exchange old notes at official branches — branches that exist only in SAF territory. Civilians in RSF areas were effectively told their cash savings were worthless unless they could cross a front line. The RSF responded by building its own banking rail.

blocks.question: What is the standard purpose of a sudden banknote recall in a civil war?
options: Strand the enemy's cash holdings and force exchange through your banks
Reduce inflation by removing old notes
blocks.explanation: India's 2016 demonetization and Sudan's 2024 recall share the mechanic: invalidating notes forces holders through state-controlled exchange points, exposing untaxed wealth or stranding rival-held cash.

timeline.heading: THE PARTITION PRECEDENTS
timeline.body: Monetary splits almost always precede or cement political partition. Yugoslavia's republics issued separate dinars before independence; Sudan and South Sudan ran a shared pound for barely a year after 2011 before splitting it; Yemen has had rival central banks in Aden and Sana'a since 2016, with two exchange rates and two banknote series that increasingly cannot be exchanged for each other.

events.label: Yemen splits CBY between Aden and Sana'a
SAF banknote recall strands RSF areas

timeline.heading: WHY DIGITAL TRANSFER MATTERS
timeline.body: A rebel-held central bank with only paper notes is fragile — the notes have to be printed somewhere, smuggled in, and trusted. A digital transfer app sidesteps all three problems: balances exist as database entries, settlement is instant, and the network effect grows with each merchant who accepts it. This is why the RSF's app, not the bank charter, is the structural threat to reunification.

timeline.heading: THE FLOOR PROBLEM
timeline.body: Visa and Mastercard rails were designed for human-scale transactions. Interchange fees, network assessments, and acquirer markups stack up to a roughly 30-cent minimum per swipe. Anything smaller loses money to process — which is why newspapers never charged per article and APIs never charged per call.

blocks.text: The economic term is the *sub-cent transaction problem*: a payment system whose **fixed cost per transaction** exceeds the value being transferred is structurally unable to serve that market, no matter how much demand exists.

timeline.heading: WHY STABLECOINS CLEAR IT
timeline.body: A USDC transfer on a Layer-2 like Base or Solana settles in seconds for a fraction of a cent. There is no acquirer, no issuer, no chargeback window — the token moves on a public ledger and finality is the block confirmation. The 30-cent floor disappears because the rail itself has no floor.

timeline.heading: WHY USDC AND NOT USDT
timeline.body: Tether (USDT) dominates global stablecoin volume — but its reserves are opaque and it has been banned or restricted in the US, EU, and Singapore. Circle's USDC publishes monthly attestations, holds reserves at BNY Mellon, and is the only major stablecoin pre-cleared under MiCA. For an agent operated by a US company, USDC is the only choice that survives compliance review.

timeline.heading: THE LIABILITY VOID
timeline.body: Card networks have 60 years of case law on who pays when a transaction goes wrong — issuer, acquirer, merchant, consumer. None of it applies when the buyer is a piece of software with no legal personhood. If an agent overpays, gets phished, or buys something its principal didn't authorize, current law has no clear answer.

blocks.question: Under US law, who is liable when an AI agent makes an unauthorized purchase on behalf of its user?
options: The agent's developer, under product liability
The user, as principal of the agent
The merchant who accepted the payment
Unsettled — no statute or precedent directly addresses it
blocks.explanation: Agent liability is a genuine legal void; the GENIUS Act and MiCA both regulate the stablecoin issuer, not the autonomous spender.

timeline.heading: THE GENIUS ACT
timeline.body: The 2025 GENIUS Act (Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins) creates a federal license for payment stablecoin issuers, mandates 1:1 reserves in cash or short Treasuries, and preempts state money-transmitter law. It legitimizes USDC as a payment instrument — but says nothing about who is operating the wallet on the other end.

timeline.heading: THE TREASURY DEMAND LOOP
timeline.body: USDC's reserves are mostly short-dated US Treasury bills. Every dollar that moves into stablecoins becomes a marginal bid for T-bills. If agent commerce scales to the trillions Stripe and Visa are projecting, stablecoin issuers become structurally significant Treasury buyers — a quiet form of dollar entrenchment running through software, not central banks.

blocks.label: how an agent's USDC payment flows

timeline.heading: WHAT Q DAY MEANS
timeline.body: Q Day is the hypothetical date a quantum computer can break RSA-2048 or elliptic-curve cryptography in hours rather than billions of years. It is not about breaking all encryption — symmetric ciphers like AES-256 only lose half their effective key length against quantum attacks, which still leaves them secure.

blocks.text: The asymmetry matters: *public-key* schemes (RSA, ECDSA) collapse; *symmetric* schemes (AES, SHA-2) merely need bigger keys.

timeline.heading: SHOR'S ALGORITHM
timeline.body: Peter Shor proved in 1994 that a sufficiently large quantum computer can factor integers and solve discrete logarithms in polynomial time. Every public-key system in production — RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ECDSA — rests on the assumption these problems are hard. Shor's algorithm is the only reason quantum computers matter for cryptography.

timeline.heading: WHY AI CHANGES THE TIMELINE
timeline.body: The bottleneck is not qubit count — it is error correction. A logical qubit currently needs hundreds of physical qubits, decoded in real time. Machine learning has begun outperforming hand-designed decoders, shrinking the overhead ratio and pulling forward the date when a useful machine is built.

timeline.heading: WHAT BITCOIN ACTUALLY USES
timeline.body: Bitcoin relies on ECDSA over the secp256k1 curve. Your private key is a 256-bit number; your public key is a point on an elliptic curve derived from it. The security assumption — you cannot work backwards from public to private — is exactly what Shor's algorithm breaks.

blocks.question: Which Bitcoin addresses are most exposed to a quantum attack?
options: Addresses that have never sent a transaction
Addresses that have already revealed their public key on-chain
blocks.explanation: Bitcoin addresses are hashes of public keys. Until you spend from an address, only the hash is on-chain. Once you spend, the public key is exposed — and that's what a quantum attacker would target.

timeline.heading: HARVEST NOW, DECRYPT LATER
timeline.body: Intelligence agencies are already collecting encrypted traffic — diplomatic cables, banking flows, medical records — on the assumption it can be decrypted years later. Anything whose secrecy must outlast Q Day is effectively compromised the moment it crosses a wire today.

timeline.heading: THE MIGRATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: In 2024 NIST finalised three post-quantum standards based on lattice problems. Migrating TLS, VPNs, and firmware channels is painful but tractable — there is a central authority to push the change. A blockchain has no such authority: changing Bitcoin's signature scheme requires a hard fork, coordinated across miners, exchanges, and wallets holding coins whose owners may be dead.

timeline.heading: THE DEFENDER'S ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: An attacker needs one exploitable bug; a defender needs to fix all of them. Tools that lower the cost of finding bugs help both sides — but the side with the patching pipeline, not the side with the scanner, decides whether the discovery becomes a fix or a zero-day.

blocks.text: The industry shorthand is **N-day** for a disclosed-and-patched bug versus **0-day** for one being exploited before any patch exists. Glasswing's output is a flood of N-day candidates — useful only as fast as the patch pipeline can absorb them.

timeline.heading: THE FUZZING LINEAGE
timeline.body: Automated bug-finding is not new. Barton Miller coined fuzzing at the University of Wisconsin in 1988 by piping random bytes at Unix utilities. AFL (2013) made coverage-guided fuzzing mainstream; Google's OSS-Fuzz (2016) has found tens of thousands of bugs in open-source projects. LLM-driven discovery is the latest rung on a 38-year ladder, not a new game.

timeline.heading: WHY MOST BUGS ARE THE SAME BUG
timeline.body: Across Microsoft, Chrome, Android, and the Linux kernel, roughly 70% of critical security vulnerabilities are memory-safety bugs — buffer overflows, use-after-frees, double-frees — in C and C++ code. This is why Rust adoption matters as a structural fix, not a fashion: rewriting the substrate eliminates a category, not a bug.

blocks.label: share of critical CVEs that are memory-safety bugs

blocks.question: Roughly what share of critical vulnerabilities in large C/C++ codebases are memory-safety bugs?
blocks.explanation: Microsoft, Google, and the Linux kernel maintainers have all independently reported the ~70% figure over the past decade — the consistency is why memory-safe languages are now a national-security talking point.

timeline.heading: THE CVE PIPELINE
timeline.body: A vulnerability becomes a CVE — a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures ID — only after a CNA (CVE Numbering Authority) assigns it. MITRE has run the program since 1999 under US government contract. The National Vulnerability Database scores severity using CVSS, a 0–10 metric where 9.0+ counts as critical. 'Critical' is not a synonym for 'exploited' — it is an estimate of worst-case impact.

blocks.text: A bug with no CVE is not less real — it's just unnumbered. Many internal bugs at large vendors are patched silently and never receive an ID, which is one reason raw CVE counts undercount the real population.

timeline.heading: THE 90-DAY NORM
timeline.body: Google's Project Zero established the modern disclosure standard in 2014: the finder privately notifies the vendor and publishes details 90 days later, patched or not. The deadline forces patching velocity. Anthropic withholding details until patches ship is the conservative end of this spectrum — the alternative is researchers who publish on day 90 regardless.

blocks.text: Project Zero will publicly disclose details of the vulnerability 90 days after the initial report, whether or not it has been fixed.
blocks.speaker: Google Project Zero disclosure policy

timeline.heading: THE PATCHING BOTTLENECK
timeline.body: Finding bugs has never been the binding constraint at scale — OSS-Fuzz already files thousands of bugs annually that maintainers cannot triage. Median time-to-patch for critical vulnerabilities in enterprise software is measured in months, not days. A scanner that produces 10,000 leads per month doesn't shrink the gap; it widens it, and shifts the strategic question from 'can we find them' to 'who can patch fastest'.

timeline.heading: THE CLOSED BORDER
timeline.body: Turkey shut its land border with Armenia in 1993 in solidarity with Azerbaijan during the First Nagorno-Karabakh War. For three decades, goods between two neighbors had to detour through Georgia or Iran — a closure unusual in modern Europe for its duration and totality.

blocks.text: The border closure made Armenia one of only two **doubly landlocked-by-hostility** states in Eurasia — surrounded by open borders only with *Georgia* and *Iran*, with Turkey and Azerbaijan sealed shut.

timeline.heading: THE 1915 SHADOW
timeline.body: The diplomatic freeze rests on the unresolved question of the Armenian Genocide — the 1915 deportations and massacres under the late Ottoman state that killed roughly 1.5 million Armenians. Turkey rejects the genocide designation; Armenia's constitution references it. Every normalization attempt since the 1990s has run into this wall.

timeline.heading: WHY KARABAKH UNLOCKED IT
timeline.body: Armenia lost the 2020 war and the remaining Armenian population of Nagorno-Karabakh was displaced in 2023. With the territorial dispute resolved on Azerbaijan's terms, Ankara's condition for opening — Armenian concessions on Karabakh — was met by force of facts rather than diplomacy.

timeline.heading: THE CORRIDOR GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: The Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway was deliberately routed through Georgia to bypass Armenia. Akhalkalaki is the Georgian junction where Armenian freight can now interchange — Armenia accesses Turkish rail without Turkish track ever touching Armenian soil.

timeline.heading: THE ZANGEZUR QUESTION
timeline.body: Pashinyan's reference to direct Azerbaijan links via Nakhichevan points to the proposed Zangezur corridor — a route across Armenia's southern Syunik province that would connect Azerbaijan proper to its Nakhichevan exclave, and onward to Turkey. Yerevan resists extraterritorial control; Baku and Ankara push for it. This is the next pressure point.

blocks.question: Why does Azerbaijan want the Zangezur corridor through Armenia?
options: To reach its Nakhichevan exclave and connect to Turkey by land
blocks.explanation: Nakhichevan is an Azerbaijani exclave separated from the main country by a strip of Armenian territory; the corridor would close that gap and connect Baku to Turkey overland.

timeline.heading: THE RUSSIAN LOSER
timeline.body: For thirty years Moscow was Armenia's only guarantor — basing troops at Gyumri, controlling rail and energy infrastructure, mediating with Azerbaijan. Every kilometer of Turkish-Armenian trade is a kilometer Russia no longer controls. Pashinyan's pivot toward the EU and now Turkey is the slow unwinding of the post-Soviet security architecture in the Caucasus.

timeline.heading: THE 2019 RULE CHANGE
timeline.body: Benin's parliament rewrote the electoral code in 2018, requiring presidential candidates to secure endorsements from a supermajority of sitting legislators and mayors. After Talon's party swept the 2019 legislative elections — which the opposition boycotted — no opposition figure could clear the threshold. The lock was procedural, not coercive.

blocks.text: The mechanism has a name in comparative politics: ***competitive authoritarianism***. Elections happen, results are counted honestly, but the *rules of entry* are tilted so the outcome is never in doubt.

timeline.heading: FROM DEMOCRATIC MODEL TO CAUTIONARY TALE
timeline.body: Benin held Africa's first sovereign national conference in 1990 — a template later copied across francophone Africa — and rotated power peacefully through four elections. Freedom House rated it 'Free' as recently as 2018. The slide since has been one of the sharpest documented democratic reversals on the continent.

timeline.heading: THE COTTON STATE
timeline.body: Talon built his fortune on cotton — Benin's largest export and the livelihood of roughly a third of the rural workforce. Control of the ginning sector translated into political patronage long before he ran for office; the presidency formalized what was already a commercial monopoly.

timeline.heading: THE FINANCE MINISTER PIPELINE
timeline.body: Wadagni came from Deloitte, ran the Eurobond program that built Benin's investor reputation, and was the regime's face to the IMF and rating agencies. Installing the technocrat-financier preserves the external story — fiscal discipline, market access — while keeping the political machine intact.

blocks.label: Benin and its neighbors
blocks.caption: Wedged between Nigeria's economy and the Sahel's coup belt

timeline.heading: THE COUP-BELT CONTEXT
timeline.body: Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, and Guinea have all seen military takeovers since 2020. Benin's path — an elected leader closing the electoral door behind him — is the constitutional mirror of those coups: same end state, different paperwork. Western capitals find the second pattern harder to sanction.

blocks.question: What changed in Benin's 2018 electoral code that effectively barred the opposition?
options: A ban on opposition parties by name
A sponsorship rule requiring endorsements from sitting legislators and mayors
blocks.explanation: The sponsorship requirement was facially neutral but unmeetable once Talon's party held nearly every legislative and mayoral seat.

timeline.heading: THE STRAIN MATTERS
timeline.body: Ebola is not one virus but six species. Zaire ebolavirus — the strain behind the 2014 West Africa and 2018 Kivu outbreaks — has an approved vaccine (Ervebo) and two monoclonal-antibody treatments. Bundibugyo has none. Each outbreak's lethality and response options depend on which species is circulating.

timeline.heading: WHY VOLUNTEERS DIE FIRST
timeline.body: Ebola transmits through direct contact with bodily fluids — and viral load is highest in the dying and the dead. Burial workers, nurses, and family caregivers face exposure orders of magnitude greater than the general population. In the 2014 outbreak, healthcare workers were infected at 21–32 times the rate of other adults.

blocks.text: The traditional West and Central African funeral rite of washing and touching the deceased is one of the highest-risk acts on earth during an Ebola outbreak — which is why *safe and dignified burials* became a Red Cross technical specialty after 2014.

timeline.heading: THE ITURI CORRIDOR
timeline.body: Ituri sits on a porous border with Uganda's West Nile region. The same trading routes that move cassava, fish, and motorcycles move pathogens. Cross-border outbreaks here are not anomalies — the 2007 Bundibugyo discovery itself happened in a Ugandan district that abuts DRC.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE WHO DECLARATION TRIGGERS
timeline.body: A Public Health Emergency of International Concern is a legal instrument under the 2005 International Health Regulations, not a slogan. It unlocks emergency funding, authorizes WHO to issue temporary recommendations on travel and trade, and obliges member states to share case data. It has been declared only eight times since the framework began.

blocks.question: Which event was the FIRST Public Health Emergency of International Concern declared under the 2005 IHR?
blocks.explanation: The 2005 IHR took force in 2007; H1N1 in 2009 was its first invocation. SARS predated the framework.

timeline.heading: THE RESERVOIR
timeline.body: Ebola's natural reservoir is almost certainly fruit bats of the family Pteropodidae — the same family that hosts Marburg and Nipah. Spillover happens when humans handle bushmeat or enter caves where bats roost. Every outbreak begins with one zoonotic event; everything after is human-to-human.

timeline.heading: THE 2018–20 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: DRC's last major Ebola outbreak — North Kivu, Zaire strain — killed 2,287 people over two years. It was eventually contained with ring vaccination, but armed groups attacked treatment centers and community mistrust of outsiders slowed response. Eastern Congo's security environment, more than the virus itself, has historically determined how long these outbreaks last.

timeline.heading: THE WITHDRAWAL PERIOD
timeline.body: Every registered pesticide carries a withdrawal interval — the days that must elapse between the last spray and harvest, so residues decay below safe limits. Skip it and the active ingredient is still on the leaf when it reaches the market.

blocks.text: The technical term is the **pre-harvest interval (PHI)**. It is printed on the label in regulated markets and treated as legally binding — enforcement depends on residue testing at point of sale.

timeline.heading: WHAT AN MRL IS
timeline.body: A Maximum Residue Limit is the highest concentration of a pesticide legally permitted on food, set by Codex Alimentarius and adopted nationally. Without an MRL framework, there is no number to test against and no basis to reject a contaminated batch.

timeline.heading: WHY DRYLANDS SPRAY MORE
timeline.body: Arid-zone vegetable plots face concentrated pest pressure — irrigated greenery in a dry landscape is a magnet for whiteflies, aphids, and leaf miners. Farmers compensate with frequent broad-spectrum sprays, often organophosphates and pyrethroids sold without prescription.

timeline.heading: THE INFORMAL MARKET PROBLEM
timeline.body: Residue testing happens at organized wholesale markets where lots are traceable to a farm. Informal roadside markets aggregate from dozens of smallholders with no paperwork — even a functioning regulator cannot sample what it cannot identify.

blocks.question: Why does buying from informal markets defeat pesticide residue regulation?
options: Informal vendors charge less, so farmers cut corners
Produce cannot be traced back to a specific farm or spray date
Informal markets sell older produce with degraded residues
Regulators are barred from inspecting informal vendors
blocks.explanation: Traceability is the precondition for enforcement — without a chain from plot to plate, a failed residue test has no one to penalise.

timeline.heading: THE RECOGNITION GAP
timeline.body: Somaliland has functioned as a de-facto state since 1991 but holds zero UN recognition. That gap blocks accession to Codex, FAO technical assistance programmes, and the regional standards bodies that would normally publish an MRL list for its growers.

blocks.label: food-safety regulatory capacity in the Horn

timeline.heading: THE EXPORT CEILING
timeline.body: EU and Gulf importers reject produce on residue grounds routinely; a single failed shipment can suspend a country from a category. Without a domestic testing regime, dryland growers are locked out of the premium export markets that would justify investing in safer practice — a chicken-and-egg trap common across recognition-deficient economies.

timeline.heading: THE RECOGNITION DEFICIT
timeline.body: Somaliland declared independence in 1991, has held competitive elections, prints its own currency, and polices its own borders — yet sits at zero formal UN recognition.
