timeline.body: The ridge often takes the shape of the Greek letter omega (Ω) on weather charts — a high-pressure bulge flanked by two lows. This pattern is unusually stable. Once locked in, it can persist for a week or more, which is what turns a hot day into a mass-casualty event.

timeline.heading: WHY EUROPE WARMS FASTER
timeline.body: Europe is warming at roughly twice the global average — the fastest-warming continent on Earth. Reduced aerosol pollution since the 1980s (cleaner air lets more sunlight through), a warming Arctic that weakens the jet stream, and Mediterranean sea-surface temperatures running 3-5°C above normal all compound.

timeline.heading: THE 2003 BASELINE
timeline.body: The August 2003 European heatwave killed an estimated 70,000 people across the continent, mostly elderly. France alone lost 15,000 in two weeks — morgues overflowed, refrigerated trucks were requisitioned. It rewrote European public health: national heat-action plans, cooling centers, and excess-mortality monitoring all date from the post-2003 reforms.

timeline.heading: WHY HUMIDITY IS THE KILLER
timeline.body: The human body cools by evaporating sweat. Above a wet-bulb temperature of ~35°C, sweat no longer evaporates and core temperature climbs regardless of shade or hydration. Dry European heat is survivable at higher dry-bulb temperatures than Gulf humidity — but urban heat islands and overnight lows above 25°C remove the body's recovery window.

blocks.question: Which factor most determines whether a heatwave becomes deadly?
options: Overnight low temperatures over consecutive days
Wind speed during the hottest hour
blocks.explanation: Bodies recover from heat stress at night. When overnight lows stay above 25°C for several days, cumulative strain kills — which is why heatwaves with high nighttime temperatures are deadlier than hotter but cooler-night events.

timeline.heading: THE SHIFTING SEASON
timeline.body: What made May 2022 a once-in-decades event is arriving in May 2026 — and the underlying climatology is shifting the heatwave season earlier. Spring heat is more dangerous than summer heat at the same temperature: bodies haven't acclimatized, infrastructure isn't primed, and vulnerable populations haven't yet activated cooling routines.

timeline.heading: THE SCARCITY MODEL
timeline.body: Ferrari's business is the opposite of automotive scale. It produces roughly 13,000 cars a year — fewer than Toyota builds before lunch — and maintains operating margins above 25%, higher than Hermès. The constraint is deliberate: demand must always exceed supply, or the brand premium collapses.

timeline.heading: THE 2035 DEADLINE
timeline.body: The EU's combustion ban prohibits the sale of new internal-combustion passenger cars from 2035. A narrow carve-out for e-fuels survived 2023 negotiations after German pressure, but the default path forces every European automaker — including the ones whose entire identity is engine noise — to electrify.

blocks.text: Ferrari's V12 is not a powertrain; it is the *product*. The 2035 deadline is why a €550,000 electric five-seater exists at all — without the regulatory cliff, the Luce would not be the lineup's priority.

timeline.heading: THE SOUND PROBLEM
timeline.body: A combustion Ferrari's exhaust note is engineered like a musical instrument — tuned pipe lengths, firing order, resonance chambers. Electric motors hum. Porsche, Audi, and now Ferrari have all filed patents on synthetic powertrain sound; the engineering question is whether buyers accept simulation when authenticity was the entire purchase.

timeline.heading: WHY FIVE SEATS
timeline.body: Ferrari has historically refused four-door cars. The GTC4Lusso was a 2+2 shooting brake; the Purosangue (2022) was the first SUV. A five-seater breaks a deeper taboo than electrification — it admits Ferraris are bought by families, not just collectors. The Chinese and Gulf markets, where chauffeured ownership is normal, drove the decision.

blocks.question: Until the Purosangue in 2022, how many seats did every production Ferrari have?
blocks.explanation: Ferrari produced strictly 2-seat and 2+2 layouts for 75 years. The Purosangue SUV broke the rule; the Luce extends it to a true five-seater.

timeline.heading: THE LUXURY EV PARADOX
timeline.body: Electric powertrains compress what used to differentiate luxury cars. A €30,000 EV and a €300,000 EV both deliver instant torque, silent acceleration, and similar 0-100 times. Luxury EVs must justify the premium through craft, materials, and brand — the same logic that sustains a €15,000 watch when a €50 quartz keeps better time.

timeline.heading: THE IVE CONNECTION
timeline.body: Jony Ive — Apple's former design chief — has reportedly consulted on Ferrari's electric program since 2024. His design language (radical minimalism, hidden seams, single-piece surfaces) suits an EV's lack of grille and exhaust. The challenge is that minimalism is the opposite of Maranello's traditional baroque visual identity.

timeline.heading: THE ISLAMIC RULING
timeline.body: Classical Sunni jurisprudence prohibits maysir — gain contingent on pure chance — and gharar, excessive uncertainty in a contract. Prediction markets sit squarely in both categories: the payoff depends on an external event, and neither party transfers a real underlying asset. Every major Sunni fiqh council (AAOIFI, OIC Islamic Fiqh Academy, Saudi Permanent Committee) has ruled conventional futures and event contracts impermissible on these grounds.

blocks.text: The Quranic prohibition on *maysir* appears alongside the prohibition on *khamr* (intoxicants) in Surah al-Ma'ida — the two are paired as social harms, not merely individual sins.

timeline.heading: HOW PREDICTION MARKETS WORK
timeline.body: Polymarket lets users buy contracts that pay $1 if an event happens and $0 if it doesn't. The price becomes a real-time probability — a contract at $0.30 means the market collectively assigns 30% odds. Settlement runs on the Polygon blockchain in USDC stablecoin, which is why crypto rails matter to the regulatory question.

blocks.question: If a Polymarket contract trades at $0.18, what probability is the market assigning to the event?
blocks.explanation: Contract price equals implied probability: pays $1 if yes, $0 if no, so $0.18 = 18% chance.

timeline.heading: THE CLASSIFICATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: Regulators worldwide struggle with the same question: is an event contract a derivative (hedging real-world exposure) or a wager (entertainment risk)? The US CFTC has allowed some Kalshi contracts as derivatives; states have sued, calling them gambling. Indonesia skipped the debate and applied its existing gambling statute — a simpler legal route most Muslim-majority states can copy.

timeline.heading: THE INDONESIAN STATUTE
timeline.body: Indonesia's gambling prohibition derives from Article 303 of the Criminal Code (inherited from Dutch colonial law) and was sharpened by the 2008 Electronic Information and Transactions Law, which lets the ministry block any online service facilitating prohibited activity. The same authority has blocked Reddit segments, Steam, and PayPal in past enforcement waves — Polymarket joins an established pattern, not a new doctrine.

blocks.label: Muslim-majority states' approach to online gambling

timeline.heading: THE TEMPLATE EFFECT
timeline.body: Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim-majority country — 280 million people, roughly 13% of the global Muslim population. When Jakarta sets a regulatory precedent on a religiously-coded question, it travels. The 2018 ban on Tumblr over pornographic content was cited verbatim in subsequent Pakistani and Bangladeshi enforcement orders.

timeline.heading: THE CRYPTO RAIL PROBLEM
timeline.body: Polymarket runs on Polygon and settles in USDC. A national IP block stops casual access but not determined users with a VPN and a self-custody wallet. Indonesia's central bank already prohibits crypto as a payment method (2017) while permitting it as a commodity for trading — a split that leaves prediction-market settlement in a legal grey zone the gambling order now closes.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'FROZEN' MEANS
timeline.body: Sovereign assets are frozen when a foreign jurisdiction blocks the owner from moving them — the money still exists on a bank's books, but transfers require a license from the sanctioning treasury. Iran's blocked funds are scattered across South Korea, Japan, Iraq, and European correspondent banks, accumulated from oil sales that buyers paid into escrow rather than into Tehran's accounts.

blocks.text: The technical term is **blocking** under OFAC's Iranian Transactions Regulations — distinct from outright **confiscation**, which would require a court judgment. Frozen funds remain Iran's property; Iran simply cannot touch them.

timeline.heading: WHY QATAR
timeline.body: Qatar shares the world's largest gas field — South Pars / North Dome — with Iran across the Persian Gulf seabed. The two states cannot afford open hostility; Doha has hosted Iranian negotiators through every nuclear cycle since 2015. Qatar also hosts Al-Udeid, the largest US military base in the region. Sitting on both sides of the table is the entire business model.

timeline.heading: THE 2023 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Washington released $6 billion of Iranian funds held in South Korea into Qatari accounts in September 2023 as part of a prisoner swap. After October 7, the deal was effectively frozen again — the money sits in Doha, accessible only for humanitarian goods under US Treasury supervision. Every subsequent negotiation references this template.

timeline.heading: THE HUMANITARIAN CHANNEL
timeline.body: Even hardline sanctions regimes carve out food, medicine, and medical devices. The mechanism is escrow accounts in third countries where Iran's customers deposit oil revenue, which Iran can only draw down to pay vendors of approved goods. The system is designed so cash never enters Iran's banking system — circumventing the SWIFT disconnection imposed in 2018.

blocks.question: What does Iran's frozen oil revenue in third-country escrow accounts allow Tehran to purchase?
options: Cash withdrawals for general budget use
Only food, medicine, and approved humanitarian goods
Any goods except those originating in the US
blocks.explanation: US Treasury licenses limit drawdowns to humanitarian categories — food, medicine, agricultural commodities — with vendor invoices reviewed before each transfer.

timeline.heading: THE OIL-PRICE TELL
timeline.body: Crude reacted before any agreement was signed because the market prices the tail risk of Hormuz disruption directly into Brent. A 5% one-day move signals traders are unwinding war-premium hedges, not pricing Iranian barrels returning to market — sanctions relief on assets is separate from sanctions relief on exports.

blocks.label: Iran closes its airspace by May 24?

timeline.heading: THE DEEPER ARC
timeline.body: The US has held Iranian assets since 1979, when the Carter administration froze roughly $12 billion in response to the embassy seizure. The Algiers Accords of 1981 returned some funds and created the Iran-US Claims Tribunal at The Hague — still adjudicating cases 45 years later. Frozen assets have been a bargaining chip in every US-Iran negotiation since the Shah fell.

timeline.heading: WHY LITHIUM, WHY NOW
timeline.body: Lithium is the irreplaceable cathode metal in every EV battery and grid storage system. Demand grew roughly 30% per year through the 2020s, pushing miners into deposits — and communities — that would never have been touched at 2015 prices.

blocks.text: The chemistry matters: **lithium-ion** batteries store energy by shuttling Li+ ions between electrodes. No commercial substitute matches its *energy density per kilogram* — sodium-ion comes close but is heavier, and solid-state remains pre-commercial.

timeline.heading: WHO PRODUCES IT
timeline.body: Australia, Chile, and China dominate primary production. Africa is the new frontier — Zimbabwe, Mali, Namibia, and now South Africa are being prospected aggressively, often by Chinese-financed operators racing ahead of Western majors.

timeline.heading: THE EIA CAPTURE PROBLEM
timeline.body: South African law requires an Environmental Impact Assessment before mining, but the mining company hires and pays the consultant who writes it. The structural conflict is global — the same pattern produced rubber-stamp assessments for Brumadinho in Brazil before its 2019 tailings dam collapse killed 270 people.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE LAW PROMISED
timeline.body: South Africa's Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act (2002) and the Interim Protection of Informal Land Rights Act (1996) require relocation agreements with affected communities before mining begins. Both were post-apartheid laws designed to prevent the forced removals that defined the previous era.

blocks.question: Under the Interim Protection of Informal Land Rights Act, who must consent before a community is relocated for mining?
blocks.explanation: The Act protects individual informal land rights — each household holds a right that cannot be overridden by a chief or province alone.

timeline.heading: THE APARTHEID ECHO
timeline.body: Between 1960 and 1983, the apartheid state forcibly relocated roughly 3.5 million Black South Africans under the Group Areas Act and homeland consolidation. The Magog community's resistance reads against that memory — relocation is not a neutral administrative step in South Africa, it is the defining trauma of the 20th century.

events.label: Natives Land Act restricts Black land ownership

timeline.heading: THE RESOURCE CURSE LOCALLY
timeline.body: KwaZulu-Natal's coastal strip is among the country's poorest. Mineral discoveries in poor regions typically deepen inequality rather than alleviate it — royalties flow to the central treasury and corporate shareholders while environmental and social costs stay local. Economists call this the resource curse; affected communities call it theft.

timeline.heading: THE EVACUATION WARNING AS DOCTRINE
timeline.body: Pre-strike warnings to evacuate civilians or diplomats are a recognized signaling move: they shift legal and moral responsibility onto the target while preserving the option to strike. The US used them before Tomahawk salvos in Iraq; Israel uses them in Gaza via the 'roof-knock'; Russia is now adapting the playbook against capital infrastructure.

blocks.text: The term of art is **'decision-making centers'** — a euphemism for political and military command nodes that, under the laws of armed conflict, sit closer to legitimate targets than civilian areas. The phrasing matters because it pre-loads the legal framing.

timeline.heading: WHY DIPLOMATS ARE THE TRIPWIRE
timeline.body: The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961) makes embassies inviolable and host states liable for their protection. Striking near a foreign mission risks dragging that mission's government into the war — which is precisely why an evacuation warning is both a threat and an off-ramp.

timeline.heading: THE KYIV TARGET MAP
timeline.body: Ukraine's executive, defense, and intelligence headquarters cluster within roughly two kilometers around Bankova Street. Most G7 embassies sit in the same Pechersk district. There is no geometry in which 'decision-making centers' can be hit without endangering diplomatic compounds.

timeline.heading: THE LAVROV–RUBIO CHANNEL
timeline.body: Direct foreign-minister-to-secretary-of-state calls during active wars are rare and deliberate. The Kissinger–Gromyko channel during the 1973 October War is the canonical precedent: a back-line used to communicate red lines without committing either side publicly.

timeline.heading: THE SANCTIONS LEVER
timeline.body: Kyiv's reflexive response — ask Western partners for more sanctions — reflects a structural truth: Ukraine has no economic retaliation of its own. Every escalatory move by Moscow is answered through third-party financial systems, primarily the EU's sanctions packages and the US Treasury's OFAC designations.

timeline.heading: THE BLACKMAIL FRAME
timeline.body: Calling an evacuation warning 'blackmail' is itself a diplomatic move. It refuses the legitimacy of the warning, denies Russia the legal cover the warning was meant to create, and forces Western capitals to choose between honoring the warning (validating Moscow's framing) or ignoring it (accepting the risk).

blocks.question: What is the diplomatic purpose of a pre-strike evacuation warning to a third country?
options: To genuinely protect civilians from harm
To shift legal and moral responsibility onto the target if casualties occur
To delay the strike for further negotiation
To comply with UN Security Council resolutions
blocks.explanation: Evacuation warnings are primarily a legal-framing tool: if the target ignores them and casualties follow, responsibility shifts. Civilian protection is the stated rationale, not the operational purpose.

timeline.heading: WHAT FRANÇAFRIQUE WAS
timeline.body: After 1960 independence, France kept a parallel system across its former African colonies: defense pacts, basing rights, a shared currency, and a network of intelligence officers who could make or unmake presidents. The formal label was cooperation; the operative word was tutelage.

blocks.text: The system had a nickname inside the Élysée — *la Françafrique* — coined approvingly by Côte d'Ivoire's Houphouët-Boigny and later weaponized by critics like François-Xavier Verschave to describe the **opaque circuits of money, arms, and influence** that survived decolonization.

timeline.heading: THE CFA FRANC
timeline.body: Fourteen African states still use a currency pegged to the euro and historically backed by reserves deposited at the French Treasury. The peg delivers low inflation; the cost is that monetary policy is set in Frankfurt and Paris, not Dakar or Niamey. Reform in 2019-2020 rebranded the West African version as the eco and ended the reserve-deposit rule, but the peg remains.

timeline.heading: THE URANIUM QUESTION
timeline.body: Niger supplied roughly 15-20% of the uranium fueling France's nuclear reactors through the Areva/Orano concessions at Arlit and Imouraren. France generates about 70% of its electricity from nuclear power — the highest share of any major economy. Niger's break is not just symbolic; it touches the metal that keeps French lights on.

timeline.heading: THE COUP BELT
timeline.body: Mali (2020, 2021), Burkina Faso (2022, twice), Niger (2023), Gabon (2023). Five francophone African states have seen successful coups in four years. Each new junta expelled French forces and, in the Sahel three, invited Russian Wagner/Africa Corps trainers. The pattern is too consistent to be coincidence — and too uneven to be Moscow's single design.

timeline.heading: WHAT BAZOUM REPRESENTED
timeline.body: Mohamed Bazoum, elected in 2021, was the first peaceful transfer of power in Niger's history and a vocal partner of Paris and Washington in counter-terror operations against ISIS-Sahel and JNIM. His detention since the July 2023 coup is why ECOWAS sanctions stayed in place longer than for prior coups — and why the junta's break with France was eventually total.

timeline.heading: THE RUSSIAN ALTERNATIVE
timeline.body: The Wagner Group — rebranded Africa Corps after Prigozhin's 2023 death — offers a different deal than Paris: no human-rights conditionality, payment partly in mining concessions, and a small footprint of trainers rather than visible French bases. The trade is sovereignty optics for counter-terror capability that, by most measures, performs worse than what it replaced.

blocks.question: Which Sahel country still hosts French forces under a defense agreement?
blocks.explanation: Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger have all expelled French forces since 2022. Chad — though it has expelled French troops from some bases — retains the broader defense cooperation framework.

timeline.heading: THE OLD FRAME
timeline.body: For decades, habitability meant one thing: liquid water on a planet orbiting at the right distance from its star. The 'Goldilocks zone' became shorthand for where to look for life.

blocks.text: The classical **circumstellar habitable zone** asks one question — is the planet warm enough for liquid water? It ignores everything happening at scales larger than the solar system.

timeline.heading: THE NEW FRAME
timeline.body: A galactic habitable zone adds a second filter: where in the galaxy does the planet sit. Too close to the center and radiation sterilizes; too far out and heavy elements needed for rocky planets are scarce.

timeline.heading: WHY THE CENTER IS LETHAL
timeline.body: Supermassive black holes are not always quiet. When they actively accrete matter, they become quasars — emitting more energy than every star in the host galaxy combined. X-rays and UV strip atmospheres and shred ozone layers across thousands of light-years.

timeline.heading: WHY SGR A* IS UNUSUAL
timeline.body: The Milky Way's central black hole, Sgr A*, weighs 4.3 million suns yet emits roughly a hundred million times less radiation than its theoretical maximum. It has been dormant for most of cosmic history — an accident of low gas supply that may explain why we are here to notice.

blocks.text: Sgr A* sits in a state astronomers call *quiescent* — actively starving, not actively feeding. Andromeda's central black hole and most galactic nuclei spent significant time in radiation-blasting *active* phases.

timeline.heading: THE GOLDILOCKS GALAXY
timeline.body: Earth sits about 26,000 light-years from the galactic center — far enough to escape Sgr A*'s ancient outbursts, close enough that supernovae enriched the local gas with the iron, oxygen, and carbon that built our planet and our bodies.

blocks.question: Roughly how far is Earth from the Milky Way's supermassive black hole?
blocks.explanation: Earth sits about 26,000 light-years from Sgr A* — in the galactic suburbs, outside the radiation-bathed bulge but inside the metal-rich disk where rocky planets form.

timeline.heading: THE FERMI IMPLICATION
timeline.body: If most galaxies pass through long active-nucleus phases that sterilize their interiors, the volume of the universe where complex life can persist shrinks dramatically. The Fermi paradox — 'where is everybody?' — gets a partial answer: most of the real estate was uninhabitable for most of cosmic time.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE ACCORDS ACTUALLY ARE
timeline.body: Signed in September 2020, the Accords normalised relations between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, then Sudan and Morocco. They are bilateral normalisation deals dressed as a regional framework — there is no multilateral treaty text, no secretariat, no membership criteria. 'Joining' means signing a separate agreement with Israel.

timeline.heading: THE ARAB PEACE INITIATIVE
timeline.body: In 2002 the Arab League unanimously offered Israel full normalisation with all 22 Arab states in exchange for withdrawal to 1967 borders and a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as capital. The Accords inverted this sequence — normalisation first, Palestinian question deferred indefinitely. Riyadh authored the 2002 plan; abandoning its precondition would mean repudiating its own diplomatic legacy.

blocks.question: What did the 2002 Arab Peace Initiative offer Israel in exchange for Palestinian statehood?
options: Full normalisation with all 22 Arab League states
A non-aggression pact with the Gulf states
Lifting of the Arab League economic boycott
blocks.explanation: The initiative offered comprehensive normalisation by the entire Arab League — the maximalist Arab diplomatic offer, and the one the Accords' sequencing bypassed.

timeline.heading: WHY SAUDI ARABIA IS DIFFERENT
timeline.body: The Saudi monarch holds the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques — Makkah and Madinah. Normalising with Israel while al-Aqsa remains under occupation is not a diplomatic calculation alone; it is a question of religious legitimacy that no other Arab state carries. This is the structural reason Riyadh has held the Palestinian precondition where Abu Dhabi did not.

blocks.text: Al-Aqsa is the *first qibla* — the direction Muslims faced in prayer before the revelation changed it to Makkah — and is named in **Surah al-Isra** as the destination of the Prophet's night journey. Custodianship language is not ceremonial.

timeline.heading: THE PAKISTAN ANOMALY
timeline.body: Pakistan has never recognised Israel and its passport still reads 'valid for all countries except Israel.' Its constitution ties foreign policy to Muslim solidarity, and Imran Khan's 2020 refusal to join the Accords — despite reported Saudi and Emirati pressure — became a marker of domestic legitimacy. Including Islamabad in a normalisation push extends the Accords beyond the Arab world for the first time.

timeline.heading: THE QATAR PARADOX
timeline.body: Qatar hosts the largest US military base in the Middle East (Al Udeid) and Hamas's political bureau simultaneously. Doha has been the indispensable mediator for every Gaza ceasefire negotiation since 2008 precisely because it talks to everyone. Forcing Qatar to normalise collapses the mediator role that Washington itself relies on.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'MANDATORY' MEANS IN PRACTICE
timeline.body: The Accords have no enforcement mechanism — they are executive agreements, not Senate-ratified treaties. 'Mandatory' therefore reads as a precondition for continued US security guarantees, arms sales, or sanctions relief rather than a legal obligation. The leverage runs through F-35 deliveries to Riyadh, the Pakistan IMF programme, and Qatar's MNNA (Major Non-NATO Ally) status.

timeline.heading: THE 1967 BAN
timeline.body: After WWII, Japan adopted the Three Principles on Arms Exports in 1967, effectively banning weapons sales abroad. The constraint was self-imposed, rooted in Article 9 of the postwar constitution renouncing war as a sovereign right.

blocks.text: The principles barred exports to **communist bloc** states, **UN-embargoed** countries, and any nation **involved in conflict** — a list so broad it functioned as a near-total ban.

timeline.heading: THE ABE REVERSAL
timeline.body: Shinzo Abe replaced the ban with the Three Principles on Defense Equipment Transfer in 2014, permitting exports that serve peace or Japan's security. A decade of attempted deals followed — almost all failed.

events.label: Loses Australia submarine bid to France
Philippines radar deal — first major export

timeline.heading: THE 2016 GHOST
timeline.body: Australia rejected Japan's Soryu submarine bid in 2016 and picked France's Naval Group. That programme collapsed in 2021 when Canberra switched to AUKUS nuclear subs — wasting nine years. Tokyo remembered the snub; Canberra remembered the lesson about delivery risk.

blocks.question: Why did Australia cancel the French submarine deal in 2021?
options: Australia switched to nuclear-powered subs under AUKUS
blocks.explanation: AUKUS gave Australia access to US/UK nuclear propulsion — a capability France's conventional Barracuda design couldn't match, regardless of price.

timeline.heading: THE MOGAMI DESIGN
timeline.body: The Mogami is a stealth-shaped multi-mission frigate displacing 5,500 tonnes, crewed by just 90 sailors — roughly half a comparable Western frigate's complement. Heavy automation is the selling point for navies struggling to recruit.

timeline.heading: THE STRATEGIC ARC
timeline.body: The deal locks Australia and Japan into a shared industrial base facing China — beyond AUKUS, beyond the Quad. Two US treaty allies sharing warship production is the kind of integration Washington has pushed for since the Obama pivot.

blocks.label: the Indo-Pacific frame
blocks.caption: Mogami hulls would patrol the same sea lanes Japanese destroyers do

timeline.heading: THE BUILD RISK
timeline.body: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries must transfer the production line to Australian shipyards — the same shipyards that took 14 years to deliver three Hobart-class destroyers, with cost overruns of roughly A$1 billion per hull. The political survival of the deal turns on whether Japanese industrial discipline transfers with the blueprints.

timeline.heading: WHAT A MAZAR IS
timeline.body: A mazar is the shrine-tomb of a Sufi saint — a site of ziyarat (visitation) where devotees recite Quran, distribute food to the poor, and seek the saint's intercession. Across South Asia, mazars are also social institutions: free kitchens, music gatherings, and refuges that cross caste and class lines.

blocks.text: The Arabic root *z-w-r* means *to visit*. **Ziyarat** is distinct from *ibadah* (worship) in Sufi practice — the saint is honored, not worshipped — though this distinction is precisely what reformist movements reject.

timeline.heading: HOW BENGAL BECAME MUSLIM
timeline.body: Bengal's conversion to Islam, beginning in the 13th century, was driven not by Arab armies but by Sufi missionaries — figures like Shah Jalal in Sylhet and Khan Jahan Ali in Khulna — who cleared forests, built mosques, and integrated local Bengali agrarian culture with Islamic practice. The mazars dotting Bangladesh are the physical inheritance of that syncretic conversion.

timeline.heading: THE DEOBANDI-SUFI SPLIT
timeline.body: Since the 19th century, South Asian Islam has been contested between Deobandi/Salafi-influenced reformers — who view shrine veneration as bidah (innovation) bordering on shirk (associating partners with God) — and the Barelvi/Sufi tradition that defends mazar devotion as legitimate intercession. Jamaat-e-Islami sits in the reformist camp; the shrine attacks are a theological argument expressed with sledgehammers.

timeline.heading: WHO JAMAAT-E-ISLAMI IS
timeline.body: Founded by Abul A'la Maududi in 1941 in British India, Jamaat-e-Islami is the oldest Islamist political party in South Asia, advocating an Islamic state governed by sharia. In Bangladesh, it was banned for opposing independence in 1971 and siding with Pakistan; the ban was lifted, reimposed under Hasina, and de-facto lifted again after her August 2024 ouster.

events.label: Founded by Maududi in British India
Sided with Pakistan in liberation war

timeline.heading: THE POWER VACUUM
timeline.body: Sheikh Hasina's Awami League had positioned itself as the secular guardian of Bengali pluralism, and its police protected major shrines from periodic attacks. Her August 2024 flight to India removed that shield overnight; the caretaker government under Muhammad Yunus has prioritized economic stabilization and not rebuilt shrine security.

timeline.heading: THE BROADER PATTERN
timeline.body: Shrine destruction is a recurring marker of reformist ascendancy across the Muslim world — the Saudi state's leveling of Ottoman-era tombs in Makkah and Madinah, the Taliban's 2001 destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas, ISIS's demolition of Sufi shrines in Mosul and Palmyra. Each event is local; the theological logic is shared.

blocks.question: Which Sufi missionary is most associated with the Islamization of northeastern Bengal in the 14th century?
blocks.explanation: Shah Jalal arrived in Sylhet around 1303 and is credited with converting much of the region; his mazar remains one of Bangladesh's most visited shrines.

timeline.heading: THE SITE
timeline.body: Bhojshala sits in Dhar, named for Raja Bhoja, the 11th-century Paramara king whose court was a center of Sanskrit learning and Saraswati devotion. Adjacent to it stands the dargah of Kamal Maula, a 14th-century Chishti Sufi. Since a 2003 ASI arrangement, Hindus pray there on Tuesdays and Muslims on Fridays — a sharing regime that lasted twenty-three years.

timeline.heading: THE PLACES OF WORSHIP ACT
timeline.body: The 1991 Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act froze the religious character of every site in India as it stood on 15 August 1947. Babri Masjid in Ayodhya was the single explicit carve-out. The law was written precisely to prevent the litigation now reaching courts across north India.

blocks.text: The act was passed under **P.V. Narasimha Rao** months before the Babri demolition. Its purpose was to draw a line: *one* dispute would be litigated, no others. That line is what is now being crossed.

blocks.question: What does India's 1991 Places of Worship Act protect?
options: The religious character of every site as it stood on 15 August 1947
All sites built before British rule
Only mosques built during Mughal rule
Sites listed by the Archaeological Survey of India
blocks.explanation: The Act froze every site's religious character at independence — with Ayodhya as the lone carve-out — to foreclose exactly the kind of suits now succeeding.

timeline.heading: THE AYODHYA TEMPLATE
timeline.body: In 2019 the Supreme Court awarded the Babri Masjid site to Hindu petitioners, citing an Archaeological Survey of India excavation that reported a pre-existing non-Islamic structure beneath the mosque. The ruling established that an archaeological report could carry religious title — the procedural template now invoked at every contested site.

timeline.heading: THE ASI AS ARBITER
timeline.body: The Archaeological Survey of India was founded in 1861 under colonial rule to catalogue antiquities. It now functions as a quasi-judicial body whose surveys frame title disputes. A court orders a survey; the survey finds older fragments beneath a mosque; the finding becomes evidence of original religious character. The chain repeats.

timeline.heading: THE QUEUE
timeline.body: Gyanvapi in Varanasi (adjacent to the Kashi Vishwanath temple), the Shahi Idgah in Mathura (adjacent to Krishna Janmabhoomi), the Qutb Minar complex in Delhi, and the Ajmer Sharif dargah have all faced suits invoking the same procedure. Bhojshala extends the precedent from Mughal-era mosques to a Sufi shrine.

timeline.heading: THE SUFI DIMENSION
timeline.body: Kamal Maula belonged to the Chishti order, the Sufi tradition that took root in the subcontinent from the 13th century onward and built a religious culture deeply entwined with local devotion. Shared shrines — where Hindus and Muslims venerated the same saint — were once common across north India. The Bhojshala ruling redraws that map by sorting one such site into a single category.

timeline.heading: INTENSITY VS ABSOLUTE
timeline.body: China's Paris pledge is denominated in carbon intensity — emissions per unit of GDP — not absolute tonnes. As long as GDP grows faster than emissions, intensity falls even while the atmosphere absorbs more CO2. This is the structural loophole every developing-economy pledge exploits.

blocks.text: The distinction matters: an *intensity* target is a ratio, an *absolute* target is a ceiling. Only absolute caps actually bound atmospheric carbon.

timeline.heading: WHY THE BASELINE YEAR MATTERS
timeline.body: Every percentage reduction is measured against a baseline. Move the baseline year, redefine what counts as GDP, or revise historical emissions upward, and the same future trajectory suddenly meets the target. The math doesn't change the physics — but it changes the compliance report.

timeline.heading: WHO EMITS WHAT
timeline.body: China emits roughly 30% of annual global CO2 — more than the US, EU, and India combined. The 700-million-tonne revision gap is itself larger than the total annual emissions of all but a handful of countries.

timeline.heading: THE KYOTO PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The 1997 Kyoto Protocol imposed absolute caps on developed countries and none on developing ones — including China, then the world's second-largest emitter. By the time Paris arrived in 2015, the framework had shifted to nationally-determined contributions, where each country writes its own pledge and its own metric. Self-reporting replaced binding caps.

events.label: Kyoto Protocol — binding caps on rich states

timeline.heading: THE VERIFICATION GAP
timeline.body: There is no independent global authority that measures national emissions. Every country self-reports to the UNFCCC using its own methodology. Satellite-based atmospheric measurement (TROPOMI, OCO-2) consistently finds discrepancies with reported figures — methane in particular runs 50-100% higher than official inventories in many countries.

timeline.heading: WHAT A METHODOLOGY CHANGE LOOKS LIKE
timeline.body: Carbon intensity can be revised by reclassifying which industries count, updating emission factors per unit of coal or cement, or restating historical GDP. Each is technically defensible in isolation; combined, they can shift the apparent trajectory by a Germany-sized margin without a single power plant changing operation.

blocks.question: China's Paris pledge commits it to peak emissions by which year?
blocks.explanation: China pledged peak CO2 before 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2060 — but 'peak' is defined against intensity metrics it controls.

timeline.heading: THE OCEAN AS INDIA'S MOAT
timeline.body: The Indian Ocean carries roughly 80% of global seaborne oil trade and half of all container traffic. Unlike the Pacific or Atlantic, it has one dominant littoral state on its northern rim — India — whose peninsula juts 1,600km into the sea lanes. Geography made New Delhi the default security manager long before it had the navy to act on it.

blocks.label: Colombo Security Conclave members
blocks.caption: five founding states plus observers

timeline.heading: THE CONCLAVE'S ORIGIN
timeline.body: Founded in 2011 as a trilateral India-Sri Lanka-Maldives coast guard forum, the Conclave was dormant for most of the 2010s as Sri Lanka pivoted toward Chinese port financing. India revived it in 2020 after the Hambantota lease — when Sri Lanka handed China a 99-year concession on a debt-financed port — turned Indian Ocean security from a regional concern into a strategic one.

timeline.heading: THE STRING OF PEARLS
timeline.body: The phrase originated in a 2005 US Department of Defense contractor report describing Chinese-funded ports across the Indian Ocean rim — Gwadar, Hambantota, Kyaukpyu, Djibouti. The Conclave is India's counter-architecture: not military bases, but a governance forum that gives smaller states an alternative coordination venue.

blocks.text: India calls its own variant the **Necklace of Diamonds** — partnerships and access agreements with Oman (Duqm), Indonesia (Sabang), Singapore (Changi), and France (Réunion) that ring the Chinese pearls.

timeline.heading: WHY UNDERSEA CABLES
timeline.body: Roughly 99% of intercontinental data traffic moves through undersea fiber-optic cables, not satellites. The Indian Ocean carries trunk routes linking Europe to East Asia via the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb. A single cable cut near Yemen in early 2024 disrupted 25% of Asia-Europe internet traffic for weeks. Cable governance is now naval business.

timeline.heading: AUSTRALIA'S ABSENCE
timeline.body: Canberra's maritime strategy runs through the Quad (US, Japan, India, Australia) and AUKUS, both Pacific-tilted frameworks. The Conclave is structured around Indian Ocean littoral and island states — Australia, despite a 12,000km Indian Ocean coastline, sits outside the geographic definition the Conclave uses. The gap is doctrinal, not accidental.

blocks.question: Which country runs the largest foreign military base on the Indian Ocean rim?
blocks.explanation: China's Djibouti base, opened 2017, is its only overseas military facility. Diego Garcia is US-operated but on UK territory; France's Réunion presence is sovereign, not foreign-based.

timeline.heading: THE ORIGINAL INSIGHT
timeline.body: PageRank, published by Brin and Page in 1998, treated a hyperlink as a vote. A page was important if important pages linked to it — a recursive definition borrowed from academic citation analysis. The web suddenly had a quality signal, and Google had a 10x better index than AltaVista or Yahoo overnight.

blocks.text: The founders' 1998 paper, *The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine*, contained a now-famous appendix arguing that **advertising-funded search engines will be inherently biased toward the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers**. They built one anyway.

timeline.heading: THE BARGAIN
timeline.body: For two decades the open web ran on an implicit deal: publishers wrote pages, Google crawled them and sent traffic, advertisers paid Google for attention alongside the results. Everyone got paid in someone else's currency. The deal worked as long as users clicked through to the source.

timeline.heading: THE MONOPOLY RULING
timeline.body: In August 2024, Judge Amit Mehta of the DC District Court ruled that Google had illegally monopolized general search and search-text ads, citing the ~$26 billion/year it paid Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to be the default. The remedies phase — what Google must divest or stop doing — was the proximate trigger for the AI-first pivot.

blocks.text: Google is a monopolist, and it has acted as one to maintain its monopoly.
blocks.speaker: Judge Amit Mehta, US v. Google

timeline.heading: WHY ZERO-CLICK BREAKS PUBLISHERS
timeline.body: When Google answers a query directly — with an AI summary or a featured snippet — the user never visits the source. The publisher served the crawler, paid the hosting bill, and got no ad impression. Studies through 2024 already showed roughly 60% of searches ended without a click; an AI-only interface pushes that toward 100%.

blocks.label: Where a search query's value lands

timeline.heading: THE ALTERNATIVES
timeline.body: A handful of independent indexes survived Google's dominance. Each made a different bet about how to fund search without selling the user.

timeline.heading: WHY CRAWLING IS HARD
timeline.body: Building a fresh web index from scratch costs hundreds of millions in storage and bandwidth, and most large sites now block unknown crawlers in robots.txt — a moat Google itself made deeper by training the publisher class to whitelist its bot. The barrier to a new entrant is not the algorithm; it is permission to read the web.

blocks.question: Roughly how many independently-crawled general web indexes exist worldwide?
blocks.explanation: Google, Bing, Yandex, Baidu, Mojeek, Brave, and Marginalia maintain their own crawls. Almost every other 'search engine' resells one of these — DuckDuckGo and Ecosia front Bing; Startpage fronts Google.

timeline.heading: WHY INDIA IMPORTS LPG
timeline.body: India consumes roughly 28 million tonnes of LPG a year and produces less than 40% of it domestically. The rest arrives by tanker, overwhelmingly from the Persian Gulf — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and Iran. Every cargo transits Hormuz.

blocks.caption: Gulf-to-India LPG corridor

timeline.heading: THE UJJWALA LOCK-IN
timeline.body: Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana, launched in 2016, gave 100 million below-poverty-line households a free LPG connection and a subsidised cylinder. It was the largest cooking-fuel transition in history — but it bet the kitchen of rural India on a fuel that arrives by sea.

blocks.text: Ujjwala converted households from **biomass** (firewood, dung cakes) to LPG in under a decade. The health gains were real — indoor air pollution kills an estimated *half a million* Indians annually — but the supply chain was never hardened against a Hormuz event.

timeline.heading: LPG VS PNG, MECHANICALLY
timeline.body: LPG is propane and butane compressed to liquid in a steel cylinder — portable, deliverable by truck, usable anywhere. PNG is methane at low pressure flowing through a buried pipe — cheaper per unit, but only available where the pipeline reaches. The two fuels are not interchangeable at the appliance level; burners and regulators differ.

timeline.heading: WHY THE PIPELINE ISN'T READY
timeline.body: India's City Gas Distribution rollout covers about 70% of the population on paper but far less in practice — last-mile household connections lag the trunk network by years. Rural districts in particular have authorised concessions but no laid pipe. A forced switch presumes infrastructure the geography doesn't yet have.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of India's LPG demand is met by imports?
blocks.explanation: India imports roughly 60% of its LPG, overwhelmingly from the Persian Gulf — making Hormuz the single chokepoint for the country's cooking fuel.

timeline.heading: THE HORMUZ EXPOSURE
timeline.body: The strait is 33 km wide at its narrowest, with shipping lanes hugging the Iranian coast. Roughly 21 million barrels of oil and most of the world's seaborne LPG transit it daily. For an importing country, there is no pipeline workaround — the Saudi East-West and UAE Habshan-Fujairah lines move crude, not LPG cylinders bound for village kitchens.

timeline.heading: THE POLICY REVERSAL
timeline.body: Forcing households to surrender LPG connections before a piped alternative is in the wall is a textbook sequencing error — the kind governments make when an external shock outruns infrastructure planning. Backing it down is the right call; the harder question is what the next cargo from Ras Laffan costs.

timeline.heading: WHAT BASELOAD MEANS
timeline.body: Baseload is the minimum power demand a grid faces around the clock — the floor below which consumption never falls. Coal, nuclear, and large hydro were designed to run flat against it because their fuel is cheap once the plant is built but ramping them up and down wastes heat and wears the turbines.

blocks.text: The opposite is *peaking* power — gas turbines and batteries that fire only when demand spikes. A grid needs both shapes; losing one means the other must stretch.

timeline.heading: THE IRREVERSIBILITY
timeline.body: A coal plant is a precision-engineered assembly of boilers, turbines, cooling towers, and grid interconnects built over years. Once the chimneys come down and the turbine hall is gutted, rebuilding costs more than a new plant and takes a decade. Demolition is the political point of no return.

timeline.heading: WHY BATTERIES AREN'T BASELOAD
timeline.body: A 500MW battery can discharge 500MW — but only for a few hours. Liddell ran 1,680MW continuously for decades. Batteries shift energy across hours; they do not generate it. Replacing a coal plant with a battery is replacing a reservoir with a bucket.

timeline.heading: THE AUSTRALIAN PARADOX
timeline.body: Australia is the world's second-largest coal exporter and is rapidly retiring its domestic coal fleet while approving new export mines. The coal stays in the ground long enough to be dug up — just for someone else to burn.

timeline.heading: THE DUCK CURVE
timeline.body: Solar floods grids at noon and vanishes by sundown — exactly when households switch on lights, ovens, and air conditioning. The resulting demand curve looks like a duck's silhouette, and the steep evening ramp is the hardest engineering problem in a decarbonising grid.

blocks.question: Why is the evening ramp the hardest part of integrating solar?
options: Solar panels degrade fastest at sunset
Demand peaks just as solar generation collapses
Transmission lines overheat in evening sun
blocks.explanation: As the sun sets, solar output falls to zero within an hour while household demand peaks — the grid must ramp up gigawatts of dispatchable power on a steep curve every evening.

timeline.heading: THE EIGHT NEW MINES
timeline.body: New South Wales has approved eight coal mine expansions since 2023, all export-oriented. The political economy is unchanged: coal royalties fund state budgets, mining unions deliver Labor seats, and the climate cost is exported with the cargo.

blocks.label: where NSW coal goes
blocks.caption: Asia takes ~85% of Newcastle's thermal coal exports

timeline.heading: WHY CMOS IS HITTING A WALL
timeline.body: Every transistor switch leaks current even when 'off,' and that leakage scales with the number of devices on a die. Modern chips spend a substantial share of their power budget on leakage, not computation. Shrinking the transistor further makes the leak worse, not better.

blocks.text: The industry calls this the **power wall** — the point where adding transistors stops giving you more performance because you can't cool what you've already added. It arrived around 2005 and has shaped every architectural decision since.

timeline.heading: WHAT SPIN IS
timeline.body: Electrons carry charge, which is what transistors manipulate, but they also carry spin — an intrinsic magnetic moment with two states, up or down. Spintronics encodes information in spin rather than charge. Flipping a spin costs far less energy than moving an electron across a channel, and the state persists when power is removed.

timeline.heading: THE MAGNETIC TUNNEL JUNCTION
timeline.body: An MTJ sandwiches a thin insulator between two magnetic layers. When the layers' spins align, electrons tunnel through easily; when they oppose, resistance jumps. The same structure already ships at scale in MRAM memory and hard-drive read heads — the new work repurposes it as a logic readout amplifier.

timeline.heading: THE VOLTAGE THRESHOLD
timeline.body: For one logic gate to drive the next, its output voltage must exceed the next gate's switching threshold. Earlier spin-orbit devices produced microvolt-scale signals — too weak to cascade. Reaching 1.5 mV is the gating number where the output of one stage can actually flip the input of another without an amplifier in between.

timeline.heading: WHY NON-VOLATILITY MATTERS
timeline.body: A transistor forgets its state the moment power is cut; a spin device remembers. Logic that retains state through power-down enables instant-on computing and eliminates the energy cost of reloading registers from memory after sleep — the dominant overhead in battery-powered devices.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of a modern CPU's power budget is spent on leakage current rather than active computation?
blocks.explanation: Leakage routinely consumes 30-50% of total chip power at advanced nodes — which is why non-volatile logic that draws zero static power is so attractive.

timeline.heading: THE INTEGRATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: A working device in a lab is not a working chip. CMOS won because billions of transistors can be lithographed onto silicon with yields above 99.99% per device. Every post-CMOS candidate — carbon nanotubes, tunnel FETs, spintronics — has cleared the physics bar and stalled at the manufacturing bar. Cascading thousands of MTJs reliably is the unsolved engineering problem.

timeline.heading: THE PATTERN
timeline.body: States killing dissidents on foreign soil is not new, but it has accelerated since 2010. Freedom House counts hundreds of incidents across dozens of host countries — assassinations, renditions, assaults — by governments that calculate the diplomatic cost is lower than the threat the exile poses at home.

blocks.text: The technical term is **transnational repression** — coined to distinguish state-directed extraterritorial violence from ordinary émigré crime.

timeline.heading: THE SANDINISTA ARC
timeline.body: Ortega led the 1979 revolution that overthrew the Somoza dictatorship, lost the 1990 election to Violeta Chamorro, then returned to power in 2007. The 2018 protests — sparked by a pension reform and met with live ammunition — killed over 300 and triggered a wave of exile that turned former comrades into the regime's most dangerous critics.

timeline.heading: WHY COSTA RICA
timeline.body: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948 and has hosted Central American dissidents for generations — Salvadoran, Guatemalan, and now Nicaraguan. Its open border with Nicaragua and large exile community make it the natural haven, and the natural hunting ground.

timeline.heading: THE PEER SET
timeline.body: Nicaragua joins a small club of states that have crossed the line into killing dissidents on foreign soil. Each case reshaped the host country's intelligence posture and forced an awkward diplomatic calculation about how loudly to respond.

timeline.heading: THE CITIZENSHIP WEAPON
timeline.body: In February 2023, Ortega's government stripped 222 political prisoners of their Nicaraguan citizenship and expelled them — then did the same to 94 more exiles by decree. Statelessness is itself a form of repression: no passport, no consular protection, no legal standing to return.

blocks.question: What did Nicaragua do to 222 political prisoners in February 2023?
options: Stripped them of citizenship and expelled them
Released them under a general amnesty
blocks.explanation: Ortega expelled them to the US and revoked their Nicaraguan citizenship by decree — leaving them stateless under international law.

timeline.heading: THE COST CALCULUS
timeline.body: For an authoritarian government, killing a high-profile exile signals that distance is no shield — the deterrent effect on the remaining diaspora is the point. The diplomatic cost is usually contained: expulsions of a few diplomats, a sanctions package, no military response. The math has historically favored the regime.

timeline.heading: THE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: Hormuz is 33 km wide at its narrowest; shipping lanes are just 3 km each. Roughly a fifth of global oil consumption transits it daily. The deepest channel hugs the Iranian side — which is why Iranian small-boat and mine positioning matters disproportionately to clearance navies.

timeline.heading: WHO THE GUARDS ARE
timeline.body: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is a parallel military, separate from Iran's regular army (Artesh). The IRGC Navy — not the Artesh Navy — controls the Persian Gulf and Hormuz; its small-boat swarm doctrine, mine warfare, and anti-ship missiles are the instruments by which Iran threatens the strait.

blocks.text: Centcom's strike killed **IRGC** personnel specifically — the branch reporting to the Supreme Leader, not the elected government. Hitting Artesh would be a strike on the state; hitting IRGC is a strike on the *parallel* state.

timeline.heading: STRIKE-AND-TALK PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Negotiating while bombing is a doctrine, not an accident. The US bombed North Vietnam through the Paris talks (1968–73). Israel kept striking Hezbollah through the 2024 Lebanon negotiations. The logic: the strikes set the price of walking away from the table, so the table-side concessions look cheaper by comparison.

timeline.heading: THE FROZEN ASSETS
timeline.body: Roughly $100bn of Iranian central bank reserves sit frozen across South Korean, Japanese, Iraqi, and European accounts under US sanctions. Tehran has traded prisoners, paused enrichment, and accepted IAEA inspections in past rounds to unlock tranches. The CBI governor flying to Doha — not the foreign minister — signals reserves, not politics, are the bargaining chip.

timeline.heading: WHY QATAR HOSTS
timeline.body: Qatar shares the world's largest gas field — South Pars / North Dome — with Iran. Doha cannot afford a Gulf war and cannot afford to alienate either Washington or Tehran, which is exactly why it has hosted every backchannel from the 2020 Taliban talks to the current Iran file. Neutrality is the product Qatar exports.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR RHYME
timeline.body: From 1984–88, Iran and Iraq attacked 400+ commercial ships in the Gulf. Oil spiked briefly; markets adapted by reflagging tankers under US and Kuwaiti colors with naval escort. The lesson planners took then still holds: closing Hormuz is easier to threaten than to sustain — but the insurance market closes the lane long before the mines do.

blocks.question: What typically closes a shipping lane during a Hormuz crisis before the mines themselves do?
options: Lloyd's of London war-risk insurance premiums
blocks.explanation: Once war-risk premiums spike, commercial vessels reroute regardless of how many mines remain — the financial chokepoint tightens faster than the physical one.

timeline.heading: THE QT INTERVAL
timeline.body: The QT interval on an ECG measures how long the heart's ventricles take to electrically reset between beats. When it stretches beyond ~500 milliseconds, the next beat can fire into a vulnerable window and trigger a chaotic rhythm called torsades de pointes — which degenerates into ventricular fibrillation and sudden death.

blocks.text: The killing mechanism is *repolarization* — the outward potassium current (**IKr**, carried by the hERG channel) that ends each heartbeat. Almost every QT-prolonging drug works by blocking this single channel.

timeline.heading: WHY ANTIPSYCHOTICS
timeline.body: Dopamine D2 blockers share a structural quirk: many of them also bind the hERG potassium channel as an off-target effect. Thioridazine was withdrawn for this reason; haloperidol, ziprasidone, and quetiapine all carry black-box or labeled warnings. The risk is dose-dependent and compounds when two are prescribed together.

timeline.heading: THE COMBINATION TRAP
timeline.body: QT-prolonging drugs do not add — they multiply. Two moderate blockers given together can push a patient past the threshold that neither would cross alone. Antibiotics (azithromycin, fluoroquinolones), antiemetics (ondansetron), and antifungals (fluconazole) routinely co-prescribed in hospitals all extend the QT, layering on top of any antipsychotic regimen.

blocks.question: What does a prolonged QT interval on an ECG actually measure?
options: How fast the heart is beating
How long the ventricles take to electrically reset between beats
How much oxygen the heart muscle is using
The thickness of the heart wall
blocks.explanation: QT measures ventricular repolarization — the reset phase. Stretch it too far and the next beat can trigger a fatal arrhythmia called torsades de pointes.

timeline.heading: WHY THE ECG MATTERS
timeline.body: A baseline ECG and a follow-up after dose changes is the standard of care because QT prolongation is silent until it kills. The patient feels nothing; the arrhythmia, when it comes, arrives without warning. Monitoring is not optional surveillance — it is the only way to catch the signal before the event.

timeline.heading: YEMEN'S COLLAPSE
timeline.body: Yemen's health system has been degraded by a decade of war and blockade. Cholera outbreaks, malnutrition, and the destruction of hospitals by Saudi-led airstrikes have hollowed out specialist capacity. Psychiatric care — never well-resourced — runs on whatever antipsychotic stock arrives, without the ECG machines, electrolyte panels, or cardiology consults that make safe prescribing possible.

blocks.label: Yemen's divided health system
blocks.caption: Sana'a under Houthi control; Aden the internationally-recognized government's seat

timeline.heading: THE BROADER PATTERN
timeline.body: Polypharmacy — prescribing multiple psychiatric drugs to one patient — is widespread globally, not just in war zones. The clinical evidence rarely supports it; the practice persists because each individual prescription seems rational and no one audits the stack. Yemen is an extreme case of a problem that exists everywhere monitoring is weak.

timeline.heading: THE PATHOGEN
timeline.body: Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped bacterium that colonizes the small intestine and secretes a toxin forcing cells to dump water and electrolytes into the gut lumen. Death comes not from the infection but from hypovolemic shock — a healthy adult can lose 10 liters of fluid in 24 hours.

blocks.text: The lethal mechanism is *dehydration*, not infection. This is why **oral rehydration salts** — a sachet of glucose and electrolytes mixed with clean water — cut cholera mortality from ~50% to under 1%. It is arguably the most cost-effective medical intervention ever devised.

timeline.heading: THE SNOW MAP
timeline.body: In 1854, London physician John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in Soho to a single contaminated water pump on Broad Street. By removing the pump handle he ended the outbreak — and founded modern epidemiology. Every cholera outbreak since has been, fundamentally, a water-infrastructure failure.

timeline.heading: WHY BORNO KEEPS BURNING
timeline.body: ISWAP and Boko Haram have spent over a decade attacking boreholes, water-treatment plants, and the engineers who maintain them. Maiduguri's population swelled past 2 million with displaced people, but the water and sanitation system was built for a fraction of that. The pathogen is not the cause — the collapsed infrastructure is.

timeline.heading: THE VACCINE LOGISTICS PROBLEM
timeline.body: Oral cholera vaccine (OCV) exists, works, and is stockpiled globally by Gavi. The bottleneck is delivery: two doses, cold chain, and trained vaccinators reaching the population at risk. In territory contested by ISWAP, none of those three conditions hold reliably, which is why pre-positioning fails even when supply is available.

timeline.heading: THE LGA TIER
timeline.body: Nigeria's 774 Local Government Areas are the constitutional delivery unit for primary healthcare — including outbreak response. But LGAs are the weakest fiscal tier, funded through federal transfers routed via state governors. When Borno's LGA health offices sit in towns the state cannot secure, the constitutional plumbing for response simply does not run.

blocks.text: The phrase **"primary healthcare"** sounds like clinics, but in Nigerian federal law it specifically means the LGA-level facility that handles immunization, surveillance, and outbreak first-response. State and federal hospitals are downstream — they treat the cases the LGA tier failed to prevent.

timeline.heading: THE EMERGENCY DECLARATION
timeline.body: A formal public health emergency declaration unlocks federal funds, WHO coordination, and emergency procurement powers. Governments routinely delay declarations to avoid signaling state failure — but the delay itself amplifies the outbreak, since vaccination and chlorination only work before transmission saturates a population.

blocks.question: What is the case-fatality rate of severe cholera when oral rehydration therapy is administered promptly?
blocks.explanation: ORT — glucose and electrolytes in clean water — cuts mortality from ~50% (untreated) to under 1%. The deaths in Borno are deaths of access, not of medicine.

timeline.heading: THE PHYSICS
timeline.body: Within roughly one wingspan of the surface, an aircraft's downwash hits the ground and bounces, compressing the air beneath the wing. Lift jumps, induced drag collapses. A wing in ground effect is two to three times more efficient than the same wing at altitude.

blocks.text: The technical name is a **wing-in-ground-effect** craft, or *ekranoplan* in Russian — literally 'screen-plane,' the screen being the sea surface itself.

timeline.heading: THE SOVIET PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The USSR built the Caspian Sea Monster in 1966 — a 544-tonne, eight-engine machine longer than a 747, designed to skim 5 meters above the waves at 500 km/h. The KM and its successor the Lun were Cold War oddities: too fast for ships, too low for radar, too fragile for open ocean.

timeline.heading: WHY BELOW RADAR
timeline.body: Ground-based and ship-based radars are limited by Earth's curvature — a target flying at 3 meters disappears below the horizon at roughly 20 km, versus 400+ km for an aircraft at cruise altitude. Airborne early-warning radar helps, but sea clutter at low grazing angles still degrades detection.

timeline.heading: WHY NOBODY ELSE BUILT THEM
timeline.body: Ground effect only works over flat surfaces. A 2-meter swell ends the flight. Maneuvering is sluggish because the cushion resists banking. The Lun could only operate in calm Caspian conditions; in the open Pacific or Atlantic, the operating envelope collapses to a handful of days per month.

timeline.heading: THE TAIWAN STRAIT ANGLE
timeline.body: The Strait averages 180 km wide and is one of the calmer semi-enclosed seas in the region for much of the year. A WIG craft carrying tanks or marines at 400 km/h crosses it in under 30 minutes, beneath the radar horizon of Taiwan's coastal defenses — closing a window that hovercraft, which top out near 90 km/h, leave open for hours.

timeline.heading: THE PAYLOAD CLASS
timeline.body: WIG craft sit between ships and aircraft on the cost-per-tonne curve: roughly 10× the payload of a same-sized aircraft for similar fuel, but 10× faster than a same-tonnage ship. Arming one turns a logistics oddity into a missile platform that no existing doctrine — naval or air — has a clean answer for.

blocks.question: At what altitude does a wing-in-ground-effect craft typically operate?
options: Within one wingspan of the surface
Just above the boundary layer, around 50 meters
At sea level, in physical contact with the water
blocks.explanation: Ground effect only works within about one wingspan of the surface — for a large WIG, that's a few meters. Higher and the lift bonus disappears; lower and waves become a hazard.

timeline.heading: WHAT CNG ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: Compressed natural gas is methane squeezed to ~200 times atmospheric pressure so it fits in a vehicle tank. India's auto-rickshaws, taxis, and city buses converted en masse after a 2002 Supreme Court order on Delhi air quality — making the capital uniquely exposed to gas prices in a way that petrol-driven cities are not.

blocks.text: Delhi's CNG fleet exists because of a court order, not a market choice — the **Supreme Court's 2002 mandate** forced public transport off diesel onto gas to fight smog. The exposure to import prices is a side effect of that ruling.

timeline.heading: THE IMPORT-PARITY MECHANIC
timeline.body: India produces only about half the gas it consumes. The rest arrives as LNG — chilled to -162°C, shipped from Qatar, the UAE, and US Gulf terminals, regasified at Dahej and Hazira. Distributors price domestic CNG against this imported cost, so a spike in spot LNG at Asian benchmarks shows up at the Delhi pump within days.

timeline.heading: WHY HORMUZ MATTERS HERE
timeline.body: Roughly a third of global LNG passes through the Strait of Hormuz, almost all of it from Qatar — the world's second-largest LNG exporter. When the strait is contested, the JKM (Japan-Korea Marker) spot price jumps, and every importer bidding for the same cargoes pays the new mark. India has no Hormuz bypass for gas the way Saudi Arabia has the East-West Pipeline for oil.

timeline.heading: WHO ABSORBS THE SHOCK
timeline.body: Petrol and diesel sit outside India's GST regime, letting the centre cushion price spikes via excise cuts. CNG is inside GST and lightly taxed already — there is no fat to trim. The shock passes through to the auto-rickshaw driver who cannot raise fares without state approval.

timeline.heading: THE LPG PARALLEL
timeline.body: Commercial LPG — the 19-kg cylinders that fuel restaurants and tea stalls — tracks the Saudi CP (Contract Price), revised monthly. Domestic 14-kg cylinders are subsidised; commercial ones are not. When global LPG and LNG move together, both ends of India's informal economy — the rickshaw and the dhaba — get squeezed at once.

blocks.question: Why does Delhi feel global gas price shocks more than other Indian cities?
options: A 2002 Supreme Court order forced public transport onto CNG
Delhi has no domestic gas pipeline connection
Delhi imports gas directly from Qatar, bypassing other states
CNG is taxed higher in Delhi than other states
blocks.explanation: The 2002 Supreme Court order on Delhi air quality forced auto-rickshaws, taxis, and buses onto CNG — locking the city's transport into gas prices.

timeline.heading: THE INELASTICITY TRAP
timeline.body: An auto-rickshaw driver cannot substitute away from CNG — the vehicle is converted, the alternative fuels are banned within the NCR, and fares are state-regulated. This is textbook inelastic demand: when the input price rises, the driver eats the margin until fare revisions catch up, often months later.

timeline.heading: THE TWO-TRACK SYSTEM
timeline.body: Congress moves emergency defense and foreign aid supplementals in days through expedited procedures, but domestic disaster relief routes through authorizing committees, EPA rulemaking, and appropriations cycles that take years. The speed gap reflects which constituencies have standing committees built around them.

blocks.label: emergency supplementals: days from introduction to signing

timeline.heading: THE POLLUTER-PAYS FICTION
timeline.body: CERCLA — the 1980 Superfund law — was supposed to make polluters fund cleanup. In practice, the responsible party negotiates a consent decree with EPA that defines cleanup scope but rarely covers long-term health surveillance. Residents become claimants in tort litigation, not beneficiaries of a public health program.

blocks.text: The original Superfund had a **dedicated tax on chemical and petroleum industries** funding cleanup when polluters couldn't pay. Congress let that tax expire in **1995**; the trust fund ran dry by 2003. Cleanup now depends on whether the polluter is solvent and cooperative.

timeline.heading: THE VINYL CHLORIDE PROBLEM
timeline.body: The Norfolk Southern derailment released vinyl chloride, a known human carcinogen linked to liver angiosarcoma — a cancer with a latency period of 15 to 30 years. Standard epidemiological studies can't detect the signal for decades, which is exactly why a long-term cohort surveillance program would matter, and exactly why none gets funded.

blocks.question: Why is a long-term health registry essential after a vinyl chloride exposure event?
options: Vinyl chloride causes immediate symptoms that need tracking
Associated cancers have 15-30 year latency periods
blocks.explanation: Vinyl chloride's signature cancer, liver angiosarcoma, can take decades to appear. Without a registry started now, the causal link to the derailment may never be provable.

timeline.heading: THE 9/11 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act — which funds healthcare and monitoring for first responders and lower Manhattan residents — was not passed until 2010, nine years after the attacks. It took a sustained advocacy campaign led by Jon Stewart and dying firefighters to force a vote. The pattern is: chemical exposure, decades of denial, eventual program only after political theater.

events.label: First responders begin dying of rare cancers

blocks.label: 9/11 health fund: nine years to law

timeline.heading: WHO HAS STANDING
timeline.body: East Palestine is a village of about 4,700 people in rural eastern Ohio. It has no dedicated congressional caucus, no industry lobby aligned with its interests, and its two senators sit in different parties. Disaster relief in the US correlates less with severity than with the political weight of the affected jurisdiction.

blocks.label: the derailment site
blocks.caption: Village of ~4,700 on the Ohio-Pennsylvania border

timeline.heading: WHY THE GLOBAL SOUTH ABSORBS THE SHOCK FIRST
timeline.body: Wealthy economies hedge oil exposure through strategic reserves, futures markets, and currency strength. Low-income importers pay spot prices in dollars they must earn from exports. A Gulf supply shock hits Nairobi before it hits Berlin because Kenya has neither the reserves to release nor the credit to defer payment.

blocks.text: The technical term is **pass-through**: how fast a global price move reaches a retail pump. In OECD countries it takes months and gets cushioned by taxes; in frontier markets it lands in *weeks* and consumes scarce FX.

timeline.heading: THE FERTILIZER CHANNEL
timeline.body: Natural gas is the feedstock for synthetic nitrogen fertilizer — roughly 70-80% of urea production cost is gas. When Gulf LNG flows wobble, European and Asian gas prices spike, fertilizer plants idle, and the next planting season's yields collapse. The food crisis arrives one harvest after the energy crisis.

timeline.heading: THE 1973 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The OPEC embargo quadrupled oil prices in five months. Western economies hit recession; the developing world hit something worse — a debt spiral. African and Latin American states borrowed petrodollars recycled through Western banks to pay for fuel, and the 1980s lost decade was the bill. The transmission mechanism — fuel shock to sovereign debt crisis — is the template still in play.

timeline.heading: WHO BUYS GULF OIL
timeline.body: Persian Gulf crude does not primarily flow to the West. Roughly 80% goes east — China, India, Japan, South Korea — and a growing share to African and South Asian refiners with no alternative supplier. A Hormuz disruption is felt sharpest in Karachi, Colombo, Dar es Salaam, and Mombasa.

blocks.label: Indian Ocean rim — most exposed to a Gulf shock
blocks.caption: importers with thin reserves and no pipeline alternative

timeline.heading: THE FUEL SUBSIDY TRAP
timeline.body: Most Global South governments cap retail fuel prices to prevent unrest. When global prices rise, the gap becomes a budget deficit the state absorbs. Cut the subsidy and riots follow; preserve it and the IMF arrives. Nigeria, Egypt, Indonesia, and Kenya have all cycled through this trap in the last three years.

blocks.question: What typically forces a Global South government to cut fuel subsidies?
options: A democratic vote by the legislature
A fall in global oil prices
blocks.explanation: Subsidy cuts almost always arrive as IMF conditionality — the fiscal math becomes unsustainable, and external financing comes with strings.

timeline.heading: WFP AND THE HUNGER METRIC
timeline.body: The World Food Programme's 'acute hunger' threshold (IPC Phase 3 or above) means a household cannot meet minimum food needs without selling productive assets — livestock, tools, land. Once crossed, recovery takes years even if prices normalize, because the asset base that generated income is gone.

timeline.heading: WHY SUBMARINES WANT URANIUM
timeline.body: A nuclear reactor lets a submarine stay submerged for months — diesel boats must surface or snorkel every few days to recharge batteries, and that is when satellites and sonar arrays find them. The reactor's fuel determines refueling cadence: low-enriched fuel needs a mid-life core swap requiring the hull to be cut open; highly enriched fuel can run the boat's entire 30-year service life without ever opening the reactor.

blocks.text: US and UK boats run on **weapons-grade** uranium (>93%). France runs on roughly **6–7%** LEU and pays for it with mid-life refuels. The fuel choice is a doctrine, not just an engineering pick.

timeline.heading: THE 20% LINE
timeline.body: Under the 1973 US–ROK 123 Agreement, Seoul cannot enrich uranium above 20% — the international threshold separating low-enriched fuel from highly enriched uranium (HEU). The same line runs through every Iran negotiation. Above 20% is treated as a weapons-relevant capability whether or not the stated end-use is civilian.

blocks.question: What is the international threshold separating low-enriched uranium (LEU) from highly enriched uranium (HEU)?
blocks.explanation: 20% U-235 is the regulatory line. Below it is LEU; above it is HEU and treated as weapons-relevant regardless of stated use.

timeline.heading: WHAT A 123 AGREEMENT IS
timeline.body: Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act requires a bilateral pact before any US nuclear material, technology, or know-how can be exported. Each agreement sets the partner's enrichment and reprocessing limits. The US has roughly two dozen in force; they are the connective tissue of the nonproliferation regime outside the NPT itself.

blocks.label: selected 123-Agreement partners and their enrichment ceiling

timeline.heading: THE AUKUS PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In 2021 the US and UK agreed to transfer naval nuclear propulsion technology to Australia — the first such transfer since the 1958 US–UK Mutual Defense Agreement. The deal cracked a 63-year bright line: nuclear-propelled submarines for a non-nuclear-weapons state. Seoul now points at Canberra and asks why not.

events.label: US signals openness to ROK enrichment

timeline.heading: THE NORTH KOREAN BACKDROP
timeline.body: Pyongyang launched its first ballistic-missile submarine, the Sinpo-class, in 2014 and tested a submarine-launched ballistic missile a year later. A sea-based deterrent is the leg of a nuclear triad that survives a first strike. Seoul's case for nuclear propulsion rests on the argument that diesel boats cannot trail and target a hidden SSBN.

timeline.heading: WHY THIS ERODES THE REGIME
timeline.body: The NPT treats peaceful nuclear use as a right but naval propulsion sits in a loophole — Article 14 allows the removal of fissile material from IAEA safeguards when used in 'non-proscribed military activity.' Every state that activates this loophole hands the same argument to the next aspirant. Iran, Brazil, and Saudi Arabia have all cited naval propulsion as a stated rationale for enrichment programs.

timeline.heading: WHAT A STABLECOIN ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: A token whose issuer claims to hold one dollar of reserves — mostly short-dated US Treasuries — for every token minted. The peg is not algorithmic; it is the promise that the T-bill is there and redeemable.

blocks.text: Two issuers dominate: **Tether (USDT)** registered in the British Virgin Islands, and **Circle (USDC)** based in the US. Together they hold over *$200 billion* in US Treasuries — more than Germany.

timeline.heading: WHY THE SOUTH WANTS THEM
timeline.body: In a country with capital controls or a depreciating currency, a citizen who converts savings into USDT has effectively dollarized — without a US bank account, without crossing a border, without notifying the central bank. The dollar arrives through a phone, not a wire.

blocks.label: FX reserves vs stablecoin market cap

timeline.heading: THE BIS WARNING
timeline.body: When residents flee local currency for dollar tokens, the central bank loses two things at once: the deposit base its banks lend against, and the demand for local currency that anchors the exchange rate. Depreciation accelerates, which drives the next wave of flight.

timeline.heading: WHO HOLDS THE TREASURIES
timeline.body: Tether's reserve disclosures show roughly $100bn in short-dated US government debt. If Tether were a country, it would sit around the 18th-largest foreign holder of Treasuries — above the UAE, below Germany. A private firm in the BVI has become a Treasury market participant on the scale of a G20 state.

blocks.question: Where is Tether, the largest stablecoin issuer, legally domiciled?
blocks.explanation: Tether Holdings is registered in the BVI. No US bank regulator, no EU MiCA supervisor, no IMF reporting obligation reaches it directly.

timeline.heading: THE REGULATORY VOID
timeline.body: Banks issuing dollar liabilities sit inside Basel capital rules, deposit insurance, and central bank lender-of-last-resort facilities. Stablecoin issuers sit outside all three. The 1930s bargain — banks accept regulation in exchange for backstops — has not been struck for tokens.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: This is not the first private dollar. Eurodollars — dollar deposits held in non-US banks — grew from nothing in the 1950s to trillions by the 1980s, largely because Soviet bloc and Gulf depositors wanted dollars outside US jurisdiction. Regulators chased it for decades before accepting it as permanent plumbing. Stablecoins are the retail version of the same trade.

timeline.heading: WHAT HAPPENED IN MAY 1980
timeline.body: After Park Chung-hee's assassination, General Chun Doo-hwan seized power and declared martial law. When Gwangju students protested, paratroopers and armored units were sent in. Over roughly ten days, hundreds of civilians were killed — official figures say ~200, civic groups count over 600.
