timeline.body: The violence almost never targets European, American, or Chinese migrants — it targets other Africans, especially Zimbabweans, Mozambicans, Nigerians, and Somalis. Scholars call it afrophobia for that reason: the hostility tracks African origin, not foreignness as such.

blocks.text: The street slur for African migrants is *makwerekwere* — an onomatopoeia mocking languages South Africans can't understand. The word does the sorting that the violence enforces.

timeline.heading: THE 33% ENGINE
timeline.body: Official unemployment above 33% — and over 42% on the broad measure that counts those who stopped looking — is the fuel. With no jobs and a frayed welfare net, migrants become the visible scapegoat for a crisis whose real causes are structural: a mining economy that shed labor and an education system that never replaced it.

timeline.heading: THE DEBT SOUTH AFRICA OWES
timeline.body: The cruel irony is that the countries now being attacked once sheltered the anti-apartheid struggle. Zambia hosted the ANC's exiled headquarters in Lusaka; Tanzania, Mozambique, and Angola trained and housed its fighters. The 'Frontline States' paid in bombing raids and assassinations for harboring the movement that now governs South Africa.

blocks.label: the Frontline States that sheltered the ANC

blocks.question: Which country hosted the ANC's headquarters during its decades in exile?
blocks.explanation: The ANC ran its government-in-exile from Lusaka, Zambia — one of the Frontline States whose citizens are now targeted in South Africa.

timeline.heading: OPERATION DUDULA
timeline.body: The threatened June shutdown traces to Operation Dudula — Zulu for 'force out' — which began in Soweto in 2021 as vigilante patrols demanding the removal of foreign-owned businesses and undocumented workers. It has since registered as a political party, normalizing into electoral politics what started as street action.

timeline.heading: THE CONTINENTAL CONTRADICTION
timeline.body: The African Union adopted a Free Movement Protocol in 2018 promising visa-free travel across the continent. Years later only a handful of states have ratified it, and South Africa — the continent's most industrialized economy and biggest migrant magnet — is not among them. The summit Ghana plans to raise this at is the same body whose flagship integration project its largest member quietly resists.

timeline.heading: WHY ENERGY LEAKS
timeline.body: Any oscillating charge acts as an antenna: it radiates electromagnetic waves outward into all of space, and that radiation is energy you can never recover. The faster and sharper the oscillation, the more it leaks. Confining energy means stopping it from becoming a wave that escapes.

timeline.heading: THE NEAR FIELD
timeline.body: Close to a source — within a fraction of a wavelength — energy sits in a non-radiating 'evanescent' field that clings to the surface and decays exponentially with distance. It carries no power away; it just stores it locally. Tap it before it fades and the transfer is loss-free, but the window has always been brutally short.

timeline.heading: THE FÖRSTER CEILING
timeline.body: The textbook rule for near-field transfer between two molecules — Förster resonance energy transfer — is that its efficiency collapses as the inverse sixth power of distance. Double the gap and the transfer drops by a factor of 64. That ruthless falloff is why nanoscale energy coupling was assumed to be a nanometre-range game.

blocks.text: **FRET** is the same mechanism that lets biologists use fluorescent proteins as molecular rulers — because the *1/r⁶* falloff is so steep it resolves distances of a few nanometres inside living cells.

blocks.question: How does Förster (near-field) energy-transfer efficiency fall off with the distance between source and target?
options: With the sixth power of distance (1/r⁶)
It stays constant until a hard cutoff
blocks.explanation: FRET rate scales as 1/r⁶, so transfer drops 64-fold when the gap doubles — which is why the effect was thought to die within a few nanometres.

timeline.heading: WHY GOLD
timeline.body: Gold's free electrons oscillate collectively as a 'plasmon,' a wave of charge that squeezes light into volumes far smaller than its wavelength. Shaping the metal into a rod tunes that resonance precisely, which is why noble-metal nanostructures are the standard tool for manipulating light below the size limits that govern ordinary optics.

blocks.text: A **surface plasmon** is light and electron-density sloshing in lockstep at a metal surface — it is what makes gold colloids appear ruby red rather than gold, an effect medieval glassmakers exploited centuries before anyone could explain it.

timeline.heading: THE DIFFRACTION WALL
timeline.body: Conventional optics cannot focus light to a spot smaller than roughly half its wavelength — hundreds of nanometres for visible light. That diffraction limit is why photonic components can't shrink to transistor scale, and why chips still shuttle data as slow electrons rather than fast photons. Plasmonics is the main route around the wall.

timeline.heading: WHAT MILLIMETRES BUY
timeline.body: Pushing loss-free coupling from nanometres to millimetres is a roughly million-fold jump in usable range. At that scale you can wire light across an actual chip or harvest stray energy across a real device — the difference between a laboratory curiosity and something that fits into manufacturable hardware.

timeline.heading: THE FABLESS BARGAIN
timeline.body: Nvidia owns no factories. It designs chips and emails the blueprints to a contract manufacturer — a foundry — that physically prints them. Every flagship Nvidia GPU is fabricated by TSMC in Taiwan. The $150B is not a bet on building things; it is the cost of locking supply at the one place that can build them.

blocks.text: The model is called *fabless*: the designer owns the intellectual property, the **foundry** owns the multi-billion-dollar fabrication plant. Nvidia, AMD, Apple, and Qualcomm are all fabless — and all queue at the same Taiwanese door.

timeline.heading: WHY YOU CAN'T BUY AN ECOSYSTEM
timeline.body: A fab in isolation is useless. It needs hundreds of specialized suppliers within truck distance — photoresist makers, etch-gas providers, mask shops, wafer polishers. Taiwan spent 40 years growing this cluster organically around Hsinchu Science Park. Onshoring a single building is easy; replicating the dense web of suppliers around it is what no government has managed.

blocks.label: the East Asian chip cluster
blocks.caption: Decades of supplier density packed around one corridor

timeline.heading: THE FOUNDRY CONCENTRATION
timeline.body: TSMC isn't merely the largest foundry; it is the foundry. It controls well over half of all contract chip revenue, and for the most advanced nodes — the ones AI accelerators require — its share approaches a near-monopoly. The runner-up, Samsung, is a distant second; everyone else fabricates older, less demanding chips.

timeline.heading: THE SILICON SHIELD
timeline.body: Taiwan's chip dominance doubles as deterrence. Both Washington and Beijing depend on TSMC's output, so neither can afford a war that flattens Hsinchu. Concentrating the world's most advanced manufacturing on one contested island is, paradoxically, the island's strongest insurance policy.

blocks.text: Strategists call it the *silicon shield*: the theory that Taiwan is too valuable to the global economy to be allowed to burn. A blockade or invasion that halted TSMC would crater the supply chains of **both** rivals at once.

timeline.heading: THE ONSHORING GAP
timeline.body: The US CHIPS Act and TSMC's Arizona fabs aim to pull manufacturing onshore, but the bleeding edge stays in Taiwan. Advanced packaging — the step that stitches AI chips together — and the newest process nodes remain Taiwan-only. Nvidia's choice to pour $150B into Taipei rather than Texas is the market voting on where the capability actually lives.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of the world's most advanced (sub-5nm) chips is fabricated in Taiwan?
blocks.explanation: Taiwan, almost entirely via TSMC, produces close to 90% of the leading-edge chips that power AI accelerators and flagship phones.

timeline.heading: THE GENDARMERIE
timeline.body: The Civil Guard is not ordinary police — it is a gendarmerie, a militarized force under both the Interior and Defense ministries, founded in 1844 to pacify the countryside and bandit-ridden roads. Its Central Operative Unit (UCO) is the elite team that builds financial-crime and corruption cases.

blocks.text: The **Guardia Civil** answers to two ministries at once — Interior in peacetime, Defense in war. Its **UCO** has become the most feared investigative body in Spanish public life.

timeline.heading: THE INVESTIGATING MAGISTRATE
timeline.body: Spain runs an inquisitorial system: a juez de instrucción directs the probe, orders searches, and assembles the case before any trial — unlike the adversarial model where police and prosecutors lead. The Audiencia Nacional is the special national court reserved for corruption, terrorism, and organized crime, which is why a party HQ search is a court-ordered act, not a police initiative.

timeline.heading: THE GÜRTEL IRONY
timeline.body: Sánchez is prime minister because of a corruption scandal. In 2018, after a court convicted figures in the Gürtel kickback network tied to Rajoy's People's Party, Sánchez won the first successful no-confidence vote in Spanish democratic history — taking power without an election. The party that rode graft into office now has its own headquarters searched.

events.label: Court convicts PP figures; Sánchez wins no-confidence vote
Sánchez re-forms govt on separatist votes

timeline.heading: WHY HE CAN'T BE FORCED OUT
timeline.body: Feijóo can demand snap elections, but he cannot trigger them. Spain's constructive vote of no confidence — borrowed from postwar Germany's Basic Law — requires the opposition to win an absolute majority while simultaneously naming a replacement prime minister. Rejecting the incumbent is not enough; you must agree on a successor.

blocks.text: The *moción de censura* is built to make governments hard to topple — you cannot vote a leader out without voting a named alternative *in*.

blocks.question: Under Spain's constructive vote of no confidence, ousting a sitting PM requires what?
options: A simple majority voting against the government
An absolute majority that names a replacement PM at the same time
A two-thirds supermajority in both chambers
A referendum called by the king
blocks.explanation: Copied from Germany's Basic Law, the rule forces the opposition to agree on a successor — not just reject the incumbent — which is why minority governments often survive scandal.

timeline.heading: THE MINORITY MATH
timeline.body: Sánchez has never commanded a parliamentary majority. His government survives on the votes of Catalan and Basque nationalist parties, which extract concessions — amnesty, fiscal autonomy — in return. The greater threat to his term is not the probe but losing those partners over a budget vote.

timeline.heading: THE SIDE CHANNEL
timeline.body: A side-channel attack steals secrets without breaking any lock. Instead of attacking the data or the cryptography directly, it watches a system's physical behavior — how long an operation takes, how much power it draws, what sound it makes — and infers the secret from the leak. The logic is perfect; the hardware betrays it.

blocks.text: A *side channel* leaks information not by defeating the math but by listening to the machine — the **timing**, power draw, or even sound a computation gives off while it runs.

timeline.heading: HOW THE SSD LEAK WORKS
timeline.body: Browsers forbid one tab from reading another's content. But JavaScript can time its own file operations. Because every tab shares one physical drive, the delay on those operations shifts depending on what other tabs are reading or writing — and that timing fingerprint reveals which sites are open.

timeline.heading: WHY VPNS AND AD-BLOCKERS CAN'T STOP IT
timeline.body: Privacy tools each guard one layer. A VPN hides your network path, an ad-blocker strips known tracking scripts, incognito clears stored data. This attack operates beneath all of them — at the hardware timing of your own disk — so none of them are even looking in the right place.

timeline.heading: THE FINGERPRINT THAT CROSSES BROWSERS
timeline.body: Most fingerprinting is browser-specific — canvas rendering quirks, font lists, the user-agent string change when you switch from Chrome to Firefox. A hardware side channel reads the machine underneath the browser, so the same identifier follows you across every browser on the device.

blocks.question: Why can this tracking method identify a visitor across different browsers on the same computer?
options: It reads SSD hardware timing beneath the browser layer
It silently syncs cookies between Chrome and Firefox
It exploits a shared bug in every browser's engine
It reads the visitor's saved browser passwords
blocks.explanation: The leak comes from physical drive timing shared by the whole machine, so no per-browser setting can hide it.

timeline.heading: THE LINEAGE
timeline.body: Side channels are old. Cold War spies read screens from electromagnetic leakage; cryptographers learned to recover keys by timing how long a decryption took. The modern era began when Spectre and Meltdown showed the chips powering nearly every computer leaked secrets through speculative execution — and side channels went from academic curiosity to front-page emergency.

events.label: van Eck: CRT screens readable from afar
Kocher's timing attacks break crypto keys
Spectre & Meltdown hit nearly every CPU

timeline.heading: THE FIX AND ITS COST
timeline.body: The proposed defense caps the file-size allocation the attack measures, flattening the timing signal that leaks. It's the canonical side-channel mitigation: you can't delete the physical behavior, so you add noise or constrain the resource — and accept a small performance hit as the price of closing the channel.

timeline.heading: WHY THE HEART CAN'T REBUILD ITSELF
timeline.body: Heart muscle cells stop dividing shortly after birth. Scientists measured this using carbon-14 left in the atmosphere by Cold War bomb tests, which dates a cell's birth year: the adult heart renews under 1% of its muscle cells annually. A heart attack kills around a billion of them in hours, and they are gone for good.

blocks.question: Roughly how much of an adult human's heart muscle is replaced each year?
blocks.explanation: Carbon-14 from atomic-bomb fallout let researchers date cardiomyocyte birth years — turnover is under 1% per year and falls with age.

timeline.heading: WHAT SCAR TISSUE COSTS
timeline.body: With no replacement muscle available, fibroblasts seal the dead zone with collagen. The scar holds the wall together but is electrically silent and cannot contract — it is dead weight that stiffens the pump and seeds arrhythmias, driving the slow slide into heart failure.

blocks.text: The repair is a structural patch, not a functional one: scar **stabilizes** the wall but contributes **zero contraction**. Every square centimeter of it is force the heart has permanently lost.

timeline.heading: THE REGENERATION GRADIENT
timeline.body: The lost ability isn't universal across animals. Zebrafish and salamanders regrow heart muscle completely after injury; a newborn mouse can for about a week after birth, then the window slams shut. Mammals appear to have traded regeneration away for the thick, high-pressure walls that warm-blooded circulation demands.

timeline.heading: HOW THE PATCH WORKS
timeline.body: BioVAT sidesteps the heart's refusal to regenerate by growing the muscle outside the body: stem cells are coaxed into beating heart tissue in a 3D engineered scaffold, then the sheet is sewn onto the scarred wall. The graft cells contract and wire into the host's electrical network, adding the pumping force the scar can't.

timeline.heading: THE iPSC TRICK BEHIND IT
timeline.body: The cells come from a 2006 breakthrough: an adult cell can be rewound to an embryo-like state by switching on just four genes. This sidesteps the ethical and supply problems of embryonic stem cells and means the graft can, in principle, be grown from the patient's own cells.

blocks.text: *Shinya Yamanaka* showed four transcription factors turn an adult skin cell back into a blank-slate stem cell — an **induced pluripotent stem cell**. It won the Nobel in 2012, six years after the discovery.

timeline.heading: THE COUPLING DANGER
timeline.body: The hard part was never growing muscle — it's making graft cells beat in time with the host. In primate trials, immature graft cells fired on their own schedule and triggered dangerous arrhythmias for weeks until they matured. This is why the open questions are durability and safety, not whether the tissue takes.

timeline.heading: A PLEDGE IS NOT A DEPOSIT
timeline.body: The headline number at every donor conference is the pledge — a political announcement, revocable and unaudited. The number that rebuilds anything is the disbursement: money actually wired into an account that can pay contractors. In post-conflict aid the gap between the two routinely swallows half or more of the announced total, because a pledge costs a government nothing until it chooses to honor it.

blocks.text: A **pledge** is a press release; a **disbursement** is a wire transfer. Tracking the *gap* between them is the single most reliable way to read whether reconstruction is real or theater.

timeline.heading: WHY THE MONEY USUALLY GOES THROUGH THE WORLD BANK
timeline.body: Donors funding contested territory normally insist on a multi-donor trust fund administered by the World Bank — competitive bidding, audited disbursement, published contracts. Those fiduciary controls are what a foreign ministry points to when defending aid to a place it cannot directly oversee. Routing $17B into a private JPMorgan account with no transparency requirements removes exactly that layer: no independent audit trail, no procurement rules, no public record of who gets paid.

blocks.question: Why do reconstruction donors usually route funds through a World Bank trust fund instead of a private account?
options: It provides independent auditing and procurement oversight
It exempts the funds from local taxation
It guarantees a fixed exchange rate
blocks.explanation: The Bank's fiduciary standards — competitive bidding and audited disbursement — are the controls donors cite to justify aid to territory they cannot directly supervise.

timeline.heading: WHO IS MEANT TO PAY
timeline.body: Reconstruction money for Gaza has historically come from the Gulf — the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar — with Egypt and Jordan as the logistical gatekeepers controlling what crosses into the strip. The geography matters: nothing rebuilds Gaza City without material physically passing through Egyptian and Israeli-controlled crossings, which is why the funders and the gatekeepers are rarely the same governments.

timeline.heading: THE 2014 RHYME
timeline.body: This has happened before. After the 2014 assault, the Cairo conference pledged roughly $5.4B and created the Gaza Reconstruction Mechanism to track every bag of cement. Years later much of the pledge had never arrived and reconstruction had barely moved. The pattern — destruction, a glittering pledge conference, then a stalled mechanism — has repeated across 2009, 2014, and 2021. Each time the announced figure was the easy part.

timeline.heading: THE EMPTY FUND AS LEVERAGE
timeline.body: An account holding zero dollars is not necessarily a failure — it can be the policy. Withholding reconstruction is a standard instrument: money is released only when political conditions are met (disarmament, a governance structure, recognition of a new authority). The board's Palestinian committee cannot disburse what was never deposited, which keeps every party dependent on whoever controls the spigot. The leverage lives in the gap between the promise and the transfer.

timeline.heading: THE BACK CHANNEL
timeline.body: Oman is the Gulf's designated middleman. Under Sultan Qaboos it hosted the secret 2013 Muscat talks between US and Iranian envoys that became the framework for the 2015 nuclear deal — negotiations so quiet that even allied governments learned of them late. Threatening the mediator is threatening the only open line to Tehran.

timeline.heading: WHY OMAN AND NOT A GULF RIVAL
timeline.body: Oman is the world's only Ibadi-majority state — a branch of Islam older than the Sunni-Shia split and distinct from both. That theological independence is the structural reason it stays out of the Saudi-Iran sectarian contest and can talk to everyone: Tehran, Washington, the Houthis, even Israel.

blocks.text: **Ibadism** traces to the 7th-century Kharijite movement but evolved into a quietist, consensus-driven school. It is why Oman has no stake in the *Sunni-Shia* rivalry that defines its neighbors.

blocks.question: Which branch of Islam is the majority in Oman?
blocks.explanation: Oman is the only Ibadi-majority country, a school that predates and sits apart from the Sunni-Shia divide — the root of its neutral diplomacy.

timeline.heading: OMAN OWNS THE SOUTH SIDE OF HORMUZ
timeline.body: The strait's narrowest point runs between Iran's coast and Oman's Musandam Peninsula — an Omani exclave separated from the rest of the country by the UAE. The outbound shipping lane actually passes through Omani territorial waters, which is why Muscat, not Abu Dhabi, is the Arab side of the chokepoint.

blocks.label: the narrows
blocks.caption: Oman's Musandam exclave forms the southern shore

timeline.heading: WHY HORMUZ HAS NO REAL BYPASS
timeline.body: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil moves through Hormuz, and the overland pipelines built as hedges can absorb only a fraction of it. Saudi Arabia's East-West line and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah route together reroute maybe a third of Gulf exports; the rest has no alternative path to sea.

blocks.label: Hormuz flow vs pipeline bypass capacity (mn bbl/day)

timeline.heading: THE ABRAHAM ACCORDS LEVER
timeline.body: Tying an Iran ceasefire to Arab normalization with Israel revives the 2020 Abraham Accords — the US-brokered deals that broke the old Arab consensus of no recognition without a Palestinian state. Four states signed in five months; the larger prizes, Saudi Arabia and Oman, have held out.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 ships in the Gulf from 1984 to 1988, yet oil never stopped flowing — tankers were reflagged under US colors and escorted by warships. The lesson planners drew: closing Hormuz is far easier to threaten than to sustain, because the world adapts within weeks.

timeline.heading: THE RITE
timeline.body: Eid al-Adha commemorates Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son and God's substitution of a ram. The qurbani — slaughter of a sheep, goat, cow, or camel — is a Sunnah mu'akkadah, with one-third for the family, one-third for relatives, one-third for the poor. The poor are not an afterthought; they are written into the rite.

blocks.text: The Arabic terms are *udhiyya* (the sacrificial animal) and *qurbani* (the act). The three-way division is **wajib** in practice — the meat distribution is the worship, not a byproduct of it.

timeline.heading: WHY THE PRICE TELLS YOU EVERYTHING
timeline.body: In a functioning market, a sheep is a commodity with a known cost — feed, transport, slaughter, margin. When one animal costs eleven times its pre-war price, the number is not inflation in any normal sense. It is the price of scarcity engineered by a closed border, and a measure of how many families will perform the rite by proxy or skip it entirely.

timeline.heading: THE CROSSINGS
timeline.body: Gaza has five potential entry points — Erez and Kerem Shalom with Israel, Rafah with Egypt, plus Karni and Sufa long since shut. Every truck of feed, every live animal, every sack of flour crosses inspection lanes Israel controls. Throughput, not distance, is the binding constraint.

timeline.heading: THE LIVESTOCK MATH
timeline.body: Roughly 15,000 sheep remain for 2.1 million people — one animal per 140 residents. A standard qurbani sheep feeds about seven shares under classical fiqh. Even if every remaining sheep were slaughtered and distributed perfectly, the meat would reach a small fraction of households.

blocks.question: Under classical Islamic jurisprudence, how many people can share a single sheep's qurbani?
blocks.explanation: A sheep or goat counts as one share — for one person or household. A cow or camel can be shared among seven. This is why livestock scarcity directly limits how many families fulfill the rite.

timeline.heading: THE SIEGE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Siege as a weapon predates Gaza by millennia, but the modern legal frame is the 1949 Geneva Convention IV, which forbids starvation of civilians and collective punishment of occupied populations. The blessed land of Palestine has lived under variations of this pressure — Mandate-era curfews, 1948 expulsions, post-1967 closures, the 2007 blockade — for nearly a century.

blocks.label: closures on Palestinian movement and goods

timeline.heading: THE RITE WHEN THE ANIMAL IS UNREACHABLE
timeline.body: Classical Sunni scholarship — Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali — holds qurbani as a strong Sunnah for those who can afford it; inability removes the obligation without sin. Many in Gaza will fulfill the rite via wakala, paying a relative or charity abroad to slaughter on their behalf and distribute the meat there. The intention travels even when the animal cannot.

timeline.heading: THE SIGNAL BENEATH SEARCH
timeline.body: Google's internal trend tools see query spikes hours before news breaks publicly. A surge in searches for a company name, a politician's health, or a city in conflict zone is itself a leading indicator — the crowd knows something is happening before the wire services report it.

blocks.text: Internal tools like **Google Trends Pro** and the unreleased **Search Console for Trends** expose query volume at minute-level granularity — orders of magnitude finer than the public Trends product, which smooths to days.

timeline.heading: WHY INSIDERS ARE THE FEATURE
timeline.body: In stock markets, insider trading is illegal because it breaks a level playing field. In prediction markets, informed traders are the mechanism — their bets pull private knowledge into public prices. The design logic cuts in the opposite direction.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL GRAY ZONE
timeline.body: US insider-trading law hinges on breach of fiduciary duty regarding a security. A Polymarket contract has no issuer, no shareholders, no fiduciary. Prosecutors here are reaching for commodities fraud and wire fraud — not securities law — because the securities framework simply does not fit.

blocks.question: Why is this case charged as commodities and wire fraud rather than insider trading?
options: Polymarket contracts are not securities, so insider-trading statutes don't apply
Insider trading is only a civil offense, not criminal
The defendant was not a corporate officer
blocks.explanation: US insider-trading law covers securities. Prediction-market contracts have no issuer or fiduciary, so prosecutors use commodities fraud and wire fraud statutes instead.

timeline.heading: THE 2004 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: DARPA's Policy Analysis Market would have let traders bet on Middle East events including assassinations. Senators killed it within 24 hours, branding it a terrorism futures market. Two decades later Polymarket runs analogous contracts in size — the Overton window on event markets has moved, but the misuse cases the senators warned about are now arriving.

timeline.heading: THE FIDUCIARY THAT DOES EXIST
timeline.body: Even without a securities tie, Spagnuolo owed Google a duty over its proprietary data. The classic misappropriation theory — affirmed in US v. O'Hagan (1997) — lets prosecutors charge someone who trades on confidential information stolen from an employer, regardless of whether the trader has any relationship to the asset traded.

blocks.text: A fiduciary who pretends loyalty to the principal while secretly converting the principal's information for personal gain dupes or defrauds the principal.
blocks.speaker: US v. O'Hagan, 521 U.S. 642

timeline.heading: WHY POLYMARKET IS TRACEABLE
timeline.body: Every Polymarket bet settles on the Polygon blockchain — a public ledger. Once the FBI links a wallet to an identity (via the on-ramp KYC at the exchange that funded it), every prior trade is visible forever. Polymarket is, paradoxically, the worst venue on Earth for someone trying to hide insider activity.

timeline.heading: THE KILL SWITCH MECHANICS
timeline.body: A national internet shutdown is not a single switch. States either order ISPs to null-route BGP announcements (Iran's 2019 method), throttle bandwidth at international gateways, or block specific protocols. Iran has built all three capabilities into a tiered system the regime can escalate or relax in hours.

blocks.text: The architecture is called the **National Information Network** (*Shabakeh-ye Melli-ye Ettela'at*) — a domestic intranet that keeps banking, messaging, and government services running *internally* even when the international gateway is severed.

timeline.heading: THE 2019 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In November 2019, Iran cut the country off for roughly six days after fuel-price protests. It was, at the time, the most complete national disconnection ever measured — and it normalized the playbook. Every subsequent shutdown has been longer than the last.

events.label: Mahsa Amini protests: ~75 days mobile cut

timeline.heading: WHY DOMESTIC PLATFORMS MATTER
timeline.body: During the shutdown, Iranians were funneled onto Bale, Rubika, and Soroush — state-licensed messaging apps whose servers sit inside Iran and whose operators must comply with judicial data requests. A blackout is not just a denial of foreign services; it is a forced migration onto surveilled domestic ones.

timeline.heading: THE ECONOMIC COST
timeline.body: NetBlocks and the Brookings Institution estimate national shutdowns cost an economy roughly 0.4% of daily GDP for a full blackout, more when banking and remittance flows are affected. For Iran, sanctions already constrain the formal economy; the shutdown taxes the informal one that keeps households afloat.

timeline.heading: THE JUDICIAL TWIST
timeline.body: That Iran's judiciary suspended the body that ordered restoration is the structural story. The Islamic Republic has parallel institutions — elected government, Supreme Leader's office, IRGC, judiciary — each with veto power over the others. Internet policy sits at the intersection where the elected presidency loses every fight.

blocks.question: Which Iranian institution holds final authority over internet policy in practice?
options: The elected president and his cabinet
The Supreme Council of Cyberspace, chaired by the Supreme Leader
blocks.explanation: The Supreme Council of Cyberspace, established by Khamenei in 2012, sits above the elected government and sets binding internet policy.

timeline.heading: THE REGIONAL MAP
timeline.body: Iran is not an outlier. The broader region has built shutdown capabilities as standard counter-protest infrastructure, with Iraq, Pakistan, and Turkey each cutting access during recent unrest.

blocks.label: shutdown-capable states in Iran's neighborhood
blocks.caption: each has cut national or regional internet within the last 3 years

timeline.heading: THE INVENTION THAT FEEDS HALF THE WORLD
timeline.body: In 1909, Fritz Haber figured out how to pull nitrogen from the air and fix it into ammonia. The Haber-Bosch process now produces roughly 150 million tonnes of ammonia per year. Without it, Earth could feed about half its current population. The other half exists because of this single chemical reaction.

blocks.text: The reaction breaks the **N₂ triple bond** — one of the strongest in chemistry — using *400°C* and *200 atmospheres* of pressure, with natural gas as both fuel and feedstock.

timeline.heading: THE GAS-TO-FOOD PIPELINE
timeline.body: Natural gas is roughly 80% of urea production cost. This is why fertilizer plants cluster near cheap gas fields. A gas supply disruption is, mechanically, a food supply disruption — the chemistry does not care about the politics.

blocks.label: share of global traded urea exports (approx.)

timeline.heading: WHY HORMUZ MOVES NEBRASKA
timeline.body: Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Iran all ship LNG and urea through or past the Strait of Hormuz. When the strait's risk premium spikes, European and Asian buyers bid up the gas and fertilizer that would otherwise have stayed in their region — and American producers, who sell into the same global market, raise their prices to match.

timeline.heading: THE CORN BELT MARGIN
timeline.body: A US corn farmer's three biggest input lines are seed, land rent, and nitrogen. Nitrogen alone can be a quarter of cash cost per acre. When urea or anhydrous ammonia jumps 30%, the operating margin on a 200-bushel acre can flip from modestly positive to negative before harvest insurance kicks in.

blocks.label: US corn input share (approx. cash cost per acre)

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988, Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. Oil prices spiked briefly but markets adapted — tankers were reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags and escorted by warships. The lesson planners took: disruption is easier to threaten than to sustain. Fertilizer markets, with smaller buffer stocks than oil, are slower to adapt.

timeline.heading: THE FARM VOTE
timeline.body: Nebraska sends two senators from a state where roughly 45% of land is cropland and a further 45% is rangeland. Farm-economy shocks translate directly into Senate races in ways that rarely happen in coastal states — which is why a Hormuz-driven urea price is, eventually, a Washington vote count.

blocks.question: Which input is the single largest swing cost for a US corn farmer when natural gas prices spike?
blocks.explanation: Nitrogen fertilizer is made from natural gas via Haber-Bosch; a gas price move passes through to urea and anhydrous ammonia within weeks. Land rent and seed are contracted ahead of the season.

timeline.heading: THE 1891 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum, issued in 1891, was the Church's response to industrial capitalism. It defended workers' right to organize, condemned both unrestrained markets and socialism, and established that the Church would speak on economic structure — not just personal morality. Every subsequent social encyclical builds on it.

blocks.text: The new document's title *Magnifica Humanitas* deliberately echoes **Rerum Novarum** — Latin for *of new things* — signaling that AI is the new industrial revolution.

timeline.heading: WHY THE NAME LEO
timeline.body: Popes choose regnal names as policy signals. Taking the name Leo — last used by the labor-encyclical pope — telegraphs the intent before any document is written. John XXIII signaled aggiornamento; Francis signaled the poor; Leo XIV signals capital-and-labor for the AI age.

timeline.heading: THE DOCTRINE OF UNIVERSAL DESTINATION
timeline.body: Catholic social teaching holds that the goods of creation are destined for all humanity. Private property is legitimate but instrumental — it serves the universal destination, not the reverse. Applied to AI, this doctrine treats compute, models, and training data as goods whose concentration in a few hands requires moral justification, not the other way around.

blocks.question: In Catholic social teaching, private property is treated as:
options: A legitimate but instrumental good serving the universal destination of created goods
A necessary evil to be minimized
A purely civil construct with no moral weight
blocks.explanation: From Aquinas through Rerum Novarum to today, the Church defends private property — but subordinate to the principle that creation is destined for all.

timeline.heading: WHY ANTHROPIC, NOT OPENAI
timeline.body: Chris Olah's appearance signals which lab the Vatican views as a moral interlocutor. Anthropic was founded in 2021 by ex-OpenAI researchers who left over safety disagreements; its corporate structure includes a Long-Term Benefit Trust meant to override shareholders on safety questions. That structural posture maps more cleanly onto Catholic social teaching's subordination of capital to the common good than the standard Silicon Valley model.

timeline.heading: THE DISTRIBUTION PROBLEM
timeline.body: Industrial gains took roughly a century to broadly distribute through unions, progressive taxation, and welfare states. AI productivity gains, if concentrated in a handful of model developers and compute owners, could compress that century into a decade with no equivalent institutional countervailing force. The encyclical's argument is that waiting for redistribution after concentration is too late.

blocks.text: Leo XIII watched the **gilded age** — robber barons, factory children, no unions — and concluded the Church could not be neutral on structure. Leo XIV is making the same wager about the **token age**.

timeline.heading: THE ENCYCLICAL'S WEIGHT
timeline.body: An encyclical is the second-highest form of papal teaching, below only an apostolic constitution. It binds Catholic bishops, schools, hospitals, and universities to align teaching with its principles. With 1.4 billion Catholics — including roughly a quarter of the US population and majorities across Latin America and the Philippines — a doctrinal position on AI distribution enters policy debates in dozens of countries simultaneously.

blocks.label: Catholic-majority and Catholic-plurality nations
blocks.caption: Encyclicals enter politics across all of these capitals at once.

timeline.heading: WHY COMPLIANCE IS EXPENSIVE
timeline.body: Global banks spend roughly $200bn a year on financial-crime compliance — more than they spend on cybersecurity. The cost is structural: every cross-border payment triggers sanctions screening, beneficial-ownership checks, and transaction monitoring against thousands of rule patterns. Headcount scaled because the rules did.

blocks.text: Industry surveys put the global financial-crime compliance bill at **~$206bn** (LexisNexis, 2023) — a figure that has doubled since 2018 as sanctions regimes multiplied.

timeline.heading: STANDARD CHARTERED'S RAP SHEET
timeline.body: This is the bank that paid $667m to US authorities in 2012 for sanctions-busting Iran transactions, another $1.1bn in 2019 for continued violations through 2014, and £102m to the UK FCA in the same settlement. Cutting 15% of fraud staff is being announced by a firm whose recent history is the canonical case study in why those staff exist.

timeline.heading: WHAT MODELS ACTUALLY DO WELL
timeline.body: Machine-learning systems reduce false-positive rates in transaction monitoring — the rule-based legacy systems flag 95-98% noise, and human reviewers spend their day clearing it. Models trained on labelled outcomes can cut alert volume by half without missing more true positives. That is the genuine productivity case.

blocks.question: What share of alerts from legacy bank transaction-monitoring systems are false positives?
blocks.explanation: Industry studies consistently put rule-based AML false-positive rates at 95-98% — most compliance staff time is spent clearing noise, not catching crime.

timeline.heading: WHAT MODELS DO BADLY
timeline.body: Novel fraud typologies — the ones not yet in training data — are exactly where supervised models fail. Synthetic-identity rings, deepfake-authorised push payments, and AI-generated KYC documents are all post-2023 attack patterns. The arms race is now model-vs-model, and the bank cutting its human reviewers is betting its defenders generalize faster than the attackers' generators evolve.

blocks.text: UK Finance reported **authorised push payment (APP) fraud** losses of £459m in 2023 — a category that barely existed a decade ago and which transaction-monitoring rules struggle to flag because the customer themselves authorises the transfer.

timeline.heading: THE ACCOUNTABILITY GAP
timeline.body: Under the UK's Senior Managers Regime and the US OCC framework, a named individual is legally responsible for compliance failures — they can be fined, banned, or prosecuted. No model has a license to revoke. When an automated system misses a suspicious transaction at scale, regulators look for the human who signed off on the system's design, which is why most automation projects end up adding senior oversight roles even as they cut junior ones.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT FROM TRADING FLOORS
timeline.body: Cash equity dealing desks were the first banking function to be largely automated, starting in the early 2000s. Goldman Sachs went from 600 cash traders in 2000 to under 5 by 2017. But compliance, risk, and surveillance headcount around those automated desks grew — because the regulatory liability did not transfer to the algorithm.

blocks.label: automation arc on the Goldman cash-equities desk

timeline.heading: THE HEJAZ INHERITANCE
timeline.body: The original Damascus-Medina line — the Hejaz Railway — was built by the Ottomans between 1900 and 1908, financed by donations from Muslims across the empire to ease the Hajj. T.E. Lawrence and Arab irregulars destroyed long stretches of it in 1916-18; most of the southern track has never been restored.

events.label: Construction begins under Abdul Hamid II

timeline.heading: THE CORRIDOR LOGIC
timeline.body: A working Syrian rail spine would let Gulf cargo reach the Mediterranean without rounding the Arabian Peninsula or transiting the Suez Canal. The distance from Riyadh to a Syrian port is roughly a third of the sea route to Europe via Suez, which is why every regional power has periodically tried to build it.

timeline.heading: WHY SOVIET LOCOMOTIVES
timeline.body: Syria was a Soviet client from the 1960s onward; rolling stock, signaling, and the 1435mm gauge sections were standardized to Eastern Bloc suppliers. After 1991 the supply of spare parts collapsed, and Western sanctions after 2011 closed off alternatives. The fleet aged in place.

blocks.text: The working freight line — Damascus to Latakia — now averages roughly **5 km/h** over track designed for *60 km/h*. A locomotive failure on the line can idle cargo for weeks.

timeline.heading: THE GAUGE PROBLEM
timeline.body: Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Iraq each built their modern rail networks to different specifications. The old Hejaz line was 1050mm narrow gauge; Saudi's new North-South Railway is 1435mm standard gauge; Iran runs 1435mm but Turkey's eastern lines have historically been a patchwork. Any real corridor requires either regauging or break-of-gauge transshipment yards at every border.

blocks.label: rail gauge across the proposed corridor

timeline.heading: WHO PAYS, WHO DECIDES
timeline.body: Gulf reconstruction money for Syria has been announced repeatedly since 2017 and disbursed sparingly. The constraint is rarely the headline figure — it is who controls procurement, which contractors get awarded, and whether sanctions waivers cover the equipment imports. An accord without a financing mechanism and a sanctions carve-out is a press release.

blocks.question: What has historically been the binding constraint on Gulf-funded reconstruction in post-war Arab states?
options: Sanctions, procurement control, and disbursement mechanics
blocks.explanation: Pledges are easy; the binding constraints are who controls procurement, whether sanctions permit the equipment, and whether the recipient government can actually receive the funds.

timeline.heading: THE BLESSED LAND
timeline.body: Damascus and the broader region of al-Sham hold particular weight in Islamic tradition. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes the people of al-Sham as being under divine protection, and classical scholars including Ibn Kathir wrote extensively on the region's role in end-times narratives. Infrastructure that reconnects Damascus to the wider Muslim world carries a resonance beyond its commercial logic.

timeline.heading: THE BOND THAT WON'T BREAK
timeline.body: PFAS molecules are built on carbon-fluorine bonds — among the strongest in organic chemistry. Nothing in nature evolved to break them because nothing in nature ever made them. They pass through soil, water, sunlight, and bacteria essentially unchanged, which is why they accumulate indefinitely in groundwater and bloodstreams.

blocks.text: The class name covers thousands of compounds; the two most studied are **PFOS** (used in firefighting foam) and **PFOA** (used to make Teflon). Both are now found in the blood of essentially every human tested.

timeline.heading: WHY DEFENCE BASES
timeline.body: Military airfields used aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) for fuel-fire training from the 1970s onward. The foam was sprayed directly onto open ground, soaked into aquifers, and migrated to surrounding farms and water supplies. Australia, the US, and most NATO militaries face structurally identical contamination at hundreds of bases.

blocks.caption: AFFF contamination sites cluster around defence airfields

timeline.heading: THE 3M KNEW DOCUMENTS
timeline.body: Internal 3M studies from the 1970s found PFOS in employee blood. By the 1980s, the company knew it bioaccumulated in fish and humans. 3M did not disclose the findings to the EPA until 1998 and exited PFOS production in 2000. Discovery in US litigation has produced thousands of internal memos showing the gap between what was known and what was reported.

events.label: Internal studies find PFOS in worker blood

timeline.heading: THE US PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In 2023, 3M agreed to pay up to $10.3 billion to US public water systems over PFAS contamination — one of the largest environmental settlements in American history. DuPont and Chemours settled separately for $1.2 billion. The Australian suit fits a global litigation pattern that is still expanding into Europe and Asia.

timeline.heading: THE HEALTH SIGNAL
timeline.body: Epidemiology links PFAS exposure to kidney and testicular cancer, thyroid disease, ulcerative colitis, high cholesterol, and pregnancy-induced hypertension. The C8 Science Panel — established as part of a 2005 DuPont settlement — spent seven years studying 69,000 exposed residents and produced the strongest evidence base linking a single industrial chemical to specific diseases.

timeline.heading: THE REMEDIATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: Because PFAS bonds don't break, you cannot neutralize the chemicals in place — you can only concentrate and contain them. Granular activated carbon filters trap PFAS in spent media that must then be incinerated at over 1000°C, and even incineration may release shorter-chain PFAS into the atmosphere. The AU$1B Australia has already spent largely bought concentration, not destruction.

blocks.question: Why can't PFAS contamination simply be broken down in place?
options: The chemicals are radioactive and require shielded handling
Carbon-fluorine bonds are among the strongest in chemistry; nothing biological breaks them
PFAS only degrade in saltwater, which most contaminated sites lack
Patents prevent third parties from using the necessary enzymes
blocks.explanation: The C-F bond requires extreme heat or specialized chemistry to break — no soil microbe, sunlight, or natural process touches it, which is why PFAS persist for generations.

timeline.heading: THE CONSTITUTIONAL TENSION
timeline.body: States cannot tax the federal government directly — McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) established that 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy.' But states can tax individuals who receive federal payments, which is the lane California is trying to use.

blocks.text: That the power to tax involves the power to destroy; that the power to destroy may defeat and render useless the power to create...
blocks.speaker: Chief Justice Marshall, McCulloch v. Maryland

timeline.heading: THE 100% RATE PROBLEM
timeline.body: A confiscatory tax — one designed to seize rather than raise revenue — has historically been struck down as a regulatory penalty in disguise. The Supreme Court's Bailey v. Drexel Furniture (1922) voided a 10% tax on child-labor goods for exactly this reason: it was a punishment dressed as revenue.

blocks.text: The legal term of art is a ***pretextual tax*** — one whose stated purpose (raising money) is contradicted by a design that ensures no money flows. Courts look at structure, not labels.

timeline.heading: THE PARDON POWER
timeline.body: Article II §2 gives the president unconditional pardon authority for federal offenses. What it does not grant is the power to compensate the pardoned — that requires an appropriation, which under Article I §9 must originate in Congress, not executive order.

blocks.text: No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law
blocks.speaker: US Constitution, Article I §9

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT THAT ISN'T
timeline.body: Federal payments to individuals are normally taxable as ordinary income at both federal and state levels — unemployment, Social Security above thresholds, even disaster relief in some cases. What makes a 100% rate novel is its targeting: a tax that applies only to recipients of one specific federal program.

blocks.question: Which constitutional clause is most often cited against state laws targeting a specific federal program?
blocks.explanation: The Supremacy Clause (Article VI) bars states from passing laws that frustrate federal policy — the doctrine of intergovernmental immunity flows from it.

timeline.heading: CALIFORNIA AS COUNTER-FEDERALISM
timeline.body: Sacramento has spent a decade building a parallel regulatory state — emissions standards stricter than EPA, immigration sanctuary policies, cannabis legalization ahead of federal law. A targeted tax on federal pardonees extends this from regulation into fiscal retaliation, which is constitutionally newer ground.

blocks.label: California vs federal posture, selected fights

timeline.heading: THE FIRE TRIANGLE
timeline.body: Wildfire needs fuel, oxygen, and heat — and spreads on three variables: fuel moisture, wind, and terrain slope. Forecasting fire risk is forecasting the joint state of all three weeks ahead, which is why it sits downstream of weather prediction, not alongside it.

blocks.text: The operational term is **fire weather** — the conjunction of low *relative humidity*, high wind, and dry fuels. A single dry day doesn't matter; a *fuel-moisture deficit* accumulated over weeks does.

timeline.heading: WHY THE GLOBAL SOUTH IS BLIND
timeline.body: Conventional fire forecasts depend on dense ground weather stations to calibrate fuel-moisture indices. Sub-Saharan Africa has roughly one-eighth the WMO-standard station density of Europe; large stretches of the Amazon and Sahel have none. The forecast skill gap is a measurement gap, not a modeling one.

blocks.label: highest fire-exposure, lowest station density
blocks.caption: countries where conventional forecasts have historically failed

timeline.heading: WHAT DEEP LEARNING REPLACES
timeline.body: The Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index, the global standard since 1970, is a chain of empirical equations tuned on boreal forest. Deep-learning models skip the equations entirely — they learn the mapping from satellite-observed vegetation, soil moisture, and reanalysis weather directly to fire occurrence, with no assumption that boreal physics transfers to the Cerrado or the miombo woodlands.

timeline.heading: THE 31-DAY HORIZON
timeline.body: Numerical weather prediction loses skill past about 10 days — chaos eats the signal. Subseasonal forecasting (10–45 days) instead leans on slower-moving drivers: sea-surface temperatures, soil moisture memory, the Madden-Julian Oscillation. Fire risk at a month's lead is forecastable precisely because vegetation dryness changes slowly.

blocks.question: Why can wildfire risk be forecast 31 days ahead when weather itself can't?
options: Fires are easier to predict than rain
Vegetation dryness changes on weekly-to-monthly timescales, not daily
Satellites can directly see future fires
AI models bypass the chaos limit
blocks.explanation: Fuel moisture has memory measured in weeks; this slow-moving signal survives past the 10-day chaos horizon that kills daily weather forecasts.

timeline.heading: THE BIAS METRIC
timeline.body: Forecast bias is the systematic over- or under-prediction averaged across many forecasts — distinct from error on any single day. A model can be unbiased on average while still missing individual fires; conversely, a biased model misallocates resources year after year. Closing the bias gap in poor, high-exposure cells means evacuation planning and pre-positioned firefighting assets finally line up with where fires actually occur.

timeline.heading: THE DECAPITATION DOCTRINE
timeline.body: Targeted killing of leadership assumes organizations are top-down and brittle. Decades of counterterrorism data suggest the opposite for ideological networks: removing commanders accelerates fragmentation but rarely ends the movement. The RAND Corporation's 2008 study of 648 terrorist groups found military force ended only 7 percent of them.

blocks.text: Political scientists call this the **decapitation paradox**: the more decentralized the target, the less effective leadership removal becomes — and the harder negotiation becomes afterward.

timeline.heading: HAMAS'S ORGANIZATIONAL SPLIT
timeline.body: Hamas has long operated as two parallel structures: the political bureau, historically based in Doha and Beirut, and the Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades inside Gaza. Decisions on negotiations require alignment between them. When the military wing's leadership is decapitated, the political wing loses its enforcement partner — and Israel loses anyone empowered to sign.

timeline.heading: THE INTERLOCUTOR PROBLEM
timeline.body: Every ceasefire framework since October 2023 has required a Hamas figure with authority to bind the movement. Phase-2 talks demand disarmament — a decision no mid-level commander can credibly make. Killing the chain of command faster than it can be reconstituted is militarily efficient and diplomatically self-defeating.

timeline.heading: THE BLESSED LAND
timeline.body: In Islamic tradition, the land of Palestine — al-Quds and its surroundings — is described in the Quran as blessed, in Surah al-Isra and elsewhere. Classical scholars including Ibn Kathir identified the region as central to end-times events. For Muslims worldwide, military operations in Gaza resonate with a prophetic geography that predates and transcends the modern conflict's political framing.

timeline.heading: THE HYDRA PATTERN
timeline.body: Israel killed Hezbollah's founder Abbas al-Musawi in 1992; Hassan Nasrallah replaced him and built the organization into a regional military force. Hamas's own founder Sheikh Ahmed Yassin was killed in 2004; Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian elections. Decapitation has historically produced harder, less negotiable successors.

timeline.heading: WHAT DISARMAMENT MEANS
timeline.body: In every comparable conflict — Northern Ireland, Colombia, the Balkans — armed groups disarmed only after binding political settlements with international guarantors. Hamas is being asked to disarm before withdrawal, before recognition, and now without leadership empowered to negotiate the terms.

blocks.question: What ended the IRA's armed campaign in Northern Ireland?
options: British military decapitation of IRA leadership
The 1998 Good Friday Agreement with political guarantees
blocks.explanation: The IRA decommissioned weapons only after a binding political framework with US and Irish guarantors — not in response to military pressure.

timeline.heading: THE COLOR CODE
timeline.body: Hydrogen is classified by how it's made. Grey hydrogen comes from natural gas via steam methane reforming and emits ~10 tonnes of CO2 per tonne of H2. Blue captures those emissions. Green splits water using renewable electricity. Today over 95% of global hydrogen is grey.

blocks.text: The industry talks about *green*, *blue*, *grey*, *pink* (nuclear), and *turquoise* (methane pyrolysis) — but only **green** has a path to zero emissions, and only at electricity prices below ~$20/MWh.

timeline.heading: WHAT HYDROGEN IS ACTUALLY FOR
timeline.body: Most hydrogen today doesn't fuel anything — it's a chemical feedstock. Roughly half goes to ammonia (fertiliser), a third to oil refining, and the rest to methanol and steel. Decarbonising these uses matters more than hydrogen cars, which lost the passenger-vehicle race to batteries.

blocks.label: global hydrogen demand by use (~95 Mt/yr)

timeline.heading: THE ELECTROLYSER
timeline.body: An electrolyser splits water (H2O) into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity. Two dominant designs: alkaline (cheaper, mature, what China builds) and PEM (proton-exchange membrane — more flexible, responds faster to variable renewables, what Europe and the US favor). The cost gap is roughly 3-to-1 in China's favor.

timeline.heading: THE SOLAR PLAYBOOK
timeline.body: In 2010 Germany, Japan, and the US led solar panel manufacturing. By 2015 China controlled 70% of global production; today it's over 80%. The mechanism was state-directed capacity buildout, below-cost pricing, and Western firms going bankrupt one by one. Beijing is applying the same template to electrolysers.

events.label: China lists solar as strategic industry

timeline.heading: THE ELECTROLYSER LEAGUE
timeline.body: Chinese electrolyser makers — Longi, Sungrow, Envision — already ship units at roughly a third the price of European competitors like Nel, ITM Power, and Thyssenkrupp. The cost gap has widened, not narrowed, since 2022.

timeline.heading: WHY GREEN STAYS HARD
timeline.body: Green hydrogen costs ~3-5x grey hydrogen at current electricity prices. The breakeven requires either cheap renewables (under $20/MWh, which China increasingly has), a carbon price on grey (which most of Asia doesn't have), or subsidy (the EU and US route). Even at 1% green today, China builds the world's largest green hydrogen projects because its solar floor is already there.

blocks.question: Roughly how much of global hydrogen production today is 'green' (from renewable electrolysis)?
blocks.explanation: Despite a decade of headlines, green hydrogen remains under 1% of supply — the rest is made from fossil fuels, mostly natural gas.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'CUSTODY' ACTUALLY MEANS
timeline.body: In IAEA language, custody is a spectrum. At one end: seals and cameras on material that stays in country. At the other: physical removal to a third state. The 2015 JCPOA shipped 11 tonnes of low-enriched uranium to Russia. The current talks reportedly keep the stockpile on Iranian soil — closer to monitoring than disarmament.

blocks.text: The distinction matters: *in-country custody* is reversible within weeks. *Out-of-country custody* takes months to undo and creates a diplomatic incident if attempted.

timeline.heading: THE ENRICHMENT LADDER
timeline.body: Natural uranium is 0.7% U-235. Power reactors run on 3-5%. Research reactors use 20%. Weapons require 90%. Iran's stockpile sits at 60% — a level with no civilian justification but short of weapons-grade. The jump from 60% to 90% takes weeks, not years; most of the separation work is already done at 60%.

blocks.question: How much enrichment work remains between 60% U-235 and weapons-grade?
options: Most of it — 60% is still far from a bomb
A small fraction — most of the work is done by 60%
blocks.explanation: Separative work is logarithmic. Going from 0.7% to 60% does ~90% of the total work needed to reach 90%.

timeline.heading: WHY HORMUZ IS THE LEVER
timeline.body: Roughly a fifth of global oil and a third of seaborne LNG transits the strait. Iran cannot win a naval war there, but it can raise war-risk insurance premiums enough to spike crude within hours. The threat is the deal — reopening is what the US is paying for.

timeline.heading: PAKISTAN AS MEDIATOR
timeline.body: Islamabad sits in an unusual diplomatic slot: a Sunni nuclear power with working relations with Tehran, Riyadh, and Washington simultaneously. It mediated the 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement alongside Beijing. The choice of a Pakistani channel signals neither side wants Gulf Arab states inside the room.

timeline.heading: THE 60-DAY PATTERN
timeline.body: Short rolling extensions — 60 or 120 days — are how nuclear diplomacy buys time without political ratification. The 2013 Joint Plan of Action that preceded the JCPOA was structured the same way: a six-month interim deal extended twice before the final agreement. Extensions favor whoever benefits from the status quo freeze.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE MARKET THINKS
timeline.body: Prediction markets have been pricing a permanent deal in the single digits for months — the structural distrust on both sides is too deep for a comprehensive settlement. The relevant question is whether the short extensions keep stacking. The market is more bullish on the ceasefire rolling than on it ending in a treaty.

timeline.heading: WHAT RCEP ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: RCEP is the 15-member trade bloc signed in 2020 covering ASEAN plus China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand. It is the largest free-trade area by GDP, but it is shallow by design — a tariff schedule with rules of origin, not a deep integration treaty.

blocks.text: The bloc's signature trick is **regional cumulation**: a Vietnamese factory using Chinese inputs and Japanese components counts the whole product as RCEP-origin, qualifying for preferential tariffs across all 15 members. This is what makes the *supply chain*, not the tariff, the real product.

timeline.heading: THE MEMBERS
timeline.body: RCEP unites economies that don't otherwise sit in the same room — China and Japan have no bilateral FTA, Japan and South Korea have no bilateral FTA, but all three are inside RCEP. The bloc is the only forum where they grant each other preferential market access.

blocks.label: the 15 RCEP members
blocks.caption: ASEAN-10 plus China, Japan, Korea, Australia, New Zealand

timeline.heading: WHO ISN'T IN
timeline.body: India walked out in 2019 over fears of Chinese import surges and a refusal to open agriculture and dairy. The US was never a candidate — it had pulled out of the rival TPP in 2017. RCEP is therefore the Asian trade order minus its two largest democracies-by-population.

timeline.heading: WHY SHALLOW WAS THE POINT
timeline.body: RCEP's tariff cuts phase in over 20 years and leave sensitive sectors untouched. Services, digital trade, state-owned enterprises, labour, environment, and IP enforcement are largely absent — the deliberate price of getting China and the ASEAN least-developed countries inside the same tent. The 2027 review is the first scheduled chance to deepen the text.

blocks.question: Why does RCEP exclude binding rules on state-owned enterprises?
options: China refused to accept disciplines its SOE-heavy economy couldn't meet
ASEAN members blocked the chapter to protect Singaporean GLCs
The WTO already covers SOE rules so RCEP defers to it
blocks.explanation: The CPTPP's SOE chapter — drafted partly to constrain Chinese practices — is exactly what RCEP omits. That omission was the price of Beijing's participation.

timeline.heading: THE FRAGMENTATION BACKDROP
timeline.body: The IMF estimates a hard split of the global economy into US-aligned and China-aligned blocs would cost roughly 7% of world GDP over the long run — worse than any post-1945 trade shock. RCEP's upgrade question is whether Asia builds a genuinely integrated middle ground or remains a loose tariff club that each member hedges from.

timeline.heading: WHY ROMANIA
timeline.body: Romania became a cybercrime hub through a specific accident: heavy Soviet-era investment in technical universities, collapse of the post-1989 economy, and fiber infrastructure that arrived faster than wages rose. The town of Râmnicu Vâlcea earned the nickname Hackerville in the 2000s for its concentration of online fraud operations.

blocks.text: The Romanian word for the craft is **șmecherie** — cleverness, working the system. A cultural register the prosecutions inherited.

timeline.heading: THE EU FRAMEWORK
timeline.body: Since 2004, the European Arrest Warrant replaced traditional extradition between EU members with a near-automatic surrender procedure. A judge in Bucharest receives a warrant from a judge in Portland's circuit and must execute it within 60 days absent narrow exceptions. No diplomatic channel, no political review.

timeline.heading: THE DUAL CRIMINALITY RULE
timeline.body: Classical extradition treaties require that the alleged conduct be a crime in both countries. The EAW abolished this for 32 listed offenses including computer crime, fraud, and money laundering — the exact menu cyber prosecutors need.

timeline.heading: THE SAFE-HAVEN MAP
timeline.body: Russia, Belarus, China, Iran, and North Korea have no extradition treaty with the US. A Russian indicted in Manhattan can vacation in Dubai but not Düsseldorf; the FBI's most-wanted cyber list is effectively a no-fly list for the Schengen zone.

blocks.label: jurisdictions without US extradition
blocks.caption: travel for indicted hackers is a map of these gaps

timeline.heading: THE ARREST-IN-TRANSIT TRICK
timeline.body: US prosecutors routinely wait for non-extradition-treaty suspects to travel. Roman Seleznev was grabbed in the Maldives in 2014; Alexander Vinnik in Greece in 2017; Aleksei Burkov in Israel in 2015. The indictment is sealed for years; the arrest happens at a layover.

timeline.heading: THE BUDAPEST CONVENTION
timeline.body: The 2001 Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime is the only binding international treaty on the topic. 70+ countries have ratified, including the US. Russia has refused to sign, citing sovereignty concerns over cross-border data access — the exact provision that makes the treaty useful.

blocks.question: Which major country has refused to ratify the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime?
blocks.explanation: Russia objects to Article 32, which permits cross-border access to stored data without consent of the host state — viewing it as a sovereignty violation.

timeline.heading: THE CONQUEST
timeline.body: The Russian Empire absorbed the Kyrgyz lands in the 1860s-70s as part of the broader conquest of Turkestan. This was settler colonialism in the classical sense: Slavic peasants were resettled onto Kyrgyz pastoral lands, displacing nomadic herders from their summer grazing routes.

events.label: Russian conquest of northern Kyrgyz tribes
Soviet national delimitation creates Kyrgyz ASSR

timeline.heading: THE URKUN
timeline.body: In 1916, tsarist Russia conscripted Central Asians for rear-line labor in WWI, breaking earlier exemptions. The Kyrgyz revolt was crushed; up to a third of the Kyrgyz population was killed or fled across the Tien Shan into Qing China. Kyrgyz call this the Urkun — the exodus.

blocks.text: The **Urkun** of 1916 is to Kyrgyz historical memory what the *Holodomor* is to Ukrainian — a foundational atrocity whose naming itself is now contested.

timeline.heading: WHY THE WORD MATTERS
timeline.body: Moscow's official line is that Russia brought modernization — railways, literacy, industry — to a backward region, a civilizing mission narrative. Calling the period colonial reframes Russians as conquerors rather than developers, which undercuts the legitimacy of present-day Russian influence in the region.

timeline.heading: THE TEXTBOOK CHANNEL
timeline.body: Joint historian commissions are a standard Russian tool across the post-Soviet space — used with Kazakhstan, Belarus, Armenia, and previously Ukraine. They produce shared narratives that constrain how each country's schools can describe the imperial past.

blocks.label: states where Moscow has pushed joint history projects

timeline.heading: THE LEVERAGE
timeline.body: Roughly a million Kyrgyz citizens work in Russia; their remittances equal about a third of Kyrgyz GDP — one of the highest ratios in the world. Bishkek cannot easily refuse Moscow on symbolic matters when the household economy depends on Russian labor markets.

timeline.heading: THE QUIZ
timeline.body: Central Asia's relationship to the Russian and Soviet states is layered — and the dates of each layer matter.

blocks.question: When was Kyrgyzstan first incorporated into the Russian Empire?
options: 1936, when the Kyrgyz SSR was established
1991, in reverse — they joined the CIS
blocks.explanation: Tsarist Russia conquered the Kyrgyz lands in the 1860s-70s; the Soviet-era dates are about administrative reorganization within an already-incorporated territory.

timeline.heading: WHY THE IEA EXISTS
timeline.body: The International Energy Agency was created in 1974 in direct response to the OPEC oil embargo. Its founding mandate was coordinating strategic petroleum reserves among consumer nations — 90 days of net imports, releasable in concert during a supply shock.

blocks.text: The IEA was built by the **OECD** as a consumers' cartel to counter a producers' cartel. Its analytical authority came later; the **strategic reserve** coordination role came first.

timeline.heading: THE HORMUZ NUMBER
timeline.body: Roughly 21 million barrels per day — about one-fifth of global oil consumption — pass through a shipping channel 3 km wide on each side. There is no real alternative route for most of it; Saudi and Emirati bypass pipelines can reroute perhaps a third of Gulf exports, leaving the rest stranded.

timeline.heading: WHY COAL COMES BACK FIRST
timeline.body: In an oil or gas shock, coal is the swing fuel of last resort. It is stockpilable, transportable by rail rather than pipeline, and burns in plants that exist on every continent. Germany did this in 2022 after Nord Stream; Japan did it after Fukushima; the pattern is structural, not ideological.

timeline.heading: THE INVESTMENT GAP
timeline.body: Oil and gas projects take 5–10 years from sanction to first production. When upstream capex collapses for three consecutive years, the supply gap shows up a decade later — long after the political crisis that caused the underinvestment has passed. Today's $500bn floor is shaping the 2032–2035 supply curve.

blocks.label: Annual upstream oil & gas investment ($bn, approx.)

timeline.heading: THE 1973 TEMPLATE
timeline.body: The first oil shock quadrupled crude prices in six months and ended the postwar economic order. It birthed not only the IEA but also fuel-economy standards, the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, French nuclear buildout, and Japan's pivot to efficiency. Every energy crisis since has been measured against it.

events.label: Nord Stream sabotage; Europe gas crisis

timeline.heading: WHAT 'ENERGY SECURITY' MEANS
timeline.body: Energy security is the availability of energy at affordable prices, with tolerable risk of disruption. It rests on four pillars: diversity of supply, reliability of infrastructure, affordability, and environmental acceptability. A crisis is when two or more pillars fail at once.

blocks.question: Which event prompted the founding of the International Energy Agency?
blocks.explanation: The IEA was established in 1974 by OECD members to coordinate responses to the 1973-74 Arab oil embargo, which quadrupled crude prices.

timeline.heading: WHY INTERIM DEALS EXIST
timeline.body: Full trade agreements take years — the US-Korea FTA took four years to negotiate and another four to ratify. Interim deals lock in tariff terms while the legal text catches up, giving exporters pricing certainty before lawyers finish drafting.

blocks.text: The distinction matters: a **full FTA** requires congressional approval under Trade Promotion Authority, but an **executive tariff arrangement** can be set unilaterally by the President under Section 232 or IEEPA — no Senate vote required.

timeline.heading: INDIA'S TARIFF WALL
timeline.body: India has historically been one of the most protectionist large economies. Its simple average applied tariff sits near 17%, against the US at roughly 3.4% and the EU at 5%. The asymmetry is why every US administration since Clinton has pushed for reciprocity — and why India has resisted.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'ECONOMIC SECURITY ALIGNMENT' MEANS
timeline.body: It is the post-2022 vocabulary for tying trade access to geopolitical posture — export controls on China-bound tech, restrictions on Russian oil intermediation, semiconductor supply-chain commitments. The text reads as commerce; the substance is alignment.

blocks.text: The framework traces to the 2022 *CHIPS and Science Act* and the *Indo-Pacific Economic Framework* — both designed to make market access conditional on **friend-shoring** rather than open trade on WTO most-favored-nation terms.

timeline.heading: THE GSP PRECEDENT
timeline.body: India was the largest beneficiary of the US Generalized System of Preferences — duty-free access on ~$6bn of exports — until Trump revoked it in 2019 over dairy and medical-device market access. The revocation took 11 months of failed talks; restoration has never happened.

timeline.heading: WHO TRADES WHAT
timeline.body: India runs a goods surplus with the US of roughly $45bn — pharma generics, gems, textiles, and software services flow west; aircraft, LNG, almonds, and crude flow east. The composition matters: pharma is the politically protected category on both sides.

timeline.heading: THE JULY 24 DEADLINE
timeline.body: The flat 10% baseline tariff applies to all US trading partners while bilateral deals are negotiated. When it expires, country-specific 'reciprocal' rates snap back — for India that rate was set at 26% in April 2025. The 18% interim figure is the negotiated discount.

blocks.question: What happens to US tariffs on Indian goods if no deal is reached by July 24?
options: They fall to zero under WTO rules
They stay at the flat 10% baseline
They snap to the 26% reciprocal rate set in April 2025
They rise to match India's average tariff
blocks.explanation: The 10% flat tariff is a pause on the country-specific reciprocal rates announced in April 2025; expiry restores India's assigned 26% rate.

timeline.heading: WHY KUWAIT
timeline.body: Kuwait hosts Ali Al Salem Air Base and Camp Arifjan — the logistics spine for US Central Command since 1991. Striking Kuwait is not striking a peripheral ally; it is striking the platform that makes American Gulf power projection possible.

blocks.label: the US footprint Iran can reach

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988, Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. The US responded with Operation Earnest Will — reflagging Kuwaiti tankers under the American flag and escorting them with warships. It was the largest naval convoy operation since WWII, and it pulled Washington directly into the war.

blocks.text: We will fight the United States until the complete elimination of its influence in the region.
blocks.speaker: Ayatollah Khomeini, on the Tanker War

timeline.heading: THE IRGC, NOT THE ARMY
timeline.body: Iran has two parallel militaries. The Artesh is the conventional army inherited from the Shah; the **IRGC** (Pasdaran) is the post-1979 revolutionary force that answers directly to the Supreme Leader. The IRGC controls the ballistic missile program, the drone fleet, and the Quds Force proxies — every tool Iran uses to project outside its borders.

blocks.text: The IRGC is not a service branch — it is a parallel state with its own navy, air arm, intelligence wing, and an industrial empire (*Khatam al-Anbiya*) estimated at a double-digit share of Iranian GDP.

timeline.heading: BANDAR ABBAS
timeline.body: Bandar Abbas is the headquarters of the IRGC Navy and the principal port for the Iranian regular navy. It sits at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz, hosts Iran's submarine pens, and is the launch point for the small-boat swarms Iran has practiced against US warships for two decades. Striking it is striking the operational hub of Iran's Gulf strategy.

timeline.heading: THE CHOKEPOINT NEXT DOOR
timeline.body: Roughly 21 million barrels per day — about a fifth of global oil consumption — pass through the Strait of Hormuz, in shipping lanes just 3 km wide on the Iranian side. Every escalation step is priced through that channel: insurance war-risk premiums spike before any mine is laid.

blocks.metric: Crude oil passing through global chokepoints

timeline.heading: KUWAIT'S DILEMMA
timeline.body: Kuwait was invaded by Iraq in 1990 and liberated by a US-led coalition staging from its soil. The 1991 defense agreement that followed made Kuwait one of the most US-dependent states in the Gulf — but Kuwait also shares the Dorra/Arash gas field with Iran and has no strategic depth. It cannot afford either patron's exit.

blocks.question: What share of Kuwait's freshwater comes from desalination?
blocks.explanation: Kuwait has no rivers and almost no aquifers — desalination plants on the Gulf coast supply over 90% of drinking water, and they are within Iranian missile range.

timeline.heading: THE ESCALATION LADDER
timeline.body: Iran's doctrine is calibrated retaliation: respond visibly enough to restore deterrence, but not so hard that it triggers a regime-ending US response. The 2020 Ain al-Asad strike after the Soleimani killing was the template — telegraphed, sized to wound facilities rather than personnel, framed as 'concluded' the next morning.

2026-05-28-iran-strikes-us-airbase-kuwai.label: Iran, Kuwait & the Gulf Escalation Ladder

timeline.heading: THE PATTERN
timeline.body: Kenya has had a recurring epidemic of fatal boarding school fires for over three decades. The 2001 Kyanguli Secondary fire killed 67 boys; the 1998 Bombolulu Girls fire killed 26. Investigations repeatedly find the same proximate cause: locked dormitory doors.

timeline.heading: WHY DOORS LOCK
timeline.body: Kenyan boarding schools — a colonial-era inheritance still housing roughly a million students — lock dormitories at night to prevent unauthorized exits, theft between students, and intrusion. The discipline logic is older than the fire codes; the lock survives every reform cycle.

blocks.text: After Kyanguli, the Ministry of Education issued the **2008 Safety Standards Manual** mandating unlocked emergency exits and fire drills every term. Enforcement is delegated to school heads — the same authority that wants the doors locked.

timeline.heading: THE ARSON FACTOR
timeline.body: A 2018 government taskforce found that the majority of Kenyan school fires are set by students themselves — typically before national exams or after disciplinary crackdowns. The pattern is so established that the Ministry runs a dedicated arson-prevention curriculum. This reframes "fire safety" from accident-prevention to a question about adolescent agency inside coercive institutions.

timeline.heading: THE FLASHOVER WINDOW
timeline.body: A dormitory fire reaches flashover — the point at which every combustible surface ignites simultaneously — in roughly 3 to 5 minutes once curtains and bedding catch.
