timeline.body: A fishery is a classic commons: no one owns the fish in the open ocean, so each boat's rational move is to catch as much as possible before a rival does. Left alone, this drives stocks toward collapse — the cost of overfishing is shared by all, but the catch belongs to whoever lands it first.

blocks.text: Economists call this the *tragedy of the commons*. The fish that recover a stock are the ones left in the water — but no single fleet has an incentive to leave them, because a competitor will simply take them instead.

timeline.heading: WHY SUBSIDIES MAKE IT WORSE
timeline.body: Most fishing fleets would lose money on distant, depleted grounds if they paid full costs. Government subsidies — above all cheap fuel — keep uneconomic boats at sea, sustaining fishing pressure that would otherwise stop on its own. The treaty's target is this exact category.

blocks.text: The deal bans *capacity-enhancing* subsidies — fuel, vessel construction, gear — that build bigger fleets, while leaving room for support that doesn't expand catch. Fuel subsidies alone are the single largest harmful category worldwide.

timeline.heading: WHO PAYS THE FLEETS
timeline.body: Global harmful fisheries subsidies run to roughly $22 billion a year, and they are highly concentrated. A handful of states account for most of it, with China far in front of the rest.

timeline.heading: THE DISTANT-WATER FLEET
timeline.body: The treaty matters most for distant-water fishing — fleets that leave home waters to work the high seas and other nations' coasts. One country dominates this category by an order of magnitude, which is why enforcement against distant fleets is the whole point of the deal.

blocks.question: Which country operates the world's largest distant-water fishing fleet?
blocks.explanation: China's distant-water fleet numbers in the thousands of vessels — roughly an order of magnitude larger than any rival.

timeline.heading: A TWENTY-YEAR NEGOTIATION
timeline.body: This is the WTO's first agreement with an environmental sustainability goal at its core, and it took two decades. Talks launched in the Doha Round in 2001, failed repeatedly, and only produced a text at the 2022 ministerial in Geneva.

blocks.label: the road to a fish deal

timeline.heading: WHY THE HOLDOUTS HOLD OUT
timeline.body: WTO agreements take effect only when two-thirds of the membership formally deposit acceptance — so a few large states can stall a treaty most others have signed. India and Indonesia invoke 'special and differential treatment,' arguing developing nations and small-scale fishers shouldn't face the same caps as industrial distant-water powers; the US faces its own domestic ratification politics.

blocks.text: The sticking point is **special and differential treatment** — carve-outs for poorer members. India argues its millions of subsistence fishers are nothing like China's industrial high-seas fleet, and shouldn't be disciplined by the same rule.

timeline.heading: THE FRAGMENTATION PARADOX
timeline.body: Negotiating with an armed group doesn't always shrink it — it can shatter it. When the FARC signed in 2016, the units that rejected the deal kept their guns, their coca, and their territory, becoming 'dissidents.' Petro's 'Total Peace' opened parallel talks with everyone at once, which gave each faction an incentive to splinter and claim its own seat at the table.

blocks.text: Petro's doctrine, *Paz Total* ('Total Peace'), tried to negotiate with all armed groups simultaneously — a reversal of the one-group-at-a-time approach that produced the 2016 accord.

timeline.heading: WHY THE WAR NEVER ENDS
timeline.body: The fighting is funded by the world's largest cocaine supply. Colombia produces well over half the planet's cocaine, and eradicating coca in one region just pushes cultivation to another — the 'balloon effect.' As long as the coca rent exists, whoever controls the land can pay fighters, so demobilizing one group only frees the turf for the next.

timeline.heading: THE 2016 BARGAIN
timeline.body: The FARC began in 1964 as a peasant Marxist insurgency and grew into a state-within-a-state. The 2016 accord — which won President Santos the Nobel Peace Prize — demobilized roughly 13,000 fighters in exchange for transitional justice and political seats. The deal closed the war's largest front but left the drug economy and the smaller ELN untouched.

timeline.heading: NOT ONE ENEMY BUT MANY
timeline.body: The 27,000 figure isn't one army — it's a fractured market. The ELN remains an ideological holdout that never disarmed; FARC dissidents reject the 2016 deal; and the Gulf Clan (Clan del Golfo) is a profit-driven successor to the old right-wing paramilitaries. They fight each other as often as the state, for coca corridors and mining rents.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY OF COCA
timeline.body: Production clusters on borders and coasts — where the state is thinnest and the export routes shortest. The Catatumbo region hugs Venezuela; Nariño and Putumayo run to Ecuador and the Pacific. Control of these frontier zones, not the capital, is what the armed groups actually fight over.

blocks.label: coca frontier zones
blocks.caption: Cultivation clusters on borders where the state is weakest.

timeline.heading: WHO PAID FOR THE WAR ON SUPPLY
timeline.body: Plan Colombia, launched in 2000, sent roughly $10 billion in mostly military and counter-narcotics aid from Washington. It weakened the FARC militarily and is credited with helping force them to the table — but coca acreage today is near record highs, a reminder that supply-side enforcement rarely shrinks a market built on global demand.

blocks.question: What happens to coca cultivation when one growing region is aggressively eradicated?
options: It shifts to another region — the 'balloon effect'
Farmers switch permanently to legal crops
Prices fall and the trade dies out
blocks.explanation: Squeezing supply in one area pushes cultivation elsewhere; as long as global demand and the price premium hold, the balloon just bulges somewhere new.

timeline.heading: THE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: No international flight can legally discharge passengers or cargo without federal customs officers on site to inspect them. A state cannot supply its own — immigration and customs are exclusively federal. Pull the officers and the airport's international terminal goes dark even though no flight has been banned and no airspace closed. The closure is administrative, not aerial.

blocks.question: What would actually halt international flights at Newark under this threat?
options: Withdrawing federal customs officers who clear arrivals
Closing the airspace over New Jersey
blocks.explanation: Only federal CBP officers can admit international arrivals; remove them and flights have nowhere to legally land, without any formal ban.

timeline.heading: THE ANTI-COMMANDEERING DOCTRINE
timeline.body: Washington cannot order New Jersey to enforce federal immigration law. In Printz v. United States (1997) the Supreme Court held that the federal government may not conscript state or local officials into federal programs. This doctrine — rooted in the Tenth Amendment — is the legal foundation on which every 'sanctuary' policy rests.

blocks.text: The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.
blocks.speaker: US Constitution, Tenth Amendment

timeline.heading: THE INVERSE LEVER
timeline.body: Because it cannot command the state, Washington threatens to withdraw a federal service the state depends on. But coercion has limits too: in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) the Court struck down a funding threat so severe it amounted to 'a gun to the head' of states. The line between persuasion and unconstitutional coercion is exactly what a Newark threat would test.

blocks.text: The maneuver inverts the usual fight: instead of *commandeering* the state, the threat is to **subtract** a service — the same lever, run in reverse.

timeline.heading: WHY NEWARK IS LEVERAGE
timeline.body: Newark is one of the busiest international gateways in the United States — a primary trans-Atlantic hub feeding the New York metro. Choking it ripples through global schedules, not just New Jersey. And the timing is pointed: the World Cup final is set for nearby MetLife Stadium on July 19, when international arrivals peak.

timeline.heading: THE SHUTDOWN PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Air traffic is the most politically explosive pressure point in the federal apparatus. The 35-day 2018–19 shutdown collapsed within hours of customs and air-traffic staffing shortages triggering ground stops at LaGuardia and Newark — proof that disrupted flights, more than missed paychecks, force a resolution.

blocks.text: The 2019 shutdown ended the *same afternoon* a staffing-driven ground stop hit **LaGuardia** — the disruption lasted hours, the political surrender was immediate.

timeline.heading: WHAT A TOBA IS
timeline.body: A toba is not a well or a spring — it is a shallow clay-lined depression scraped to catch and hold monsoon runoff. It taps no aquifer; it stores only the rain that falls on it. When the monsoon fails, there is no second source to fall back on. The entire freshwater economy of Cholistan rests on whether the sky delivers in July and August.

blocks.text: The herders call these ponds *tobas*. A full toba can water a herd for months; an empty one offers nothing at all — there is no half-measure, no trickle to ration. The system is **binary**: wet or dead.

timeline.heading: THE GROUNDWATER TRAP
timeline.body: Cholistan does sit over groundwater — but most of it is brackish to saline, undrinkable for people and harmful to livestock. This is why drilling more wells is not the obvious fix it seems: the desert is not short of water underground, it is short of fresh water. Surface rain capture is the only viable source, which is exactly why the tobas can never be fully replaced by tankers or boreholes.

timeline.heading: THE LOST RIVER BENEATH THE SAND
timeline.body: Cholistan was not always desert. The Ghaggar-Hakra river — which some scholars identify with the Saraswati of ancient texts — once flowed through it. Hundreds of Bronze Age settlement mounds line its dry bed, a sister-civilization to the Indus cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. When the river shifted and died around 1900 BCE, the towns were abandoned and the land reverted to desert. Today's herders live in the ruins of a place that a river once made green.

blocks.label: Cholistan and the Thar desert belt
blocks.caption: The dry Hakra bed runs through Cholistan into the Thar

timeline.heading: MIGRATION AS THE OLD ANSWER
timeline.body: Seasonal movement of herds toward water and pasture — transhumance — is not a sign of collapse here; it is the design. Cholistani pastoralists have always moved between the desert in the wet season and the irrigated canal lands toward the Indus when the tobas fail. The crisis is not that they migrate, but that the dry-season refuge is shrinking and the failures are coming more often.

blocks.question: Why can't water tankers permanently solve Cholistan's shortage?
options: The roads are too poor for trucks
Tankers reach only a fraction of scattered settlements, and tobas refill only with monsoon rain
Tanker water is too expensive for herders
blocks.explanation: Settlements are too dispersed for tankers to cover, and the underlying source — monsoon-fed ponds — only replenishes when the rains come.

timeline.heading: WHY THE MONSOON IS THE WHOLE STORY
timeline.body: A region with no perennial river and no fresh aquifer has zero buffer against a weak monsoon. In wetter climates a bad rain year is absorbed by reservoirs, rivers, and groundwater; in Cholistan the rainfall total for two months is, almost directly, the year's drinking water. That is what makes it one of the most sensitive places on earth to small shifts in monsoon timing and strength.

timeline.heading: THE HIGH COMMAND
timeline.body: Congress chief ministers do not control their own tenure. Since Indira Gandhi dismantled the party's regional power brokers in the late 1960s, state leaders serve at the pleasure of a Delhi 'high command' — a handful of national leaders who pick, transfer, and remove CMs. That is why a Karnataka swearing-in waits on a party meeting in the capital.

timeline.heading: THE ROTATION DEAL
timeline.body: When two rivals both have a claim, the high command's classic fix is an unwritten power-sharing pact: one takes the chair first, the other is promised the back half of the term. These deals are rarely honored cleanly — the incumbent always has reasons to stay, and the rival has every incentive to collect.

timeline.heading: WHY FOUR DEPUTIES
timeline.body: India's Constitution never mentions a 'deputy chief minister' — the post carries no extra constitutional power, only protocol and prestige. That is precisely why it is useful: a party can mint several of them to placate competing factions without splitting real authority.

blocks.text: A *deputy chief minister* is a **purely political title** — the Supreme Court has noted it confers no powers beyond those of an ordinary cabinet minister. It exists to manage egos, not to govern.

blocks.question: What does India's Constitution say about the office of 'deputy chief minister'?
options: It is a constitutional post with defined succession powers
It is not mentioned at all — it carries no extra legal authority
It automatically becomes acting CM if the CM resigns
blocks.explanation: The title is a political convenience; a deputy CM is legally just another cabinet minister with no guaranteed succession.

timeline.heading: THE CASTE ARITHMETIC
timeline.body: The rivalry maps onto caste blocs. Siddaramaiah built his base on AHINDA — a coalition of minorities, backward classes and Dalits — while Shivakumar draws on the dominant Vokkaliga community of southern Karnataka. Congress cannot hand the state to one bloc without compensating the other.

blocks.text: *AHINDA* is a Kannada acronym for **minorities, backward classes, and Dalits** — Siddaramaiah's signature vote bank, set against Shivakumar's **Vokkaliga** landholding base.

timeline.heading: THE GOVERNOR'S ROLE
timeline.body: A state governor is appointed by the central government, not elected. Their job is largely ceremonial — but accepting a resignation and inviting the next leader to form a government is a real lever, and in contested transitions the governor's timing can decide who gets the first move.

timeline.heading: WHAT ARTICLE 5 ACTUALLY SAYS
timeline.body: The North Atlantic Treaty's collective-defense clause treats an attack on one member as an attack on all — but it never defines what counts as an 'armed attack,' and each member decides for itself what response is 'necessary.' The vagueness is deliberate: it lets allies signal solidarity without committing in advance to war.

blocks.text: an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all
blocks.speaker: North Atlantic Treaty, Article 5

timeline.heading: INVOKED EXACTLY ONCE
timeline.body: In 76 years NATO has triggered Article 5 a single time — by the United States after September 11, 2001. Not the Cold War, not Crimea, not the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The bar for invocation is political will, not the severity of the incident.

blocks.question: How many times has NATO invoked Article 5 in its history?
blocks.explanation: The only Article 5 invocation came after 9/11 — and ironically it was the US, the alliance's protector, that called it in.

timeline.heading: THE ARTICLE 4 OFF-RAMP
timeline.body: When members feel threatened but don't want to trigger collective defense, they reach for Article 4 — consultations. It commits NATO to nothing but a meeting. Poland, the Baltics, and Romania have used Article 4 repeatedly to register alarm over Russian strikes without forcing the alliance toward escalation.

timeline.heading: WHY GALAȚI
timeline.body: Galați sits on the Danube where Romania, Moldova, and Ukraine nearly meet. Ukraine's river ports of Izmail and Reni — repeatedly hit by Russian drones since the Black Sea grain corridor collapsed — lie just across the water. A drone overshooting those targets by a few kilometers lands in NATO territory.

blocks.label: the Danube tripoint
blocks.caption: Ukraine's Danube ports sit within a few km of NATO soil

timeline.heading: WHY CHEAP DRONES STRAY
timeline.body: The Iranian-designed Shahed-136 — built in Russia as the Geran-2 — navigates by satellite and inertial guidance, not a live pilot. Jamming, signal loss, or a programming error sends it drifting off course with no human to recall it. At a few tens of thousands of dollars each, they are launched in swarms precisely because losing some is acceptable.

blocks.text: The **Shahed-136** flies as a *loitering munition* — it cannot be steered home once airborne, so a knocked-out GPS link doesn't abort the flight, it just makes the impact point random.

timeline.heading: THE POLAND PRECEDENT
timeline.body: In November 2022 a missile killed two people in Przewodów, Poland — the first NATO deaths of the war. Investigators concluded it was a stray Ukrainian air-defense interceptor, not a Russian strike. NATO declined to treat it as an attack at all, establishing the working rule: spillover from the war, even lethal, does not automatically cross the Article 5 line.

blocks.label: the alliance and its red lines

timeline.heading: WHAT THE LABEL ACTUALLY DOES
timeline.body: A Foreign Terrorist Organization designation under Section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act is signed by the Secretary of State alone, with no court involved. Its real bite is not the gang — it is the 'material support' statute, which criminalizes anyone, anywhere, who knowingly handles the group's money or assets, and exposes correspondent banks to US secondary sanctions.

blocks.text: The key phrase is *material support* — under **18 U.S.C. §2339B** it covers funds, services, even expert advice, and carries up to 20 years. It is the statute that turns a designation into a global enforcement tool, not just a label.

timeline.heading: BORN IN A MASSACRE
timeline.body: The Primeiro Comando da Capital was founded in 1993 inside São Paulo's prison system, organized explicitly as a response to the 1992 Carandiru massacre, when military police killed 111 inmates while suppressing a riot. A grievance born behind bars became Brazil's largest criminal network, dominant in cocaine logistics across the southern cone.

blocks.question: What event directly preceded the founding of the PCC?
blocks.explanation: The 1992 killing of 111 inmates at Carandiru became the founding grievance the PCC organized around the following year.

timeline.heading: THE DICTATORSHIP'S ACCIDENT
timeline.body: Comando Vermelho formed in the late 1970s in Rio's prisons, where the military dictatorship jailed ordinary criminals alongside leftist political prisoners. The criminals absorbed the guerrillas' cell structure, discipline, and collective-finance model — the state inadvertently trained its own underworld in clandestine organization.

timeline.heading: WHY BRAZIL HEARS 'INTERVENTION'
timeline.body: In 2025 Washington designated several Latin American cartels — Tren de Aragua, MS-13, Sinaloa, CJNG — as terrorist organizations, and US officials openly floated military strikes on the basis of those labels. Lula's government reads the Brazilian designation through that precedent: not as a financial tool but as legal scaffolding for action inside a sovereign state.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY OF THE TRADE
timeline.body: The PCC's power rests on controlling cocaine flow from Bolivia and Paraguay through Brazilian ports toward Europe; Comando Vermelho dominates Rio. The two syndicates are headquartered a few hundred kilometers apart but project across a continental supply chain.

timeline.heading: THE LONG ARC
timeline.body: Both groups grew from carceral grievances into transnational enterprises over four decades. The designation is the latest move in a long pattern of treating criminal economies as security threats.

events.label: Comando Vermelho forms in Rio prisons
PCC paralyzes São Paulo in coordinated attacks
US designates Latin cartels as FTOs

timeline.heading: THE FALSE-POSITIVE FLOOD
timeline.body: Bank anti-money-laundering systems are tuned to miss nothing, so they flag almost everything: industry estimates put false-positive rates above 90%. Each alert is cleared by a human analyst. The CEO's 'lower-value human capital' jab describes the tens of thousands of people paid to dismiss alarms a rule generated and a machine could close.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of alerts from bank transaction-monitoring systems turn out to be false positives?
blocks.explanation: Rules are set to over-flag rather than risk a missed launderer, so the vast majority of alerts are noise cleared by human reviewers.

timeline.heading: THE ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: A defender has to catch every laundering route; an attacker needs one that works. Generative models hand the attacker scale — synthetic identities, deepfake KYC selfies, and personalized scam scripts produced for pennies — while the bank's detection still runs on rules written for a slower era. Automation favors the side that only needs to win once.

timeline.heading: WHY 'COMPLIANCE' MEANS PAPERWORK, NOT OUTCOMES
timeline.body: Under the US Bank Secrecy Act and its global imitators, a bank discharges its duty by filing a Suspicious Activity Report — not by stopping the crime. This breeds 'defensive filing': flood regulators with reports so that, whatever happens, the box was ticked. AI that auto-generates compliant-looking SARs satisfies the letter of the rule while the fraud sails through.

blocks.text: The key term is the **SAR** (Suspicious Activity Report). Banks practice *defensive filing* — over-reporting to transfer liability, not to catch criminals.

timeline.heading: WHAT MISSING IT COSTS
timeline.body: AML failures are punished with landmark fines, which is why banks over-invest in process. BNP Paribas paid nearly $9bn in 2014 for sanctions breaches; Standard Chartered itself has been fined repeatedly. The penalties dwarf the cost of any single compliance team, which is exactly why the work was never automated away before now.

timeline.heading: THE UNRESOLVED QUESTION
timeline.body: When an AI compliance system clears an AI-generated fraud, no legal regime yet says who is accountable — the bank that deployed the model, the vendor that built it, or no one. Liability law assumes a negligent human in the loop. Remove the human from both attack and defense, and the chain of responsibility has a missing link the courts have not yet filled.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE METRIC MEASURES
timeline.body: Carbon intensity is emissions divided by GDP — tonnes of CO2 per dollar of output. It can fall every single year while the total tonnage in the atmosphere keeps climbing, because the denominator is growing too.

blocks.text: The distinction is *relative* decoupling (emissions grow slower than GDP) versus *absolute* decoupling (emissions actually fall). An intensity target only ever promises the first.

timeline.heading: WHY IT LETS EMISSIONS RISE
timeline.body: If the economy grows 5% and intensity improves 4%, total emissions still rise about 1%. The metric rewards efficiency gains even as the physical volume of carbon released increases — which is why a country can claim climate progress and burn more coal in the same year.

timeline.heading: THE COPENHAGEN CHOICE
timeline.body: China first pledged an intensity target — not an absolute cap — at the 2009 Copenhagen summit, and carried that framing into its Paris commitments. The 2020 'dual carbon' pledge added dates: peak emissions before 2030, neutrality by 2060.

timeline.heading: THE OTHER MODEL
timeline.body: The EU does the opposite: its Emissions Trading System sets an absolute cap on tonnage and shrinks it yearly. A capped system guarantees the volume falls; an intensity system only guarantees the ratio falls. The June overcapacity dispute is partly this clash of accounting philosophies.

timeline.heading: THE TEST THAT MATTERS
timeline.body: The real question is not whether intensity falls — it almost always does as economies modernize — but whether absolute emissions peak and then decline. Britain, Germany, and the US have achieved absolute decoupling; the open question is when China's curve bends down.

blocks.question: A country's carbon intensity drops 4% while GDP grows 5%. What happens to its total emissions?
blocks.explanation: Growth (5%) outpaces the intensity improvement (4%), so absolute emissions still climb roughly 1% — the gap intensity targets allow.

timeline.heading: THE MEMORY WALL
timeline.body: An AI accelerator's GPU cores can compute far faster than memory can feed them data. The chip spends most cycles waiting for weights to arrive, not multiplying. This gap — not raw FLOPS — is the binding constraint, and it is what HBM exists to close.

blocks.question: What is the binding bottleneck in modern AI accelerators?
options: Memory bandwidth — feeding data to the cores fast enough
Electricity cost of the data center
The price of the silicon wafer
blocks.explanation: Cores idle waiting for data; bandwidth into and out of memory is what caps real-world throughput, which is why HBM commands a premium.

timeline.heading: HOW HBM WORKS
timeline.body: High Bandwidth Memory stacks DRAM dies vertically and wires them together with through-silicon vias — copper columns drilled straight through the chips. Twelve layers in a single stack sit millimeters from the GPU, trading the long, slow trip to ordinary memory for a short, massively parallel one.

blocks.text: The vertical wiring is the trick: **through-silicon vias** (TSVs) replace thousands of slow edge pins with short vertical channels, multiplying bandwidth without growing the chip's footprint.

timeline.heading: THE OLIGOPOLY
timeline.body: Only three firms on earth can make HBM at scale: SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron. Two of the three are South Korean, which is why Seoul effectively controls the supply of the scarcest input in the AI buildout.

timeline.heading: WHY HBM WINS THE WAFER
timeline.body: An HBM stack uses several times the wafer area of commodity DRAM for the same gigabyte, but its margins run 5–10× higher. Every wafer a fab assigns to HBM is a wafer not making the DDR5 that phones, laptops, and cars depend on — which is how an AI memory boom quietly raises the price of consumer memory.

blocks.text: This is the same dynamic that has gutted commodity supply before: fabs chase margin, so an HBM order doesn't just sell a chip — it *removes* capacity from everything cheaper.

timeline.heading: QUALIFICATION IS THE REAL GATE
timeline.body: Shipping samples is not a contract. Nvidia runs each new HBM through months of qualification — thermal cycling, yield validation, power-integrity testing — before it converts to mass-production orders. A supplier can lead on the spec sheet and still lose the order if its stacks fail to qualify, which is why Samsung's sample shipment is a starting line, not a finish.

timeline.heading: THE CONFOUNDER PROBLEM
timeline.body: People who take aspirin daily tend to be older, sicker, and under medical supervision — exactly the people prone to macular degeneration anyway. For decades, every observational link between aspirin and the retina drowned in this kind of confounding: you can never measure all the reasons a person ended up on the drug.

timeline.heading: THE GENETIC INSTRUMENT
timeline.body: Mendelian randomization sidesteps the problem with a loophole: your genes are dealt at conception, effectively at random. If a genetic variant mimics aspirin's effect on the body, and people carrying it also get more macular degeneration, no lifestyle confounder can explain it — your alleles didn't choose your habits. The technique was named in 1986 but only became powerful once genome-wide studies supplied thousands of variants to use as instruments.

blocks.question: Why can Mendelian randomization claim causation where observational studies can't?
options: It uses far larger sample sizes
Genes are assigned at conception, before any confounder can act
It runs an actual randomized drug trial
It corrects for confounders statistically after the fact
blocks.explanation: Because alleles are fixed at conception and unrelated to later lifestyle, a gene-outcome link can't be explained by confounders the way a behavior-outcome link can.

timeline.heading: FULLY MEDIATED
timeline.body: The striking finding isn't just that aspirin raises the risk — it's that the entire effect runs through lipids. Aspirin's association with lower LDL cholesterol accounts for all of the retinal risk; strip out the lipid change and no direct aspirin-to-retina pathway survives. The drug is a passenger, not the driver.

timeline.heading: HOW ASPIRIN WORKS
timeline.body: Aspirin irreversibly blocks the COX enzymes, shutting down the prostaglandins behind pain, fever, and clotting. That same chemistry quietly nudges lipid metabolism — the side door through which, this study argues, the retinal risk enters.

blocks.text: Aspirin's *irreversible* block of **COX-1** is why a single low dose thins the blood for a platelet's entire ~10-day life — platelets can't make new enzyme.

timeline.heading: DRY VERSUS WET
timeline.body: Macular degeneration comes in two forms. The dry form, by far the more common, is a slow thinning and accumulation of debris (drusen) under the retina. The wet form, where leaky new blood vessels grow, is rarer but causes most of the sudden, severe vision loss. The study's open question is whether aspirin touches the wet form at all.

timeline.heading: WHAT IT CAN'T TELL YOU
timeline.body: Mendelian randomization measures the effect of a lifetime of slightly altered biology, not the effect of starting or stopping a pill. So it cannot say whether quitting aspirin reverses the risk — a small genetic nudge from birth and a deliberate mid-life intervention are not the same experiment.

timeline.heading: THE MISSION CLASS
timeline.body: Scout is ESA's smallest science class, capped near €35m per mission and meant to fly within three years. The cap is the point: a hard ceiling forces engineers to design to cost rather than design to ambition, which is what keeps the schedule short.

timeline.heading: THE FLAGSHIP TRAP
timeline.body: Big space missions overrun because requirements ratchet up during a decade of development, each addition justified on its own but compounding into billions. Once a flagship is too expensive to cancel, every delay is cheaper to absorb than to fight — so delays accumulate.

timeline.heading: WHY EARTH OBSERVATION GOT CHEAP
timeline.body: Cheap small missions only became possible once commercial off-the-shelf electronics, miniaturized sensors, and rideshare launch slots collapsed the cost of getting a working instrument into orbit. A capability that once required a bus-sized satellite now fits on a platform a startup could build.

blocks.text: The pivot is from *design-to-requirement* — build whatever the science demands, then find the money — to **design-to-cost**: fix the budget first, then take the best science that fits inside it.

timeline.heading: WHO BUILDS WHAT
timeline.body: ESA contracts are governed by geographical return — the principle that each member state wins industrial work roughly proportional to the money it pays in. This is why the Industrial Policy Committee, not the scientists, signs off: the committee balances the contracts across countries before anything is built.

blocks.text: The doctrine is called ***juste retour*** ("fair return"). It is what makes ESA politically stable across 22 members — and what makes its procurement slower and pricier than a single-government agency like NASA.

timeline.heading: THE TRADEOFF
timeline.body: Small-fast missions trade redundancy for speed. A flagship carries backup systems and years of testing so it cannot fail; a Scout accepts that a cheap mission can be lost and simply flown again. The risk model, not the technology, is what changes.

blocks.question: Why does ESA's Industrial Policy Committee — not its scientists — approve mission contracts?
options: To balance industrial work across member states by their contributions
Because scientists lack security clearance for launch data
To negotiate the launch price with rocket providers
Because EU law requires civilian oversight of all spacecraft
blocks.explanation: Under 'juste retour', each member state's firms win work proportional to what it pays in — so contracts are a political balancing act, not just a technical one.

timeline.heading: THE NORTHWEST WAS A CRIME ECONOMY, NOT A CALIPHATE
timeline.body: For a decade the Zamfara-Sokoto-Katsina belt was ruled by bandit militias whose business was cattle rustling, village taxation, and mass kidnap-for-ransom — a profit machine with no flag and no creed. They burned schools to extract ransom, not to impose doctrine. An Islamic State claim in this zone is a category shift: from armed crime to armed ideology.

blocks.text: The northwest banditry is a *for-profit* insurgency — SBM Intelligence put northern ransom payments above **$18M** in a single half-year, almost all of it paid quietly by families. Ideology was never the point; the gun paid for itself.

timeline.heading: NIGERIA ALREADY HAD TWO JIHADS — IN DIFFERENT CORNERS
timeline.body: The northeast around Lake Chad belongs to ISWAP (Islamic State West Africa Province), grown out of Boko Haram. The Sahel Province (ISSP) operates far to the northwest, in the Mali-Niger-Burkina tri-border. Sokoto sits between them — turf neither franchise had touched. A claim here means the Sahel insurgency has reached down across the Niger border into Nigeria itself.

blocks.label: the two theaters and the gap between them

timeline.heading: THE LINEAGE OF NIGERIAN JIHAD
timeline.body: Boko Haram rose in Maiduguri in 2009, pledged to ISIS in 2015, then fractured: in 2016 the Islamic State disowned Abubakar Shekau and installed a rival faction as ISWAP, precisely because Shekau slaughtered Muslim civilians. That split is the through-line — every escalation since has been about which group can claim the mantle of legitimate jihad.

timeline.heading: THE CLAIM CAME BEFORE THE CONFIRMATION
timeline.body: Islamic State runs a weekly Arabic newsletter that catalogs and claims attacks across its provinces — a propaganda ledger published before any government acknowledges the dead. Claiming a debut in new territory is itself the strategy: it signals expansion to followers and rivals, whether or not the operation matched the boast. This is why the military's silence and the claim's confidence can coexist.

blocks.text: *Al-Naba* — "the news" — is IS's weekly bulletin and the closest thing the group has to an official record. A claim there is a marketing act as much as a military one: the **franchise** advertises reach to recruit, even where its footprint is thin.

timeline.heading: HOW A BANDIT BECOMES A JIHADIST
timeline.body: The boundary the article calls disputed is real and porous: jihadist groups recruit by offering bandits ideology, weapons, and a transnational brand, while bandits offer local knowledge and manpower. Nigeria has seen this before — Ansaru, an al-Qaeda-aligned splinter, embedded in the northwest years ago. Armed criminality is the raw material that ideological movements refine.

blocks.question: Why did Islamic State replace Abubakar Shekau with a rival faction (ISWAP) in 2016?
options: He refused to pledge allegiance to ISIS
He wanted to merge with al-Qaeda
He lost all his territory to the army
blocks.explanation: IS distanced itself from Shekau's mass killing of Muslims, installing ISWAP as the faction that would target the state and spare civilians — a split over legitimacy, not strategy alone.

timeline.heading: THE ROTATION GAMBIT
timeline.body: Rotational chief-minister deals — split a five-year term down the middle — are a recurring fix when a party wins but can't choose between two rival claimants. They are private, unwritten, and legally unenforceable: nothing in India's constitution obliges a sitting CM with a majority to step down halfway. The man holding the chair almost always wants to keep it, which is why these pacts are famous for breaking, not honoring.

timeline.heading: THE HIGH COMMAND
timeline.body: Congress is run on a 'high command' model: state chief ministers serve at the pleasure of the central leadership in Delhi, which arbitrates succession, brokers deals, and can summon a sitting CM to resign. A swap like this is never purely local — it is ratified, and often engineered, from the party's national headquarters.

timeline.heading: THE CASTE ARITHMETIC
timeline.body: The rivalry maps onto Karnataka's two power blocs. Siddaramaiah, a Kuruba, built his career on a coalition of minorities, backward classes, and Dalits; Shivakumar belongs to the Vokkaligas, the dominant landowning community of southern Karnataka. The leadership question is also a question of which social base the party tilts toward.

blocks.text: Siddaramaiah's vote bank is known by the acronym **AHINDA** — a Kannada compression of *minorities, backward classes, and Dalits*. Shivakumar's strength is the **Vokkaliga** belt around the old Mysore region. The two rarely overlap.

timeline.heading: WHY KARNATAKA IS THE PRIZE
timeline.body: This is not just any state. Bengaluru, its capital, is the center of India's software industry and accounts for the single largest slice of the country's IT exports — making Karnataka's treasury and its chief minister's patronage among the most valuable in Indian politics.

timeline.heading: THE NUMBERS GAME
timeline.body: Whoever leads must hold a majority of the 224-seat assembly together, and India's 1985 anti-defection law strips a legislator of their seat for crossing the floor. That makes blocs of loyal MLAs the real currency of a leadership fight — which is why such standoffs sometimes end with rival camps sequestered in resorts to prevent poaching.

blocks.question: Bengaluru's dominance means Karnataka accounts for roughly what share of India's software exports?
blocks.explanation: Karnataka, led by Bengaluru, contributes roughly two-fifths of India's IT/software exports — the largest of any state.

timeline.heading: THE WORLD'S FASTEST-DYING LAKE
timeline.body: The Aral was the fourth-largest lake on Earth in 1960. Soviet planners knew diverting its rivers would shrink it — Moscow's own ministries called the lake's death an acceptable price for cotton. This was not an accident; it was a deliberate engineering trade.

events.label: Lake splits into north and south

timeline.heading: TWO RIVERS, TWO FATES
timeline.body: The Aral was fed by two great Central Asian rivers: the Syr Darya from the north and the Amu Darya from the south. The Kok-Aral Dam works by trapping the entire Syr Darya in the smaller northern basin — which is why Kazakhstan's half recovered while Uzbekistan's, starved of the still-diverted Amu Darya, did not.

blocks.label: the divided sea
blocks.caption: Syr Darya feeds the north; Amu Darya the dried south

timeline.heading: WHITE GOLD
timeline.body: The water went to cotton — Soviet planners called it 'white gold' and pushed Uzbekistan into monoculture. Uzbekistan is still among the world's largest cotton producers, which is precisely why the Amu Darya cannot simply be returned to the lake: the crop that emptied the sea is now the economy that depends on it.

blocks.text: Cotton is brutally thirsty — roughly **2,700 litres** of water for a single t-shirt's worth of fibre. Forcing it onto the arid steppe meant draining an inland sea to grow it.

timeline.heading: THE POISON DESERT
timeline.body: The exposed seabed became a new desert — the Aralkum — coated in salt and decades of accumulated pesticide and fertilizer runoff. Winds lift this toxic dust and scatter it across the region, where infant mortality, respiratory disease, and certain cancers rank among the highest in the former Soviet world.

blocks.text: The new desert has a name: the *Aralkum*. It is the only desert on Earth whose dust is laced with industrial agricultural chemicals — including residues of DDT banned decades ago.

timeline.heading: WHY A SMALLER TARGET WORKED
timeline.body: Restoration succeeded by abandoning the goal of refilling the whole lake. By damming off and concentrating one river's flow into one northern basin, Kazakhstan raised the water level fast enough to outpace evaporation — a lesson that a partial, achievable fix can beat an impossible total one.

blocks.question: Why did the North Aral Sea recover while the southern half stayed desert?
options: A dam trapped the Syr Darya's flow in the smaller northern basin
The southern seabed was permanently salted
blocks.explanation: The Kok-Aral Dam concentrated the Syr Darya into the small northern basin, raising its level faster than evaporation could remove it.

timeline.heading: THE 20% LINE
timeline.body: OKX stopped at 19.6% deliberately. Under Korean financial law, crossing roughly 20% of an exchange's shares can classify a buyer as a controlling party, triggering a fit-and-proper review of the acquirer itself. Staying just under buys market access without inviting regulators to audit OKX's own history.

blocks.text: This is *threshold arbitrage* — the deal is structured around a regulatory tripwire at **20%**, not around what economic stake OKX actually wants. The same logic governs takeover-disclosure rules in most markets.

timeline.heading: THE REAL-NAME MOAT
timeline.body: Since 2018, Korean crypto exchanges may only let users trade with won if those users hold a real-name bank account at a partner bank that verifies identity. Banks are cautious about which exchanges they'll service, so the binding constraint on a Korean exchange isn't technology — it's whether a domestic bank will issue it real-name accounts. That moat is what a foreign player is really paying to get behind.

blocks.question: What does a Korean exchange most need before it can offer won trading to retail users?
options: A real-name banking partnership with a domestic bank
A listing on the Kospi stock exchange
A minimum Bitcoin reserve held in cold storage
Approval from the central bank's monetary committee
blocks.explanation: The 2018 real-name rule routes all won deposits through verified bank accounts, so a bank partnership is the gatekeeper to the retail market.

timeline.heading: WHY BUY IN, NOT BUILD
timeline.body: A foreign exchange cannot simply open a Seoul branch and start serving Korean users — licensing, real-name banking, and local-entity rules effectively wall out outsiders. The practical route in is an equity stake in an already-licensed incumbent. OKX, which has been pushed out of or fined in several Western jurisdictions, gains a compliant Korean foothold without building one from scratch.

timeline.heading: THE KIMCHI PREMIUM
timeline.body: Korea's market is so insulated by capital controls and the closed won-banking rail that Bitcoin has historically traded at a persistent markup there — the 'kimchi premium,' which spiked above 50% during the 2017-18 mania. The gap exists because arbitrageurs can't freely move won out to buy cheaper coins abroad and sell them back in. A closed market is exactly what makes a stake in it valuable.

timeline.heading: WHO RUNS KOREAN CRYPTO
timeline.body: Coinone is a second-tier player. The Korean market is overwhelmingly concentrated in Upbit, with Bithumb a distant second — together they handle the vast majority of won-denominated volume, leaving Coinone and Korbit fighting over the remainder.

timeline.heading: ARTICLE 4, NOT ARTICLE 5
timeline.body: The treaty most people know is Article 5 — an attack on one is an attack on all. But it requires an 'armed attack' and unanimous agreement on the response, a bar no ally wants to test over a drone. Romania's actual lever is Article 4: any member may demand formal consultations when it feels threatened. It triggers a meeting, not a war.

blocks.question: Which NATO treaty article lets a member demand formal alliance consultations without invoking collective defense?
blocks.explanation: Article 4 obliges allies to consult when one feels its security threatened; Article 5 is the collective-defense clause requiring an armed attack.

timeline.heading: THE SHAHED IN RUSSIAN PAINT
timeline.body: The Geran-2 is not a Russian design. It is the Iranian Shahed-136, transferred after 2022 and now license-produced inside Russia at the Alabuga plant in Tatarstan. A delta-wing flying bomb with a moped engine and a roughly 50kg warhead, it loiters at low altitude and crashes into its target — cheap, slow, and built to be expended in waves.

blocks.text: The **Geran-2** (Russian for *geranium*) is the rebranded Iranian **Shahed-136** — a one-way attack drone costing perhaps **$20–50k** apiece, designed to be fired in saturating swarms rather than aimed with precision.

timeline.heading: THE COST ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: The reason these drones are a strategic weapon is arithmetic. A defender who downs a $30,000 drone with a million-dollar surface-to-air missile wins the engagement and loses the war of attrition. Russia builds them by the thousand precisely to drain Western interceptor stockpiles that take months to replace.

timeline.heading: WHY THEY DRIFT INTO ROMANIA
timeline.body: Galați sits on the Danube directly across from the Ukrainian river ports of Izmail and Reni, which Russia bombs to choke Ukraine's grain exports. Drones that overshoot, are jammed, or are knocked off course by air defense have only a few kilometers of water to cross before they are over Romanian — and therefore NATO — soil. The incursions are a geographic byproduct of the strike campaign next door.

blocks.label: the Danube frontier
blocks.caption: Russian strikes on Ukraine's Danube ports spill across a few km of river into NATO airspace

timeline.heading: WHY 'RECKLESS,' NOT 'DELIBERATE'
timeline.body: NATO's choice of words is a policy, not a description. Calling a strike 'reckless' rather than 'deliberate' preserves the off-ramp: a deliberate attack on an ally would pressure the alliance toward an Article 5 reckoning it has no appetite for. Ambiguity lets both sides avoid the rungs of the escalation ladder neither wants to climb. The deniability is a feature Moscow exploits and Brussels quietly accepts.

timeline.heading: THE PRZEWODÓW TEMPLATE
timeline.body: This script was written in November 2022, when a missile killed two people in Przewodów, Poland. Within hours it looked like a Russian strike on NATO territory — then evidence pointed to a stray Ukrainian air-defense round. NATO seized the ambiguity to de-escalate, and that response became the template: investigate slowly, condemn loudly, retaliate never.

events.label: Shahed debris found in Romania's Danube delta
Galați strike — first NATO civilian injuries

timeline.heading: WHO GUARDS THE GATE
timeline.body: The Black Sea has one exit: the Turkish Straits. Under the 1936 Montreux Convention, Turkey controls passage through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles and can close them to warships in wartime — which it did in 2022, barring Russian naval reinforcement from the Mediterranean. This legal chokehold is why Ankara, not Brussels or Washington, brokered the grain deal.

blocks.label: the enclosed sea and its only exit

blocks.text: Montreux lets Turkey shut the straits to belligerent warships but **not** to commercial traffic — the legal seam that kept grain moving while Russia's Black Sea Fleet stayed bottled up.

timeline.heading: THE CORRIDOR THAT FED CONTINENTS
timeline.body: Before 2022, Ukraine and Russia together supplied roughly a third of the world's wheat exports. The Black Sea Grain Initiative, signed in Istanbul in July 2022, let inspected vessels run a humanitarian corridor out of Odesa. Russia walked away in July 2023; what moves now does so without that guarantee — which is what makes a single drone strike a market event.

timeline.heading: WHO GOES HUNGRY UPSTREAM
timeline.body: Black Sea grain doesn't feed rich economies — it feeds wheat-import-dependent states with thin reserves, where bread is a political commodity. Egypt is the world's largest wheat importer; Lebanon's silos held weeks of supply even before the 2020 port blast. A corridor strike registers as a price tremor in Cairo and Beirut, not in Chicago.

blocks.label: wheat import dependence (share consumed that is imported)

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: It is not the drones that close a shipping lane — it is the war-risk premium. Once Lloyd's underwriters reprice a route as a conflict zone, the per-voyage surcharge can swamp the cargo's margin, and owners reroute or refuse regardless of how many vessels actually get hit. A single burning freighter resets the premium for every ship behind it.

blocks.text: The corridor's real toll booth sits in London: a **war-risk premium** quoted as a percentage of hull value per voyage. Spike it and commercial shipping stops itself — no blockade required.

timeline.heading: THE STRAITS, ACROSS HISTORY
timeline.body: Whoever holds the Bosphorus holds Russia's warm-water access. Tsarist Russia fought repeated wars for it; the 1853–56 Crimean War was, at root, about keeping Russia out of the straits. Montreux froze that contest into a treaty — and handed the referee's whistle permanently to Turkey.

blocks.question: Which treaty gives Turkey legal authority over warship passage into the Black Sea?
blocks.explanation: Montreux returned full control of the straits to Turkey and lets it restrict warship transit, especially in wartime.

timeline.heading: THE MULTIPLE
timeline.body: A $1.8tn valuation against $18.7bn of 2025 revenue is roughly 96 times sales. Mature profitable giants trade in the single digits to low tens; a number this high is not pricing today's rockets and Starlink subscriptions — it is pricing a story about the future.

blocks.question: Roughly how many times its 2025 revenue is SpaceX's $1.8tn IPO floor?
blocks.explanation: $1.8tn divided by $18.7bn revenue is ~96x — far above the single-digit multiples mature firms command.

timeline.heading: THE TAM REFRAME
timeline.body: The number only works if you change the question SpaceX answers. Priced as a launch-and-broadband company, it is worth a few hundred billion; priced as 'AI infrastructure' addressing a $28.5tn services market, almost any multiple looks cheap. The pivot is a valuation tool as much as a strategy.

blocks.text: The lever is the *total addressable market*. Anchor a story to a **$28.5tn** TAM and a 96x sales multiple reads as a rounding error — which is exactly why founders reach for the biggest credible market they can name.

timeline.heading: THE PRIVATE GIANT
timeline.body: SpaceX is already the most valuable private company on earth, ahead of the AI labs and the Chinese platform giants. Staying private this long is itself unusual — most firms this size went public a decade ago to raise capital.

timeline.heading: WHO ACTUALLY CONTROLS IT
timeline.body: Concentrated ownership means the float sold to the public carries little say. Founders typically retain supervoting shares so that selling a minority economic stake never threatens voting control — the structure Musk has used at every company he runs.

timeline.heading: WHAT GOING PUBLIC EXPOSES
timeline.body: Private companies choose what to disclose; an S-1 filing ends that. SpaceX would have to publish audited GAAP financials, every related-party deal with xAI and Tesla, and executive pay. Consolidation rules can also force a subsidiary's losses onto the parent — an accounting structure, not the rocket business, can turn an operating profit into a reported net loss.

timeline.heading: WHY IT STAYED PRIVATE
timeline.body: SpaceX never needed an IPO for cash — recurring tender offers let employees and early backers sell shares while the company set the price and stayed off public markets. Going public now trades that control for the one thing tenders can't deliver: a deep, liquid market to fund capital at AI-infrastructure scale.

timeline.heading: THE NAME IS THE ARGUMENT
timeline.body: A pope's chosen name signals his program. Leo XIV reached past a century of Johns, Pauls, and a Francis to revive 'Leo' — the name of the pope who confronted the last great machine age. The choice tells you the encyclical is coming before a word of it is read.

people.name: Leo XIII
people.role: wrote Rerum Novarum on industrial labor

blocks.label: popes behind the landmark social encyclicals

timeline.heading: THE 1891 TEMPLATE
timeline.body: Modern Catholic social teaching begins with Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum in 1891 — a response to the Industrial Revolution that defended workers' right to organize, a living wage, and private property, while rejecting both unchecked capitalism and socialism. Every social encyclical since has been written in its shadow, often timed to its anniversaries.

timeline.heading: WHY 'ENCYCLICAL'
timeline.body: An encyclical is not a law and not infallible dogma. The word comes from the Greek for 'circular' — historically a letter circulated among bishops. It carries the ordinary teaching authority of the office: binding on conscience, persuasive rather than juridical, addressed increasingly not just to Catholics but to 'all people of good will.'

blocks.text: An encyclical sits between an off-the-cuff homily and a defined *dogma* — it is **authoritative teaching**, not **infallible decree**. Catholics owe it 'religious submission of intellect and will,' not the assent reserved for articles of faith.

timeline.heading: 'NOT NEUTRAL' IS AN OLD CLAIM
timeline.body: The idea that a technology embeds the values of its makers predates AI by decades — the French theologian Jacques Ellul argued in the 1950s that technique reshapes the society that adopts it, on its own logic. The encyclical's novelty is institutional, not philosophical: it puts the weight of a global church behind a thesis academics have argued for seventy years.

blocks.question: By choosing the name 'Leo,' which predecessor was Pope Leo XIV most clearly invoking?
options: Leo XIII, who confronted the Industrial Revolution
Leo I, who turned back Attila the Hun
Leo X, who excommunicated Martin Luther
blocks.explanation: Leo XIII's 1891 Rerum Novarum founded modern Catholic social teaching on the last great machine age — the obvious template for an AI encyclical.

timeline.heading: THE DISTRIBUTION MACHINE
timeline.body: When a pope speaks, the message reaches every parish the following Sunday. The infrastructure is unmatched: roughly 17,000 parishes in the US alone, each a captive weekly audience, and over 200,000 worldwide. No political organization commands comparable reach at zero marginal cost — which is why a doctrinal statement can move public opinion that a think-tank report cannot.

timeline.heading: HOW IT REACHES THE BOARDROOM
timeline.body: The article's real mechanism is the shareholder proxy resolution. Once a company is public, investors holding a small threshold of stock can force a vote at the annual meeting on issues like human-rights due diligence. Catholic orders and pension funds have run this playbook for decades — and an encyclical gives faith-based investors a shared rationale to file in coordination.

blocks.text: The lever isn't excommunication — it's the *proxy ballot*. A resolution rarely needs to **win** the vote; a **20–30% yes** tally is enough to signal a board that institutional capital is watching.

timeline.heading: THE MULTIPLIER
timeline.body: Climate impact is measured in Global Warming Potential — how much heat a gas traps over 100 years versus the same mass of CO₂. CO₂ is the baseline of 1. Common AC refrigerants score in the thousands, so a few kilograms leaking from a single unit can equal years of a car's tailpipe.

blocks.text: The reason is the **atmospheric window** — a band of infrared wavelengths that CO₂ and water vapor leave open. Fluorinated refrigerants absorb light *precisely in that gap*, so each molecule does outsized warming work.

timeline.heading: THE GENERATIONAL TREADMILL
timeline.body: Refrigerant chemistry has been replaced wholesale three times, each fix breeding the next problem. CFCs destroyed ozone, so they were banned for HCFCs; HCFCs still harmed ozone, so HFCs replaced them — but HFCs turned out to be potent greenhouse gases. The current frontier, HFOs, breaks down fast but raises toxicity and flammability questions.

timeline.heading: THE MONTREAL IRONY
timeline.body: The 1987 Montreal Protocol is the most successful environmental treaty ever signed — it healed the ozone layer by phasing out CFCs. But its replacements, HFCs, were chosen for being ozone-safe, not climate-safe. The 2016 Kigali Amendment exists to clean up the warming mess that Montreal's own success created.

timeline.heading: WHERE THE LEAKS HAPPEN
timeline.body: Most refrigerant emissions occur not in daily use but at the end of life — when a unit is scrapped and its charge vents to the air instead of being recovered. This is why disposal rules matter more than efficiency standards, and why the coming equipment boom in regions with the weakest recovery enforcement is the real risk.

blocks.question: When does an air conditioner release most of its refrigerant emissions?
options: At manufacture, when it is charged
At end of life, if the charge isn't recovered
blocks.explanation: A sealed unit leaks little in use; the bulk vents at scrappage unless the refrigerant is captured — which weak disposal regimes rarely require.

timeline.heading: THE COOLING PARADOX
timeline.body: Cooling is the rare technology that worsens the problem it solves: every air conditioner running on a fossil grid, leaking high-GWP gas, makes the heat it was bought to escape slightly worse. As warming pushes more of the world past the threshold where cooling is survival rather than comfort, the feedback loop tightens.

timeline.heading: SUR, THE ROCK
timeline.body: Tyre's Arabic and Phoenician name, Sur, means 'rock' — the city began as a fortified island just offshore, which is exactly why it survived sieges that flattened mainland rivals. Its defensibility is not incidental to its history; it is the entire story of the place.

blocks.text: The island made Tyre the dominant Phoenician sea power — it founded *Carthage* and gave the world *Tyrian purple*, a dye extracted drop by drop from murex sea snails, so costly it became the literal color of emperors.

timeline.heading: THE CAUSEWAY THAT STUCK
timeline.body: When Alexander the Great couldn't storm island Tyre in 332 BC, he spent seven months building a causeway of rubble out to it. The siege ended, but the causeway never washed away — silt built up around it, and Tyre has been a peninsula joined to the mainland ever since. A modern city sits on a 2,300-year-old siege work.

blocks.question: How did Alexander's 332 BC siege permanently change Tyre's geography?
options: His causeway fused the offshore island to the mainland
He diverted the Litani river to flood the city
He demolished the island, leaving only a reef
He cut a canal that turned the coast into islands
blocks.explanation: Silt accumulated around the rubble causeway, turning the former island into the peninsula Tyre occupies today.

timeline.heading: THE LITANI LINE
timeline.body: Tyre sits just north of the Litani river, the natural line that has defined every southern Lebanon conflict. UN Resolution 1701, which ended the 2006 war, drew its buffer along this river: Hezbollah south, the Lebanese army and UN peacekeepers in between. Strikes on Tyre are strikes on the edge of that contested zone.

blocks.label: southern Lebanon
blocks.caption: Tyre lies just north of the Litani, the 1701 buffer line

timeline.heading: WHY DISPLACEMENT ORDERS PRECEDE STRIKES
timeline.body: A blanket order to evacuate a city converts it, in the issuing army's framing, from a protected civilian space into a presumed combat zone. Under the laws of war, warnings are required, but a warning does not by itself make a strike on a residential building lawful — proportionality and distinction still apply to whoever remains.

blocks.text: The legal pivot is **distinction** — the duty to separate combatants from civilians. A mass evacuation order cannot dissolve that duty; the people who *cannot* leave, or who return, retain full protection regardless of the order.

timeline.heading: THE PATTERN OF INVASION
timeline.body: Southern Lebanon has been crossed and re-crossed for half a century. Each ceasefire has been a pause in a recurring cycle rather than a settlement, and Tyre — the largest city below the Litani — has sat in the path of every wave.

timeline.heading: THE HIDING TRICK
timeline.body: A feeding black hole blazes brighter than its entire host galaxy — but only if you can see it. Wrap it in enough dust and the visible glare is absorbed and re-radiated as infrared heat, so the monster reads as ordinary warm gas. The light isn't gone; it's been laundered into a longer wavelength.

blocks.text: Astronomers call a black hole this heavily veiled *Compton-thick* — the surrounding column of gas is so dense that even most X-rays scatter before escaping. These are the **AGN** (active galactic nuclei) that census after census keeps undercounting.

timeline.heading: WHY MERGERS FEED MONSTERS
timeline.body: A black hole can only grow if gas falls in, and gas in a quiet galaxy orbits stably forever. A collision wrecks that order: tidal forces strip angular momentum from the gas, and it pours toward the center — simultaneously igniting a starburst and feeding the black hole. The same crash that builds stars buries the black hole in the dust those stars produce.

timeline.heading: THE CONFUSION PROBLEM
timeline.body: Newborn massive stars and an accreting black hole both dump enormous energy into surrounding dust, which glows in the infrared either way. From the outside the two engines can look nearly identical, which is why a hidden black hole can sit unnoticed inside what everyone catalogued as a star-forming knot.

blocks.label: what each wavelength reveals through dust

timeline.heading: HOW YOU PROVE IT
timeline.body: Hard X-rays and radio waves pierce dust that stops visible light cold. A black hole betrays itself through signatures starbursts can't fake: X-rays with the specific spectrum of gas heated to millions of degrees as it spirals in, or a compact radio core with relativistic jets. That's why the article notes X-ray or radio surveys are needed to confirm the claim.

blocks.question: Why do astronomers turn to X-rays to find a dust-hidden black hole?
options: X-rays penetrate dust that blocks visible light
X-rays are only emitted by stars, not black holes
Dust amplifies X-rays, making them easy to detect
X-rays travel faster than other light through gas
blocks.explanation: Hard X-rays pass through obscuring dust and carry the spectral signature of gas heated to millions of degrees near the black hole — a fingerprint star formation can't reproduce.

timeline.heading: THE ANTENNAE
timeline.body: The Antennae (NGC 4038/4039) are the nearest major galaxy merger, roughly 60 million light-years away, named for the two long tidal tails the collision flung out. Being close and clearly mid-collision makes them the textbook laboratory for what the Milky Way and Andromeda will become in a few billion years.

timeline.heading: THE PREPRINT CAVEAT
timeline.body: The finding lives on arXiv, the physics preprint server where papers post before peer review. arXiv accelerates science — results circulate in days, not months — but a preprint has cleared no referee. Until an X-ray or radio detection independently confirms the source, this is a strong hypothesis, not an established discovery.

timeline.heading: THE INVISIBLE LEDGER
timeline.body: When you buy a US stock, you almost never become its registered owner. The shares are held in the name of Cede & Co., a nominee of DTCC's depository, and your broker records a 'security entitlement' against that pool. Nearly every publicly traded American share sits in one giant electronic vault — DTCC is the unglamorous monopoly underneath the entire market.

blocks.question: When you buy shares through a US broker, who is the registered legal owner of those shares?
blocks.explanation: Almost all US shares are held in 'street name' under Cede & Co.; investors hold a book-entry entitlement, not the certificate itself.

timeline.heading: WHAT SETTLEMENT ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: A trade and its settlement are two different events. The price is agreed instantly, but the actual swap of cash for ownership happens later — historically days later. That delay exists because the plumbing batches and nets millions of trades overnight, and the whole industry has spent decades compressing the lag.

timeline.heading: WHY THE LAG IS DANGEROUS
timeline.body: During the settlement window, the clearinghouse carries the risk that one side defaults — so it demands collateral. In January 2021, DTCC's clearing arm demanded billions in extra margin from brokers amid the GameStop frenzy, and Robinhood, unable to post it, halted buying. The settlement gap, invisible most days, became the choke point of the whole episode.

blocks.text: Robinhood faced a roughly **$3B** collateral call overnight and restricted trading within hours — a vivid demonstration that **T+2** is not free. Every day of lag is a day of default risk the clearinghouse must collateralize.

timeline.heading: WHAT ATOMIC SETTLEMENT CHANGES
timeline.body: On a blockchain, the security and the cash can move in the same transaction — either both legs execute or neither does. This is delivery-versus-payment taken to its limit: settlement becomes instantaneous and final, collapsing the window in which a counterparty can fail and eliminating the collateral buffer that window requires.

timeline.heading: TOKENS VS THE RAILS
timeline.body: The article's real point: putting securities on-chain is infrastructure, not speculation. DTCC tokenizing real Treasuries and equities is the blockchain working as plumbing — like TCP/IP under a browser — and has nothing to do with whether bitcoin rises or falls. That is why the rail can advance on the same day the speculative coins sink.

timeline.heading: DIFFERENT MARKETS, DIFFERENT SPEED
timeline.body: Settlement speed is a policy choice, not a law of nature, and the world's exchanges sit at different points. The US only reached T+1 in 2024; Europe still runs a day slower; parts of Asia already settle same-day. On-chain settlement is an attempt to leapfrog the whole queue to T+0.

timeline.heading: STELLAR'S LINEAGE
timeline.body: The chain DTCC plugged into was not chosen at random. Stellar was built in 2014 explicitly for cheap, fast cross-institution payments rather than open-ended speculation — a pedigree that matters when a settlement monopoly is picking infrastructure.

blocks.text: Stellar was co-founded by **Jed McCaleb**, who earlier created the **Mt. Gox** exchange and co-founded **Ripple** before leaving — its design goal was institutional payment settlement, not a store-of-value bet.

timeline.heading: WHAT COUNTS AS A DISASTER
timeline.body: EM-DAT does not log every flood or quake. An event enters only if it crosses a threshold: at least 10 deaths, 100+ people affected, a declared state of emergency, or a call for international assistance. Those rules are why a single archive can claim to be comparable across two centuries.

blocks.question: An event is logged in EM-DAT only if it meets a set threshold. Which one qualifies?
blocks.explanation: EM-DAT requires one of: 10+ deaths, 100+ affected, a state-of-emergency declaration, or an appeal for international aid.

timeline.heading: THE KEEPER
timeline.body: The database is run not by the UN or a government but by CRED, a small research center at the Université catholique de Louvain in Belgium, founded in 1973. A global public record sits on the budget of one university lab — which is exactly why a single donor's withdrawal can end it.

blocks.text: CRED — the **Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters** — has compiled EM-DAT since 1988, but US aid covered roughly **90%** of the running cost. One funder, one point of failure.

timeline.heading: THE REPORTING GAP
timeline.body: Wealthy states record disasters meticulously; poor ones often cannot. So the archive already undercounts the Global South — yet those same governments rely on it because they have no national equivalent. Defunding the database widens the very blind spot its users most need closed.

timeline.heading: THE ONLY OPEN ONE
timeline.body: Comprehensive disaster data does exist elsewhere — but mostly inside reinsurers who sell it. Munich Re and Swiss Re keep proprietary catastrophe records to price risk. EM-DAT is the rare open, free, comparable archive, which is why scientists treat its loss as a public-knowledge emergency, not a budget line.

timeline.heading: WHY THE CLIMATE FILES NEED IT
timeline.body: UN climate assessments and the new loss-and-damage fund both rest on counting disasters consistently over time — you cannot prove events are growing more frequent or costly without a long, uniform baseline. Lose the baseline and every future trend claim loses its denominator.

timeline.heading: WHAT SWIFT ACTUALLY IS
timeline.body: SWIFT moves no money. It is a Belgium-based messaging cooperative that lets 11,000 banks send standardized payment instructions to each other. The actual money settles through correspondent accounts at central banks. But because almost every cross-border transaction starts with a SWIFT message, controlling the network is a chokepoint on global finance.

blocks.text: The crucial distinction: **SWIFT** is the *messaging layer*, not the *settlement layer*. Cut a bank off and its money still exists — it just can no longer tell anyone where to send it.

timeline.heading: THE WEAPON DISCOVERED
timeline.body: SWIFT was apolitical infrastructure until 2012, when EU sanctions forced it to disconnect Iranian banks — the first time the network was used as a coercive tool. The success of that cutoff turned SWIFT access into a strategic asset and triggered a quiet, decade-long race to build alternatives.

events.label: EU sets up INSTEX for Iran trade
Major Russian banks cut from SWIFT

timeline.heading: THE RAILS ALREADY EXIST
timeline.body: An SCO bank would not be built from scratch — the components exist. China's CIPS clears yuan payments, Russia's SPFS carries domestic messaging, and the EU's INSTEX was a barter-style workaround for Iran. The problem has never been technology; it is getting counterparties to actually use a parallel system.

timeline.heading: WHY LOCAL CURRENCIES STALL
timeline.body: Settling trade in rials, rubles, and rupees runs into a liquidity wall: an exporter paid in a soft currency cannot easily spend it elsewhere, so it piles up unwanted. India and Russia hit exactly this in 2023 — Indian refiners paid for Russian oil in rupees that Moscow then had billions of and no way to use. Currencies become global only when everyone wants to hold them.

blocks.text: Economists call a usable currency a *medium of exchange* and a *store of value* at once. A rupee-for-oil deal solves the first and breaks the second — which is why these arrangements quietly collapse back toward dollars.

timeline.heading: THE DOLLAR'S ACTUAL GRIP
timeline.body: Despite a decade of dedollarization talk, the dollar still makes up the clear majority of global central-bank reserves, with the euro a distant second and the yuan barely a sliver. Network effects compound: you hold dollars because everyone else does, and a new system has to overcome that gravity before its first transaction is worth more than a press release.

blocks.question: What does being disconnected from SWIFT actually do to a bank?
options: Freezes the money in its accounts
Cuts its ability to message other banks about payments
blocks.explanation: SWIFT is a messaging network — the money still exists, but the bank can no longer instruct counterparties on where to send it.

timeline.heading: THE AMNESTY BARGAIN
timeline.body: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission was not a blanket pardon. Amnesty was individual and conditional: a perpetrator had to apply, appear, and make full disclosure of a politically motivated crime. Those who stayed silent, lied, or were refused were supposed to face ordinary prosecution. The 'truth' in the name was the price of the 'reconciliation.'

blocks.question: How did the TRC's amnesty actually work?
options: Blanket pardon for all apartheid-era crimes
blocks.explanation: Amnesty was granted individually only for full, truthful disclosure of politically motivated acts — non-applicants and liars were meant to be prosecuted.

timeline.heading: THE CASES THAT VANISHED
timeline.body: The TRC referred roughly 300 cases — perpetrators who refused amnesty or were denied it — to the National Prosecuting Authority when it closed. Over two decades, almost none were pursued. Families of the dead and disappeared have long argued this was not prosecutorial backlog but a deliberate decision to let apartheid's enforcers walk.

blocks.text: The reopened inquests into *Ahmed Timol* (fell from the 10th floor of John Vorster Square, 1971) and *Neil Aggett* overturned decades-old 'suicide' findings — proof the evidence to prosecute had existed all along.

timeline.heading: THE BACKDOOR AMNESTY
timeline.body: In 2005 the NPA quietly amended its prosecution policy, granting prosecutors discretion that effectively re-offered amnesty to those the TRC had denied it. Courts later struck the amendment down as unconstitutional — but by then the window of witnesses, memory, and political will had closed. The suppression worked through paperwork, not decrees.

timeline.heading: WHY BOTH SIDES WANTED SILENCE
timeline.body: The negotiated transition exposed everyone. Apartheid's security police feared the dock, but so did ANC figures implicated in camp abuses and bombings. A live prosecutions track threatened the architects of the new order as much as the old one — a mutual interest in burying the files that cut across the racial divide of the conflict itself.

blocks.label: the figures now in the frame

timeline.heading: THE KHAMPEPE COMMISSION
timeline.body: Retired Constitutional Court justice Sisi Khampepe now chairs a judicial commission of inquiry into who ordered the prosecutions stopped. It was forced into being by survivors and families suing the state — meaning the accountability mechanism exists because citizens dragged a reluctant government to it, not because the government volunteered.

events.label: TRC established by Act of Parliament

blocks.label: truth, then silence, then the reckoning

timeline.heading: THE BACKCHANNEL PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Pakistan's most famous act of diplomacy was invisible at the time: in 1971 it secretly hosted the channel that carried Henry Kissinger to Beijing, enabling Nixon's opening to China. Islamabad's value to great powers has long been as a discreet conduit between rivals who cannot be seen talking directly.

blocks.question: Which diplomatic breakthrough did Pakistan secretly help arrange in 1971?
blocks.explanation: Yahya Khan's government relayed messages and hosted the channel that flew Kissinger covertly to Beijing, opening US–China relations.

timeline.heading: WHY PAKISTAN CAN TALK TO BOTH
timeline.body: Pakistan is a US major non-NATO ally yet shares a 900-km border with Iran and deep religious and trade ties across it. Even after the two traded cross-border airstrikes against Baluch militants in January 2024, working diplomatic relations resumed within weeks — the dual standing that lets Islamabad carry messages neither capital would deliver itself.

timeline.heading: WHAT SHUTTLE DIPLOMACY IS
timeline.body: Carrying proposals back and forth between parties who refuse to sit in the same room is a defined diplomatic technique, not improvisation. The mediator distorts and softens positions just enough to keep both sides at the table — and gains leverage simply by being the only one who knows what each side will actually accept.

blocks.text: The term *shuttle diplomacy* was coined for Kissinger's 1973–74 flights between Israeli and Arab capitals after the Yom Kippur War — the mediator as the only moving part.

timeline.heading: WHY THE VENUE IS NEVER NEUTRAL ABOUT VENUE
timeline.body: Hosting a signing is itself a prize: it confers prestige and a permanent place in the accord's name. Oslo, Camp David, Doha, Dayton — peace deals are remembered by where they were signed, and the host claims a share of the credit. That is why neither Tehran nor Washington has rushed to confirm Islamabad as the location.

timeline.heading: A CEASEFIRE IS NOT A PEACE
timeline.body: Diplomacy sharply distinguishes a ceasefire — an agreement to stop shooting — from a peace accord that resolves the underlying dispute. The first is cheap and reversible; the second is rare and slow. Prediction markets price exactly this gap: a near-term agreement reads far more likely than a durable settlement.

series.label: US x Iran permanent peace deal by May…

timeline.heading: THE SOFT TARGET
timeline.body: Public package registries run on trust at a scale no human can audit. Millions of packages, anyone can publish, and a modern app pulls in hundreds of transitive dependencies the developer never reads. The attack surface isn't a bug — it's the model.

blocks.text: The classic tricks: *typosquatting* (publish `colours` next to `colors`) and *dependency confusion* (push a public package with the same name as a company's private one, and the build tool grabs the higher version number).

timeline.heading: THE NEW VECTOR
timeline.body: TrapDoor's twist is that the payload isn't executable code — it's text. AI coding assistants read project config files (rules files, instruction files) as authoritative context. Hide commands in that config and the assistant obeys them, exfiltrating secrets while the developer thinks they're getting help. It's prompt injection laundered through a config file.

blocks.text: This is a **confused deputy** attack: the AI assistant has the developer's full permissions, and the malicious config tricks it into misusing them. The human never runs anything — the *trusted agent* does the dirty work.

timeline.heading: WHY CRYPTO WALLETS
timeline.body: Two properties make wallet keys the ideal loot. Blockchain transactions are irreversible — there's no chargeback, no fraud department to call. And developers building wallet apps keep private keys and seed phrases in plaintext config and environment files on the same machine the AI assistant can read.

blocks.question: Why did TrapDoor target AI assistant config files rather than just shipping malware that runs on install?
options: Config files execute faster than code
AI assistants treat config as trusted instructions and act with the developer's permissions
Registries don't scan config files at all
Config files can't be removed once published
blocks.explanation: The assistant is a confused deputy — it has the developer's access and follows hidden instructions in the config without the human ever running anything.

timeline.heading: THE PULL-REQUEST TRUST MODEL
