blocks.text: Roughly **90%** of the world's ship-protection cover is written through the London-based **International Group of P&I Clubs** — which is why a price ceiling set in Brussels reaches a tanker loading in the Baltic.

timeline.heading: WHY SIXTY, NOT ZERO
timeline.body: The cap was deliberately designed as a ceiling, not an embargo. Set it too low and Russia halts exports, global supply tightens, and prices spike — punishing the buyers, not Moscow. The $60 line was pitched above Russia's production cost but below the market, the idea being to keep the oil flowing while shaving the Kremlin's per-barrel margin.

blocks.question: Why did the G7 set the Russian oil cap at $60 rather than near zero?
options: To keep Russian oil flowing and avoid a global price spike
To inflict maximum pain regardless of supply effects
Because $60 is Russia's exact break-even cost
To match OPEC's official price target
blocks.explanation: A near-zero cap would have pushed Russia to cut exports, tightening global supply and raising prices for the cap's own backers.

timeline.heading: THE URALS DISCOUNT
timeline.body: Russia's flagship grade, Urals, does not trade at the world price. Since 2022 it has sold at a steep discount to Brent because the pool of buyers who will handle sanctioned crude is small and demands a premium for the risk. The cap targets Urals specifically — which is why a jump in the global benchmark can drag the discounted Russian grade up past the $60 line.

timeline.heading: THE SHADOW FLEET
timeline.body: To sell above the cap, Russia assembled a fleet of aging tankers with murky ownership and non-Western insurance — vessels that never touch a London broker and so are not bound by the ceiling. The cap's bite depends on how much oil it can keep inside the Western-serviced system versus how much slips into this parallel fleet.

blocks.text: Estimates put the **shadow fleet** at hundreds of tankers — old, often uninsured to Western standards, and a growing environmental as well as sanctions concern in chokepoints like the **Danish Straits**.

timeline.heading: THE REVENUE SQUEEZE
timeline.body: The cap's whole purpose is to drain hydrocarbon revenue, which funds the bulk of the Russian state budget. When oil money tightens, the pressure shows up in the ruble — the cleanest public read on how hard sanctions are actually biting at any given moment.

timeline.heading: THE SANCTIONS ARC
timeline.body: The cap was the second act, not the first. The EU banned seaborne Russian crude outright in mid-2022; the price cap followed in December as a softer instrument once a full embargo threatened to spike prices worldwide. The semi-annual revision now in question is a routine valve built into that machinery.

timeline.heading: THE FLAW BEHIND THE FLAW
timeline.body: The classic way 'millions of records' leak is rarely a sophisticated hack. It is usually an insecure direct object reference: the URL ends in ?id=10421, you change it to 10422, and the server hands you a stranger's file because it never checked whether you were allowed to see it. No password cracked, no firewall breached — just a counter you can increment.

blocks.text: This is called an **IDOR** — *insecure direct object reference*. It sits at the top of the OWASP risk list precisely because it requires zero tooling: a teenager with a browser address bar can find one.

timeline.heading: WHY OUTSOURCING IS THE WEAK LINK
timeline.body: A government board's security is only as strong as the cheapest vendor it subcontracts to. On-screen marking, payment gateways, and document portals are routinely handed to private firms whose contracts specify uptime and price but rarely specify penetration testing. Security becomes nobody's billable line item.

blocks.question: What flaw most commonly exposes 'millions of records' on a government web portal?
options: Guessable URLs with no access check (IDOR)
blocks.explanation: Most mass exposures are access-control failures — the data was never gated — not broken cryptography or stolen hardware.

timeline.heading: THE WHISTLEBLOWER'S TRAP
timeline.body: A researcher who reports a flaw responsibly can still be prosecuted. India's IT Act criminalizes 'unauthorized access' broadly, with no statutory safe harbor for good-faith security research — so the person who warns you about the open door can be charged for having tried the handle. This is why many flaws go unreported until a bad actor finds them first.

timeline.heading: THE PATTERN, NOT THE INCIDENT
timeline.body: India digitized identity and services faster than almost any state on earth, but the legal and security scaffolding lagged. The data-protection regime arrived decades after the systems it was meant to govern — and after the largest exposures had already happened.

events.label: Supreme Court strikes down IT Act §66A
DPDP Act passed — no researcher safe harbor

timeline.heading: WHY THE CONTRACT IS THE STORY
timeline.body: The opposition is demanding a court inquiry into how the marking contract was awarded — not just the breach itself. That instinct is sound: in outsourced public IT, the security failure is usually downstream of the procurement failure. When a contract is awarded on price or proximity rather than capability, the audit trail of how it was won predicts how it will fail.

timeline.heading: THE PHYSIOLOGICAL CEILING
timeline.body: The human body sheds heat by sweating, but sweat only cools if it can evaporate. Above a wet-bulb temperature of about 35°C — heat plus humidity combined — evaporation stops and core temperature climbs no matter how fit, hydrated, or shaded you are. A few hours at that threshold is fatal. The 47.6°C dry-bulb reading in the headline is survivable in dry air; the danger is when humidity rides alongside it.

blocks.text: The metric that kills is not the thermometer reading but the **wet-bulb temperature** — air temperature measured by a thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth, capturing how much cooling evaporation can still deliver. Beyond **~35°C wet-bulb**, a healthy human in the shade dies within hours.

blocks.question: Why can a humid 38°C kill an outdoor worker faster than a dry 47°C?
options: Humid air carries more heat energy per breath
High humidity stops sweat from evaporating, so the body can't cool
The sun is stronger in humid climates
Dry heat triggers more sweating, which protects the body
blocks.explanation: Sweat only cools by evaporating; saturated air blocks evaporation, so the body retains heat even at a lower thermometer reading.

timeline.heading: WHY CITIES COOK
timeline.body: Concrete and asphalt absorb solar radiation by day and release it slowly at night, while glass and steel re-radiate it sideways into streets. The result is the urban heat island: a dense city can run 5–8°C hotter than its rural surroundings, and crucially it stays hot after dark — denying the body the nighttime recovery that prevents heat stroke from accumulating day over day.

blocks.text: The cruelest part is the *night*: rural land cools after sunset, but a city's stored heat keeps temperatures elevated, erasing the recovery window. Consecutive hot nights, not single hot days, are what drive heat-death curves upward.

timeline.heading: THE SOUTH ASIAN HEAT BELT
timeline.body: The Indo-Gangetic plain is one of the planet's most dangerous heat zones — flat, densely populated, and increasingly humid as pre-monsoon moisture builds. Jacobabad in Pakistan has already crossed the survivability threshold in recent years, and the same air mass that bakes it sweeps across northern India.

blocks.label: the Indo-Gangetic heat zone
blocks.caption: Flat, humid, densely populated — among Earth's deadliest heat terrain

timeline.heading: THE LARGEST MIGRATION ON EARTH
timeline.body: India's internal migration is the biggest human movement of its kind anywhere — hundreds of millions who leave villages for construction sites, brick kilns, and informal urban labor. Because they are documented in their home districts, not their workplaces, they fall through nearly every welfare and protection scheme designed around fixed residence.

timeline.heading: THE INFORMAL TRAP
timeline.body: Roughly 90% of India's workforce is informal — no contract, no fixed employer, paid by the day. A formal worker can demand shade, water breaks, or a paused shift; an informal one who stops working simply isn't paid. Heat protection costs the worker income directly, which is why behavioral advice ('avoid midday sun') fails for the people most exposed.

timeline.heading: THE GOVERNANCE GAP
timeline.body: India pioneered Heat Action Plans after a 2010 Ahmedabad heatwave killed over a thousand — early-warning systems, cooling centers, hospital readiness. But these plans are built around fixed residents. The Nature study's finding — fewer than 5 of 94 policies address both heat and migrant status — captures a structural blind spot: the people who move are the people the system can't see.

blocks.text: The 2010 **Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan** became the template copied across South Asia — yet a decade on, its successors still assume a worker has a *home address the warning can reach*. Migrants don't.

timeline.heading: THE PERPETUAL FRONTLINE
timeline.body: The strip from the Litani River to the border has been buffer zone, occupation zone, and battleground continuously since 1978. The same geography that makes it a buffer — high ground overlooking northern Israel, a Shia-majority population, broken terrain — makes it a permanent frontline. Ceasefires pause the fighting here; they have never ended it.

blocks.label: the Litani–border strip
blocks.caption: From the Litani to the line: ~30km of contested ground

timeline.heading: WHAT RESOLUTION 1701 PROMISED
timeline.body: The UN resolution that ended the 2006 war was meant to make the zone south of the Litani a weapons-free space, policed by the Lebanese army and a reinforced UNIFIL. It never fully held: Hezbollah kept its positions, Israel kept its overflights, and both treated the line as a posture to be tested rather than a border to be respected.

blocks.text: 1701's core demand was that the area south of the **Litani** hold *no armed personnel, assets, or weapons* other than the Lebanese state's and **UNIFIL's** — a condition neither side ever let fully take effect.

timeline.heading: TYRE, THE ANCIENT PORT
timeline.body: Tyre is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth — a Phoenician maritime power that Alexander besieged for seven months in 332 BC by building a causeway to its island. Today it is the largest city in the war zone and a Shia population center, which is why its casualty counts carry political weight far beyond the numbers.

timeline.heading: THE 2006 PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Bint Jbeil, a few kilometers from Tyre, was the fiercest battle of the 2006 war. Israel sent elite Golani units to take the town; Hezbollah held it through days of close urban combat and Israel withdrew without holding it. In Hezbollah's narrative this is their Stalingrad — proof that Israeli ground forces can be fought to a standstill on this terrain.

blocks.question: What did UN Resolution 1701, ending the 2006 war, require for south Lebanon?
options: A demilitarized zone south of the Litani, policed by the Lebanese army and UNIFIL
Permanent Israeli occupation up to the Litani
Joint Israeli–Lebanese patrols of the border
blocks.explanation: 1701 envisioned a weapons-free strip under Lebanese state and UNIFIL control — a condition that was never fully enforced.

timeline.heading: WHY CEASEFIRES LEAK HERE
timeline.body: A ceasefire holds only when both sides believe the framework delivers more than continued fighting. In south Lebanon, each side reads the other's restraint as weakness and each violation as a probe. Without a deadline either party is willing to enforce, the line erodes by attrition — strikes continue, the toll climbs, and the 'ceasefire' becomes a name for a slower war.

timeline.heading: WHAT GELIGNITE IS
timeline.body: Gelignite is a nitroglycerin explosive Alfred Nobel patented in 1875 as a safer, putty-like successor to dynamite. It is the workhorse of quarrying and mining because it can be packed into drill holes — but it degrades with age and temperature, sweating raw nitroglycerin that makes a stockpile dangerously sensitive to shock.

blocks.text: Old gelignite *exudes* nitroglycerin as it ages — the leaked droplets are far more shock-sensitive than the stick itself. A warehouse of decaying stock near a population center is the worst-case storage scenario.

timeline.heading: WHY REBELS HOLD EXPLOSIVES
timeline.body: Shan State's armed groups fund themselves partly through mining — jade, tin, rare earths, and gemstones — which runs on industrial blasting agents. Controlling a quarry means stockpiling the explosives that work it, so munitions and commercial mining stock blur into the same supply.

blocks.label: Shan State & its borders
blocks.caption: Namkham sits in northern Shan, ~3 km from China's Yunnan frontier

timeline.heading: WHO THE TA'ANG ARE
timeline.body: The Ta'ang (also called Palaung) are a highland ethnic minority of northern Shan State. Their armed wing, the Ta'ang National Liberation Army, is one of dozens of ethnic armed organizations that have fought Myanmar's central state since independence in 1948 — the world's longest-running civil war.

timeline.heading: OPERATION 1027
timeline.body: In October 2023 the TNLA, MNDAA, and Arakan Army launched a coordinated offensive named for its start date — Oct 27 — that overran dozens of junta posts across northern Shan. It was the most serious military setback the army had suffered since seizing power in the 2021 coup, and it redrew control along the China border.

timeline.heading: WHY CHINA SITS AT THE TABLE
timeline.body: The blast hit a village 3 km from Yunnan. Beijing's pipelines, rare-earth imports, and trade corridors all run through this exact ground, which is why China — not the UN or ASEAN — repeatedly brokers and breaks the ceasefires between the junta and the border groups. Proximity gives Beijing leverage no other outside power has.

blocks.question: The TNLA belongs to which coalition behind the 2023 Operation 1027 offensive?
blocks.explanation: The Three Brotherhood Alliance unites the TNLA, MNDAA, and Arakan Army; the Tatmadaw is the junta army they fight.

2026-05-31-myanmar-shan-state-village-ex.label: Shan State & the Ethnic Armed Groups

timeline.heading: WHY GEOGRAPHY DECIDES THE FIGHT
timeline.body: In every river system the upstream user holds physical leverage — water must be released before it can reach the tail. Punjab sits at the head of Pakistan's canal network; Sindh sits at the tail. The Indus descends through a ladder of barrages, and whoever controls the upper gates shapes a shortage before the water ever moves south.

blocks.label: the Indus barrage ladder, head to tail
blocks.caption: Punjab's intakes lie upstream of Sindh's at Guddu, Sukkur, Kotri

timeline.heading: THE 1991 ACCORD
timeline.body: Pakistan's provinces don't share the Indus by goodwill — they share it by a fixed formula. The 1991 Water Apportionment Accord split the basin into province-by-province allocations and created IRSA to police them. Two giants dominate the table; the real contest is always Punjab versus Sindh.

timeline.heading: WHAT 'EQUALISING' ACTUALLY MEANS
timeline.body: When the river runs short, IRSA can spread the pain two ways: cut every province by the same percentage, or honour historical canal withdrawals first. 'Equalising' shortages means the same percentage cut for all — which Sindh objects to, because the baseline those percentages are measured against is itself disputed. The argument is never about the water alone; it is about which number you start from.

blocks.text: The accord's *three-tier formula* — fixed shares, historical use, and balance-of-river — was never fully operationalised, so each shortage reopens the question of **which rule governs the cut**.

timeline.heading: THE WATER THAT 'WASTES' INTO THE SEA
timeline.body: The accord deliberately reserves a flow to pass the last barrage at Kotri and reach the ocean. It looks like waste, but it isn't: without that freshwater pressure, the Arabian Sea pushes inland. Decades of upstream diversion have let seawater intrude tens of kilometres into the Indus delta, salting farmland and collapsing the mangrove fishery that once anchored southern Sindh.

blocks.question: Why does the accord reserve water to flow past the final barrage into the sea?
options: To hold back seawater intruding into the Indus delta
To meet treaty obligations with India
To maintain a shipping channel to Karachi
blocks.explanation: Freshwater flow below Kotri counters tidal seawater intrusion; without it, salt destroys delta farmland and fisheries.

timeline.heading: THE TRUST PROBLEM
timeline.body: Why does this dispute recur every dry season? Because there is no agreed measurement. IRSA installed a telemetry system to gauge flows automatically at each barrage, but it never worked reliably — so allocations rest on manual readings that each province accuses the other of fudging. With no neutral fact about how much water actually passed a gate, every shortage becomes a political negotiation rather than an engineering calculation.

timeline.heading: ARMIES RUN ON SUPPLY, NOT VALOR
timeline.body: A division in combat consumes hundreds of tons of fuel, shells, food, and water every day, all of it trucked forward from rail depots. Interdiction — striking those depots and routes rather than the troops themselves — is the cheapest way to break an offensive, because a gun without shells is scrap and a tank without diesel is a pillbox.

blocks.text: The doctrine has a name: *interdiction* — attacking the enemy's logistics in the rear so the front withers from starvation rather than from frontal assault. It is why air forces have always prized **rail junctions and fuel dumps** over front-line trenches.

timeline.heading: THE COST ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: The drone economy inverts the old math of war. A long-range strike drone costs a few tens of thousands of dollars; the ammunition depot or fuel train it destroys is worth orders of magnitude more, and the air-defense missile fired to stop it often costs more than the drone itself.

blocks.label: cost to attack vs cost to defend

timeline.heading: OPERATIONAL DEPTH
timeline.body: A strike 205 km behind the line is not a tactical poke — it reaches the rear echelon where supplies are marshaled before the final truck run forward. Holding that depth under threat forces an army to disperse depots, move them farther back, and lengthen its own supply lines, which slows every offensive whether or not a single depot is actually hit.

blocks.label: occupied Luhansk Oblast
blocks.caption: Drones reached supply routes deep inside occupied territory

timeline.heading: THE DONBAS BACKSTORY
timeline.body: Luhansk did not become a war zone in 2022. Russian-backed separatists declared a 'People's Republic' there in 2014, and the line of contact barely moved for eight years until the full-scale invasion. The 'occupied oblast' the drones now strike is the product of a conflict over a decade old.

timeline.heading: CONTROL IS NOT PRESENCE
timeline.body: A flag on a map claims a province; controlling it means the rear is safe enough to stockpile fuel and shells without losing them. When deep-strike drones range freely over the supply routes, the territory is held on paper but contested in practice — which is exactly why a drone operation can 'challenge' a declaration of full occupation.

blocks.question: Why do militaries prioritize striking supply depots over front-line troops?
options: Depots are easier to find than troops
A unit without fuel and ammunition cannot fight, at far lower cost than killing it
International law forbids targeting front-line soldiers
blocks.explanation: Interdiction breaks combat power cheaply: starve the supply and the guns, tanks, and trucks at the front become useless without a shot fired at them.

timeline.heading: THE CONTEXT TAX
timeline.body: A tool definition isn't called on demand — its full schema sits in the context window on every single turn, whether the model uses it or not. Connect four servers and you pay for all four descriptions, names, and parameter specs on every message, before the user has typed a word.

timeline.heading: WHY IT COMPOUNDS
timeline.body: Context bloat isn't just storage — transformer attention compares every token against every other token, so cost scales with the square of the length. Doubling the context roughly quadruples the work the model does on each generated token. Idle tool schemas are taxed on every word of every reply.

blocks.text: This is the **quadratic attention** problem: an N-token context costs on the order of **N²** compute. It's why a 21,000-token tool preamble is expensive even when no tool is ever called.

blocks.question: Why does a bloated context window slow down every response, not just consume memory?
options: Attention compares every token to every other, so compute grows with the square of length
The model re-reads the entire context aloud before answering
Longer contexts force the model to use a slower CPU fallback
blocks.explanation: Self-attention is O(N²): each new token attends to all prior tokens, so doubling context length roughly quadruples per-token compute.

timeline.heading: THE FIX: DEFER THE LOAD
timeline.body: Deferred loading flips the default: instead of injecting every tool schema upfront, the model is shown only a short index of tool names and fetches the full definition the moment it actually needs one. The heavy specs leave the context until they earn their place — the same idea as lazy-loading images that scroll into view.

blocks.text: The reported **85%** context cut comes not from better tools but from *not loading what you don't use yet* — a scheduling change, not a capability one.

timeline.heading: THE WINDOW IS FINITE
timeline.body: Every model has a hard context ceiling, and tools, system prompt, history, and the answer all compete for the same fixed pool. Burning 16.5% of a 128k window on idle schemas means that much less room for the document, the code, or the conversation the user actually came for.

timeline.heading: THE PROTOCOL TRADEOFF
timeline.body: MCP's pitch is interoperability — one standard socket so any model can talk to any tool, the 'USB-C for AI' framing. But standards always tax the common case to serve the general one: the same critique sank SOAP's verbose XML envelopes in favor of leaner REST. A protocol that wins on connectivity can still lose on the overhead it imposes per call.

blocks.text: It's the recurring systems tradeoff: **generality** (any tool, any model) bought with **overhead** (schema weight on every turn). The winner is usually whoever shrinks the tax without giving up the socket.

timeline.heading: WHY LAW ALWAYS LAGS
timeline.body: Regulation is reactive by design: legislators must observe a harm before they can name it, draft a rule, and pass it. Technology deploys on engineering timelines measured in months; law moves on parliamentary timelines measured in years. The gap is structural, not a failure of any one government — it is the same lag that left social media, gene editing, and ride-hailing unregulated during their fastest growth.

timeline.heading: THE BRUSSELS EFFECT
timeline.body: Most countries do not write AI rules from scratch — they import them. The EU's GDPR became the de-facto global privacy template because multinationals found it cheaper to apply one standard everywhere than to maintain separate ones. The EU AI Act (2024), the world's first comprehensive AI law, is now exporting the same way. Ecuador's eventual rulebook will likely be a localized echo of Brussels, not an original draft.

blocks.text: The pattern has a name: the **Brussels Effect** — the EU exports regulation through market size alone, without treaties or pressure, because compliance scales cheaper than fragmentation.

timeline.heading: THE COORDINATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: When ministries, regulators, and academia advance on separate timelines with no coordinating authority, the result is not no policy — it is contradictory policy. One agency may procure facial-recognition cameras while another drafts a privacy code that would ban them. The absence of a single owner is itself the governance failure the forum is trying to fix.

timeline.heading: SURVEILLANCE FIRST, RULES LATER
timeline.body: Across Latin America the sequence is consistent: states acquire surveillance capability — Chinese-built 'safe city' camera networks, biometric ID systems, predictive policing tools — before any legal framework governs their use. Ecuador's own ECU-911 emergency network, built with Chinese technology, is a surveillance backbone that predates any AI law that would constrain it. Capability outruns law, and the law inherits a fait accompli.

timeline.heading: THE THREE REGULATORY MODELS
timeline.body: The world has converged on three rival approaches. The EU regulates by risk tier — banning some uses outright, auditing others. The US relies on sectoral rules and litigation after the fact. China governs AI as an instrument of state control, mandating alignment with social stability. A latecomer like Ecuador must effectively pick a parent model, and that choice shapes everything downstream.

timeline.heading: WHO WRITES THE RULES
timeline.body: A 60-stakeholder forum sounds inclusive, but multi-stakeholder bodies without binding authority tend to produce consensus documents rather than enforceable law. The reader should know which institution can actually compel compliance.

blocks.question: What most often determines whether an AI 'governance forum' produces real rules?
options: Whether it has binding legal authority to enforce outcomes
The number of stakeholders who attend
blocks.explanation: Without an enforcement mandate, forums generate recommendations; only a body with statutory power can turn them into binding rules.

timeline.heading: THE INDIGENOUS DEFICIT
timeline.body: Brand Africa surveys consumers across the continent for the brands they most admire — and African-owned names take only about 15% of the top 100. On a continent of 1.4 billion people, the brands Africans love most are overwhelmingly foreign.

blocks.text: The survey separates *admiration* from ownership: a brand can feel African — built around local marketing — while its profits flow abroad. **Indigenous** means African-owned, and that is the share stuck near **15%**.

timeline.heading: WHY FOREIGN BRANDS WIN
timeline.body: The pattern traces to a colonial trade structure that never fully unwound: African economies were built to export raw commodities — cocoa, oil, copper — and import finished goods. Branding is the final, highest-margin step of manufacturing, and that step was historically located outside the continent.

blocks.label: Brand Africa most-admired — top names by origin

timeline.heading: THE VERTICAL EMPIRE
timeline.body: Dangote's model is integration, not diversification: cement needs limestone and energy, fertiliser needs gas, and a refinery supplies the fuel that moves all of it. Each business feeds the next, so the group captures margins competitors must buy on the open market.

blocks.text: Cement is the foundation — Dangote is Africa's largest producer — but the *crown* is the **Lekki refinery**: a single 650,000-barrel-a-day train, the largest of its kind in the world.

timeline.heading: THE REFINERY PARADOX
timeline.body: Nigeria is Africa's largest crude oil producer, yet for decades it imported almost all of its refined petrol — pumping crude out and buying fuel back at a premium because its state refineries barely functioned. Dangote's plant exists to close that gap.

blocks.question: Before the Dangote refinery, why did oil-rich Nigeria import most of its petrol?
options: It had no crude oil reserves of its own
Its state-owned refineries had collapsed to near-zero output
OPEC rules banned it from refining domestically
Refined fuel was cheaper to import than crude to export
blocks.explanation: Nigeria exported crude but its four state refineries ran far below capacity for years, forcing it to re-import refined product.

timeline.heading: WHAT A BRAND IS WORTH
timeline.body: A brand is an economic moat: it lets a firm charge more than a generic rival for the same physical product, and that premium compounds into pricing power, easier financing, and resilience in downturns. The 15% deficit is therefore a measure of where the continent's pricing power sits — mostly offshore.

timeline.heading: POLICING VERSUS WAR
timeline.body: Two legal regimes govern killing. Law enforcement may use lethal force only against an imminent threat, must attempt arrest, and owes suspects a trial. Armed conflict lets a state kill enemy combatants on sight. For decades, drug interdiction lived entirely on the first side of that line — the Coast Guard boards a vessel, seizes the cargo, and arrests the crew for prosecution. A strike that kills the crew treats them as combatants, not suspects.

blocks.text: The crucial legal phrase is *hostis humani generis* — "enemy of all mankind," historically applied to pirates, who could be attacked anywhere. Reclassifying traffickers under a war framework is what makes killing-without-trial arguable at all.

timeline.heading: THE TERRORIST DESIGNATION
timeline.body: The pivot that converts a smuggler into a target is the Foreign Terrorist Organization label. Once a cartel is designated, the government can argue trafficking is not crime but armed attack, and reach for the war powers Congress passed after 9/11 rather than the criminal code.

blocks.text: An **FTO** designation was built for groups like al-Qaeda; applying it to drug networks imports the entire post-9/11 lethal-targeting toolkit into a domain that was law enforcement the day before.

timeline.heading: THE TARGETED-KILLING PRECEDENT
timeline.body: The legal machinery here was not invented for boats. It was built incrementally — a 2001 authorization to use force, then a 2011 drone strike that killed a US citizen in Yemen without trial, each step widening who could be killed, where, and on whose say-so.

events.label: al-Awlaki killed by drone, no trial

timeline.heading: WHY THE OPEN SEA
timeline.body: The strikes happen on the water for a reason. The Posse Comitatus Act bars the US military from domestic policing, and a strike on land would need host-nation consent. International waters are the one arena where neither constraint bites — no foreign sovereign to ask, no domestic-policing bar to clear.

blocks.label: the interdiction zone
blocks.caption: strikes reported in Caribbean and eastern Pacific waters

timeline.heading: THE SUPPLY GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: Nearly all the world's cocaine originates in just three Andean countries, with Colombia far ahead. The maritime routes the strikes target are the seaward end of that funnel — the Pacific run from Colombia's Nariño coast and the Caribbean run toward Central America.

blocks.label: global cocaine production by origin (approx. share)

timeline.heading: THE OVERSIGHT GAP
timeline.body: A criminal prosecution produces a public record — charges, evidence, a verdict that can be appealed. A strike produces a body and a press release. With no charges filed and no hearings held, there is no forum in which the government's claim that a given boat carried traffickers is ever tested.

blocks.question: Historically, what happened when US forces intercepted a suspected drug vessel at sea?
options: The vessel was boarded, cargo seized, and crew arrested for trial
The vessel was sunk on sight
The crew was killed and the boat impounded
The vessel was escorted to international court
blocks.explanation: Maritime drug interdiction was a law-enforcement operation — the Coast Guard boarded, seized, and arrested for prosecution; lethal strikes are the new departure.

timeline.heading: WHY THERE'S A RUNOFF
timeline.body: Colombia elects its president by absolute majority. If no candidate clears 50% in the first round, the top two meet three weeks later. The system forces a left-right showdown that the first round, with its splintered field, only previews.

blocks.question: What triggers a second-round runoff in Colombia's presidential election?
options: No candidate wins an absolute majority in round one
The top two candidates finish within 5 points
Congress fails to certify a winner
blocks.explanation: A candidate must clear 50%+1; otherwise the top two advance to a runoff, which is why a fragmented field almost guarantees a second round.

timeline.heading: THE PETRO BREAK
timeline.body: Gustavo Petro, elected in 2022, was Colombia's first leftist president — a former M-19 guerrilla in a country governed by conservative and centrist elites since its founding. Cepeda's candidacy is an attempt to make that break permanent rather than a one-term anomaly.

timeline.heading: PLAN COLOMBIA
timeline.body: From 2000, Washington poured roughly $10bn into Colombia — military aid, aerial coca spraying, counterinsurgency. It made Colombia the closest US security partner in Latin America. De la Espriella's pledge to resume fumigation is a promise to restore that alignment; Petro's drug policy quietly buried it.

timeline.heading: THE FUMIGATION FIGHT
timeline.body: Colombia suspended aerial glyphosate spraying in 2015 after its health agency flagged the herbicide as a probable carcinogen and the Constitutional Court demanded safeguards. Restarting it isn't just a policy switch — it's a legal battle, which is why the promise signals a whole governing posture.

blocks.text: The herbicide is *glyphosate* — the active ingredient in Roundup. Its 2015 suspension was driven by a WHO cancer classification, making the spray plane a courtroom question as much as a coca one.

timeline.heading: WHY THE WORLD WATCHES COCA
timeline.body: Colombia grows the majority of the world's cocaine, far ahead of Peru and Bolivia. Whoever governs in Bogotá sets the supply policy for a global market — which is why a domestic vote becomes a US foreign-policy concern.

timeline.heading: THE URIBE SHADOW
timeline.body: Colombia's right has organized around Álvaro Uribe for two decades — his hardline 'democratic security' doctrine defined an era. The right's splintering in this race reflects life after Uribe: no single heir commands the coalition he once held together.

blocks.label: Colombia and its neighbors
blocks.caption: Border instability shapes the security debate as much as Washington does.

timeline.heading: WHY AUTONOMY IS HARD
timeline.body: An agent that is 99% reliable on a single step is not 99% reliable on a task. Reliability multiplies across steps, so a 50-step workflow at 99% per step succeeds only about 60% of the time. The longer the chain, the steeper the cliff — which is why demos impress and production disappoints.

blocks.text: The math is unforgiving: **0.99⁵⁰ ≈ 0.61**. To hit **99%** reliability over 50 steps, each step must clear **99.98%** — a different engineering problem entirely.

blocks.question: An AI agent that is 99% reliable per step is roughly how reliable across a 50-step task?
blocks.explanation: Per-step reliability compounds multiplicatively: 0.99^50 ≈ 0.61, so errors accumulate far faster than intuition suggests.

timeline.heading: WHY A CHIPMAKER IS THE TELL
timeline.body: Marvell builds none of the AI models in the headlines — it makes the custom silicon and optical interconnects that wire datacenter accelerators together. When a networking-chip CEO forecasts demand, it is the 'picks and shovels' signal: infrastructure capex is committed years before the applications that justify it pay off.

timeline.heading: THE VERIFICATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: The bottleneck is not getting an agent to act — it is knowing whether the action was correct without a human checking each step. For many real tasks, verifying the answer is nearly as hard as producing it, so 'autonomous' systems quietly require a human in the loop, which erases most of the promised savings.

timeline.heading: THE GHOST OF EXPERT SYSTEMS
timeline.body: This is not the first wave of autonomous-reasoning hype. 1980s expert systems promised to encode professional judgment into software; they sold for billions, then collapsed into the second AI winter because they were brittle at every edge case the rules did not anticipate. Each cycle since has overpromised autonomy and underdelivered reliability.

timeline.heading: THE EXECUTION GAP
timeline.body: Tracking returns is not the same as earning them. That 72% of enterprise leaders now measure AI ROI signals seriousness, but measurement tends to precede payoff — the same pattern seen with ERP in the 1990s and cloud migration in the 2010s, where benefits trailed spending by years while organizations rebuilt processes around the tool.

timeline.heading: THE TURF WAR
timeline.body: The Clarity Act is fundamentally a jurisdiction bill: does a tokenised asset answer to the SEC (securities) or the CFTC (commodities)? The stakes are lopsided — the CFTC is a fraction of the SEC's size, so handing it crypto means handing a vast new market to a far smaller cop.

timeline.heading: THE HOWEY TEST
timeline.body: Whether something is a 'security' in the US has turned on one 1946 Supreme Court case about Florida orange groves. SEC v. Howey set a four-part test — money invested in a common enterprise with profit expected from others' efforts — that still decides whether a token falls under the SEC's reach.

blocks.text: The case wasn't about stocks at all — it was about selling rows of orange trees plus a service contract to tend them. The Court held the *package*, not the fruit, was an **investment contract**, and that logic now governs tokens.

blocks.question: Which test determines whether an asset counts as a 'security' under US law?
blocks.explanation: SEC v. Howey (1946) set the four-prong investment-contract test still used to classify tokens today.

timeline.heading: WHAT TOKENISING ACTUALLY CHANGES
timeline.body: Putting an equity or treasury 'on-chain' doesn't change the asset — it changes the plumbing of ownership. Today a stock trade settles two days after you click buy; the promise of tokenisation is settlement in seconds, with payment and delivery happening in the same instant.

blocks.text: The current standard is **T+2** — trade date plus two days. Tokenised markets aim for **atomic settlement**: the asset and the cash swap simultaneously, so neither side can default mid-transaction.

timeline.heading: THE PAPERWORK PRECEDENT
timeline.body: America already lived through one settlement revolution. In the late 1960s, Wall Street volume buried back offices in physical stock certificates — the 'paperwork crisis' forced exchanges to close on Wednesdays just to catch up. The fix was to stop moving paper: the DTCC was created to hold certificates centrally and settle by ledger entry. Tokenisation is the next step in that same 50-year arc.

events.label: DTC founded to end paper certificates

timeline.heading: WHY THE LABEL IS THE WHOLE GAME
timeline.body: Classification isn't bureaucratic trivia — it dictates disclosure rules, who can trade, custody requirements, and enforcement powers. The same token treated as a commodity faces light-touch CFTC oversight; treated as a security, it inherits the full registration burden built for IPOs. The 12-month rulemaking is a fight over which rulebook a trillion-dollar market inherits.

timeline.heading: WHAT AN ANALOG MISSION IS
timeline.body: You cannot send researchers to Mars to study what the trip does to them, so space agencies build the trip on Earth — sealed habitats, polar stations, submarines, now a sail-training ship. The hardware is irrelevant; the goal is to reproduce the human stressors: confinement, isolation, monotony, and a crew that cannot walk away from each other.

timeline.heading: THE LINEAGE
timeline.body: ICE-Blue joins a decades-long tradition. The benchmark is Mars500 — six men locked in a Moscow mock-spacecraft for 520 days in 2010-11, the full duration of a round trip. Antarctica's Concordia station and Hawaii's HI-SEAS habitat run the same experiment in real isolation.

timeline.heading: WHY THE NUMBER MATTERS
timeline.body: A minimum-energy transfer to Mars takes roughly seven to nine months one way, dictated by orbital mechanics — you launch only in the ~26-month window when the planets align. 107 days is a partial analog of the outbound leg, long enough to surface the psychological breakdowns that short missions never reach.

timeline.heading: THE SLEEP TRAP
timeline.body: On a spacecraft there is no sunrise to anchor the body clock, and crews drift into fragmented, shortened sleep within weeks. A Mars surface day — a 'sol' — runs 24 hours 39 minutes, just long enough that the human circadian system cannot lock onto it, the same mismatch that wrecks the sleep of the rover-operations teams on Earth.

blocks.text: A Martian day is a **sol**, 39 minutes longer than ours. That tiny surplus compounds: it shifts your schedule about *40 minutes later each day*, the same jet-lag-without-end that ground crews running Mars rovers report after a few weeks.

timeline.heading: THE THIRD-QUARTER PHENOMENON
timeline.body: Isolation researchers find morale does not decline steadily — it sags hardest after the midpoint, once the novelty is gone but the end is not yet in sight. This 'third-quarter phenomenon' shows up in Antarctic winter-overs and submarine patrols alike, which is why the back half of a confinement study yields the most useful data.

blocks.question: Why is sending astronauts to Mars constrained to roughly one launch window every 26 months?
options: Rockets need that long to refuel and refit
Earth and Mars only align favorably for a low-energy transfer that often
Solar radiation peaks on a 26-month cycle
Crews need 26 months of training between flights
blocks.explanation: Orbital mechanics: the cheapest Earth-to-Mars trajectory only exists when the two planets reach the right relative position, which recurs about every 26 months.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE SHIP CAN'T FAKE
timeline.body: The sea reproduces confinement and crew dynamics, but not microgravity — and that is where the body actually fails. In freefall, bone demineralizes at roughly 1-2% per month, fluids shift toward the head and reshape the eye, and muscles atrophy without load. The ICE-Blue samples test the mind; the Axiom-3 astronaut samples it's compared against carry the physiology a ship can never simulate.

timeline.heading: TWO NICARAGUAS
timeline.body: Nicaragua's Caribbean coast was never really Spanish. For two centuries it was a British protectorate — the Mosquito Kingdom — Anglican, English-speaking, and self-governing, while Spanish Catholic Nicaragua ruled the Pacific side. Managua only absorbed the coast by force in 1894, an event the coast still calls 'the Reincorporation,' not the unification.

blocks.label: the Miskito Coast
blocks.caption: Indigenous autonomous regions on Nicaragua's Caribbean edge

timeline.heading: WHO THE MISKITO ARE
timeline.body: The Miskito are an indigenous people of the Caribbean lowlands, distinct in language, religion, and history from the Spanish-speaking Pacific majority. Through centuries of contact with British traders and escaped slaves, their identity fused indigenous, African, and English strands — which is why their politics has always been about autonomy, not assimilation.

blocks.text: Rivera co-founded *YATAMA* — Yapti Tasba Masraka Nanih Aslatakanka, 'the children of Mother Earth' — the Miskito political movement that fought first the Sandinistas, then ran as an opposition party.

timeline.heading: RED CHRISTMAS
timeline.body: When the Sandinistas took power in 1979, they treated coastal autonomy as counter-revolution. In 1981-82 the army forcibly relocated thousands of Miskito inland and burned villages — an episode the Miskito call Navidad Roja, 'Red Christmas.' Rivera took up arms then; the regime that jailed him in 2023 was the same one he first resisted four decades earlier.

timeline.heading: THE FAMILY STATE
timeline.body: Ortega returned to power in 2007 and never left. Power is now openly dynastic: his wife Rosario Murillo, long the regime's spokesperson and vice president, was elevated to co-president — making Nicaragua one of the few states with a formal husband-and-wife executive.

timeline.heading: WHY 'DISAPPEARANCE' IS A LEGAL TERM
timeline.body: Enforced disappearance is not loose language. Under international law it means state agents detain a person and then refuse to acknowledge the detention or reveal their whereabouts — placing the victim outside all legal protection. It is classed as a crime against humanity precisely because withholding information about the prisoner is itself the weapon. Refusing to return a body to the family extends that crime past death.

blocks.question: What made Nicaragua's Caribbean coast historically distinct from the rest of the country?
options: It was a British protectorate, not Spanish-ruled
It was never inhabited until the 20th century
It was a Portuguese colony like Brazil
blocks.explanation: The Mosquito Coast was a British protectorate — Anglican and English-speaking — until Nicaragua annexed it by force in 1894.

timeline.heading: THE TERRITORY THAT ISN'T A PROVINCE
timeline.body: Gilgit-Baltistan is administered by Pakistan but has never been made a constitutional province. It is not named in the constitution, its residents do not vote for the National Assembly, and it has no Supreme Court representation — a population of roughly two million in permanent legal suspension.

blocks.label: Gilgit-Baltistan at the junction
blocks.caption: Borders China, the Afghan Wakhan, and Indian-administered Kashmir

timeline.heading: WHY KASHMIR FREEZES ITS STATUS
timeline.body: Pakistan refuses to formally annex Gilgit-Baltistan because doing so would contradict its own position that the entire Kashmir dispute must be settled by a UN-mandated plebiscite. To absorb GB as a province would concede that borders can be redrawn unilaterally — the exact argument Pakistan makes against India. So the territory stays in limbo to protect a diplomatic claim.

timeline.heading: THE 1949 HANDOVER
timeline.body: Under the Karachi Agreement of 1949, the Azad Kashmir government ceded administration of the region — then called the Northern Areas — directly to Pakistan's federal government. That single agreement, signed by parties with no GB representatives present, is why the region has been governed from Islamabad rather than locally ever since.

timeline.heading: ELECTIONS MANAGED FROM ISLAMABAD
timeline.body: The 2009 order created an elected Gilgit-Baltistan Assembly, but real authority sits with federal appointees and the centre retains power over key portfolios. Because the territory lacks constitutional protection, the safeguards a province takes for granted — judicial review, an entrenched election commission — are weaker here, which is precisely what makes pre-poll rigging allegations harder to adjudicate.

blocks.text: The deployment of **6,000 Punjab police** — an out-of-territory force from Pakistan's largest province — into a region with no provincial police autonomy is itself the story: GB cannot insulate its own vote.

timeline.heading: WHY THE CENTRE CARES SO MUCH
timeline.body: Gilgit-Baltistan is the only land link between Pakistan and China. The Karakoram Highway and the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor both run through it, and it borders China's Xinjiang directly. A territory this strategically valuable is one Islamabad has every incentive to control tightly — and little incentive to fully empower.

blocks.question: Why has Pakistan never made Gilgit-Baltistan a full constitutional province?
options: Its population is too small to qualify
Doing so would undercut Pakistan's UN-plebiscite position on Kashmir
The region voted against provincial status
China objects to any change in its legal status
blocks.explanation: Formal annexation would contradict Pakistan's stance that all of Kashmir's fate must be decided by plebiscite — so GB is left in limbo.

timeline.heading: THE BOTTLENECK
timeline.body: Hormuz is 33 km wide at its narrowest, but the usable shipping lanes are only about 3 km in each direction, separated by a buffer. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil — around 20 million barrels a day — funnels through that thread. There is no wider stretch to spread the traffic out.

blocks.label: the Hormuz chokepoint
blocks.caption: shipping lanes hug the Omani side; Iran's coast runs the northern edge

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: The strait sits between Iran and Oman, not Iran and any Arab Gulf state. Iran's coastline runs along the entire northern edge, and the deepest channel hugs the Iranian side — which is why Iranian naval positioning matters out of all proportion to its fleet's size.

blocks.question: The Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes pass between Iran and which country?
blocks.explanation: The lanes run through Omani territorial waters on the southern side, with Iran on the north — not any Arab Gulf state.

timeline.heading: WHY THE NAVY ESCORTS
timeline.body: Convoying merchant ships under a flag's protection is an old answer to an old problem. In 1987 the US reflagged Kuwaiti tankers as American and escorted them through the same strait during the Iran-Iraq Tanker War — Operation Earnest Will. Coordinating 70 crossings today is a quieter version of the same move: a state navy lending its flag to commercial hulls.

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: What actually closes a sea lane is rarely the threat itself — it is the price of insuring against it. When Lloyd's war-risk premiums spike, commercial vessels reroute or refuse to sail regardless of how many ships are still getting through. A US escort matters partly because it can hold those premiums down.

blocks.text: The binding constraint is financial, not physical: a *war-risk surcharge* of even **0.5% of hull value** per voyage can erase a tanker's margin and freeze traffic before a single shot is fired.

timeline.heading: WHY IT CAN'T BE BYPASSED
timeline.body: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah line were built partly as Hormuz hedges, but together they can reroute only a fraction of Gulf exports. Most barrels have no alternative path to open water.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL REGIME
timeline.body: Under UNCLOS Article 38, ships have a right of 'transit passage' through international straits — coastal states cannot suspend it or impose conditions. Iran signed the convention in 1982 but never ratified it, and argues Hormuz is governed by its own domestic law. That gap is the legal hinge every standoff turns on.

timeline.heading: THE WORD MEANS NOTHING ALONE
timeline.body: Everything biodegrades eventually — a steel beam, a glass bottle, given enough centuries. "Biodegradable" without a stated timeframe and environment is technically true and practically empty. That is precisely why marketers love it: no regulator can call it a lie.

timeline.heading: THREE WORDS THAT ARE NOT SYNONYMS
timeline.body: Bio-based means made from plants, not that it breaks down. Biodegradable means microbes can consume it, but says nothing about speed or conditions. Compostable is the only one with a legal bar — it must fully break down within a set time under defined composting conditions. A cup can be bio-based and still last for decades.

blocks.text: The poster child is **PLA** (polylactic acid), made from corn starch. It is bio-based *and* compostable — but only in an **industrial composter** running near **58°C**. In your garden bin or the ocean, it behaves like ordinary plastic.

timeline.heading: THE TEMPERATURE TRAP
timeline.body: Industrial composting holds material at roughly 55–60°C for weeks — hot enough for the microbial activity that cracks these polymers apart. Landfills are anaerobic and cool; oceans are cold and salty. The lab certificate that says "compostable" was earned in an oven the discarded item will almost never see.

blocks.label: where a PLA cup actually ends up

timeline.heading: DEGRADES INTO WHAT
timeline.body: The first of the three questions is the one labels never answer. Some plastics don't mineralize into CO2 and water — they just fragment into microplastics, which are arguably worse than the intact item because they enter food chains and water supplies invisibly.

timeline.heading: THE OXO-PLASTIC CAUTIONARY TALE
timeline.body: "Oxo-degradable" plastics were sold for years as a green fix: metal additives made them crumble in sunlight. They crumbled into microplastics. The EU banned them outright in 2021 under the Single-Use Plastics Directive — a rare case of a green claim being legislated off the shelf.

events.label: EU science review finds microplastic risk

timeline.heading: THE CERTIFICATION YOU CAN TRUST
timeline.body: Reputable compostable goods carry a standard mark — EN 13432 in Europe or ASTM D6400 in the US — which requires ~90% breakdown within a set period under industrial conditions, with no toxic residue. The absence of such a mark beside a "biodegradable" claim is itself the tell.

blocks.question: A label says "100% biodegradable" with no other detail. What does that guarantee?
options: It will break down in your home compost
It will break down in the ocean if littered
Almost nothing — no timeframe or conditions are specified
It is made entirely from plants
blocks.explanation: Without a stated environment and timeframe, "biodegradable" is unverifiable — which is why certified marks like EN 13432 specify both.

timeline.heading: WHY "UNTREATABLE"
timeline.body: Every approved Ebola countermeasure — the Ervebo vaccine, the Inmazeb and Ebanga antibody drugs — was built against one species: Zaire ebolavirus. They target that virus's surface glycoprotein, and Bundibugyo's is different enough that none is licensed to work against it. The strain isn't untreatable because it's deadlier; it's untreatable because the toolkit was built for a different relative.

blocks.text: The vaccines and drugs lock onto the viral **glycoprotein** — the spike on the virus surface. Across Ebola species that protein diverges by *30–40%*, enough that a Zaire-tuned antibody simply doesn't grip Bundibugyo.

timeline.heading: ONE NAME, SIX VIRUSES
timeline.body: "Ebola" is a genus, not a single virus. Its species differ sharply in lethality — Zaire has killed up to nine in ten of the infected, while Reston, found in monkeys, has never made a human sick. Bundibugyo sits in the middle, which is part of why five patients could pull through on supportive care alone.

timeline.heading: NAMED FOR A UGANDAN DISTRICT
timeline.body: Bundibugyo was first identified in 2007 in Bundibugyo District, western Uganda, on the same border the strain is now crossing back into. The virus's named home and its current spillover sit barely a hundred kilometres apart, across the Rwenzori range — which is why Uganda's case count moves in lockstep with DRC's.

timeline.heading: HOW PEOPLE RECOVER WITHOUT A DRUG
timeline.body: Ebola kills mainly through fluid loss and shock, not the virus directly. Aggressive supportive care — intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction, treating secondary infections — buys time for the patient's own antibodies to clear the virus. Where that care exists, survival roughly doubles, which is what "five recovered" actually measures.

timeline.heading: WHY IT KEEPS STARTING HERE
timeline.body: Ebola was first identified in 1976 near the Ebola River in what is now DRC, and the country has had more outbreaks than anywhere on Earth. The reservoir is thought to be fruit bats; spillover happens at the forest edge through bushmeat and bat contact. Dense rainforest, hunting economies, and weak rural health systems make the Congo Basin the virus's recurring launchpad.

blocks.question: Approved Ebola vaccines and antibody drugs protect against which species?
blocks.explanation: Licensed vaccines and antibody therapies target Zaire ebolavirus's glycoprotein, leaving strains like Bundibugyo without an approved countermeasure.

timeline.heading: THE GATEKEEPER
timeline.body: India's instant payments — UPI and IMPS — don't run through the central bank. They run through the NPCI, a non-profit owned by a consortium of banks. It is not formally a regulator, but its refusal to confirm that Coinbase could use UPI in 2022 was enough to freeze the rails. Access to a private network, not a law, was the chokepoint.

blocks.text: **NPCI** clears over 10 billion **UPI** transactions a month — the largest real-time retail payments system on Earth. A nod from it is worth more than a banking licence.

timeline.heading: THE SHADOW BAN
timeline.body: India's crypto fight is older than this block. In 2018 the RBI ordered banks to stop servicing crypto businesses — no formal ban, just cut off the banking pipes. The Supreme Court struck it down in 2020 as a disproportionate restriction on a legitimate trade. Regulators then switched tactics from prohibition to taxation.

timeline.heading: THE 1% BLEED
timeline.body: The real weapon wasn't prohibition. In 2022 India imposed a flat 30% tax on crypto gains and — more crippling — a 1% tax deducted at source on every single trade. A high-frequency trader churning capital loses 1% each round trip regardless of profit. Domestic exchange volume collapsed as traders fled to offshore platforms within months.

timeline.heading: WHY INDIA RANKS FIRST
timeline.body: Chainalysis ranks India first in adoption because its index weights grassroots retail usage — small transactions, peer-to-peer trade, savings — not raw dollar volume. By that measure a populous country with broad, decentralized usage outranks wealthy markets where a few institutions move billions. Adoption is a headcount, not a balance sheet.

blocks.label: where grassroots crypto adoption is highest

blocks.question: Why does India top the global crypto adoption index despite smaller transaction sizes?
options: The index weights grassroots retail usage over dollar volume
India has the most crypto exchanges by count
The rupee is pegged to Bitcoin
India holds the largest national Bitcoin reserve
blocks.explanation: Chainalysis weights population-adjusted, peer-to-peer and retail activity — so broad small-scale usage outranks a few large institutional flows.

timeline.heading: WHAT PERPETUALS ARE
timeline.body: Perpetual futures — the dominant crypto derivative — are contracts that never expire, unlike traditional futures with a settlement date. To keep their price tethered to spot, exchanges charge a funding rate: when the contract trades above spot, longs pay shorts every few hours, and vice versa. It's a self-correcting leash invented for crypto's 24/7 markets.

blocks.text: The *funding rate* is the whole trick: a periodic payment between traders that pulls the perpetual back toward spot without ever forcing settlement. BitMEX pioneered it in **2016**.

timeline.heading: THE ROTATION TRAP
timeline.body: Power-sharing pacts where two leaders agree to split a term rarely survive contact with office. The leader who holds the chair first accumulates patronage, controls the police and the treasury, and discovers reasons the handover must wait. The 2.5-year swap is a ceasefire, not a settlement.

timeline.heading: WHY KARNATAKA IS THE PRIZE
timeline.body: Karnataka is one of India's largest state economies, anchored by Bengaluru. Control of the state means control of its budget, land allocations, and contracts — which is why neither faction would yield. Among Indian states it sits near the top of the output table.

timeline.heading: BENGALURU, THE ENGINE
timeline.body: Bengaluru is India's software capital — the single largest source of the country's IT-services exports, home to the campuses of Infosys, Wipro, and the Indian arms of nearly every global tech firm. The city's tax base and global visibility make the chief ministership a national-tier post, not a regional one.

blocks.question: Which Indian state contributes the largest share of the country's IT-services exports?
blocks.explanation: Bengaluru alone accounts for the bulk of India's software exports, putting Karnataka ahead of Hyderabad's Telangana and Mumbai's Maharashtra.

timeline.heading: WHAT A CHIEF MINISTER ACTUALLY CONTROLS
timeline.body: Under India's federal scheme, states hold their own list of subjects — police, land, agriculture, public health, local industry. The chief minister is the real executive over all of these; the centrally-appointed Governor is largely ceremonial. This is why a state CM commands more day-to-day power than the post's modest title suggests.

blocks.text: India's constitution divides authority into a *Union List*, a *State List*, and a *Concurrent List* — policing and land sit squarely on the **State List**, which is the chief minister's domain.

timeline.heading: THE HIGH COMMAND
timeline.body: Congress is run on a 'high command' model — final say on state leadership rests with the central party leadership in Delhi, not the state legislators. The Karnataka deadlock was resolved not by a vote but by a brokered arrangement handed down from above, the party's defining decision-making habit since the Indira Gandhi era.

timeline.heading: THE CAST
timeline.body: The two men splitting the term came up through different bases — Siddaramaiah as a mass-backed welfare politician, Shivakumar as the party's organizational fixer and fundraiser. Cabinet posts, including a role for Siddaramaiah's son, are the currency of the handover.

timeline.heading: THE FREE-TEXT FIELD
timeline.body: A Bluetooth device name is not a credential — it is an arbitrary string the owner types in, broadcast in the clear inside the advertising packets every device emits so others can discover it. Nothing checks it, signs it, or ties it to a real identity. 'BOMB' is as valid a name as 'AirPods'.

blocks.text: The name rides in the **advertising packet** — the same beacon that lets your phone *find* a speaker before any pairing or password. Discovery happens before authentication, by design.

timeline.heading: WHY YOU CAN'T TRACE IT
timeline.body: Broadcast discovery is one-way and anonymous: a name appears in range but reveals no sender, no seat, no account. On a 250-seat cabin there is no protocol-level way to learn which passenger set it, so crew cannot quietly resolve the source — only react to the whole aircraft.

timeline.heading: THE ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: Aviation security runs on a deliberately lopsided cost function: a missed real threat is catastrophic and irreversible, a false alarm is merely expensive. Once a credible-looking bomb signal exists and cannot be ruled out, the precautionary rule forces the costly action every time — the prank wins because the downside of ignoring it is unbounded.

blocks.text: This is the **precautionary principle** colliding with a near-zero **base rate**: almost every such alert is a hoax, yet the one that isn't dominates the math, so the rational response stays 'land the plane'.

timeline.heading: THE SAME BUG, EVERYWHERE
timeline.body: This isn't a Bluetooth flaw — it's a property of every short-range discovery protocol that lets a stranger broadcast a self-chosen label to nearby devices. The same unauthenticated free-text field has triggered scares across multiple technologies.

blocks.label: names anyone in range can set

timeline.heading: THE HOAX IS A FELONY
timeline.body: A bomb joke is not legally a joke. Under US law a false threat against an aircraft is a federal crime carrying years of prison regardless of intent, and the airline can separately sue to recover the cost of the diversion — fuel dumped to reach landing weight, crew hours, rebooking, and the aircraft out of rotation.

blocks.question: Why can't crew simply ignore an anonymous Bluetooth name reading 'BOMB'?
options: The name can carry malware that infects the avionics
There's no way to identify who set it or rule out a real threat
Bluetooth must be disabled for the autopilot to function
FAA rules ban all Bluetooth devices in flight
blocks.explanation: Broadcast names reveal no sender, so the threat can't be located or dismissed — and the cost of being wrong is total, forcing the precautionary response.

timeline.heading: WHY COAST GUARD, NOT NAVY
timeline.body: A warship in disputed water is an act of war; a white-hulled coast guard cutter is 'law enforcement.' By sending the Coast Guard, Beijing asserts that the water is its own jurisdiction to police — a sovereignty claim dressed as routine patrol, and far harder for a rival to fire on.

blocks.text: This is the **gray zone**: coercion calibrated to stay below the threshold of armed conflict, where the other side has no clean military response.

timeline.heading: THE WORLD'S LARGEST COAST GUARD
timeline.body: China's Coast Guard is not a customs service — it is a paramilitary fleet larger by tonnage than most navies, including cutters that dwarf anything its neighbors float. Its flagship, the 'Monster,' displaces more than a guided-missile destroyer.

timeline.heading: THE FIRST ISLAND CHAIN
timeline.body: Cold War planners drew a line of US-aligned territory — Japan, the Ryukyus, Taiwan, the Philippines — that walls China's navy into its near seas. Patrolling EAST of Taiwan is the point: it puts Chinese hulls on the Pacific side of that wall, signaling the chain no longer contains them.

blocks.label: the first island chain
blocks.caption: the arc that walls China's fleet into its near seas

timeline.heading: THE CABBAGE STRATEGY
timeline.body: China layers its presence like leaves of a cabbage: fishing-boat 'maritime militia' on the inside, Coast Guard around them, navy held over the horizon. Each layer lets the next deny involvement, so a contested reef gets wrapped without a single shot fired.

blocks.question: Why is China patrolling EAST of Taiwan more provocative than patrolling the Taiwan Strait?
options: It is the Pacific side, beyond the first island chain meant to contain China
The water there is too deep for coast guard ships
It is internationally recognized Japanese territory
Taiwan has no forces on its eastern coast
blocks.explanation: Taiwan's east coast faces the open Pacific; Chinese hulls there mean the island-chain containment line has been crossed.

timeline.heading: WHY MANILA AND TOKYO ARE TALKING
timeline.body: Japan and the Philippines sit at the chain's northern and southern anchors, and both face Chinese coast-guard pressure — Japan around the Senkakus, the Philippines at Second Thomas Shoal. Their 2024 Reciprocal Access Agreement lets each station forces on the other's soil, knitting the two ends of the wall together.

blocks.text: The 2024 **RAA** was Japan's first such pact with an Asian nation — a quiet admission that the island chain only holds if its anchors coordinate.

2026-06-01-china-coast-guard-east-of-tai.label: Gray-Zone Coercion & the First Island Chain

timeline.heading: THE ARCHITECTURE
timeline.body: Ethiopia is not a normal federation. Its 1995 constitution divides the country into ethnically-defined regions, each with a constitutional right to secede. The state was deliberately built around ethnicity rather than against it — a design unique among major nations.

blocks.text: The model is called **ethnic federalism**. Article 39 of the constitution grants every "nation, nationality and people" the *right to self-determination, including secession* — a clause no other large state writes into its founding law.

timeline.heading: WHO BUILT IT
timeline.body: The Tigrayans — barely 6% of the population — ran Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 through the TPLF, the guerrilla front that toppled the Derg. Abiy Ahmed's rise ended Tigrayan dominance, and the 2020 war was, structurally, the former rulers fighting their own displacement.

timeline.heading: THE PROSPERITY PARTY
timeline.body: Abiy dissolved the old ruling coalition in 2019 and merged its ethnic parties into a single pan-Ethiopian Prosperity Party. The TPLF refused to join — that refusal, not the election timing, was the spark that set the 2020 war in motion.

blocks.question: What triggered the breach between Abiy and the TPLF in 2019?
options: The TPLF refused to merge into the new Prosperity Party
blocks.explanation: The TPLF rejected dissolving its ethnic party into Abiy's unitary Prosperity Party, then held its own regional vote in defiance of Addis Ababa.

timeline.heading: THE WAR'S TOLL
timeline.body: The 2020–22 conflict killed an estimated 600,000 people — by some counts deadlier than the entire war in Ukraine over the same window — driven as much by famine and a blockade of Tigray as by combat.

events.label: Nobel Peace Prize; Prosperity Party formed

timeline.heading: THE LANDLOCKED PROBLEM
timeline.body: Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea seceded in 1993, leaving Africa's second-most populous country dependent on Djibouti for nearly all trade. Abiy's hunger for a port reshapes every regional alliance — and Eritrea, a 2020 war ally, is now a rival again.

blocks.label: the landlocked giant and its outlets

timeline.heading: THE TWO-TIER PRICE
timeline.body: India runs LPG on a split system: domestic household cylinders are subsidized and politically untouchable, while commercial cylinders — used by restaurants, tea stalls, small industry — track the market. When global costs rise, the state lets the commercial price move and shields the household one. The Rs 42 hike landed entirely on businesses.

blocks.text: The household 14.2 kg cylinder and the commercial 19 kg cylinder hold the *same fuel* — only the customer class and the subsidy differ.

timeline.heading: WHY INDIA IS EXPOSED
timeline.body: India consumes more LPG for cooking than any country except China, and imports more than half of it — overwhelmingly from Gulf producers whose cargoes transit the Strait of Hormuz. There is no overland substitute; the molecules arrive by sea tanker or not at all.

timeline.heading: WHO SUPPLIES THE GAS
timeline.body: The bulk of India's imported LPG comes from a handful of Gulf states — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar lead, with growing US cargoes arriving on longer voyages. Saudi Arabia alone has historically been the single largest source, which is why one kingdom's pricing decisions ripple straight into an Indian kitchen.

timeline.heading: WHAT ACTUALLY SETS THE PRICE
timeline.body: India's LPG cost is benchmarked to the Saudi Contract Price (CP) — a monthly figure Saudi Aramco publishes for propane and butane. Indian oil marketing companies import on this benchmark, so the domestic shelf price is downstream of a number set in Dhahran, not Delhi.

blocks.question: What benchmark primarily sets the price of imported LPG in India?
options: The US Henry Hub gas price
blocks.explanation: LPG (propane/butane) is priced off Aramco's monthly CP, not crude oil — so its moves can diverge sharply from headline oil prices.

timeline.heading: THE RUPEE MULTIPLIER
timeline.body: Imported LPG is paid for in dollars, so the rupee's exchange rate is a second, hidden price lever. A weaker rupee raises the import bill even when the dollar-denominated Saudi benchmark is flat — meaning Indian consumers can pay more for gas without global prices moving at all.

timeline.heading: WHY HOUSEHOLDS ARE SPARED
timeline.body: The household subsidy is electoral infrastructure. The Ujjwala scheme put cooking-gas connections into tens of millions of poor and rural homes, turning the domestic cylinder into a symbol of welfare delivery. Raising its price carries a political cost no government absorbs lightly — so commercial users take the hit first.

blocks.text: **Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana** (launched 2016) made the subsidized cylinder a flagship welfare promise — which is precisely why its price is the *last* one a government will touch.

timeline.heading: THE DECLARED-AREA TRAP
timeline.body: Australia's 2014 foreign-incursion laws made it an offence to even enter a declared zone — al-Raqqa province among them — without a legitimate reason. Prosecutors don't have to prove you fired a weapon; presence plus intent to join is the crime. This is why the case turns on when and why she left, not on any battlefield act.

blocks.text: The legal device is the *declared area offence*: the burden flips toward the traveller, who must show a lawful purpose like aid work or family. It was written precisely to convict returnees whose violent acts can never be evidenced from a collapsed warzone.

timeline.heading: WHY COURTS DISTRUST LATE RENUNCIATION
timeline.body: The prosecution's argument is structural: thousands fled only after the caliphate physically collapsed, when staying was no longer an option. Disavowal under those conditions is hard to distinguish from defeat. Courts weight the timing of departure heavily — leaving at the height of IS power reads as conscience; leaving at Baghuz reads as the tide turning.

timeline.heading: THE CALIPHATE'S ARC
timeline.body: IS was not a permanent fact of the region. It declared a 'caliphate' in mid-2014, held territory the size of Britain for three years, then was ground down city by city until its last sliver fell in eastern Syria in 2019. The window in which the defendant is charged — 2013 to 2014 — is the rise, when joining meant betting on expansion.

events.label: ISIS splits from al-Qaeda in Syria

timeline.heading: WHAT JIHAD ACTUALLY REQUIRES
timeline.body: IS appropriated the word jihad to brand mass violence, but classical Sunni jurisprudence hedges armed jihad with strict conditions: it must be called by legitimate authority, spare non-combatants, and forbids the takfir — declaring other Muslims apostate — that IS used to justify killing Muslims who opposed it. In 2014 over a hundred scholars publicly rejected al-Baghdadi's claim on exactly these grounds.

blocks.text: The doctrine IS relied on was *takfir* — excommunicating fellow Muslims to make their blood lawful. Mainstream scholarship treats unrestricted takfir as one of the gravest deviations, which is why the overwhelming majority of IS's victims were themselves Muslims.

timeline.heading: WHERE THE SOURCE OF FIGHTERS WAS
timeline.body: Some 40,000 foreigners from over 100 countries travelled to join IS. The largest contingents came not from the West but from the Arab world and the former Soviet space; Western recruits like Australia's roughly 230 were a small fraction of the flow.

timeline.heading: THE CITIZENSHIP WEAPON
timeline.body: Many states prefer that returnees never reach a courtroom. Australia, the UK and others passed laws to strip dual nationals of citizenship for terrorism, leaving thousands of women and children stranded in camps like al-Hawl in northeast Syria. Prosecution at home is the alternative to that limbo — and the harder, more accountable path.

blocks.label: from the warzone to the dock

blocks.question: When did IS lose the last of its territorial 'caliphate'?
blocks.explanation: Mosul and Raqqa fell in 2017, but the final pocket held until the battle of Baghuz in March 2019.

timeline.heading: THE 100% RULE
timeline.body: Once rabies symptoms appear, it is effectively always fatal — among the highest case-fatality rates of any disease known to medicine. Fewer than a handful of unvaccinated survivors have ever been documented. The entire fight is to immunize the patient before the virus reaches the brain.

timeline.heading: THE RACE UP THE NERVE
timeline.body: Rabies does not travel in the blood, where antibodies patrol. It creeps along nerve fibers toward the spinal cord and brain at roughly a few millimeters per day, hidden from the immune system. That slow, silent journey is exactly why a vaccine given after the bite can still win — if it starts in time.

blocks.text: Because the virus is *neurotropic* and bypasses the bloodstream, the incubation window is long — typically **1–3 months**, sometimes years — which is what makes post-exposure vaccination possible at all.

timeline.heading: WHY A FULL COURSE STILL FAILS
timeline.body: Proper post-exposure prophylaxis is two things, not one: the vaccine, which takes 7–14 days to build the patient's own antibodies, AND rabies immunoglobulin injected into the wound on day one for immediate protection during that gap. Skipping the immunoglobulin — common where it is scarce or unaffordable — leaves a deadly window even when every vaccine dose is given.

blocks.question: Why is rabies immunoglobulin given alongside the first vaccine dose?
options: It provides instant antibodies while the vaccine takes ~2 weeks to work
It replaces the need for later vaccine doses
It treats the bite wound infection
It works only after symptoms appear
blocks.explanation: The vaccine needs ~7–14 days to generate immunity; immunoglobulin supplies borrowed antibodies to cover that vulnerable gap.

timeline.heading: THE COLD-CHAIN PROBLEM
timeline.body: Rabies vaccine loses potency if it strays outside 2–8°C. In public-sector systems with patchy refrigeration and unreliable power, a vial can be administered on schedule yet be biologically inert — a 'full course' that immunizes no one. Breakthrough deaths often trace back to the fridge, not the regimen.

timeline.heading: A CHILD'S DISEASE
timeline.body: Rabies kills roughly 59,000 people a year, almost all from dog bites, and overwhelmingly in Asia and Africa. About 40% of victims are children under 15 — short stature means more bites to the face and hands, closer to the brain, and a poorer chance for slow prophylaxis to catch up. India and Pakistan together carry a vast share of the global toll.

blocks.label: annual rabies deaths by region (~59,000 total)

timeline.heading: WHY RADAR GOES FIRST
timeline.body: The opening move of almost every air campaign is to blind the enemy's air defenses. Radar sites are the eyes of a surface-to-air missile network; destroy them and the missiles below fire blind. This is why US Central Command hit radar, not airfields or cities, first — it is the doorway, not the destination.

blocks.text: The mission has a name and a heritage: **SEAD** (Suppression of Enemy Air Defenses), flown since Vietnam by crews nicknamed *Wild Weasels* whose motto was the unprintable line about being the first ones in.

timeline.heading: HOW A RADAR SITE WORKS
timeline.body: Radar fires electromagnetic pulses and times the reflections off metal aircraft. But the act of transmitting is also a beacon: every sweep broadcasts the site's exact location. Anti-radiation missiles home in on that emission, so an air-defense radar that switches on to find attackers reveals itself to be killed.

blocks.question: Why is leaving an air-defense radar switched on dangerous in wartime?
options: Its own transmissions reveal its location to anti-radiation missiles
Radar overheats and fails within minutes of use
Enemy aircraft can copy the radar's signal
It drains the missile battery's power supply
blocks.explanation: Anti-radiation missiles ride the radar's own emissions to the source, so radar operators must choose between seeing and surviving.

timeline.heading: THE COST ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: A reconnaissance drone can cost more than a fighter jet, while the missile that downs it costs a fraction as much — and the drone carries no pilot to lose. This inverts the old calculus of escalation: a state can destroy a high-value asset and kill no one, leaving the other side to decide whether a machine is worth a war.
